abstract: We show how to estimate (1) the number of functions that can be implemented by a particular network architecture, (2) how much analog precision is needed in the connections in the network, and (3) the number of training examples the network must see before it can be expected to form reliable generalizations.
originalAbstract: We show how to estimate (1) the number of functions that can be implemented by a particular network architecture, (2) how much analog precision is needed in the connections in the network, and (3) the number of training examples the network must see before it can be expected to form reliable generalizations.

paragraphs: This paper presents ways to estimate three requirements of a neural network: the range of functions its architecture can implement, the precision needed in its connections, and the number of training examples needed for reliable generalization. These questions concern what a network can represent, how accurately it must be realized, and how much evidence it needs to learn.

Counting implementable functions gives a measure of architectural generality. Estimating analog precision addresses a different aspect of the same design: how finely connection values need to be specified. Considering both quantities makes the network’s computational possibilities and its numerical requirements explicit parts of the analysis.

The third estimate concerns training data and the expectation that learning will extend beyond the examples observed. This places generalization alongside architecture and connection precision as a quantity to assess when studying a network. The contribution is a framework for estimating these three aspects of network capability and requirements, helping distinguish expressive possibilities from the practical demands of representing and learning them.
summary.tldr: The paper estimates a network’s representational range, required connection precision, and training-data needs for reliable generalization.

title: Network Generality, Training Required, and Precision Required

abstract: A pool of handwritten signatures is used to train a neural net(cid:173) work for the task of deciding whether or not a given signature is a forgery. The network is a feedforward net, with a binary image as input. There is a hidden layer, with a single unit output layer. The weights are adjusted according to the backpropagation algorithm. The signatures are entered into a C software program through the use of a Datacopy Electronic Digitizing Camera. The binary signa(cid:173) tures are normalized and centered. The performance is examined as a function of the training set and network structure. The best scores are on the order of 2% true signature rejection with 2-4% false signature acceptance.

The network is a feedforward net, with a binary image as input. There is a hidden layer, with a single unit output layer. The weights are adjusted according to the backpropagation algorithm. The signatures are entered into a C software program through the use of a Datacopy Electronic Digitizing Camera. The binary signa(cid:173) tures are normalized and centered. paragraphs: This paper trains a neural network to decide whether a handwritten signature is genuine or forged. Its input is a binary image of the signature, and its output comes from a single decision unit. A hidden layer sits between the image and the output, with connection weights adjusted through backpropagation.

The signatures are captured with an electronic digitizing camera and entered into a C program. Before reaching the network, the binary images are normalized and centered. This preprocessing gives the learning system a more consistent presentation of each signature. The study then examines how performance changes with the training set and the structure of the network.

The best reported results are approximately 2% rejection of genuine signatures and 2–4% acceptance of false signatures. These describe two distinct errors: refusing an authentic signature and accepting an impostor's signature. Reporting both makes the verification outcome more informative than a single combined score. The results demonstrate that this image-based feedforward network can learn a useful distinction between genuine and forged examples.
summary.tldr: A backpropagation network verifies signature images, with best reported errors near 2% genuine rejection and 2–4% false acceptance.

title: Backpropagation and Its Application to Handwritten Signature Verification

abstract: Spiking neurons which integrate to threshold and fire were used to study the transmission of frequency modulated (FM) signals through layered networks. Firing correlations between cells in the input layer were found to modulate the transmission of FM sig(cid:173) nals under certain dynamical conditions. A tonic level of activity was maintained by providing each cell with a source of Poisson(cid:173) distributed synaptic input. When the average membrane depo(cid:173) larization produced by the synaptic input was sufficiently below threshold, the firing correlations between cells in the input layer could greatly amplify the signal present in subsequent layers. When the depolarization was sufficiently close to threshold, however, the firing synchrony between cells in the initial layers could no longer effect the propagation of FM signals. In this latter case, integrate(cid:173) and-fire neurons could be effectively modeled by simpler analog elements governed by a linear input-output relation.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how coordinated spike timing affects the transmission of frequency-modulated signals through successive neural layers. The modeled neurons accumulate input until reaching a firing threshold. Each also receives Poisson-distributed synaptic input to maintain background activity, allowing the authors to examine signal transmission under different levels of average membrane depolarization.

When that average depolarization lies sufficiently below the firing threshold, correlations among input-layer neurons can greatly amplify the signal in later layers. The result shows that coordinated firing can influence what the network transmits even when the signal is described through frequency modulation. Timing relationships among neurons matter in this dynamical regime.

When average depolarization is sufficiently close to threshold, synchrony in the initial layers no longer affects propagation of the frequency-modulated signal. In that regime, simpler analog elements with linear input-output relationships can effectively represent the neurons. The findings make the importance of spike synchrony conditional on operating state and identify a setting in which a simpler continuous description captures the relevant transmission behavior.
summary.tldr: Firing synchrony amplifies signals below threshold, but loses its influence near threshold, where a linear analog model becomes effective.

title: Effects of Firing Synchrony on Signal Propagation in Layered Networks

abstract: The goal in this work has been to identify the neuronal elements of the cortical column that are most likely to support the learning of nonlinear associative maps. We show that a particular style of network learning algorithm based on locally-tuned receptive fields maps naturally onto cortical hardware, and gives coherence to a variety of features of cortical anatomy, physiology, and biophysics whose relations to learning remain poorly understood.
originalAbstract: The goal in this work has been to identify the neuronal elements of the cortical column that are most likely to support the learning of nonlinear associative maps. We show that a particular style of network learning algorithm based on locally-tuned receptive fields maps naturally onto cortical hardware, and gives coherence to a variety of features of cortical anatomy, physiology, and biophysics whose relations to learning remain poorly understood.

paragraphs: This paper asks which neuronal elements within a cortical column could support learning nonlinear associations. A nonlinear associative map links inputs to outputs through relationships more flexible than a simple linear combination. The authors approach this question by relating a style of neural learning algorithm to the biological organization of the cortex.

The algorithm uses locally tuned receptive fields, so its elements respond selectively to particular regions of the input space. The authors argue that this computational organization maps naturally onto cortical hardware. The point of the mapping is to identify how the elements needed for learning could correspond to actual neuronal structures and response properties.

The claimed result is a coherent interpretation of several features of cortical anatomy, physiology, and biophysics whose relationship to learning has been unclear. The contribution is thus a proposed connection between a learning mechanism and its possible biological implementation. It makes locally tuned nonlinear associative learning a framework for understanding how diverse properties of cortical columns might work together.
summary.tldr: The paper connects learning with locally tuned receptive fields to neuronal structures that could support nonlinear associations in cortical columns.

title: Sigma-Pi Learning: On Radial Basis Functions and Cortical Associative Learning

abstract: Hand-printed digits can be modeled as splines that are governed by about 8 control points. For each known digit. the control points have preferred ., home" locations, and deformations of the digit are generated by moving the control points away from their home locations. Images of digits can be produced by placing Gaussian ink generators uniformly along the spline. Real images can be recognized by finding the digit model most likely to have generated the data. For each digit model we use an elastic matching algorithm to minimize an energy function that includes both the defor(cid:173) mation energy of the digit model and the log probability that the model would generate the inked pixels in the image. The model with the lowest total energy wins. If a uniform noise process is included in the model of image generation, some of the inked pixels can be rejected as noise as a digit model is fitting a poorly segmented image. The digit models learn by modifying the home locations of the control points.

paragraphs: This paper recognizes handwritten digits by asking which flexible digit model best explains an image. Each digit is represented by a spline controlled by roughly eight points. These points have preferred positions, but moving them allows the model to accommodate variations in handwriting while retaining a reference shape.

The model generates an image by distributing Gaussian ink generators along the spline. During recognition, elastic matching adjusts each candidate digit to fit the observed pixels. The matching objective balances the cost of deforming the reference shape with the probability of producing the image. The candidate with the lowest combined energy becomes the recognized digit.

Adding a uniform noise process lets the model treat some inked pixels as noise while fitting an imperfectly segmented image. Learning changes the preferred positions of the control points, so the reference shapes themselves adapt. The approach combines shape variation, image generation, and noise handling within one recognition procedure, giving each a role in deciding which digit best accounts for the input.
summary.tldr: Flexible spline models recognize handwritten digits by balancing image fit, shape deformation, and a probabilistic account of noise.

title: Adaptive Elastic Models for Hand-Printed Character Recognition

abstract: Many cells in the dorsal part of the medial superior temporal (MST) area of visual cortex respond selectively to spiral flow patterns-specific combinations of expansion/ contraction and ro(cid:173) tation motions. Previous investigators have suggested that these cells may represent self-motion. Spiral patterns can also be gener(cid:173) ated by the relative motion of the observer and a particular object. An MST cell may then account for some portion of the complex flow field, and the set of active cells could encode the entire flow; in this manner, MST effectively segments moving objects. Such a grouping operation is essential in interpreting scenes containing several independent moving objects and observer motion. We de(cid:173) scribe a model based on the hypothesis that the selective tuning of MST cells reflects the grouping of object components undergo(cid:173) ing coherent motion. Inputs to the model were generated from sequences of ray-traced images that simulated realistic motion sit(cid:173) uations, combining observer motion, eye movements, and indepen(cid:173) dent object motion. The input representation was modeled after response properties of neurons in area MT, which provides the pri(cid:173) mary input to area MST. After applying an unsupervised learning algorithm, the units became tuned to patterns signaling coherent motion. The results match many of the known properties of MST cells and are consistent with recent studies indicating that these cells process 3-D object motion information. 166 Richard S. Zemel, Terrence J. Sejnowski

paragraphs: The paper proposes that motion-sensitive cells in visual area MST help group image components belonging to coherently moving objects. Many MST cells prefer spiral flow patterns combining expansion or contraction with rotation. Such patterns can arise from observer motion, but also from motion between an observer and a particular object, making them relevant to object grouping.

The model receives inputs derived from ray-traced image sequences containing observer movement, eye movements, and independently moving objects. Its input representation follows response properties of neurons in area MT, which supplies the main input to MST. An unsupervised learning algorithm then discovers structure in these motion signals without supplied labels for the desired response patterns.

After learning, model units become selective for patterns indicating coherent motion. Their responses match many known properties of MST cells and fit evidence that those cells process three-dimensional object motion. The findings support a grouping interpretation: different active cells can account for different portions of a complex flow field, helping distinguish moving objects within a scene that also contains observer motion.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised visual-motion model develops MST-like responses that support grouping components of coherently moving three-dimensional objects.

title: Grouping Components of Three-Dimensional Moving Objects in Area MST of Visual Cortex

abstract: A linear architectural model of cortical simple cells is presented. The model evidences how mutual inhibition, occurring through synaptic coupling functions asymmetrically distributed in space, can be a possible basis for a wide variety of spatio-temporal simple cell response properties, including direction selectivity and velocity tuning. While spatial asymmetries are included explicitly in the structure of the inhibitory interconnections, temporal asymmetries originate from the specific mutual inhibition scheme considered. Extensive simulations supporting the model are reported.
originalAbstract: A linear architectural model of cortical simple cells is presented. The model evidences how mutual inhibition, occurring through synaptic coupling functions asymmetrically distributed in space, can be a possible basis for a wide variety of spatio-temporal simple cell response properties, including direction selectivity and velocity tuning. While spatial asymmetries are included explicitly in the structure of the inhibitory interconnections, temporal asymmetries originate from the specific mutual inhibition scheme considered. Extensive simulations supporting the model are reported.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how cortical simple cells could acquire different responses to motion direction and velocity. It presents a linear architectural model in which the arrangement of connections between cells plays a central role. The proposed mechanism is mutual inhibition: connected cells suppress one another through synaptic interactions distributed unevenly across space.

The model distinguishes two sources of asymmetry. Spatial asymmetry is explicitly built into the inhibitory connections, so interactions differ according to spatial arrangement. Temporal asymmetry arises from the particular scheme of mutual inhibition. This distinction explains how a network with a specified spatial architecture can also develop differences in how it responds over time.

The authors report extensive simulations supporting this mechanism across a variety of spatial and temporal response properties, including direction selectivity and velocity tuning. The result identifies asymmetric inhibitory connectivity as a possible basis for these responses. Its significance is mechanistic: the proposed architecture connects the organization of synaptic interactions to the motion preferences expressed by the modeled cells.
summary.tldr: Asymmetric mutual inhibition provides a possible architectural explanation for cortical cells’ direction selectivity and velocity tuning.

title: An Architectural Mechanism for Direction-tuned Cortical Simple Cells: The Role of Mutual Inhibition

abstract: We propose a novel strategy for training neural networks using se(cid:173) quential sampling-importance resampling algorithms. This global optimisation strategy allows us to learn the probability distribu(cid:173) tion of the network weights in a sequential framework. It is well suited to applications involving on-line, nonlinear, non-Gaussian or non-stationary signal processing.
originalAbstract: We propose a novel strategy for training neural networks using se(cid:173) quential sampling-importance resampling algorithms. This global optimisation strategy allows us to learn the probability distribu(cid:173) tion of the network weights in a sequential framework. It is well suited to applications involving on-line, nonlinear, non-Gaussian or non-stationary signal processing.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a neural-network training strategy based on sequential sampling and importance resampling. It frames training as a global optimization problem and uses a sequential procedure to learn a probability distribution over the network's weights. The distribution over weights is therefore a central object of the method.

This formulation brings together network training and probabilistic estimation in a process that proceeds sequentially. Sampling and importance resampling provide the stated algorithmic basis for that process. The approach matters because it describes training in terms of learning about possible weight settings through a distribution, giving the optimization strategy an explicitly probabilistic form.

The authors identify online, nonlinear, non-Gaussian, and nonstationary signal processing as suitable applications. Those settings motivate a method that can operate sequentially while accommodating the kinds of signal behavior named in the abstract. The stated contribution is the training strategy and its suitability for those applications; the description of global optimization does not itself assert guaranteed recovery of a global optimum.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes sequential sampling and importance resampling to train neural networks by learning a distribution over their weights.

title: Global Optimisation of Neural Network Models via Sequential Sampling

abstract: Generative probability models such as hidden ~larkov models pro(cid:173) vide a principled way of treating missing information and dealing with variable length sequences. On the other hand , discriminative methods such as support vector machines enable us to construct flexible decision boundaries and often result in classification per(cid:173) formance superior to that of the model based approaches. An ideal classifier should combine these two complementary approaches. In this paper, we develop a natural way of achieving this combina(cid:173) tion by deriving kernel functions for use in discriminative methods such as support vector machines from generative probability mod(cid:173) els. We provide a theoretical justification for this combination as well as demonstrate a substantial improvement in the classification performance in the context of D~A and protein sequence analysis.

paragraphs: This paper combines two approaches to classification that offer complementary strengths. Generative probability models, including hidden Markov models, provide a principled treatment of missing information and sequences of different lengths. Discriminative methods, including support vector machines, offer flexible decision boundaries and often achieve better classification performance than model-based approaches.

The proposed connection is to derive kernel functions from generative probability models and use those kernels within discriminative classifiers. A kernel supplies the comparison that the discriminative method uses between inputs. Deriving it from a generative model allows information captured by that model to contribute to the classification decision.

The authors provide a theoretical justification for this combination and demonstrate a substantial classification improvement in DNA and protein sequence analysis. These results support the usefulness of combining structured probabilistic modeling with discriminative learning in the sequence-analysis setting studied. The contribution is a concrete interface between the two approaches: the generative model supplies the kernel through which the discriminative classifier works.
summary.tldr: Kernels derived from generative models connect probabilistic sequence modeling to discriminative classifiers and improve DNA and protein classification.

title: Exploiting Generative Models in Discriminative Classifiers

abstract: A system emulating the functionality of a moving eye-hence the name oculo-motor system-has been built and successfully tested. It is made of an optical device for shifting the field of view of an image sensor by up to 45 ° in any direction, four neuromorphic analog VLSI circuits imple(cid:173) menting an oculo-motor control loop, and some off-the-shelf electronics. The custom integrated circuits communicate with each other primarily by non-arbitrated address-event buses. The system implements the behav(cid:173) iors of saliency-based saccadic exploration, and smooth pursuit of light spots. The duration of saccades ranges from 45 ms to 100 ms, which is comparable to human eye performance. Smooth pursuit operates on light sources moving at up to 50 0 /s in the visual field.

It is made of an optical device for shifting the field of view of an image sensor by up to 45 ° in any direction, four neuromorphic analog VLSI circuits imple(cid:173) menting an oculo-motor control loop, and some off-the-shelf electronics. paragraphs: The authors built and successfully tested a system that emulates aspects of a moving eye. An optical device shifts an image sensor's field of view by as much as 45 degrees in any direction. Four neuromorphic analog VLSI circuits, together with off-the-shelf electronics, implement the control loop that directs this movement.

The custom circuits communicate mainly through non-arbitrated address-event buses. The integrated system supports two distinct behaviors: rapid exploration directed by visual saliency and smooth pursuit of light spots. These behaviors demonstrate both shifts toward visually prominent locations and continued tracking of a moving target within one hardware system.

Reported saccades last between 45 and 100 milliseconds, a range described as comparable to human eye performance. Smooth pursuit works for light sources moving at up to 50 degrees per second in the visual field. These findings establish concrete operating capabilities for the tested device. The comparison with human performance concerns saccade duration, while the pursuit result specifically concerns moving light sources.
summary.tldr: A tested multi-chip analog system performs saliency-driven eye-like movements and smooth tracking of moving light sources.

title: An Oculo-Motor System with Multi-Chip Neuromorphic Analog VLSI Control

abstract: We consider the existence of efficient algorithms for learning the class of half-spaces in ~n in the agnostic learning model (Le., mak(cid:173) ing no prior assumptions on the example-generating distribution). The resulting combinatorial problem - finding the best agreement half-space over an input sample - is NP hard to approximate to within some constant factor. We suggest a way to circumvent this theoretical bound by introducing a new measure of success for such algorithms. An algorithm is IL-margin successful if the agreement ratio of the half-space it outputs is as good as that of any half-space once training points that are inside the IL-margins of its separating hyper-plane are disregarded. We prove crisp computational com(cid:173) plexity results with respect to this success measure: On one hand, for every positive IL, there exist efficient (poly-time) IL-margin suc(cid:173) cessful learning algorithms. On the other hand, we prove that unless P=NP, there is no algorithm that runs in time polynomial in the sample size and in 1/ IL that is IL-margin successful for all IL> O.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning linear decision boundaries in the agnostic setting, without prior assumptions about the distribution producing examples. The corresponding sample problem is to find the boundary that agrees best with the observed labels. Even approximating this best agreement within a certain constant factor is computationally hard, motivating a different definition of learning success.

The authors introduce a margin-based success criterion. It compares the returned classifier's agreement with that of competing boundaries after disregarding training points within a specified margin of the competing separating plane. This changes the target against which an algorithm is evaluated. It allows near-boundary points to be excluded from the comparison instead of demanding the original best-agreement objective.

For every fixed positive margin, the authors prove that an efficient polynomial-time algorithm meeting this criterion exists. They also establish a complementary barrier: unless P equals NP, no algorithm can be polynomial in both sample size and inverse margin while satisfying the criterion for every positive margin. Efficiency at a fixed margin therefore does not imply uniformly efficient behavior as margins shrink.
summary.tldr: A margin-based success criterion permits efficient linear learning for each fixed positive margin, with a hardness barrier as the margin varies.

title: Efficient Learning of Linear Perceptrons

abstract: Factor analysis and principal components analysis can be used to model linear relationships between observed variables and linearly map high-dimensional data to a lower-dimensional hidden space. In factor analysis, the observations are modeled as a linear com(cid:173) bination of normally distributed hidden variables. We describe a nonlinear generalization of factor analysis, called "product analy(cid:173) sis", that models the observed variables as a linear combination of products of normally distributed hidden variables. Just as fac(cid:173) tor analysis can be viewed as unsupervised linear regression on unobserved, normally distributed hidden variables, product anal(cid:173) ysis can be viewed as unsupervised linear regression on products of unobserved, normally distributed hidden variables. The map(cid:173) ping between the data and the hidden space is nonlinear, so we use an approximate variational technique for inference and learn(cid:173) ing. Since product analysis is a generalization of factor analysis, product analysis always finds a higher data likelihood than factor analysis. We give results on pattern recognition and illumination(cid:173) invariant image clustering.

paragraphs: Factor analysis represents observations as linear combinations of normally distributed hidden variables. This paper generalizes that construction by allowing products of hidden variables to enter the representation. The resulting method, called product analysis, models observations as linear combinations of those products, introducing interactions into the relationship between hidden structure and observed data.

The authors describe the method as unsupervised linear regression on products of unobserved Gaussian variables. Although the combination of products is linear, the relationship to the underlying hidden variables is nonlinear. They therefore use an approximate variational method for both inference and learning, addressing the computational challenge introduced by this richer representation.

Because product analysis generalizes factor analysis, the paper states that it always finds a higher data likelihood. That is a claim about how well the model assigns probability to the data, distinct from a universal claim about task performance. The authors also present results on pattern recognition and image clustering that is invariant to illumination, illustrating applications of the nonlinear hidden-variable representation.
summary.tldr: Product analysis extends factor analysis with products of Gaussian hidden variables to model nonlinear structure.

title: Product Analysis: Learning to Model Observations as Products of Hidden Variables

abstract: We consider data which are images containing views of multiple objects. Our task is to learn about each of the objects present in the images. This task can be approached as a factorial learning problem, where each image must be explained by instantiating a model for each of the objects present with the correct instantiation parameters. A major problem with learning a factorial model is that as the number of objects increases, there is a combinatorial explosion of the number of conﬁgurations that need to be considered. We develop a method to extract object models sequentially from the data by making use of a robust statistical method, thus avoid- ing the combinatorial explosion, and present results showing successful extraction of objects from real images.
originalAbstract: We consider data which are images containing views of multiple objects. Our task is to learn about each of the objects present in the images. This task can be approached as a factorial learning problem, where each image must be explained by instantiating a model for each of the objects present with the correct instantiation parameters. A major problem with learning a factorial model is that as the number of objects increases, there is a combinatorial explosion of the number of conﬁgurations that need to be considered. We develop a method to extract object models sequentially from the data by making use of a robust statistical method, thus avoid- ing the combinatorial explosion, and present results showing successful extraction of objects from real images.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn models of individual objects from images containing several objects at once. Each image can be explained by instantiating a separate model for every object present, with appropriate parameters for each instance. This makes the task a factorial learning problem involving multiple contributing models.

The difficulty is that considering joint explanations becomes combinatorially expensive as the number of objects increases. The proposed method avoids this explosion by extracting object models sequentially. It uses a robust statistical method to support that sequential extraction, rather than searching through the full set of joint object configurations.

The authors present results showing successful object extraction from real images. These results support the feasibility of learning individual object models from scenes in which objects appear together. The contribution is a strategy for separating the learning task into successive model extractions while retaining the goal of explaining multiple objects. Its computational significance comes from avoiding the combinatorial configuration search described in the original factorial formulation.
summary.tldr: A robust sequential extraction method learns object models from multi-object images while avoiding combinatorial search over joint configurations.

title: Learning About Multiple Objects in Images: Factorial Learning without Factorial Search

abstract: We study the problem of hierarchical classification when labels corresponding to partial and/or multiple paths in the underlying taxonomy are allowed. We introduce a new hierarchical loss function, the H-loss, implementing the simple intuition that additional mistakes in the subtree of a mistaken class should not be charged for. Based on a probabilistic data model introduced in earlier work, we derive the Bayes-optimal classifier for the H-loss. We then empirically compare two incremental approximations of the Bayes-optimal classifier with a flat SVM classifier and with classifiers obtained by using hierarchical versions of the Perceptron and SVM algorithms. The experiments show that our simplest incremental approximation of the Bayes-optimal classifier performs, after just one training epoch, nearly as well as the hierarchical SVM classifier (which performs best). For the same incremental algorithm we also derive an H-loss bound showing, when data are generated by our probabilistic data model, exponentially fast convergence to the H-loss of the hierarchical classifier based on the true model parameters.

We introduce a new hierarchical loss function, the H-loss, implementing the simple intuition that additional mistakes in the subtree of a mistaken class should not be charged for. Based on a probabilistic data model introduced in earlier work, we derive the Bayes-optimal classifier for the H-loss. We then empirically compare two incremental approximations of the Bayes-optimal classifier with a flat SVM classifier and with classifiers obtained by using hierarchical versions of the Perceptron and SVM algorithms. The experiments show that our simplest incremental approximation of the Bayes-optimal classifier performs, after just one training epoch, nearly as well as the hierarchical SVM classifier (which performs best). For the same incremental algorithm we also derive an H-loss bound showing, when data are generated by our probabilistic data model, exponentially fast convergence to the H-loss of the hierarchical classifier based on the true model parameters.

It introduces H-loss, which avoids charging additional mistakes inside the subtree of an already mistaken class. This makes the error measure reflect the hierarchy: a mistake higher in the taxonomy changes how errors beneath it are counted.

They then compare two incremental approximations with a flat SVM and hierarchical versions of the Perceptron and SVM. In the reported experiments, the simplest incremental approximation performs nearly as well after one training epoch as the hierarchical SVM, which performs best.

This guarantee assumes that the data come from the stated probabilistic model. The work therefore combines a hierarchy-sensitive objective, an efficient empirical approximation, and a conditional theoretical convergence result.
summary.tldr: A hierarchy-aware loss supports incremental classifiers with strong empirical performance and a convergence guarantee under the proposed data model.

title: Incremental Algorithms for Hierarchical Classification

abstract: There is a long-standing controversy on the site of the cerebellar motor learning. Different theories and experimental results suggest that either the cerebellar flocculus or the brainstem learns the task and stores the memory. With a dynamical system approach, we clarify the mechanism of transferring the memory generated in the flocculus to the brainstem and that of so-called savings phenomena. The brainstem learning must comply with a sort of Hebbian rule depending on Purkinje-cell activities. In contrast to earlier numerical models, our model is simple but it accommodates explanations and predictions of experimental situations as qualitative features of trajectories in the phase space of synaptic weights, without fine parameter tuning.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a disagreement about where cerebellar motor learning occurs and where its memory is stored. The authors use a dynamical-system model to explain how memory formed in the flocculus can be transferred to the brainstem.

This ties the proposed transfer mechanism to a specific relationship between neural activity and changes in synaptic strength.

The contribution provides a simple way to understand memory transfer and savings within one dynamical framework.
summary.tldr: A dynamical model explains cerebellar memory transfer and savings through synaptic learning governed by Purkinje-cell activity.

title: Modeling Memory Transfer and Saving in Cerebellar Motor Learning

abstract: We develop a Bayesian "sum-of-trees" model, named BART, where each tree is constrained by a prior to be a weak learner. Fitting and inference are accomplished via an iterative backfitting MCMC algorithm. This model is motivated by ensemble methods in general, and boosting algorithms in particular. Like boosting, each weak learner (i.e., each weak tree) contributes a small amount to the overall model. However, our procedure is defined by a statistical model: a prior and a likelihood, while boosting is defined by an algorithm. This model-based approach enables a full and accurate assessment of uncertainty in model predictions, while remaining highly competitive in terms of predictive accuracy.

Each tree is constrained by a prior to act as a weak learner, contributing only a small part of the overall prediction. The model builds on the ensemble idea that several modest predictors can collectively form a strong predictor.

Fitting and inference use an iterative backfitting MCMC procedure. The central distinction from boosting is how the ensemble is specified: BART has an explicit statistical model consisting of a prior and a likelihood. This gives the collection of weak trees a probabilistic foundation for both learning and inference.

The authors report that this formulation supports a full and accurate assessment of predictive uncertainty while retaining highly competitive predictive accuracy. Its importance is that the ensemble produces more than a prediction alone: uncertainty about that prediction is part of the model's output. The paper thus connects weak-tree ensembles with Bayesian assessment of how confidently their predictions should be interpreted.
summary.tldr: BART combines weak decision trees in a Bayesian model that delivers competitive predictions alongside uncertainty estimates.

title: Bayesian Ensemble Learning

abstract: We show that any weak ranker that can achieve an area under the ROC curve slightly better than 1/2 (which can be achieved by random guessing) can be efﬁ- ciently boosted to achieve an area under the ROC curve arbitrarily close to 1. We further show that this boosting can be performed even in the presence of indepen- dent misclassiﬁcation noise, given access to a noise-tolerant weak ranker.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether a modest ranking capability can be amplified into a very strong one. The performance measure is area under the ROC curve, or AUC. Random guessing can achieve an AUC of one half, so the starting requirement is a weak ranker that performs slightly better than that reference level.

The authors show that such a weak ranker can be efficiently boosted to obtain an AUC arbitrarily close to one. The result concerns approaching that value as closely as desired, rather than asserting that the method must attain it exactly. Its significance is that even a small advantage over random ranking can support a much stronger ranking procedure through boosting.

The paper also extends the result to independent misclassification noise. This extension requires access to a weak ranker that tolerates that noise; noise tolerance is part of the condition for the result. Together, the findings establish an amplification principle for ranking quality, including a noisy-label setting where the required underlying learning capability remains available.
summary.tldr: A weak ranker with AUC above one half can be efficiently boosted toward AUC one, including under specified noise-tolerance conditions.

title: Boosting the Area under the ROC Curve

abstract: We propose an unsupervised method that, given a word, automatically selects non-abstract senses of that word from an online ontology and generates images depicting the corresponding entities. When faced with the task of learning a visual model based only on the name of an object, a common approach is to find images on the web that are associated with the object name, and then train a visual classifier from the search result. As words are generally polysemous, this approach can lead to relatively noisy models if many examples due to outlier senses are added to the model. We argue that images associated with an abstract word sense should be excluded when training a visual classifier to learn a model of a physical object. While image clustering can group together visually coherent sets of returned images, it can be difficult to distinguish whether an image cluster relates to a desired object or to an abstract sense of the word. We propose a method that uses both image features and the text associated with the images to relate latent topics to particular senses. Our model does not require any human supervision, and takes as input only the name of an object category. We show results of retrieving concrete-sense images in two available multimodal, multi-sense databases, as well as experiment with object classifiers trained on concrete-sense images returned by our method for a set of ten common office objects.

Images associated with an abstract meaning can enter the training collection even when the desired category is a physical object. This paper develops an unsupervised method for selecting images associated with concrete senses of a category name.

The method takes only the object category's name as input and uses an online ontology to distinguish its senses. It combines image features with accompanying text to connect latent topics to particular meanings. This addresses a weakness of visual clustering alone: a visually consistent group of images does not necessarily correspond to the intended physical object.

The authors report concrete-sense retrieval results on two multimodal databases containing multiple word senses. They also experiment with classifiers trained on the selected images for ten common office objects. The approach makes semantic filtering part of collecting visual training data, using both textual and visual evidence without requiring human supervision.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised method combines images, text, and word senses to select concrete-object images from ambiguous search results.

title: Filtering Abstract Senses From Image Search Results

abstract: How are the spatial patterns of spontaneous and evoked population responses related? We study the impact of connectivity on the spatial pattern of fluctuations in the input-generated response of a neural network, by comparing the distribution of evoked and intrinsically generated activity across the different units. We develop a complementary approach to principal component analysis in which separate high-variance directions are typically derived for each input condition. We analyze subspace angles to compute the difference between the shapes of trajectories corresponding to different network states, and the orientation of the low-dimensional subspaces that driven trajectories occupy within the full space of neuronal activity. In addition to revealing how the spatiotemporal structure of spontaneous activity affects input-evoked responses, these methods can be used to infer input selectivity induced by network dynamics from experimentally accessible measures of spontaneous activity (e.g. from voltage- or calcium-sensitive optical imaging experiments). We conclude that the absence of a detailed spatial map of afferent inputs and cortical connectivity does not limit our ability to design spatially extended stimuli that evoke strong responses.

This paper asks how the spatial patterns of these two kinds of activity are related, and how network connectivity shapes fluctuations in an input-driven response. It compares how internally generated and evoked activity are distributed across the units of a network.

The authors develop an approach complementary to principal component analysis. Their analysis uses angles between subspaces to compare the shapes of activity trajectories in different network states and the orientation of the low-dimensional spaces occupied by driven responses. This provides a way to examine relationships between population activity patterns beyond treating high-variance directions for each input condition separately.

The required spontaneous-activity measurements can be experimentally accessible through voltage-sensitive or calcium-sensitive imaging. The authors conclude that detailed maps of incoming inputs and cortical connectivity are not required to design spatially extended stimuli that evoke strong responses.
summary.tldr: Analyzing the geometry of population activity can reveal network-driven stimulus selectivity from measurements of spontaneous neural dynamics.

title: Inferring Stimulus Selectivity from the Spatial Structure of Neural Network Dynamics

abstract: Speech conveys different yet mixed information ranging from linguistic to speaker-specific components, and each of them should be exclusively used in a specific task. However, it is extremely difficult to extract a specific information component given the fact that nearly all existing acoustic representations carry all types of speech information. Thus, the use of the same representation in both speech and speaker recognition hinders a system from producing better performance due to interference of irrelevant information. In this paper, we present a deep neural architecture to extract speaker-specific information from MFCCs. As a result, a multi-objective loss function is proposed for learning speaker-specific characteristics and regularization via normalizing interference of non-speaker related information and avoiding information loss. With LDC benchmark corpora and a Chinese speech corpus, we demonstrate that a resultant speaker-specific representation is insensitive to text/languages spoken and environmental mismatches and hence outperforms MFCCs and other state-of-the-art techniques in speaker recognition. We discuss relevant issues and relate our approach to previous work.

paragraphs: Speech recordings mix information about the speaker with information about words, language, and recording conditions. A representation that preserves all of these can introduce irrelevant variation into speaker recognition. This paper proposes a deep Siamese architecture that extracts speaker-specific information from MFCC acoustic features, aiming to make the representation better suited to identifying speakers.

The training objective combines several goals. It learns characteristics associated with speaker identity while regularizing the representation to normalize interference from non-speaker information and avoid information loss. This addresses the tension between suppressing distracting variation and preserving useful information. The method therefore changes the acoustic representation itself as part of the recognition approach.

Experiments on LDC benchmark corpora and a Chinese speech corpus show that the learned representation is insensitive to spoken text, language, and environmental mismatches in the reported evaluations. It also outperforms MFCCs and other leading speaker-recognition techniques in those comparisons. These findings support learning task-specific speech features as a way to reduce interference from other information carried by speech.
summary.tldr: A regularized Siamese network learns speaker-specific acoustic features that improve recognition across the reported text, language, and environmental variations.

title: Extracting Speaker-Specific Information with a Regularized Siamese Deep Network

abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) have recently been proposed as computationally efficient probabilistic models of diverse sets for a variety of applications, including document summarization, image search, and pose estimation. Many DPP inference operations, including normalization and sampling, are tractable; however, finding the most likely configuration (MAP), which is often required in practice for decoding, is NP-hard, so we must resort to approximate inference. Because DPP probabilities are log-submodular, greedy algorithms have been used in the past with some empirical success; however, these methods only give approximation guarantees in the special case of DPPs with monotone kernels. In this paper we propose a new algorithm for approximating the MAP problem based on continuous techniques for submodular function maximization. Our method involves a novel continuous relaxation of the log-probability function, which, in contrast to the multilinear extension used for general submodular functions, can be evaluated and differentiated exactly and efficiently. We obtain a practical algorithm with a 1/4-approximation guarantee for a general class of non-monotone DPPs. Our algorithm also extends to MAP inference under complex polytope constraints, making it possible to combine DPPs with Markov random fields, weighted matchings, and other models. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms greedy methods on both synthetic and real-world data.

Greedy methods have had empirical success, but their existing approximation guarantees apply only to the special case of monotone kernels. This paper develops an alternative for a broader non-monotone setting.

Its key ingredient is a new continuous relaxation of the DPP log-probability function that can be evaluated and differentiated exactly and efficiently. summary.tldr: A tractable continuous relaxation supports approximate DPP MAP inference with a one-quarter guarantee for a general class of non-monotone models.

title: Near-Optimal MAP Inference for Determinantal Point Processes

abstract: Multi-Agent Plan Recognition (MAPR) aims to recognize dynamic team structures and team behaviors from the observed team traces (activity sequences) of a set of intelligent agents. Previous MAPR approaches required a library of team activity sequences (team plans) be given as input. However, collecting a library of team plans to ensure adequate coverage is often difficult and costly. In this paper, we relax this constraint, so that team plans are not required to be provided beforehand. We assume instead that a set of action models are available. Such models are often already created to describe domain physics; i.e., the preconditions and effects of effects actions. We propose a novel approach for recognizing multi-agent team plans based on such action models rather than libraries of team plans. We encode the resulting MAPR problem as a \emph{satisfiability problem} and solve the problem using a state-of-the-art weighted MAX-SAT solver. Our approach also allows for incompleteness in the observed plan traces. Our empirical studies demonstrate that our algorithm is both effective and efficient in comparison to state-of-the-art MAPR methods based on plan libraries.

paragraphs: Multi-agent plan recognition seeks to infer how agents form teams and what those teams are doing from observed activity sequences. Earlier approaches require a library of team plans prepared in advance. Building a library with adequate coverage can be difficult and costly, so this paper changes the knowledge required as input.

The proposed method assumes access to action models describing what must hold before an action and what changes after it. Such models may already exist to describe the domain. summary.tldr: Team plans are recognized from action models through weighted MAX-SAT, allowing incomplete observations without a predefined plan library.

title: Action-Model Based Multi-agent Plan Recognition

abstract: Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (NMF) is a promising relaxation technique for clustering analysis. However, conventional NMF methods that directly approximate the pairwise similarities using the least square error often yield mediocre performance for data in curved manifolds because they can capture only the immediate similarities between data samples. Here we propose a new NMF clustering method which replaces the approximated matrix with its smoothed version using random walk. Our method can thus accommodate farther relationships between data samples. Furthermore, we introduce a novel regularization in the proposed objective function in order to improve over spectral clustering. The new learning objective is optimized by a multiplicative Majorization-Minimization algorithm with a scalable implementation for learning the factorizing matrix. Extensive experimental results on real-world datasets show that our method has strong performance in terms of cluster purity.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a weakness of clustering with nonnegative matrix factorization: directly fitting pairwise similarities can emphasize only immediate relationships between samples. For data arranged along curved manifolds, those local comparisons may fail to capture relationships that become visible through connections among multiple samples. The authors seek to bring those farther relationships into the clustering objective.

Their method uses a random walk to smooth the similarity matrix before factorizing it. The resulting target incorporates relationships beyond immediate sample pairs. They also introduce a regularization term intended to improve on spectral clustering. A multiplicative Majorization-Minimization algorithm optimizes the resulting objective, with an implementation designed to make learning the factor matrix scalable.

Experiments across real-world datasets show strong cluster purity, meaning the discovered groups align well with the evaluated class groupings. The reported evidence supports combining graph-based smoothing with factorization. The central contribution is the change in what the factorization tries to represent: similarities enriched by paths through the data graph.
summary.tldr: Random-walk smoothing lets nonnegative matrix factorization use farther relationships between samples, with strong reported clustering purity.

title: Clustering by Nonnegative Matrix Factorization Using Graph Random Walk

abstract: Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) is a widely used statistical tool with both well established theory and favorable performance for a wide range of machine learning problems. However, computing CCA for huge datasets can be very slow since it involves implementing QR decomposition or singular value decomposition of huge matrices. In this paper we introduce L-CCA, an iterative algorithm which can compute CCA fast on huge sparse datasets. Theory on both the asymptotic convergence and finite time accuracy of L-CCA are established. The experiments also show that L-CCA outperform other fast CCA approximation schemes on two real datasets.

paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis is a widely used statistical tool with established theory and favorable results across many machine-learning problems. Its practical difficulty at large scale is computation: standard approaches require QR or singular-value decompositions of very large matrices. Those operations can make an otherwise useful analysis slow on huge datasets.

The paper introduces L-CCA, an iterative algorithm designed to compute CCA quickly on huge sparse datasets. The title identifies iterative least squares as the approach. The contribution centers on making the computation practical in this setting, where the size and sparsity of the data are central considerations.

The authors establish both asymptotic convergence and finite-time accuracy results. These address complementary questions: how the algorithm behaves as iteration continues, and how accurate its result is after a finite amount of computation. Experiments on two real datasets also report better performance than other fast CCA approximation schemes. Together, the theory and experiments support L-CCA as a scalable computational approach, with empirical comparisons limited to the two reported datasets.
summary.tldr: L-CCA computes canonical correlation analysis iteratively on huge sparse datasets, with convergence theory, finite-time accuracy results, and favorable empirical comparisons.

title: large scale canonical correlation analysis with iterative least squares

abstract: Simple decision heuristics are models of human and animal behavior that use few pieces of information---perhaps only a single piece of information---and integrate the pieces in simple ways, for example, by considering them sequentially, one at a time, or by giving them equal weight. It is unknown how quickly these heuristics can be learned from experience. We show, analytically and empirically, that only a few training samples lead to substantial progress in learning. We focus on three families of heuristics: single-cue decision making, lexicographic decision making, and tallying. Our empirical analysis is the most extensive to date, employing 63 natural data sets on diverse subjects.

A decision might rely on one cue, examine cues in sequence, or assign them equal weight. This paper asks how quickly such rules can be learned from experience, separating the simplicity of using a rule from the question of learning it.

The authors study three families: single-cue decisions, lexicographic decisions, and tallying. These correspond to relying on one piece of information, considering information in an ordered sequence, and combining it with equal weighting. The analysis therefore covers several different forms of simple decision making rather than treating all heuristics as one interchangeable approach.

Both theoretical analysis and empirical results show that a few training samples can produce substantial learning progress. The empirical study uses 63 natural datasets spanning diverse subjects. The finding concerns meaningful early improvement, rather than a claim that a handful of examples completes learning. It helps explain how simple behavioral rules can become useful even when experience is limited.
summary.tldr: Analytical results and experiments across 63 datasets show substantial early learning progress for three families of simple decision heuristics.

title: Learning From Small Samples: An Analysis of Simple Decision Heuristics

abstract: We provide two fundamental results on the population (infinite-sample) likelihood function of Gaussian mixture models with $M \geq 3$ components. Our first main result shows that the population likelihood function has bad local maxima even in the special case of equally-weighted mixtures of well-separated and spherical Gaussians. We prove that the log-likelihood value of these bad local maxima can be arbitrarily worse than that of any global optimum, thereby resolving an open question of Srebro (2007). Our second main result shows that the EM algorithm (or a first-order variant of it) with random initialization will converge to bad critical points with probability at least $1-e^{-\Omega(M)}$. We further establish that a first-order variant of EM will not converge to strict saddle points almost surely, indicating that the poor performance of the first-order method can be attributed to the existence of bad local maxima rather than bad saddle points. Overall, our results highlight the necessity of careful initialization when using the EM algorithm in practice, even when applied in highly favorable settings.

We further establish that a first-order variant of EM will not converge to strict saddle points almost surely, indicating that the poor performance of the first-order method can be attributed to the existence of bad local maxima rather than bad saddle points. Overall, our results highlight the necessity of careful initialization when using the EM algorithm in practice, even when applied in highly favorable settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies the population likelihood of Gaussian mixture models with at least three components. Population likelihood corresponds to an infinite-sample setting, so the analysis examines the objective’s underlying structure. Even for equally weighted, well-separated, spherical Gaussian components, the authors prove that poor local maxima exist.

These local maxima can have log-likelihood values arbitrarily below the global optimum. The authors also show that randomly initialized expectation-maximization, or a first-order variant, converges to bad critical points with probability at least one minus a term exponentially small in the number of components. Favorable separation and component shape therefore do not by themselves eliminate serious optimization difficulties in the settings analyzed.

A further result distinguishes local maxima from strict saddle points. The first-order EM variant almost surely does not converge to strict saddles, indicating that poor local maxima explain its failures rather than those saddles. Together, the findings emphasize careful initialization when using EM. They show why an apparently favorable statistical model can still present a difficult likelihood landscape for a local optimization algorithm.
summary.tldr: Gaussian-mixture likelihoods can contain arbitrarily poor local maxima even in favorable settings, making EM initialization consequential.

title: Local Maxima in the Likelihood of Gaussian Mixture Models: Structural Results and Algorithmic Consequences

abstract: Recommendation and collaborative filtering systems are important in modern information and e-commerce applications. As these systems are becoming increasingly popular in industry, their outputs could affect business decision making, introducing incentives for an adversarial party to compromise the availability or integrity of such systems. We introduce a data poisoning attack on collaborative filtering systems. We demonstrate how a powerful attacker with full knowledge of the learner can generate malicious data so as to maximize his/her malicious objectives, while at the same time mimicking normal user behaviors to avoid being detected. While the complete knowledge assumption seems extreme, it enables a robust assessment of the vulnerability of collaborative filtering schemes to highly motivated attacks. We present efficient solutions for two popular factorization-based collaborative filtering algorithms: the alternative minimization formulation and the nuclear norm minimization method. Finally, we test the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms on real-world data and discuss potential defensive strategies.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems can influence commercial decisions, creating incentives to manipulate their outputs. This paper studies data poisoning in collaborative filtering: an attacker supplies malicious data intended to change what the system learns. The analysis considers attacks that pursue harmful objectives while also imitating ordinary user behavior to reduce the chance of detection.

The attacker is assumed to have full knowledge of the learning system. The authors explicitly treat this as a strong assumption that enables a demanding assessment of vulnerability to a highly motivated adversary. They develop efficient attack solutions for two factorization-based approaches: an alternating-minimization formulation and a method based on nuclear-norm minimization.

The proposed algorithms are tested on real-world data, and the paper discusses possible defensive strategies. Its contribution is a way to assess how these recommendation methods can be manipulated under the stated knowledge assumption. The combination of attack effectiveness and behavior mimicry makes the assessment broader than simply asking whether arbitrary corrupted data can disrupt a model.
summary.tldr: The paper develops poisoning attacks against two factorization-based recommenders under a full-knowledge attacker assumption.

title: Data Poisoning Attacks on Factorization-Based Collaborative Filtering

abstract: We consider the problem of active sequential hypothesis testing where a Bayesian decision maker must infer the true hypothesis from a set of hypotheses. The decision maker may choose for a set of actions, where the outcome of an action is corrupted by independent noise. In this paper we consider a special case where the decision maker has limited knowledge about the distribution of observations for each action, in that only a binary value is observed. Our objective is to infer the true hypothesis with low error, while minimizing the number of action sampled. Our main results include the derivation of a lower bound on sample size for our system under limited knowledge and the design of an active learning policy that matches this lower bound and outperforms similar known algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a decision maker can identify the correct hypothesis by choosing which actions to take and observing their outcomes. The process is sequential: evidence gathered along the way can inform later choices. The objective combines two demands, keeping the final error low while using as few sampled actions as possible.

The setting restricts what the decision maker knows about the observation distributions associated with actions. Only a binary value is observed, and action outcomes are affected by independent noise. These restrictions make the choice of actions central to the problem: the decision maker must learn from limited feedback while still distinguishing among the candidate hypotheses.

The authors derive a lower bound on the number of samples needed in this setting and design an active learning policy that matches it. They also report that the policy outperforms similar existing algorithms. Matching the bound connects the policy's sample requirements to a fundamental limit for the specified system, giving theoretical support for its efficiency under limited information.
summary.tldr: An adaptive hypothesis-testing policy matches a sample-size lower bound when actions provide limited, noisy binary feedback.

title: Adaptive Active Hypothesis Testing under Limited Information

abstract: This paper focuses on best-arm identification in multi-armed bandits with bounded rewards. We develop an algorithm that is a fusion of lil-UCB and KL-LUCB, offering the best qualities of the two algorithms in one method. This is achieved by proving a novel anytime confidence bound for the mean of bounded distributions, which is the analogue of the LIL-type bounds recently developed for sub-Gaussian distributions. We corroborate our theoretical results with numerical experiments based on the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest.
originalAbstract: This paper focuses on best-arm identification in multi-armed bandits with bounded rewards. We corroborate our theoretical results with numerical experiments based on the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify the best option when each evaluation produces an uncertain but bounded reward. In the multi-armed bandit formulation, options are called arms, and repeated evaluations help estimate their average rewards. The goal here is best-arm identification: gathering evidence to determine which option has the highest mean.

The proposed algorithm combines lil-UCB and KL-LUCB, aiming to bring their favorable properties into one procedure. Its main theoretical ingredient is a new confidence bound for the mean of a bounded distribution. The bound is anytime, meaning it supports uncertainty assessment as observations accumulate, rather than being designed only for one predetermined sample count.

The authors relate this result to law-of-the-iterated-logarithm-style bounds previously developed for sub-Gaussian distributions. They also test the method numerically using the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest. This connects the statistical problem to crowdsourcing, where many candidate captions must be compared through noisy evaluations, and the experiments support the theoretical results.
summary.tldr: A hybrid bandit algorithm uses a new anytime confidence bound to identify the best option from noisy, bounded evaluations.

title: A KL-LUCB algorithm for Large-Scale Crowdsourcing

abstract: We establish the consistency of an algorithm of Mondrian Forests~\cite{lakshminarayanan2014mondrianforests,lakshminarayanan2016mondrianuncertainty}, a randomized classification algorithm that can be implemented online. First, we amend the original Mondrian Forest algorithm proposed in~\cite{lakshminarayanan2014mondrianforests}, that considers a \emph{fixed} lifetime parameter. Indeed, the fact that this parameter is fixed actually hinders statistical consistency of the original procedure. Our modified Mondrian Forest algorithm grows trees with increasing lifetime parameters $\lambda_n$, and uses an alternative updating rule, allowing to work also in an online fashion. Second, we provide a theoretical analysis establishing simple conditions for consistency. Our theoretical analysis also exhibits a surprising fact: our algorithm achieves the minimax rate (optimal rate) for the estimation of a Lipschitz regression function, which is a strong extension of previous results~\cite{arlot2014purf_bias} to an \emph{arbitrary dimension}.

paragraphs: Mondrian Forests are randomized classification models that can be updated online. This paper identifies a statistical problem with keeping their lifetime parameter fixed: that choice hinders consistency. Consistency concerns whether learning can approach the appropriate statistical target as the amount of data increases, so the parameter choice affects more than immediate predictive performance.

The authors modify the algorithm to grow trees with lifetime parameters that increase with sample size. They also introduce an alternative updating rule that preserves the ability to operate online. The resulting procedure adjusts its tree construction as more observations arrive, and the analysis gives simple conditions under which consistency holds.

The theory further establishes a minimax-optimal rate for estimating a Lipschitz regression function, extending earlier results to arbitrary dimension. Minimax optimality describes the best achievable rate over the relevant function class. The result therefore combines a consistency guarantee with a sharper statement about how quickly estimation improves under that smoothness assumption, while retaining an online implementation.
summary.tldr: A modified online Mondrian Forest achieves consistency under stated conditions and minimax-optimal rates for Lipschitz regression in arbitrary dimension.

title: Universal consistency and minimax rates for online Mondrian Forests

abstract: Differential privacy comes equipped with multiple analytical tools for the design of private data analyses. One important tool is the so-called "privacy amplification by subsampling" principle, which ensures that a differentially private mechanism run on a random subsample of a population provides higher privacy guarantees than when run on the entire population. Several instances of this principle have been studied for different random subsampling methods, each with an ad-hoc analysis. In this paper we present a general method that recovers and improves prior analyses, yields lower bounds and derives new instances of privacy amplification by subsampling. Our method leverages a characterization of differential privacy as a divergence which emerged in the program verification community. Furthermore, it introduces new tools, including advanced joint convexity and privacy profiles, which might be of independent interest.

paragraphs: A differentially private mechanism can provide stronger privacy when applied to a random subsample than when applied to the entire population. This principle, called privacy amplification by subsampling, is useful when designing private analyses. Previous treatments had established particular versions of the principle for different sampling procedures through separate, specialized arguments.

The paper develops a general analysis method that recovers earlier results, improves some of them, and derives new instances of amplification. It also produces lower bounds. Combining guarantees with lower bounds helps characterize both the privacy improvement that can be established and the limits on how strong an analysis can be.

The method uses a characterization of differential privacy in terms of a divergence, drawing on ideas from program verification. It introduces additional mathematical tools, including advanced joint convexity and privacy profiles, that the authors suggest may have independent value. The main contribution is a common analytical foundation for several subsampling settings, reducing reliance on disconnected proofs while enabling stronger and broader results.
summary.tldr: A general divergence-based framework unifies and strengthens privacy amplification analyses for random subsampling while also providing lower bounds.

title: Privacy Amplification by Subsampling: Tight Analyses via Couplings and Divergences

abstract: Deep learning models often have more parameters than observations, and still perform well. This is sometimes described as a paradox. In this work, we show experimentally that despite their huge number of parameters, deep neural networks can compress the data losslessly even when taking the cost of encoding the parameters into account. Such a compression viewpoint originally motivated the use of variational methods in neural networks. However, we show that these variational methods provide surprisingly poor compression bounds, despite being explicitly built to minimize such bounds. This might explain the relatively poor practical performance of variational methods in deep learning. Better encoding methods, imported from the Minimum Description Length (MDL) toolbox, yield much better compression values on deep networks.

However, we show that these variational methods provide surprisingly poor compression bounds, despite being explicitly built to minimize such bounds.
