paragraphs: Deep networks can contain more parameters than training observations and still perform well. This paper examines that apparent puzzle through compression: how compactly can the data be encoded when the cost of describing the network's parameters is included? The relevant quantity is the full description length, rather than the parameter count by itself.

The experiments show that deep networks can provide lossless data compression even after accounting for parameter encoding. This establishes that a large parameter count need not prevent a model from giving a compact description of the data. The paper also examines variational methods, whose motivation includes optimizing compression-related bounds, and finds their bounds surprisingly poor.

Encoding techniques drawn from Minimum Description Length yield substantially better compression values for the deep networks studied. This makes the choice of encoding method important when assessing a model through description length. The authors suggest that weak compression bounds might help explain the relatively poor practical performance of variational methods, but present that connection as a possible explanation rather than an established causal result.
summary.tldr: Deep networks can compress data losslessly despite parameter-encoding costs, and MDL encoding methods provide better compression values than the studied variational bounds.

title: The Description Length of Deep Learning models

abstract: Recent work by Cohen et al. has achieved state-of-the-art results for learning spherical images in a rotation invariant way by using ideas from group representation theory and noncommutative harmonic analysis. In this paper we propose a generalization of this work that generally exhibits improved performace, but from an implementation point of view is actually simpler. An unusual feature of the proposed architecture is that it uses the Clebsch--Gordan transform as its only source of nonlinearity, thus avoiding repeated forward and backward Fourier transforms. The underlying ideas of the paper generalize to constructing neural networks that are invariant to the action of other compact groups.
originalAbstract: Recent work by Cohen et al. has achieved state-of-the-art results for learning spherical images in a rotation invariant way by using ideas from group representation theory and noncommutative harmonic analysis. In this paper we propose a generalization of this work that generally exhibits improved performace, but from an implementation point of view is actually simpler. An unusual feature of the proposed architecture is that it uses the Clebsch--Gordan transform as its only source of nonlinearity, thus avoiding repeated forward and backward Fourier transforms. The underlying ideas of the paper generalize to constructing neural networks that are invariant to the action of other compact groups.

paragraphs: Clebsch–Gordan Nets address learning from spherical images while making the result insensitive to rotations. The paper builds on an earlier approach that used group representation theory and noncommutative harmonic analysis to achieve strong results on this problem. Its contribution is a generalization that the authors describe as both generally better performing and simpler to implement.

The central architectural choice is to use the Clebsch–Gordan transform as the network’s only source of nonlinearity. Nonlinearity lets a network express relationships beyond those available through linear operations alone. Here, that capability is incorporated into a network operating entirely in Fourier space, avoiding repeated forward and backward Fourier transforms.

This matters because the reported performance improvement comes alongside a simpler implementation, rather than requiring repeated changes of representation. The performance claim is qualified as a general tendency, not a guarantee for every case. The authors also state that the underlying ideas extend to networks invariant under other compact groups, giving the approach relevance beyond rotations of spherical images.
summary.tldr: Clebsch–Gordan Nets use a single kind of nonlinear transform to learn rotation-invariant spherical images entirely in Fourier space, with generally improved performance and simpler implementation.

title: Clebsch–Gordan Nets: a Fully Fourier Space Spherical Convolutional Neural Network

abstract: We introduce DeepProbLog, a probabilistic logic programming language that incorporates deep learning by means of neural predicates. We show how existing inference and learning techniques can be adapted for the new language. Our experiments demonstrate that DeepProbLog supports (i) both symbolic and subsymbolic representations and inference, (ii) program induction, (iii) probabilistic (logic) programming, and (iv) (deep) learning from examples. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to propose a framework where general-purpose neural networks and expressive probabilistic-logical modeling and reasoning are integrated in a way that exploits the full expressiveness and strengths of both worlds and can be trained end-to-end based on examples.

Our experiments demonstrate that DeepProbLog supports (i) both symbolic and subsymbolic representations and inference, (ii) program induction, (iii) probabilistic (logic) programming, and (iv) (deep) learning from examples. paragraphs: DeepProbLog brings neural networks into probabilistic logic programming. The objective is to combine learned representations with explicit logical reasoning and uncertainty within one framework. Its central device is the neural predicate: a point in a logic program where a neural component contributes to the program's reasoning.

The authors adapt existing inference and learning techniques to support this combined language. This matters because adding a neural component is only part of the problem; the resulting system must also reason with its outputs and learn from examples. DeepProbLog is designed for end-to-end training, allowing the neural and probabilistic-logical parts to participate in a single learning process.

Experiments demonstrate support for symbolic and subsymbolic representations and inference, program induction, probabilistic programming, and deep learning from examples. The authors describe their framework, to the best of their knowledge, as the first to integrate general-purpose neural networks and expressive probabilistic-logical reasoning while exploiting the strengths of both. The contribution is therefore both a language design and a demonstration that these capabilities can operate together.
summary.tldr: DeepProbLog integrates neural networks with probabilistic logic programs and supports end-to-end learning from examples.

title: DeepProbLog: Neural Probabilistic Logic Programming

abstract: We study the classic k-means/median clustering, which are fundamental problems in unsupervised learning, in the setting where data are partitioned across multiple sites, and where we are allowed to discard a small portion of the data by labeling them as outliers. We propose a simple approach based on constructing small summary for the original dataset. The proposed method is time and communication efficient, has good approximation guarantees, and can identify the global outliers effectively. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first practical algorithm with theoretical guarantees for distributed clustering with outliers. Our experiments on both real and synthetic data have demonstrated the clear superiority of our algorithm against all the baseline algorithms in almost all metrics.

The proposed method is time and communication efficient, has good approximation guarantees, and can identify the global outliers effectively. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first practical algorithm with theoretical guarantees for distributed clustering with outliers. Our experiments on both real and synthetic data have demonstrated the clear superiority of our algorithm against all the baseline algorithms in almost all metrics.

paragraphs: The paper considers clustering when a dataset is divided across several sites. It studies the familiar k-means and k-median objectives while allowing a small portion of the observations to be labeled as outliers and discarded. The challenge is to form useful clusters and identify outliers across the full distributed dataset.

The proposed approach constructs a compact summary of the original data. This summary is the basis for an algorithm designed to use both computation time and communication efficiently. The method also has approximation guarantees, connecting its practical resource savings to a theoretical account of the quality of the clustering solution it produces.

The authors report that the algorithm can effectively identify global outliers and describe it, to their knowledge, as the first practical distributed method for this problem with theoretical guarantees. Experiments on real and synthetic data show advantages over all tested baselines on almost all measured criteria. That evidence supports the combination of compact summaries, distributed operation, and explicit outlier handling in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Compact data summaries enable efficient distributed clustering with outlier detection and theoretical approximation guarantees.

title: A Practical Algorithm for Distributed Clustering and Outlier Detection

abstract: We consider first order expansions of convex penalized estimators in high-dimensional regression problems with random designs. Our setting includes linear regression and logistic regression as special cases. For a given penalty function $h$ and the corresponding penalized estimator $\hbeta$, we construct a quantity $\eta$, the first order expansion of $\hbeta$, such that the distance between $\hbeta$ and $\eta$ is an order of magnitude smaller than the estimation error $\|\hat{\beta} - \beta^*\|$. In this sense, the first order expansion $\eta$ can be thought of as a generalization of influence functions from the mathematical statistics literature to regularized estimators in high-dimensions. Such first order expansion implies that the risk of $\hat{\beta}$ is asymptotically the same as the risk of $\eta$ which leads to a precise characterization of the MSE of $\hbeta$; this characterization takes a particularly simple form for isotropic design. Such first order expansion also leads to inference results based on $\hat{\beta}$. We provide sufficient conditions for the existence of such first order expansion for three regularizers: the Lasso in its constrained form, the lasso in its penalized form, and the Group-Lasso. The results apply to general loss functions under some conditions and those conditions are satisfied for the squared loss in linear regression and for the logistic loss in the logistic model.

paragraphs: Regularization helps estimate regression models with many parameters, but it also complicates mathematical descriptions of their errors. This paper constructs first-order approximations of convex penalized estimators in high-dimensional regression with random designs. Its setting includes both linear and logistic regression.

For an estimator, the authors construct an approximating quantity whose distance from the estimator is smaller in order than the estimator's distance from the true parameter. This makes the approximation precise enough to capture the leading estimation error. It extends the role of influence functions to regularized estimation in high dimensions.

The expansion implies that the estimator and its approximation have asymptotically equivalent risk, enabling a precise characterization of mean squared error and supporting statistical inference. The characterization becomes particularly simple for isotropic designs. The authors provide sufficient conditions for the expansion with constrained Lasso, penalized Lasso, and Group-Lasso. Their conditions also accommodate general losses and are satisfied by squared loss in linear regression and logistic loss in the logistic model.
summary.tldr: First-order approximations characterize the leading error and risk of high-dimensional regularized estimators under sufficient conditions.

title: First order expansion of convex regularized estimators

abstract: We present an approach to learn SAT solver heuristics from scratch through deep reinforcement learning with a curriculum. In particular, we incorporate a graph neural network in a stochastic local search algorithm to act as the variable selection heuristic. We consider Boolean satisfiability problems from different classes and learn specialized heuristics for each class. Although we do not aim to compete with the state-of-the-art SAT solvers in run time, we demonstrate that the learned heuristics allow us to find satisfying assignments in fewer steps compared to a generic heuristic, and we provide analysis of our results through experiments.
originalAbstract: We present an approach to learn SAT solver heuristics from scratch through deep reinforcement learning with a curriculum. In particular, we incorporate a graph neural network in a stochastic local search algorithm to act as the variable selection heuristic. We consider Boolean satisfiability problems from different classes and learn specialized heuristics for each class. Although we do not aim to compete with the state-of-the-art SAT solvers in run time, we demonstrate that the learned heuristics allow us to find satisfying assignments in fewer steps compared to a generic heuristic, and we provide analysis of our results through experiments.

paragraphs: Boolean satisfiability asks whether truth values can be assigned to variables so that a collection of logical requirements is satisfied. Local search approaches this by repeatedly changing a candidate assignment. A central choice is which variable to change next, and this paper investigates learning that choice instead of relying on a generic handcrafted heuristic.

The authors place a graph neural network inside a stochastic local-search algorithm to serve as its variable-selection heuristic. They train it from scratch with deep reinforcement learning and a curriculum. They consider several classes of satisfiability problems and learn a specialized heuristic for each class, making the target the structure of a problem family rather than a single universal selection rule.

Experiments show that the learned heuristics find satisfying assignments in fewer search steps than a generic heuristic. The authors explicitly do not aim to compete with state-of-the-art solvers on runtime. The supported result is therefore improved search-step efficiency in the studied settings, demonstrating that learned choices can guide local search more effectively without establishing faster overall solving.
summary.tldr: Graph neural networks learn problem-class-specific SAT search heuristics that find satisfying assignments in fewer steps than a generic heuristic.

title: Learning Local Search Heuristics for Boolean Satisfiability

abstract: We develop new models and algorithms for learning the temporal dynamics of the topic polytopes and related geometric objects that arise in topic model based inference. Our model is nonparametric Bayesian and the corresponding inference algorithm is able to discover new topics as the time progresses. By exploiting the connection between the modeling of topic polytope evolution, Beta-Bernoulli process and the Hungarian matching algorithm, our method is shown to be several orders of magnitude faster than existing topic modeling approaches, as demonstrated by experiments working with several million documents in under two dozens of minutes.
originalAbstract: We develop new models and algorithms for learning the temporal dynamics of the topic polytopes and related geometric objects that arise in topic model based inference. Our model is nonparametric Bayesian and the corresponding inference algorithm is able to discover new topics as the time progresses. By exploiting the connection between the modeling of topic polytope evolution, Beta-Bernoulli process and the Hungarian matching algorithm, our method is shown to be several orders of magnitude faster than existing topic modeling approaches, as demonstrated by experiments working with several million documents in under two dozens of minutes.

paragraphs: Topics in a document collection can change over time, and new topics can emerge as more documents arrive. This paper develops models and algorithms for tracking that evolution through the geometric structures associated with topic models. In particular, it studies topic polytopes and related latent objects as quantities whose temporal dynamics can be learned.

The model uses a nonparametric Bayesian formulation, allowing its inference procedure to discover new topics as time progresses. Its computational approach connects the evolution of topic geometry with the Beta-Bernoulli process and the Hungarian matching algorithm. These connections form the basis of the proposed inference method and its ability to handle changing topic structure at scale.

Experiments demonstrate processing several million documents in less than twenty-four minutes, with speeds several orders of magnitude faster than existing topic-modeling approaches. These reported gains make computational scale a central contribution alongside the evolving-topic model itself. The result shows that tracking latent topic structures, including newly appearing topics, can be practical for very large document collections in the demonstrated setting.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric Bayesian approach tracks evolving topic geometry and discovers new topics while processing millions of documents efficiently in experiments.

title: Scalable inference of topic evolution via models for latent geometric structures

abstract: Ancestral graphs are a prevalent mathematical tool to take into account latent (hidden) variables in a probabilistic graphical model. In ancestral graph representations, the nodes are only the observed (manifest) variables and the notion of m-separation fully characterizes the conditional independence relations among such variables, bypassing the need to explicitly consider latent variables. However, ancestral graph models do not necessarily represent the actual causal structure of the model, and do not contain information about, for example, the precise number and location of the hidden variables. Being able to detect the presence of latent variables while also inferring their precise location within the actual causal structure model is a more challenging task that provides more information about the actual causal relationships among all the model variables, including the latent ones. In this article, we develop an algorithm to exactly recover graphical models of random variables with underlying polytree structures when the latent nodes satisfy specific degree conditions. Therefore, this article proposes an approach for the full identification of hidden variables in a polytree. We also show that the algorithm is complete in the sense that when such degree conditions are not met, there exists another polytree with fewer number of latent nodes satisfying the degree conditions and entailing the same independence relations among the observed variables, making it indistinguishable from the actual polytree.

paragraphs: A graphical model can describe relationships among measured variables while leaving hidden variables implicit. Ancestral graphs do this by recording conditional independence relationships among observed variables. However, that representation does not necessarily reveal the actual causal structure, including how many hidden variables exist or where they belong.

This paper develops an algorithm that recovers a fuller structure for models whose underlying graph is a polytree. Its exact recovery guarantee requires the hidden nodes to satisfy particular degree conditions, meaning conditions on their connections. Under those conditions, the algorithm identifies hidden variables and their positions rather than merely representing their effects on observed relationships.

The paper also explains why the conditions matter for identification. When they fail, another polytree with fewer hidden nodes can produce the same observed independence relationships while satisfying the conditions. Those relationships therefore cannot distinguish the original structure from the alternative. The completeness result connects the algorithm's recovery boundary to an ambiguity in the available independence information.
summary.tldr: The paper gives an algorithm for exactly recovering hidden-node polytrees under degree conditions and characterizes the ambiguity when those conditions fail.

title: An Algorithm to Learn Polytree Networks with Hidden Nodes

abstract: In this work, we move beyond the traditional complex-valued representations, introducing more expressive hypercomplex representations to model entities and relations for knowledge graph embeddings. More specifically, quaternion embeddings, hypercomplex-valued embeddings with three imaginary components, are utilized to represent entities. Relations are modelled as rotations in the quaternion space. The advantages of the proposed approach are: (1) Latent inter-dependencies (between all components) are aptly captured with Hamilton product, encouraging a more compact interaction between entities and relations; (2) Quaternions enable expressive rotation in four-dimensional space and have more degree of freedom than rotation in complex plane; (3) The proposed framework is a generalization of ComplEx on hypercomplex space while offering better geometrical interpretations, concurrently satisfying the key desiderata of relational representation learning (i.e., modeling symmetry, anti-symmetry and inversion). Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on four well-established knowledge graph completion benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper develops representations for entities and relations in knowledge graphs using quaternions. A quaternion has one real component and three imaginary components, providing a richer representation than a complex number. Entities receive quaternion embeddings, while relations act as rotations in this space, giving the model a geometric interpretation.

Interactions use the Hamilton product, which couples the components of the representations. The authors argue that this captures dependencies among all components while encouraging compact entity-relation interactions. Quaternion rotations also offer more degrees of freedom than rotations in the complex plane. The framework extends ComplEx into hypercomplex space and can represent symmetry, anti-symmetry, and inversion, three important patterns in relations.

The method achieves reported state-of-the-art results on four established knowledge graph completion benchmarks. These experiments support the usefulness of the representation for predicting missing graph relationships. The contribution combines expressive interactions with a geometric account of relations, rather than presenting additional representational dimensions without explaining how entities and relations interact.
summary.tldr: Quaternion entity embeddings and rotational relations capture rich relational patterns and achieve reported state-of-the-art knowledge graph completion results.

title: Quaternion Knowledge Graph Embeddings

abstract: From infancy, humans have expectations about how objects will move and interact. Even young children expect objects not to move through one another, teleport, or disappear. They are surprised by mismatches between physical expectations and perceptual observations, even in unfamiliar scenes with completely novel objects. A model that exhibits human-like understanding of physics should be similarly surprised, and adjust its beliefs accordingly. We propose ADEPT, a model that uses a coarse (approximate geometry) object-centric representation for dynamic 3D scene understanding. Inference integrates deep recognition networks, extended probabilistic physical simulation, and particle filtering for forming predictions and expectations across occlusion. We also present a new test set for measuring violations of physical expectations, using a range of scenarios derived from developmental psychology. We systematically compare ADEPT, baseline models, and human expectations on this test set. ADEPT outperforms standard network architectures in discriminating physically implausible scenes, and often performs this discrimination at the same level as people.

paragraphs: People form expectations about objects even in unfamiliar scenes: objects should not pass through one another, vanish, or suddenly appear elsewhere. This paper studies whether a computational model can detect comparable violations of physical expectations. The focus is on comparing observed events with predictions about how objects should move and interact.

The proposed model, ADEPT, represents scenes through individual objects with approximate geometry. It combines deep recognition networks, probabilistic physical simulation, and particle filtering to maintain predictions and expectations, including while objects are occluded. The representation deliberately uses coarse object descriptions, bringing perception and uncertain physical prediction together for dynamic three-dimensional scene understanding.

The authors also introduce a test set based on scenarios from developmental psychology and compare ADEPT with baseline models and human expectations. ADEPT is better than standard network architectures at distinguishing physically implausible scenes and often reaches human-level discrimination on this test set. These findings support the usefulness of coarse, probabilistic object representations for the evaluated expectation judgments, with human comparability applying to many tested cases rather than every case.
summary.tldr: ADEPT combines coarse object representations with probabilistic physics to detect implausible scenes, often matching human discrimination on its test set.

title: Modeling Expectation Violation in Intuitive Physics with Coarse Probabilistic Object Representations

abstract: In this paper we provide a general framework for estimating symmetric properties of distributions from i.i.d. samples. For a broad class of symmetric properties we identify the {\em easy} region where empirical estimation works and the {\em difficult} region where more complex estimators are required. We show that by approximately computing the profile maximum likelihood (PML) distribution \cite{ADOS16} in this difficult region we obtain a symmetric property estimation framework that is sample complexity optimal for many properties in a broader parameter regime than previous universal estimation approaches based on PML. The resulting algorithms based on these \emph{pseudo PML distributions} are also more practical.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate symmetric properties of a probability distribution from independent samples drawn from that same distribution. Such properties concern the distribution without depending on the particular names assigned to its outcomes. The central question is when simple estimation from observed frequencies is adequate and when more elaborate methods are needed.

The authors identify easy and difficult regions for a broad class of these properties. Empirical estimation works in the easy region. In the difficult region, their framework approximately computes a profile maximum likelihood distribution, using what they call pseudo PML distributions. This division gives the more complex estimator a specific role where empirical estimation is insufficient.

For many properties, the resulting framework achieves optimal sample complexity over a broader parameter regime than earlier universal PML approaches. This means its sample requirements meet the relevant optimum in those settings. The authors also describe the resulting algorithms as more practical, combining stronger statistical coverage with a more usable estimation approach.
summary.tldr: Separating easy and difficult estimation regions yields a practical PML-based framework with optimal sample complexity for many symmetric properties.

title: A General Framework for Symmetric Property Estimation

abstract: We consider estimating a high dimensional signal in $\R^n$ using a sublinear number of linear measurements. In analogy to classical compressed sensing, here we assume a generative model as a prior, that is, we assume the signal is represented by a deep generative model $G: \R^k \rightarrow \R^n$. Classical recovery approaches such as empirical risk minimization (ERM) are guaranteed to succeed when the measurement matrix is sub-Gaussian. However, when the measurement matrix and measurements are heavy tailed or have outliers, recovery may fail dramatically. In this paper we propose an algorithm inspired by the Median-of-Means (MOM). Our algorithm guarantees recovery for heavy tailed data, even in the presence of outliers. Theoretically, our results show our novel MOM-based algorithm enjoys the same sample complexity guarantees as ERM under sub-Gaussian assumptions. Our experiments validate both aspects of our claims: other algorithms are indeed fragile and fail under heavy tailed and/or corrupted data, while our approach exhibits the predicted robustness.

paragraphs: The paper considers recovering a high-dimensional signal from fewer linear measurements than the signal has coordinates. Recovery relies on a generative prior: the signal is assumed to be represented by a deep generative model mapping a lower-dimensional input into the signal space. This assumption supplies structure that makes reconstruction from limited measurements possible.

Standard empirical risk minimization has recovery guarantees for sub-Gaussian measurement matrices, but heavy tails or outliers can cause serious failures. The authors propose an algorithm inspired by Median-of-Means to handle those less favorable observations. Their method provides recovery guarantees for heavy-tailed data even when outliers are present, addressing robustness in both the measurement matrix and the measurements.

The theoretical results match the sample-complexity guarantees that empirical risk minimization enjoys under sub-Gaussian assumptions. Experiments support both sides of the argument: other algorithms fail on the studied heavy-tailed or corrupted data, while the proposed method exhibits the predicted robustness. The result shows that, in the analyzed setting with a generative prior, increased robustness can retain the favorable measurement requirements of the cleaner-data guarantee.
summary.tldr: A Median-of-Means-inspired reconstruction algorithm uses a generative prior to recover signals robustly from heavy-tailed measurements with outliers.

title: Robust compressed sensing using generative models

abstract: Clustering is an important topic in algorithms, and has a number of applications in machine learning, computer vision, statistics, and several other research disciplines. Traditional objectives of graph clustering are to find clusters with low conductance. Not only are these objectives just applicable for undirected graphs, they are also incapable to take the relationships between clusters into account, which could be crucial for many applications. To overcome these downsides, we study directed graphs (digraphs) whose clusters exhibit further “structural” information amongst each other. Based on the Hermitian matrix representation of digraphs, we present a nearly-linear time algorithm for digraph clustering, and further show that our proposed algorithm can be implemented in sublinear time under reasonable assumptions. The significance of our theoretical work is demonstrated by extensive experimental results on the UN Comtrade Dataset: the output clustering of our algorithm exhibits not only how the clusters (sets of countries) relate to each other with respect to their import and export records, but also how these clusters evolve over time, in accordance with known facts in international trade.

paragraphs: Graph clustering commonly seeks groups with relatively few connections crossing their boundaries. This paper studies directed graphs where the relationships between groups also carry useful structure. Direction matters because connections from one group to another can have a different meaning from connections going the other way, so finding groups alone does not capture the full organization.

The authors use a Hermitian matrix representation of the directed graph to develop a spectral clustering algorithm. They establish nearly-linear running time and show that, under suitable assumptions, the algorithm can be implemented in sublinear time. The method therefore addresses both the structural goal of representing relationships among clusters and the computational goal of handling graphs efficiently.

Experiments use the UN Comtrade dataset, with countries grouped according to import and export records. The resulting clusters reveal relationships between groups of countries and changes in those groups over time, consistent with known international trade facts. These findings illustrate how directed clustering can expose organization beyond isolated communities, while the stronger sublinear efficiency result remains conditional on the stated class of assumptions.
summary.tldr: A spectral method clusters directed graphs while capturing relationships among groups, with efficient algorithms and evidence from international trade data.

title: Higher-Order Spectral Clustering of Directed Graphs

abstract: Current deep neural networks can achieve remarkable performance on a single task. However, when the deep neural network is continually trained on a sequence of tasks, it seems to gradually forget the previous learned knowledge. This phenomenon is referred to as catastrophic forgetting and motivates the field called lifelong learning. Recently, episodic memory based approaches such as GEM and A-GEM have shown remarkable performance. In this paper, we provide the first unified view of episodic memory based approaches from an optimization's perspective. This view leads to two improved schemes for episodic memory based lifelong learning, called MEGA-\rom{1} and MEGA-\rom{2}. MEGA-\rom{1} and MEGA-\rom{2} modulate the balance between old tasks and the new task by integrating the current gradient with the gradient computed on the episodic memory. Notably, we show that GEM and A-GEM are degenerate cases of MEGA-\rom{1} and MEGA-\rom{2} which consistently put the same emphasis on the current task, regardless of how the loss changes over time. Our proposed schemes address this issue by using novel loss-balancing updating rules, which drastically improve the performance over GEM and A-GEM. Extensive experimental results show that the proposed schemes significantly advance the state-of-the-art on four commonly used lifelong learning benchmarks, reducing the error by up to 18%.

paragraphs: A network trained on successive tasks can lose skills it acquired earlier, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Episodic memory methods address this by retaining examples from previous tasks and using them during later learning. This paper develops a unified optimization perspective on such methods and uses it to design two improved schemes, MEGA-1 and MEGA-2.

Both schemes combine the gradient for the current task with a gradient computed from stored examples. Their central concern is how much emphasis each source of information receives. The authors show that GEM and A-GEM arise as degenerate cases of their schemes, with unchanged emphasis on the current task despite changes in loss during training. MEGA introduces loss-balancing update rules to adapt that tradeoff.

The authors report substantial improvements over GEM and A-GEM and advances over the state of the art on four commonly used lifelong-learning benchmarks, with error reductions of up to 18%. The findings suggest that how memory influences each update matters alongside the presence of memory itself. The reported maximum improvement is an experimental outcome, rather than a uniform reduction across tasks.
summary.tldr: MEGA-1 and MEGA-2 adapt the balance between current-task and memory gradients, reducing forgetting-related errors in lifelong-learning experiments.

title: Improved Schemes for Episodic Memory-based Lifelong Learning

abstract: We propose novel algorithms with first- and second-order regret bounds for adversarial linear bandits. These regret bounds imply that our algorithms perform well when there is an action achieving a small cumulative loss or the loss has a small variance. In addition, we need only assumptions weaker than those of existing algorithms; our algorithms work on discrete action sets as well as continuous ones without a priori knowledge about losses, and they run efficiently if a linear optimization oracle for the action set is available. These results are obtained by combining optimistic online optimization, continuous multiplicative weight update methods, and a novel technique that we refer to as distribution truncation. We also show that the regret bounds of our algorithms are tight up to polylogarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Adversarial linear bandit problems require decisions under limited feedback even when losses can vary adversarially. This paper develops algorithms whose regret guarantees reflect favorable structure in the realized losses. They perform well when some action has low cumulative loss or when losses have low variance, capturing first-order and second-order forms of adaptivity.

The algorithms support both discrete and continuous action sets without advance knowledge of the losses. Their computational efficiency is conditional on access to a linear optimization oracle for the action set. This separates the learning guarantee from the practical ability to solve the required optimization subproblem over the available actions.

The construction combines optimistic online optimization, continuous multiplicative weight updates, and a new distribution-truncation technique. The authors show that the resulting regret bounds are tight up to polylogarithmic factors. This means the dependence captured by their guarantees is close to the fundamental limit, while requiring weaker assumptions than existing algorithms. The contribution joins loss-sensitive performance guarantees with broad action-space coverage under an explicit computational condition.
summary.tldr: New adversarial linear bandit algorithms achieve nearly tight loss- and variance-sensitive regret bounds across discrete and continuous action sets.

title: Tight First- and Second-Order Regret Bounds for Adversarial Linear Bandits

abstract: Important insights towards the explainability of neural networks reside in the characteristics of their decision boundaries. In this work, we borrow tools from the field of adversarial robustness, and propose a new perspective that relates dataset features to the distance of samples to the decision boundary. This enables us to carefully tweak the position of the training samples and measure the induced changes on the boundaries of CNNs trained on large-scale vision datasets. We use this framework to reveal some intriguing properties of CNNs. Specifically, we rigorously confirm that neural networks exhibit a high invariance to non-discriminative features, and show that the decision boundaries of a DNN can only exist as long as the classifier is trained with some features that hold them together. Finally, we show that the construction of the decision boundary is extremely sensitive to small perturbations of the training samples, and that changes in certain directions can lead to sudden invariances in the orthogonal ones. This is precisely the mechanism that adversarial training uses to achieve robustness.

paragraphs: A classifier’s decision boundary separates inputs assigned to different classes. This paper investigates how features in training data determine where that boundary forms. Using tools from adversarial robustness, the authors relate dataset features to the distance between samples and the boundary, making it possible to study how controlled changes in samples reshape classification behavior.

Their framework carefully changes the positions of training examples and measures the resulting boundary changes in convolutional networks trained on large-scale vision datasets. They confirm strong invariance to features that do not help distinguish classes. They also show that maintaining a decision boundary requires training features that support it, connecting boundary geometry to the discriminative information available during learning.

The study further finds that boundary construction is highly sensitive to small changes in training samples. Perturbations along certain directions can produce sudden invariance along perpendicular directions. The authors identify this as the mechanism through which adversarial training achieves robustness. These findings explain how changing the features a network encounters can reorganize which input variations affect its predictions.
summary.tldr: Controlled training-data perturbations reveal how discriminative features shape neural decision boundaries and how adversarial training induces invariance.

title: Hold me tight! Influence of discriminative features on deep network boundaries

abstract: The dominant approaches to text representation in natural language rely on learning embeddings on massive corpora which have convenient properties such as compositionality and distance preservation. In this paper, we develop a novel method to learn a heavy-tailed embedding with desirable regularity properties regarding the distributional tails, which allows to analyze the points far away from the distribution bulk using the framework of multivariate extreme value theory. In particular, a classifier dedicated to the tails of the proposed embedding is obtained which exhibits a scale invariance property exploited in a novel text generation method for label preserving dataset augmentation. Experiments on synthetic and real text data show the relevance of the proposed framework and confirm that this method generates meaningful sentences with controllable attribute, e.g. positive or negative sentiments.

paragraphs: Text embeddings represent language as points in a learned space. This paper focuses on points far from the main concentration of that distribution. It develops a heavy-tailed embedding whose tails have regularity properties, making those distant points accessible to analysis through multivariate extreme value theory.

The authors use that structure to obtain a classifier specifically for the embedding's tails. This classifier has a scale invariance property, allowing the method to exploit changes of scale while preserving its classification behavior. That property becomes the basis of a text generation procedure intended to augment a dataset while keeping the labels of generated examples consistent.

Experiments on synthetic data and real text support the framework and show that it can generate meaningful sentences with controllable attributes, including positive or negative sentiment. The contribution connects the geometry of an embedding distribution to a practical generation task. Rather than treating extreme regions merely as unusual points, the approach gives them mathematical structure that can support classification and label-preserving augmentation.
summary.tldr: A heavy-tailed text embedding enables tail-specific classification and controlled generation of meaningful sentences for label-preserving augmentation.

title: Heavy-tailed Representations, Text Polarity Classification & Data Augmentation

abstract: In this paper, we establish a theoretical comparison between the asymptotic mean square errors of double Q-learning and Q-learning. Our result builds upon an analysis for linear stochastic approximation based on Lyapunov equations and applies to both tabular setting or with linear function approximation, provided that the optimal policy is unique and the algorithms converge. We show that the asymptotic mean-square error of Double Q-learning is exactly equal to that of Q-learning if Double Q-learning uses twice the learning rate of Q-learning and the output of Double Q-learning is the average of its two estimators. We also present some practical implications of this theoretical observation using simulations.

paragraphs: The paper compares Q-learning and Double Q-learning through their asymptotic mean-squared errors. Its focus is the behavior of estimation error in the long run. The analysis uses results for linear stochastic approximation based on Lyapunov equations, providing a theoretical framework for comparing the two algorithms.

The main result applies in tabular settings and with linear function approximation, provided that the optimal policy is unique and the algorithms converge. Under those assumptions, Double Q-learning has exactly the same asymptotic mean-squared error as Q-learning when two additional choices are made: its learning rate is doubled, and its reported estimate is the average of its two estimators.

This establishes a precise conditional equivalence between the methods. Both the learning-rate relationship and the averaging rule are part of the result, so the equality concerns a particular configuration of Double Q-learning. Simulations explore practical implications of the theoretical observation, connecting the asymptotic comparison to decisions about how the two estimators and learning rates are used.
summary.tldr: Under stated convergence and uniqueness assumptions, averaged Double Q-learning matches Q-learning's asymptotic mean-squared error when its learning rate is doubled.

title: The Mean-Squared Error of Double Q-Learning

abstract: Dense 3D object reconstruction from a single image has recently witnessed remarkable advances, but supervising neural networks with ground-truth 3D shapes is impractical due to the laborious process of creating paired image-shape datasets. Recent efforts have turned to learning 3D reconstruction without 3D supervision from RGB images with annotated 2D silhouettes, dramatically reducing the cost and effort of annotation. These techniques, however, remain impractical as they still require multi-view annotations of the same object instance during training. As a result, most experimental efforts to date have been limited to synthetic datasets. In this paper, we address this issue and propose SDF-SRN, an approach that requires only a single view of objects at training time, offering greater utility for real-world scenarios. SDF-SRN learns implicit 3D shape representations to handle arbitrary shape topologies that may exist in the datasets. To this end, we derive a novel differentiable rendering formulation for learning signed distance functions (SDF) from 2D silhouettes. Our method outperforms the state of the art under challenging single-view supervision settings on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Learning to reconstruct a three-dimensional object from an image often requires expensive training annotations. Even methods that avoid ground-truth 3D shapes can require several annotated views of each object. SDF-SRN addresses this training-data requirement by learning from only one view per object, using two-dimensional silhouette supervision to support three-dimensional shape reconstruction.

The method represents shapes implicitly through signed distance functions. This representation allows it to handle arbitrary shape topologies present in the data. To learn the representation from silhouettes, the authors derive a differentiable rendering formulation. That formulation connects the predicted three-dimensional shape to the two-dimensional supervision available during training.

The authors report better performance than the state of the art under challenging single-view supervision conditions on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The significance is the combination of a flexible shape representation and a reduced annotation requirement. Training can use a single annotated view of an object rather than requiring multiple views of that same instance, making the approach more useful for the real-world scenarios motivating the work.
summary.tldr: SDF-SRN learns implicit 3D shapes from single-view silhouette supervision through a new differentiable rendering formulation.

title: SDF-SRN: Learning Signed Distance 3D Object Reconstruction from Static Images

abstract: Randomly initialized neural networks are known to become harder to train with increasing depth, unless architectural enhancements like residual connections and batch normalization are used. We here investigate this phenomenon by revisiting the connection between random initialization in deep networks and spectral instabilities in products of random matrices. Given the rich literature on random matrices, it is not surprising to find that the rank of the intermediate representations in unnormalized networks collapses quickly with depth. In this work we highlight the fact that batch normalization is an effective strategy to avoid rank collapse for both linear and ReLU networks. Leveraging tools from Markov chain theory, we derive a meaningful lower rank bound in deep linear networks. Empirically, we also demonstrate that this rank robustness generalizes to ReLU nets. Finally, we conduct an extensive set of experiments on real-world data sets, which confirm that rank stability is indeed a crucial condition for training modern-day deep neural architectures.

It connects the problem to products of random matrices and the spectral instabilities they can produce. In unnormalized networks, intermediate representations rapidly lose rank as depth grows, meaning their outputs occupy fewer independent directions.

The authors examine batch normalization as a way to preserve those directions. Using tools from Markov chain theory, they derive a meaningful lower bound on representation rank in deep linear networks. This provides a theoretical account of how normalization can counteract rank collapse in that setting.

For networks with ReLU activations, the evidence is empirical: experiments show that the rank robustness also extends to these nonlinear networks. Additional experiments on real-world datasets support the importance of rank stability for training deep architectures. The distinction between the two forms of evidence matters: the stated rank bound concerns linear networks, while the extension to ReLU networks is demonstrated experimentally. The work identifies preservation of representation rank as an important contribution of batch normalization.
summary.tldr: Batch normalization counters representation rank collapse, with a theoretical bound for deep linear networks and supporting experiments for ReLU networks.

title: Batch normalization provably avoids ranks collapse for randomly initialised deep networks

abstract: Self-supervised frameworks that learn denoising models with merely individual noisy images have shown strong capability and promising performance in various image denoising tasks. Existing self-supervised denoising frameworks are mostly built upon the same theoretical foundation, where the denoising models are required to be J-invariant. However, our analyses indicate that the current theory and the J-invariance may lead to denoising models with reduced performance. In this work, we introduce Noise2Same, a novel self-supervised denoising framework. In Noise2Same, a new self-supervised loss is proposed by deriving a self-supervised upper bound of the typical supervised loss. In particular, Noise2Same requires neither J-invariance nor extra information about the noise model and can be used in a wider range of denoising applications. We analyze our proposed Noise2Same both theoretically and experimentally. The experimental results show that our Noise2Same remarkably outperforms previous self-supervised denoising methods in terms of denoising performance and training efficiency.

Many existing approaches share a theoretical foundation that requires a property called J-invariance. The authors analyze that foundation and argue that both the theory and the restriction may reduce denoising performance.

Noise2Same introduces a different training objective by deriving a self-supervised upper bound on the usual supervised loss. This gives the model a loss that can be optimized using noisy images while remaining linked to the supervised denoising objective. The framework requires neither J-invariance nor additional information about the noise model.

The authors study Noise2Same theoretically and experimentally, reporting substantial improvements over previous self-supervised denoising methods in both restoration performance and training efficiency. Removing the stated restrictions also allows a wider range of denoising applications. The contribution is the connection between a new self-supervised bound and a training framework that relaxes a constraint the authors identify as potentially detrimental.
summary.tldr: Noise2Same trains denoisers through a self-supervised upper bound without requiring J-invariance or extra noise-model information.

title: Noise2Same: Optimizing A Self-Supervised Bound for Image Denoising

abstract: Modern convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have massive identical convolution blocks, and, hence, recursive sharing of parameters across these blocks has been proposed to reduce the amount of parameters. However, naive sharing of parameters poses many challenges such as limited representational power and the vanishing/exploding gradients problem of recursively shared parameters. In this paper, we present a recursive convolution block design and training method, in which a recursively shareable part, or a filter basis, is separated and learned while effectively avoiding the vanishing/exploding gradients problem during training. We show that the unwieldy vanishing/exploding gradients problem can be controlled by enforcing the elements of the filter basis orthonormal, and empirically demonstrate that the proposed orthogonality regularization improves the flow of gradients during training. Experimental results on image classification and object detection show that our approach, unlike previous parameter-sharing approaches, does not trade performance to save parameters and consistently outperforms over parameterized counterpart networks. This superior performance demonstrates that the proposed recursive convolution block design and the orthogonality regularization not only prevent performance degradation, but also consistently improve the representation capability while a significant amount of parameters are recursively shared.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks often contain many repeated blocks, making parameter sharing an appealing way to reduce model size. Simply reusing parameters can, however, restrict what the network represents and cause gradients to shrink or grow excessively during training. This paper redesigns the convolution block and its training procedure to address those problems together.

The method separates out a filter basis that can be learned and reused across blocks. The authors show that making the basis elements orthonormal can control the problematic gradient behavior. They also introduce an orthogonality regularizer and empirically show that it improves gradient flow. The shared component is therefore paired with a training mechanism intended to keep recursive reuse manageable.

On image classification and object detection experiments, the proposed networks save substantial numbers of parameters while consistently outperforming their overparameterized counterparts. In these tests, sharing does more than preserve performance in a smaller model: the block design and regularization also improve representation capability. The results support this particular combination of structured sharing and gradient control, rather than parameter reuse alone.
summary.tldr: Sharing learned filter bases with orthogonality regularization reduces CNN parameters while improving gradient flow and performance in the reported experiments.

title: Deeply Shared Filter Bases for Parameter-Efficient Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Generative flows and diffusion models have been predominantly trained on ordinal data, for example natural images. This paper introduces two extensions of flows and diffusion for categorical data such as language or image segmentation: Argmax Flows and Multinomial Diffusion. Argmax Flows are defined by a composition of a continuous distribution (such as a normalizing flow), and an argmax function. To optimize this model, we learn a probabilistic inverse for the argmax that lifts the categorical data to a continuous space. Multinomial Diffusion gradually adds categorical noise in a diffusion process, for which the generative denoising process is learned. We demonstrate that our method outperforms existing dequantization approaches on text modelling and modelling on image segmentation maps in log-likelihood.

paragraphs: Generative flows and diffusion models have largely been applied to data with ordered values. This paper develops two ways to apply these model families to categorical observations, including text and image segmentation maps. The challenge is to construct a learning process that works directly with categories.

Argmax Flows combine a continuous probability distribution with an argmax operation that selects a category. Training requires connecting observed categories back to the continuous representation. The authors do this by learning a probabilistic inverse of argmax, allowing categorical observations to be lifted into continuous space for optimization.

Multinomial Diffusion follows a different route: a forward process gradually introduces categorical noise, and the model learns the corresponding generative denoising process. Both constructions adapt an established generative framework to categorical distributions through an explicit treatment of the data type. In text modeling and segmentation-map modeling, the paper reports better log-likelihood than existing dequantization approaches. These findings concern how well the models assign probability to the evaluated categorical data.
summary.tldr: Argmax Flows and Multinomial Diffusion adapt flow and diffusion models to categorical data, improving reported likelihood over dequantization approaches.

title: Argmax Flows and Multinomial Diffusion: Learning Categorical Distributions

abstract: We analyze the adaptive first order algorithm AMSGrad, for solving a constrained stochastic optimization problem with a weakly convex objective. We prove the $\mathcal{\tilde O}(t^{-1/2})$ rate of convergence for the squared norm of the gradient of Moreau envelope, which is the standard stationarity measure for this class of problems. It matches the known rates that adaptive algorithms enjoy for the specific case of unconstrained smooth nonconvex stochastic optimization. Our analysis works with mini-batch size of $1$, constant first and second order moment parameters, and possibly unbounded optimization domains. Finally, we illustrate the applications and extensions of our results to specific problems and algorithms.
originalAbstract: We analyze the adaptive first order algorithm AMSGrad, for solving a constrained stochastic optimization problem with a weakly convex objective. We prove the $\mathcal{\tilde O}(t^{-1/2})$ rate of convergence for the squared norm of the gradient of Moreau envelope, which is the standard stationarity measure for this class of problems. It matches the known rates that adaptive algorithms enjoy for the specific case of unconstrained smooth nonconvex stochastic optimization. Our analysis works with mini-batch size of $1$, constant first and second order moment parameters, and possibly unbounded optimization domains. Finally, we illustrate the applications and extensions of our results to specific problems and algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies AMSGrad, an adaptive first-order optimization algorithm, for stochastic problems with constraints and weakly convex objectives. The setting broadens the analysis beyond smooth, unconstrained nonconvex optimization. The goal is to establish how quickly the method approaches stationarity, a relevant target when global optimality is not the guarantee under study.

The authors measure progress using the squared norm of the gradient of the Moreau envelope, a smoothed representation of the objective and a standard stationarity measure for this problem class. They prove a convergence rate of approximately t to the minus one-half, with logarithmic factors suppressed. This matches known rates for adaptive methods in the more specific smooth, unconstrained setting.

The analysis permits a mini-batch size of one, fixed first- and second-moment parameters, and optimization domains that may be unbounded. These features specify the scope of the result and connect it to concrete algorithm choices. The paper also illustrates applications and extensions to particular problems and algorithms, showing how the stationarity analysis can be used beyond its central formulation.
summary.tldr: AMSGrad receives a stationarity convergence guarantee for constrained stochastic weakly convex optimization, including single-sample updates and potentially unbounded domains.

title: Convergence of adaptive algorithms for constrained weakly convex optimization

abstract: Regularization plays a major role in modern deep learning. From classic techniques such as L1, L2 penalties to other noise-based methods such as Dropout, regularization often yields better generalization properties by avoiding overfitting. Recently, Stochastic Depth (SD) has emerged as an alternative regularization technique for residual neural networks (ResNets) and has proven to boost the performance of ResNet on many tasks [Huang et al., 2016]. Despite the recent success of SD, little is known about this technique from a theoretical perspective. This paper provides a hybrid analysis combining perturbation analysis and signal propagation to shed light on different regularization effects of SD. Our analysis allows us to derive principled guidelines for choosing the survival rates used for training with SD.

paragraphs: This paper examines why stochastic depth acts as a regularizer in residual neural networks. Regularization aims to improve generalization by limiting overfitting, and stochastic depth had already shown useful performance across tasks. The authors focus on the theoretical understanding of that technique, seeking to explain the effects behind its observed success.

Their approach combines perturbation analysis with signal propagation analysis. These provide complementary perspectives: one examines the effects of perturbations introduced during training, while the other follows how signals travel through the network. Bringing them together allows the authors to investigate different regularization effects of stochastic depth within a shared analysis.

The analysis leads to principled guidelines for selecting survival rates, the probabilities governing which residual components remain active during stochastic-depth training. This connects the theoretical study to a concrete training choice. The contribution is an explanation of regularization behavior that informs how the method is configured, giving a mathematical basis for choosing an important aspect of the training procedure.
summary.tldr: A combined theoretical analysis explains stochastic-depth regularization and yields guidelines for choosing survival rates.

title: Regularization in ResNet with Stochastic Depth

abstract: Active learning has proven to be useful for minimizing labeling costs by selecting the most informative samples. However, existing active learning methods do not work well in realistic scenarios such as imbalance or rare classes,out-of-distribution data in the unlabeled set, and redundancy. In this work, we propose SIMILAR (Submodular Information Measures based actIve LeARning), a unified active learning framework using recently proposed submodular information measures (SIM) as acquisition functions. We argue that SIMILAR not only works in standard active learning but also easily extends to the realistic settings considered above and acts as a one-stop solution for active learning that is scalable to large real-world datasets. Empirically, we show that SIMILAR significantly outperforms existing active learning algorithms by as much as ~5%−18%in the case of rare classes and ~5%−10%in the case of out-of-distribution data on several image classification tasks like CIFAR-10, MNIST, and ImageNet.

paragraphs: Active learning reduces labeling effort by choosing which unlabeled examples should receive labels. This paper focuses on difficulties that arise when the available pool contains rare classes, class imbalance, out-of-distribution examples, or redundant data. Such conditions can undermine methods that work well in more standard active learning settings.

SIMILAR provides a unified framework using submodular information measures as acquisition functions, the criteria that guide example selection. The authors argue that this family of measures supports both standard active learning and the more realistic scenarios they consider. The framework is also presented as scalable to large real-world datasets.

Experiments on image classification tasks including CIFAR-10, MNIST, and ImageNet report improvements over existing active learning algorithms of approximately 5%–18% for rare-class scenarios and 5%–10% when out-of-distribution data are present. These findings provide empirical support for using the framework under challenging pool compositions. The reported ranges describe results in the studied settings rather than a guaranteed improvement for every labeling task.
summary.tldr: SIMILAR uses submodular information measures to select labels and reports gains in active learning with rare classes and out-of-distribution data.

title: SIMILAR: Submodular Information Measures Based Active Learning In Realistic Scenarios

abstract: Several works in implicit and explicit generative modeling empirically observed that feature-learning discriminators outperform fixed-kernel discriminators in terms of the sample quality of the models. We provide separation results between probability metrics with fixed-kernel and feature-learning discriminators using the function classes $\mathcal{F}_2$ and $\mathcal{F}_1$ respectively, which were developed to study overparametrized two-layer neural networks. In particular, we construct pairs of distributions over hyper-spheres that can not be discriminated by fixed kernel $(\mathcal{F}_2)$ integral probability metric (IPM) and Stein discrepancy (SD) in high dimensions, but that can be discriminated by their feature learning ($\mathcal{F}_1$) counterparts. To further study the separation we provide links between the $\mathcal{F}_1$ and $\mathcal{F}_2$ IPMs with sliced Wasserstein distances. Our work suggests that fixed-kernel discriminators perform worse than their feature learning counterparts because their corresponding metrics are weaker.

In particular, we construct pairs of distributions over hyper-spheres that can not be discriminated by fixed kernel $(\mathcal{F}_2)$ integral probability metric (IPM) and Stein discrepancy (SD) in high dimensions, but that can be discriminated by their feature learning ($\mathcal{F}_1$) counterparts. paragraphs: Generative-modeling experiments have found that discriminators which learn features can produce better sample quality than discriminators based on fixed kernels. This paper investigates a mathematical explanation by comparing the probability metrics associated with the two approaches. These metrics measure how distinguishable two distributions are through their respective discriminator function classes.

The analysis uses the F2 and F1 classes developed for studying overparameterized two-layer neural networks. The authors construct pairs of distributions on high-dimensional hyperspheres that fixed-kernel integral probability metrics and Stein discrepancies cannot discriminate, while their feature-learning counterparts can. These constructions establish concrete separations in the distinguishing power of the studied metrics.

The paper also relates the F1 and F2 integral probability metrics to sliced Wasserstein distances, further characterizing the separation. Its findings suggest that weaker probability metrics help explain the observed disadvantage of fixed-kernel discriminators. The result supplies theoretical examples and an explanatory connection to generative modeling; it does not claim that every learned-feature discriminator outperforms every fixed kernel on every distribution.
summary.tldr: Constructed high-dimensional examples show that feature-learning probability metrics can distinguish distributions that their fixed-kernel counterparts cannot.

title: Separation Results between Fixed-Kernel and Feature-Learning Probability Metrics

abstract: Motivated by sequential budgeted allocation problems, we investigate online matching problems where connections between vertices are not i.i.d., but they have fixed degree distributions -- the so-called configuration model. We estimate the competitive ratio of the simplest algorithm, GREEDY, by approximating some relevant stochastic discrete processes by their continuous counterparts, that are solutions of an explicit system of partial differential equations. This technique gives precise bounds on the estimation errors, with arbitrarily high probability as the problem size increases. In particular, it allows the formal comparison between different configuration models. We also prove that, quite surprisingly, GREEDY can have better performance guarantees than RANKING, another celebrated algorithm for online matching that usually outperforms the former.

paragraphs: Online matching makes allocation decisions as opportunities arrive. This paper studies sparse random graphs whose vertices have fixed degree distributions, using the configuration model rather than assuming independent, identically distributed connections. That setting captures a different structure from many standard random-graph analyses.

The authors approximate relevant discrete stochastic processes with continuous processes described by an explicit system of partial differential equations. This provides estimates of GREEDY’s competitive ratio and precise approximation-error bounds that hold with arbitrarily high probability as problem size increases.

The technique permits formal comparisons between degree-distribution models. It also shows that GREEDY can have better performance guarantees than RANKING, despite the latter’s usual advantage in other settings. The result is therefore distribution-sensitive: it does not say GREEDY universally dominates RANKING, but demonstrates why online-matching guarantees can change when the graph-generation assumptions change.
summary.tldr: A differential-equation analysis gives finite-size guarantees for greedy online matching in configuration-model graphs.

title: Online Matching in Sparse Random Graphs: Non-Asymptotic Performances of Greedy Algorithm

abstract: Understanding the implicit bias of training algorithms is of crucial importance in order to explain the success of overparametrised neural networks. In this paper, we study the dynamics of stochastic gradient descent over diagonal linear networks through its continuous time version, namely stochastic gradient flow. We explicitly characterise the solution chosen by the stochastic flow and prove that it always enjoys better generalisation properties than that of gradient flow.Quite surprisingly, we show that the convergence speed of the training loss controls the magnitude of the biasing effect: the slower the convergence, the better the bias. To fully complete our analysis, we provide convergence guarantees for the dynamics. We also give experimental results which support our theoretical claims. Our findings highlight the fact that structured noise can induce better generalisation and they help explain the greater performances of stochastic gradient descent over gradient descent observed in practice.

paragraphs: A training algorithm influences more than how quickly a network fits its data: it also influences which solution the network reaches. The paper studies this implicit bias in diagonal linear networks. It analyzes stochastic gradient flow, a continuous-time version of stochastic gradient descent, to make the effect of randomness mathematically explicit.

The authors characterize the solution selected by the stochastic dynamics and prove that, in the setting studied, it has better generalization properties than the solution selected by ordinary gradient flow. They also show a surprising relationship between training speed and solution preference: slower convergence of the training loss produces a stronger beneficial bias.

The analysis includes convergence guarantees, and experiments support the theoretical claims. The central implication is that structured training noise can help select solutions with better generalization, rather than merely adding variability to optimization. Because the proof concerns diagonal linear networks and continuous-time dynamics, its contribution is a precise mechanism in that setting that helps explain advantages observed for stochastic gradient descent in practice.
summary.tldr: For diagonal linear networks, stochastic gradient flow provably selects better-generalizing solutions than gradient flow, with stronger beneficial bias when training converges more slowly.

title: Implicit Bias of SGD for Diagonal Linear Networks: a Provable Benefit of Stochasticity

abstract: Deep learning has enabled algorithms to generate realistic images. However, accurately predicting long video sequences requires understanding long-term dependencies and remains an open challenge. While existing video prediction models succeed at generating sharp images, they tend to fail at accurately predicting far into the future. We introduce the Clockwork VAE (CW-VAE), a video prediction model that leverages a hierarchy of latent sequences, where higher levels tick at slower intervals. We demonstrate the benefits of both hierarchical latents and temporal abstraction on 4 diverse video prediction datasets with sequences of up to 1000 frames, where CW-VAE outperforms top video prediction models. Additionally, we propose a Minecraft benchmark for long-term video prediction. We conduct several experiments to gain insights into CW-VAE and confirm that slower levels learn to represent objects that change more slowly in the video, and faster levels learn to represent faster objects.

paragraphs: Generating a sharp video frame does not by itself solve the problem of predicting what will happen far into the future. The paper focuses on long-term dependencies in video: the relationships across time that a model must preserve to produce accurate extended predictions. Existing models can generate visually sharp images while still struggling with this longer horizon.

Clockwork VAE addresses the problem using a hierarchy of hidden sequences that update at different rates. Higher levels update less frequently, introducing temporal abstraction into the model. This gives the hierarchy distinct timescales for representing video content, instead of requiring every level to change at every step.

The authors evaluate the model on four diverse video prediction datasets with sequences reaching 1,000 frames and report that it outperforms leading video prediction models. They also introduce a Minecraft benchmark for long-term prediction. Additional experiments show that slower levels represent more slowly changing objects, while faster levels represent faster objects, supporting the intended role of the hierarchy.
summary.tldr: Clockwork VAE improves long-term video prediction using a hierarchy whose hidden representations update at different speeds.

title: Clockwork Variational Autoencoders

abstract: Several families of continual learning techniques have been proposed to alleviate catastrophic interference in deep neural network training on non-stationary data. However, a comprehensive comparison and analysis of limitations remains largely open due to the inaccessibility to suitable datasets. Empirical examination not only varies immensely between individual works, it further currently relies on contrived composition of benchmarks through subdivision and concatenation of various prevalent static vision datasets. In this work, our goal is to bridge this gap by introducing a computer graphics simulation framework that repeatedly renders only upcoming urban scene fragments in an endless real-time procedural world generation process. At its core lies a modular parametric generative model with adaptable generative factors. The latter can be used to flexibly compose data streams, which significantly facilitates a detailed analysis and allows for effortless investigation of various continual learning schemes.
