paragraphs: Continual learning studies how neural networks can keep learning as incoming data changes, while reducing interference with what they learned previously. Comparing methods is difficult when each study constructs its own sequence of tasks. The paper identifies a particular weakness in existing evaluations: they often divide and concatenate static vision datasets to imitate a changing stream.

The authors introduce a computer graphics framework that continually generates an urban world. It renders the fragments of the scene that are coming next, supporting an endless process that runs in real time. A modular generative model controls the world through adjustable parameters, so researchers can compose streams by changing the factors responsible for the generated data.

This design makes the construction of changing data streams part of the experimental framework itself. Researchers can use adjustable generative factors to investigate continual learning schemes in a more systematic way. The contribution is an evaluation resource that supports detailed analysis of learning under changing conditions, addressing the difficulty of comparing methods through separately assembled static benchmarks.
summary.tldr: A controllable urban-world simulator generates changing visual data streams for systematic continual learning evaluation.

title: A Procedural World Generation Framework for Systematic Evaluation of Continual Learning

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a novel approach enabling several clients holding sensitive data to collaboratively train machine learning models, without centralizing data. The cross-silo FL setting corresponds to the case of few ($2$--$50$) reliable clients, each holding medium to large datasets, and is typically found in applications such as healthcare, finance, or industry. While previous works have proposed representative datasets for cross-device FL, few realistic healthcare cross-silo FL datasets exist, thereby slowing algorithmic research in this critical application. In this work, we propose a novel cross-silo dataset suite focused on healthcare, FLamby (Federated Learning AMple Benchmark of Your cross-silo strategies), to bridge the gap between theory and practice of cross-silo FL.FLamby encompasses 7 healthcare datasets with natural splits, covering multiple tasks, modalities, and data volumes, each accompanied with baseline training code. As an illustration, we additionally benchmark standard FL algorithms on all datasets.Our flexible and modular suite allows researchers to easily download datasets, reproduce results and re-use the different components for their research. FLamby is available at~\url{www.github.com/owkin/flamby}.

paragraphs: Federated learning allows several participants to train a model together while keeping their data in separate locations. In the cross-silo setting, there are relatively few reliable participants, each with a medium or large dataset. Healthcare is an important example, but the shortage of realistic benchmarks makes it harder to study algorithms for this setting.

FLamby addresses that gap with a suite of seven healthcare datasets. The datasets have natural splits and span different tasks, data types, and amounts of data. Each includes baseline training code. This gives researchers several settings in which to examine cross-silo learning, with partitions grounded in the datasets' existing organization.

The authors also benchmark standard federated learning algorithms across the full suite. Their contribution is a shared experimental resource and starting point for comparing methods. Its modular design supports downloading datasets, reproducing results, and reusing components in new research. Together, the datasets and code make it easier to investigate how federated approaches behave across varied healthcare problems.
summary.tldr: FLamby provides seven naturally partitioned healthcare datasets, training code, and benchmarks for studying cross-silo federated learning.

title: FLamby: Datasets and Benchmarks for Cross-Silo Federated Learning in Realistic Healthcare Settings

abstract: There has been a significant research effort focused on explaining predictive models, for example through post-hoc explainability and recourse methods. Most of the proposed techniques operate upon a single, fixed, predictive model. However, it is well-known that given a dataset and a predictive task, there may be a multiplicity of models that solve the problem (nearly) equally well. In this work, we investigate the implications of this kind of model indeterminacy on the post-hoc explanations of predictive models. We show how it can lead to explanatory multiplicity, and we explore the underlying drivers. We show how predictive multiplicity, and the related concept of epistemic uncertainty, are not reliable indicators of explanatory multiplicity. We further illustrate how a set of models showing very similar aggregate performance on a test dataset may show large variations in their local explanations, i.e., for a specific input. We explore these effects for Shapley value based explanations on three risk assessment datasets. Our results indicate that model indeterminacy may have a substantial impact on explanations in practice, leading to inconsistent and even contradicting explanations.

paragraphs: A dataset and prediction task can admit several models with nearly equal predictive performance. This paper examines what that model indeterminacy means for explanations, which are commonly generated for a single fixed model. The central question is whether equally successful models also provide similar accounts of their decisions.

The authors show that model indeterminacy can produce explanatory multiplicity: different explanations across alternative models. Large differences can appear in explanations for a particular input even when aggregate test performance is very similar. They also find that predictive multiplicity and epistemic uncertainty are unreliable indicators of explanatory multiplicity, so those quantities cannot simply stand in for checking explanation variation.

The empirical investigation studies Shapley-value-based explanations on three risk assessment datasets. Results indicate that alternative models can yield inconsistent and even contradictory explanations in practice. This matters when interpreting a local explanation as a stable account of a decision: similar overall predictive quality does not establish that the explanation would remain similar under another comparably performing model.
summary.tldr: Models with similar predictive performance can give conflicting local explanations, and prediction uncertainty does not reliably reveal that variation.

title: Implications of Model Indeterminacy for Explanations of Automated Decisions

abstract: Interpretable and explainable machine learning has seen a recent surge of interest. We focus on safety as a key motivation behind the surge and make the relationship between interpretability and safety more quantitative. Toward assessing safety, we introduce the concept of *maximum deviation* via an optimization problem to find the largest deviation of a supervised learning model from a reference model regarded as safe. We then show how interpretability facilitates this safety assessment. For models including decision trees, generalized linear and additive models, the maximum deviation can be computed exactly and efficiently. For tree ensembles, which are not regarded as interpretable, discrete optimization techniques can still provide informative bounds. For a broader class of piecewise Lipschitz functions, we leverage the multi-armed bandit literature to show that interpretability produces tighter (regret) bounds on the maximum deviation. We present case studies, including one on mortgage approval, to illustrate our methods and the insights about models that may be obtained from deviation maximization.

paragraphs: The paper makes one connection between interpretability and safety quantitative: how far can a model's behavior depart from a reference model regarded as safe? It formulates this as an optimization problem called maximum deviation. The resulting assessment is explicitly relative to the chosen reference, giving a concrete target for examining model behavior.

For decision trees and generalized linear and additive models, the authors show that maximum deviation can be computed exactly and efficiently. For tree ensembles, discrete optimization can still produce informative bounds. These results distinguish cases where the largest departure can be found precisely from cases where it can be bounded usefully.

The analysis extends to a broader class of piecewise Lipschitz functions using ideas from multi-armed bandits. Within that setting, interpretability yields tighter regret bounds for estimating maximum deviation. Case studies, including mortgage approval, illustrate the method and the insights obtained by searching for extreme departures. The contribution makes interpretability useful for a specific safety-assessment task rather than treating comprehensibility alone as a safety guarantee.
summary.tldr: Maximum deviation quantifies departures from a reference model regarded as safe, with interpretability enabling exact computations or tighter bounds.

title: On the Safety of Interpretable Machine Learning: A Maximum Deviation Approach

abstract: Generic motion understanding from video involves not only tracking objects, but also perceiving how their surfaces deform and move. This information is useful to make inferences about 3D shape, physical properties and object interactions. While the problem of tracking arbitrary physical points on surfaces over longer video clips has received some attention, no dataset or benchmark for evaluation existed, until now. In this paper, we first formalize the problem, naming it tracking any point (TAP). We introduce a companion benchmark,TAP-Vid, which is composed of both real-world videos with accurate human annotations of point tracks, and synthetic videos with perfect ground-truth point tracks. Central to the construction of our benchmark is a novel semi-automatic crowdsourced pipeline which uses optical flow estimates to compensate for easier, short-term motion like camera shake, allowing annotators to focus on harder sections of the video. We validate our pipeline on synthetic data and propose a simple end-to-end point tracking model, TAP-Net, showing that it outperforms all prior methods on our benchmark when trained on synthetic data.

paragraphs: Understanding motion includes following particular points on a surface as an object moves or deforms. This paper formalizes tracking any point, or TAP, and introduces a benchmark for evaluating it over longer video clips.

A semiautomatic crowdsourcing pipeline uses optical-flow estimates to compensate for easier short-term motion, including camera shake. This lets annotators concentrate on harder portions of a video. The authors validate the annotation pipeline using synthetic data.

The paper also introduces TAP-Net, a simple end-to-end point-tracking model. When trained on synthetic data, it outperforms all prior methods evaluated on the new benchmark. The contribution therefore includes a defined task, a way to collect annotations, an evaluation resource, and a working model. Its reported model advantage is specific to the benchmark, while the benchmark supplies a common basis for comparing future point-tracking approaches.
summary.tldr: TAP-Vid establishes a benchmark for tracking arbitrary surface points and introduces a strong synthetic-data-trained baseline.

title: TAP-Vid: A Benchmark for Tracking Any Point in a Video

abstract: We study embedding table placement for distributed recommender systems, which aims to partition and place the tables on multiple hardware devices (e.g., GPUs) to balance the computation and communication costs. Although prior work has explored learning-based approaches for the device placement of computational graphs, embedding table placement remains to be a challenging problem because of 1) the operation fusion of embedding tables, and 2) the generalizability requirement on unseen placement tasks with different numbers of tables and/or devices. To this end, we present DreamShard, a reinforcement learning (RL) approach for embedding table placement. DreamShard achieves the reasoning of operation fusion and generalizability with 1) a cost network to directly predict the costs of the fused operation, and 2) a policy network that is efficiently trained on an estimated Markov decision process (MDP) without real GPU execution, where the states and the rewards are estimated with the cost network. Equipped with sum and max representation reductions, the two networks can directly generalize to any unseen tasks with different numbers of tables and/or devices without fine-tuning. Extensive experiments show that DreamShard substantially outperforms the existing human expert and RNN-based strategies with up to 19% speedup over the strongest baseline on large-scale synthetic tables and our production tables. The code is available.

paragraphs: DreamShard addresses how to distribute embedding tables across hardware devices in a recommender system. A good placement must balance computation with communication. The problem becomes harder when table operations are fused, because the system must reason about the cost of a combined operation, and when deployments contain different numbers of tables or devices.

The approach uses reinforcement learning supported by a learned cost network. That network predicts fused-operation costs and supplies estimated states and rewards for training the placement policy. This lets policy training proceed in an estimated decision process without real GPU execution. Sum and maximum reductions make the network representations accommodate varying numbers of tables and devices.

The authors state that these representations support direct transfer to unseen placement tasks of different sizes without fine-tuning. Experiments using large synthetic tables and production tables show improvements over human-expert and recurrent-network strategies, reaching up to 19% speedup over the strongest baseline. The result links reusable placement decisions with explicit modeling of fused-operation costs.
summary.tldr: DreamShard learns embedding-table placements using predicted execution costs and transfers across different numbers of tables and devices.

title: DreamShard: Generalizable Embedding Table Placement for Recommender Systems

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) defy the classical bias-variance trade-off: adding parameters to a DNN that interpolates its training data will typically improve its generalization performance. Explaining the mechanism behind this ``benign overfitting'' in deep networks remains an outstanding challenge. Here, we study the last hidden layer representations of various state-of-the-art convolutional neural networks and find that if the last hidden representation is wide enough, its neurons tend to split into groups that carry identical information and differ from each other only by statistically independent noise. The number of such groups increases linearly with the width of the layer, but only if the width is above a critical value. We show that redundant neurons appear only when the training is regularized and the training error is zero.

Here, we study the last hidden layer representations of various state-of-the-art convolutional neural networks and find that if the last hidden representation is wide enough, its neurons tend to split into groups that carry identical information and differ from each other only by statistically independent noise. paragraphs: Neural networks can fit their training data exactly and still generalize better as more parameters are added. This behavior, often called benign overfitting, challenges the usual expectation that additional flexibility necessarily harms performance beyond the training set. The paper investigates a possible representational mechanism by examining the last hidden layers of several leading convolutional networks.

When those layers are sufficiently wide, the authors find that neurons tend to form groups carrying identical information. Members of a group differ only through statistically independent noise. The observation distinguishes the shared information represented by a group from the noise associated with its individual neurons, revealing organization within an apparently redundant layer.

Above a critical width, the number of these groups increases linearly with layer width. The authors also report that redundant neurons appear only when training is regularized and training error reaches zero. These conditions are part of the reported finding, rather than a claim that every wide network develops the same structure. The study identifies a concrete pattern relevant to understanding generalization in networks that interpolate their training data.
summary.tldr: The studied wide convolutional networks develop groups of informationally redundant neurons, with this structure appearing only under regularization and zero training error.

title: Redundant representations help generalization in wide neural networks

abstract: Clustering models constitute a class of unsupervised machine learning methods which are used in a number of application pipelines, and play a vital role in modern data science. With recent advancements in deep learning-- deep clustering models have emerged as the current state-of-the-art over traditional clustering approaches, especially for high-dimensional image datasets. While traditional clustering approaches have been analyzed from a robustness perspective, no prior work has investigated adversarial attacks and robustness for deep clustering models in a principled manner. To bridge this gap, we propose a blackbox attack using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) where the adversary does not know which deep clustering model is being used, but can query it for outputs. We analyze our attack against multiple state-of-the-art deep clustering models and real-world datasets, and find that it is highly successful. We then employ some natural unsupervised defense approaches, but find that these are unable to mitigate our attack. Finally, we attack Face++, a production-level face clustering API service, and find that we can significantly reduce its performance as well. Through this work, we thus aim to motivate the need for truly robust deep clustering models.

paragraphs: Deep clustering uses neural networks to group data without supervised class labels and has become especially effective for high-dimensional images. This paper examines whether that success also comes with resistance to adversarial manipulation. It addresses a gap in the principled study of attacks and robustness for deep clustering, beyond earlier work on traditional clustering methods.

The authors propose a black-box attack based on a generative adversarial network. The attacker does not know which deep clustering model is operating but can submit queries and observe its outputs. Evaluations across multiple state-of-the-art models and real-world datasets find the attack highly successful, showing vulnerability under this limited-access setting.

The study also tests natural unsupervised defenses, which fail to mitigate the proposed attack in the reported evaluations. An attack on the production Face++ face-clustering API substantially reduces its performance as well. Together, these findings motivate stronger robustness methods for deep clustering and show that the concern extends to an evaluated deployed service.
summary.tldr: A GAN-based black-box attack exposes vulnerabilities in deep clustering models and Face++, while the tested unsupervised defenses fail to mitigate it.

title: On the Robustness of Deep Clustering Models: Adversarial Attacks and Defenses

abstract: Fairness has become an important topic in machine learning. Generally, most literature on fairness assumes that the sensitive information, such as gender or race, is present in the training set, and uses this information to mitigate bias. However, due to practical concerns like privacy and regulation, applications of these methods are restricted. Also, although much of the literature studies supervised learning, in many real-world scenarios, we want to utilize the large unlabelled dataset to improve the model's accuracy. Can we improve fair classification without sensitive information and without labels? To tackle the problem, in this paper, we propose a novel reweighing-based contrastive learning method. The goal of our method is to learn a generally fair representation without observing sensitive attributes.Our method assigns weights to training samples per iteration based on their gradient directions relative to the validation samples such that the average top-k validation loss is minimized. Compared with past fairness methods without demographics, our method is built on fully unsupervised training data and requires only a small labelled validation set. We provide rigorous theoretical proof of the convergence of our model. Experimental results show that our proposed method achieves better or comparable performance than state-of-the-art methods on three datasets in terms of accuracy and several fairness metrics.

paragraphs: Many fairness methods require sensitive attributes such as gender or race during training, which can be unavailable because of privacy or regulatory concerns. This paper asks how to learn useful, fairer representations without observing those attributes. It uses fully unlabeled training data, while still requiring a small labeled validation set to guide learning.

The proposed method combines contrastive learning with repeated reweighting of training examples. At each iteration, weights depend on how training-example gradient directions relate to those of validation examples. The objective is to reduce the average of the top-k validation losses, directing learning toward validation examples with relatively large errors rather than relying on demographic group labels.

The authors provide a rigorous convergence result for their model. Across three datasets, the method achieves better or comparable results to state-of-the-art methods on accuracy and several fairness measures. These findings support reweighting as a way to improve fairness without demographic annotations, while the labeled validation set remains an explicit part of the method's supervision.
summary.tldr: A contrastive-learning method reweights unlabeled examples using a small labeled validation set to improve fairness without sensitive attributes.

title: Self-Supervised Fair Representation Learning without Demographics

abstract: Geometric deep learning has broad applications in biology, a domain where relational structure in data is often intrinsic to modelling the underlying phenomena. Currently, efforts in both geometric deep learning and, more broadly, deep learning applied to biomolecular tasks have been hampered by a scarcity of appropriate datasets accessible to domain specialists and machine learning researchers alike. To address this, we introduce Graphein as a turn-key tool for transforming raw data from widely-used bioinformatics databases into machine learning-ready datasets in a high-throughput and flexible manner. Graphein is a Python library for constructing graph and surface-mesh representations of biomolecular structures, such as proteins, nucleic acids and small molecules, and biological interaction networks for computational analysis and machine learning. Graphein provides utilities for data retrieval from widely-used bioinformatics databases for structural data, including the Protein Data Bank, the AlphaFold Structure Database, chemical data from ZINC and ChEMBL, and for biomolecular interaction networks from STRINGdb, BioGrid, TRRUST and RegNetwork. The library interfaces with popular geometric deep learning libraries: DGL, Jraph, PyTorch Geometric and PyTorch3D though remains framework agnostic as it is built on top of the PyData ecosystem to enable inter-operability with scientific computing tools and libraries. Graphein is designed to be highly flexible, allowing the user to specify each step of the data preparation, scalable to facilitate working with large protein complexes and interaction graphs, and contains useful pre-processing tools for preparing experimental files. Graphein facilitates network-based, graph-theoretic and topological analyses of structural and interaction datasets in a high-throughput manner. We envision that Graphein will facilitate developments in computational biology, graph representation learning and drug discovery. Availability and implementation: Graphein is written in Python. Source code, example usage and tutorials, datasets, and documentation are made freely available under the MIT License at the following URL: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/graphein-3472/README.md

paragraphs: Biomolecular data contains relationships and geometry that are useful for machine learning, but turning raw biological records into suitable datasets can be a substantial obstacle. Graphein addresses this preparation step. It is a Python library that builds graph and surface-mesh representations of proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, and biological interaction networks.

The library retrieves data from established resources covering molecular structures, chemicals, and biological interactions. Users can specify individual preparation steps, and preprocessing utilities help prepare experimental files. This flexibility supports different choices about how biological information should be represented, while its design accommodates large protein complexes and interaction graphs.

Its outputs support machine learning as well as network, graph-theoretic, and topological analyses. The contribution is reusable infrastructure for producing analysis-ready biological datasets at scale. The authors make the code, examples, datasets, tutorials, and documentation freely available under the MIT License.
summary.tldr: Graphein turns biomolecular structures and interaction records into configurable graphs and meshes for machine learning and scientific analysis.

title: Graphein - a Python Library for Geometric Deep Learning and Network Analysis on Biomolecular Structures and Interaction Networks

abstract: Making language models bigger does not inherently make them better at following a user's intent. For example, large language models can generate outputs that are untruthful, toxic, or simply not helpful to the user. In other words, these models are not aligned with their users. In this paper, we show an avenue for aligning language models with user intent on a wide range of tasks by fine-tuning with human feedback. Starting with a set of labeler-written prompts and prompts submitted through a language model API, we collect a dataset of labeler demonstrations of the desired model behavior, which we use to fine-tune GPT-3 using supervised learning. We then collect a dataset of rankings of model outputs, which we use to further fine-tune this supervised model using reinforcement learning from human feedback. We call the resulting models InstructGPT. In human evaluations on our prompt distribution, outputs from the 1.3B parameter InstructGPT model are preferred to outputs from the 175B GPT-3, despite having 100x fewer parameters. Moreover, InstructGPT models show improvements in truthfulness and reductions in toxic output generation while having minimal performance regressions on public NLP datasets. Even though InstructGPT still makes simple mistakes, our results show that fine-tuning with human feedback is a promising direction for aligning language models with human intent.

This paper investigates a training process that uses human feedback to improve instruction following. It starts from GPT-3 and gathers prompts written by labelers as well as prompts submitted through a language-model API.

The process has two stages. First, human demonstrations of desired responses provide supervised training examples. Second, rankings of model outputs guide further training through reinforcement learning from human feedback. The resulting models are called InstructGPT. summary.tldr: Human demonstrations and preference feedback make InstructGPT better at following user intent, with evaluators preferring a much smaller model on the tested prompts.

title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback

abstract: We study the multi-step off-policy learning approach to distributional RL. Despite the apparent similarity between value-based RL and distributional RL, our study reveals intriguing and fundamental differences between the two cases in the multi-step setting. We identify a novel notion of path-dependent distributional TD error, which is indispensable for principled multi-step distributional RL. The distinction from the value-based case bears important implications on concepts such as backward-view algorithms. Our work provides the first theoretical guarantees on multi-step off-policy distributional RL algorithms, including results that apply to the small number of existing approaches to multi-step distributional RL. In addition, we derive a novel algorithm, Quantile Regression-Retrace, which leads to a deep RL agent QR-DQN-Retrace that shows empirical improvements over QR-DQN on the Atari-57 benchmark. Collectively, we shed light on how unique challenges in multi-step distributional RL can be addressed both in theory and practice.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning models a distribution of returns, rather than only a value summarizing them. This paper studies learning from multiple steps of experience collected off-policy. Although this resembles multi-step value-based learning, the authors find fundamental differences in how the learning errors must be formulated.

The central contribution is a path-dependent distributional temporal-difference error. The paper identifies this dependence on the trajectory as indispensable for a principled multi-step treatment. It also has consequences for backward-view algorithms, changing how ideas from ordinary value-based learning carry over. The authors provide the first theoretical guarantees for multi-step off-policy distributional algorithms, including results applicable to some existing approaches.

They additionally derive Quantile Regression-Retrace and use it to construct the deep reinforcement-learning agent QR-DQN-Retrace. On Atari-57, this agent empirically improves over QR-DQN. The theory and experiment serve complementary purposes: the analysis clarifies what a valid multi-step distributional update requires, while the new agent demonstrates that addressing the distinction can improve performance in a substantial benchmark setting.
summary.tldr: Path-dependent distributional temporal-difference errors underpin new multi-step off-policy guarantees and a Retrace-based agent that improves on QR-DQN in Atari-57.

title: The Nature of Temporal Difference Errors in Multi-step Distributional Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of 3D object segmentation from raw point clouds. Unlike all existing methods which usually require a large amount of human annotations for full supervision, we propose the first unsupervised method, called OGC, to simultaneously identify multiple 3D objects in a single forward pass, without needing any type of human annotations. The key to our approach is to fully leverage the dynamic motion patterns over sequential point clouds as supervision signals to automatically discover rigid objects. Our method consists of three major components, 1) the object segmentation network to directly estimate multi-object masks from a single point cloud frame, 2) the auxiliary self-supervised scene flow estimator, and 3) our core object geometry consistency component. By carefully designing a series of loss functions, we effectively take into account the multi-object rigid consistency and the object shape invariance in both temporal and spatial scales. This allows our method to truly discover the object geometry even in the absence of annotations. We extensively evaluate our method on five datasets, demonstrating the superior performance for object part instance segmentation and general object segmentation in both indoor and the challenging outdoor scenarios.

paragraphs: OGC learns to separate multiple objects in three-dimensional point clouds without human annotations. Its source of supervision is the motion visible across successive point clouds. The central idea is that rigid motion and consistent object shape provide evidence about which points belong to the same object.

The system combines three components: an object segmentation network, an auxiliary self-supervised scene-flow estimator, and an object geometry consistency component. Scene flow supplies motion information, while the consistency component connects that information to object structure. The training losses account for multiple objects' rigid behavior and shape invariance across both space and time.

Although learning uses sequential motion patterns, the segmentation network predicts multiple object masks from a single point-cloud frame in one forward pass. This distinction explains how temporal evidence can train a model whose segmentation input is a single frame. Evaluations on five datasets report strong performance for object-part instance segmentation and general object segmentation, including indoor and challenging outdoor settings. The results support rigid dynamics as a useful source of annotation-free object supervision.
summary.tldr: OGC uses rigid motion and geometry consistency across point-cloud sequences to learn single-frame multi-object segmentation without human labels.

title: OGC: Unsupervised 3D Object Segmentation from Rigid Dynamics of Point Clouds

abstract: Advanced deep neural networks (DNNs), designed by either human or AutoML algorithms, are growing increasingly complex. Diverse operations are connected by complicated connectivity patterns, e.g., various types of skip connections. Those topological compositions are empirically effective and observed to smooth the loss landscape and facilitate the gradient flow in general. However, it remains elusive to derive any principled understanding of their effects on the DNN capacity or trainability, and to understand why or in which aspect one specific connectivity pattern is better than another. In this work, we theoretically characterize the impact of connectivity patterns on the convergence of DNNs under gradient descent training in fine granularity. By analyzing a wide network's Neural Network Gaussian Process (NNGP), we are able to depict how the spectrum of an NNGP kernel propagates through a particular connectivity pattern, and how that affects the bound of convergence rates. As one practical implication of our results, we show that by a simple filtration of "unpromising" connectivity patterns, we can trim down the number of models to evaluate, and significantly accelerate the large-scale neural architecture search without any overhead.

paragraphs: Deep networks differ in how their operations connect, including the placement and arrangement of skip connections. This paper develops a theoretical account of how connectivity influences convergence under gradient descent.

The analysis uses the Neural Network Gaussian Process associated with a wide network. It tracks how the spectrum of its kernel propagates through a particular connectivity pattern and how that propagation affects bounds on convergence rates. This makes the analysis sensitive to the arrangement of connections, providing a more detailed view of architecture than a broad description of network complexity.

The authors also use their results to guide neural architecture search. By filtering out connectivity patterns judged unpromising, they reduce the number of candidate models that must be evaluated. They report a significant acceleration of large-scale architecture search without additional overhead. The practical finding connects the wide-network analysis to a concrete way of reducing search effort.
summary.tldr: A wide-network kernel analysis links connectivity patterns to convergence bounds and supports filtering candidates to accelerate neural architecture search.

title: Deep Architecture Connectivity Matters for Its Convergence: A Fine-Grained Analysis

abstract: Epistemic uncertainty quantification is a crucial part of drawing credible conclusions from predictive models, whether concerned about the prediction at a given point or any downstream evaluation that uses the model as input. When the predictive model is simple and its evaluation differentiable, this task is solved by the delta method, where we propagate the asymptotically-normal uncertainty in the predictive model through the evaluation to compute standard errors and Wald confidence intervals. However, this becomes difficult when the model and/or evaluation becomes more complex. Remedies include the bootstrap, but it can be computationally infeasible when training the model even once is costly. In this paper, we propose an alternative, the implicit delta method, which works by infinitesimally regularizing the training loss of the predictive model to automatically assess downstream uncertainty. We show that the change in the evaluation due to regularization is consistent for the asymptotic variance of the evaluation estimator, even when the infinitesimal change is approximated by a finite difference. This provides both a reliable quantification of uncertainty in terms of standard errors as well as permits the construction of calibrated confidence intervals. We discuss connections to other approaches to uncertainty quantification, both Bayesian and frequentist, and demonstrate our approach empirically.

paragraphs: Uncertainty in a fitted predictive model also affects quantities computed from that model. The classical delta method propagates asymptotically normal model uncertainty through a differentiable evaluation, producing standard errors and confidence intervals. Applying it becomes difficult with complex models or evaluations, while bootstrap alternatives can be costly when training a model is already expensive.

The implicit delta method estimates downstream uncertainty by introducing an infinitesimal regularization into the training loss. It then examines how the downstream evaluation changes. This turns the response to a small training-objective perturbation into information about the variability of the evaluation estimator.

The authors prove that this change consistently estimates the evaluation's asymptotic variance, including when a finite difference approximates the infinitesimal perturbation. The result supports standard-error estimation and calibrated confidence intervals within the asymptotic framework. The paper also relates the method to Bayesian and frequentist uncertainty approaches and demonstrates it empirically, offering another route when direct uncertainty propagation is difficult.
summary.tldr: The implicit delta method estimates downstream uncertainty from the response to a small regularization of a model's training loss.

title: The Implicit Delta Method

abstract: In this work, we propose a multi-objective decision making framework that accommodates different user preferences over objectives, where preferences are learned via policy comparisons. Our model consists of a known Markov decision process with a vector-valued reward function, with each user having an unknown preference vector that expresses the relative importance of each objective. The goal is to efficiently compute a near-optimal policy for a given user. We consider two user feedback models. We first address the case where a user is provided with two policies and returns their preferred policy as feedback. We then move to a different user feedback model, where a user is instead provided with two small weighted sets of representative trajectories and selects the preferred one. In both cases, we suggest an algorithm that finds a nearly optimal policy for the user using a number of comparison queries that scales quasilinearly in the number of objectives.

The goal is to efficiently compute a near-optimal policy for a given user. We consider two user feedback models. We first address the case where a user is provided with two policies and returns their preferred policy as feedback. In both cases, we suggest an algorithm that finds a nearly optimal policy for the user using a number of comparison queries that scales quasilinearly in the number of objectives.

paragraphs: A decision-making system may need to balance several objectives, with different users valuing them differently. This paper studies how to learn those preferences through comparisons and then compute a nearly optimal policy for an individual user. It assumes a known Markov decision process with a vector-valued reward and an unknown user preference vector.

The authors consider two feedback formats. In the first, the user compares two policies and selects the preferred one. In the second, the user compares two small weighted sets of representative trajectories. The latter changes what the user is asked to inspect while retaining comparisons as the source of preference information.

For both formats, the paper gives an algorithm whose comparison-query requirement scales quasilinearly with the number of objectives. That is close to linear growth, with additional logarithmic factors. The result concerns efficiently obtaining a near-optimal personalized policy within the stated model. Its significance is that the preference-learning burden need not grow explosively as the number of objectives increases.
summary.tldr: Under a known decision-process model, comparison-based algorithms find nearly optimal personalized policies with query counts growing quasilinearly in the number of objectives.

title: Eliciting User Preferences for Personalized Multi-Objective Decision Making through Comparative Feedback

abstract: Graph neural networks are prominent models for representation learning over graphs, where the idea is to iteratively compute representations of nodes of an input graph through a series of transformations in such a way that the learned graph function is isomorphism-invariant on graphs, which makes the learned representations graph invariants. On the other hand, it is well-known that graph invariants learned by these class of models are incomplete: there are pairs of non-isomorphic graphs which cannot be distinguished by standard graph neural networks. This is unsurprising given the computational difficulty of graph isomorphism testing on general graphs, but the situation begs to differ for special graph classes, for which efficient graph isomorphism testing algorithms are known, such as planar graphs. The goal of this work is to design architectures for efficiently learning complete invariants of planar graphs. Inspired by the classical planar graph isomorphism algorithm of Hopcroft and Tarjan, we propose PlanE as a framework for planar representation learning. PlanE includes architectures which can learn complete invariants over planar graphs while remaining practically scalable. We empirically validate the strong performance of the resulting model architectures on well-known planar graph benchmarks, achieving multiple state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: Graph representations should remain unchanged when nodes are relabeled without changing the graph's structure. Standard graph neural networks provide this invariance, but their representations can fail to distinguish genuinely different graphs. The paper asks whether stronger guarantees are possible for planar graphs, a special class with efficient graph-isomorphism algorithms.

PlanE takes inspiration from the classical Hopcroft–Tarjan planar graph-isomorphism algorithm. Its goal is to learn complete invariants: representations that respect equivalent graph structures while distinguishing non-isomorphic planar graphs. Restricting attention to this graph class allows the architecture to draw on structural knowledge that is unavailable for arbitrary graphs.

The framework includes architectures capable of learning these complete invariants while remaining practically scalable. Evaluations on established planar-graph benchmarks produce multiple state-of-the-art results. The theoretical and empirical contributions address different aspects of representation quality: the ability to distinguish structures, and performance on benchmark tasks. The completeness claim concerns planar graphs and the capacity of the proposed architectures; it does not assert that standard graph learning has become complete for unrestricted graphs.
summary.tldr: PlanE uses planar graph-isomorphism ideas to build scalable architectures capable of learning complete planar-graph invariants.

title: PlanE: Representation Learning over Planar Graphs

abstract: Distribution shift (DS) may have two levels: the distribution itself changes, and the support (i.e., the set where the probability density is non-zero) also changes. When considering the support change between the training and test distributions, there can be four cases: (i) they exactly match; (ii) the training support is wider (and thus covers the test support); (iii) the test support is wider; (iv) they partially overlap. Existing methods are good at cases (i) and (ii), while cases (iii) and (iv) are more common nowadays but still under-explored. In this paper, we generalize importance weighting (IW), a golden solver for cases (i) and (ii), to a universal solver for all cases. Specifically, we first investigate why IW might fail in cases (iii) and (iv); based on the findings, we propose generalized IW (GIW) that could handle cases (iii) and (iv) and would reduce to IW in cases (i) and (ii). In GIW, the test support is split into an in-training (IT) part and an out-of-training (OOT) part, and the expected risk is decomposed into a weighted classification term over the IT part and a standard classification term over the OOT part, which guarantees the risk consistency of GIW. Then, the implementation of GIW consists of three components: (a) the split of validation data is carried out by the one-class support vector machine, (b) the first term of the empirical risk can be handled by any IW algorithm given training data and IT validation data, and (c) the second term just involves OOT validation data. Experiments demonstrate that GIW is a universal solver for DS problems, outperforming IW methods in cases (iii) and (iv).

paragraphs: Distribution shift can change both how frequently examples occur and which examples are possible at all. The latter concerns distribution support. Ordinary importance weighting handles matching supports or a training support that covers the test support, but it can fail when test examples occupy regions absent from training.

Generalized importance weighting addresses this by dividing the test support into regions inside and outside the training support. It decomposes expected risk into a weighted classification term for the shared region and a standard classification term for the outside region. The authors establish risk consistency through this decomposition, and the formulation reduces to ordinary importance weighting when training support covers testing.

The implementation uses a one-class support vector machine to split validation data. An existing importance-weighting algorithm handles the inside portion using training and validation examples, while the outside portion contributes its own classification term. Experiments report improvements over importance-weighting methods when test support extends beyond training support or overlaps only partially, supporting the framework across the four support relationships considered.
summary.tldr: Generalized importance weighting separates shared and unseen support regions to address distribution shifts that ordinary importance weighting cannot fully cover.

title: Generalizing Importance Weighting to A Universal Solver for Distribution Shift Problems

abstract: Recently, diffusion models have achieved great success in generative tasks. Sampling from diffusion models is equivalent to solving the reverse diffusion stochastic differential equations (SDEs) or the corresponding probability flow ordinary differential equations (ODEs). In comparison, SDE-based solvers can generate samples of higher quality and are suited for image translation tasks like stroke-based synthesis. During inference, however, existing SDE-based solvers are severely constrained by the efficiency-effectiveness dilemma. Our investigation suggests that this is because the Gaussian assumption in the reverse transition kernel is frequently violated (even in the case of simple mixture data) given a limited number of discretization steps. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel class of SDE-based solvers called \emph{Gaussian Mixture Solvers (GMS)} for diffusion models. Our solver estimates the first three-order moments and optimizes the parameters of a Gaussian mixture transition kernel using generalized methods of moments in each step during sampling. Empirically, our solver outperforms numerous SDE-based solvers in terms of sample quality in image generation and stroke-based synthesis in various diffusion models, which validates the motivation and effectiveness of GMS. Our code is available at https://github.com/Guohanzhong/GMS.

paragraphs: Generating samples with a diffusion model involves solving a reverse stochastic differential equation or a corresponding ordinary differential equation. Stochastic solvers can produce higher-quality samples and suit image translation, but face a trade-off between speed and effectiveness. This paper investigates a potential cause: with few discretization steps, the distribution describing a reverse transition may not be well represented by a single Gaussian.

The proposed Gaussian Mixture Solvers replace that single-Gaussian transition assumption with a mixture of Gaussians. At each sampling step, the solver estimates moments through third order and fits the mixture’s parameters using a generalized method of moments. This provides a richer transition model while retaining the stochastic sampling formulation used by SDE-based solvers.

Experiments evaluate image generation and stroke-guided synthesis across several diffusion models. The proposed solver produces better sample quality than numerous other SDE-based solvers in those evaluations. These results support the authors’ explanation that transition-distribution mismatch contributes to the efficiency–quality problem. They also show the value of improving the sampling procedure through a more expressive transition approximation.
summary.tldr: Gaussian Mixture Solvers improve diffusion sample quality by fitting richer reverse-transition distributions at each stochastic sampling step.

title: Gaussian Mixture Solvers for Diffusion Models

abstract: Semantic image synthesis (SIS) aims to generate realistic images according to semantic masks given by a user. Although recent methods produce high quality results with fine spatial control, SIS requires expensive pixel-level annotation of the training images. On the other hand, manipulating intermediate feature maps in a pretrained unconditional generator such as StyleGAN supports coarse spatial control without heavy annotation. In this paper, we introduce a new approach, for reflecting user's detailed guiding masks on a pretrained unconditional generator. Our method converts a user's guiding mask to a proxy mask through a semantic mapper. Then the proxy mask conditions the resulting image through a rearranging network based on cross-attention mechanism. The proxy mask is simple clustering of intermediate feature maps in the generator. The semantic mapper and the rearranging network are easy to train (less than half an hour). Our method is useful for many tasks: semantic image synthesis, spatially editing real images, and unaligned local transplantation. Last but not least, it is generally applicable to various datasets such as human faces, animal faces, and churches.

paragraphs: Semantic image synthesis turns a user’s region labels into a realistic image with the requested spatial arrangement. Conventional approaches require expensive pixel-level training annotations. Pretrained unconditional generators already contain useful visual structure, but directly manipulating their intermediate features typically offers only coarse control. This paper develops a way to apply detailed user masks to such generators.

A semantic mapper translates the user’s guiding mask into a proxy mask based on clusters of the generator’s intermediate feature maps. A rearranging network then uses cross-attention to condition image generation on that proxy. The proxy provides an interface between the user’s semantic instructions and the internal features available in the pretrained generator.

The authors report that the semantic mapper and rearranging network can be trained in less than half an hour. Applications include mask-guided synthesis, spatial editing of real images, and local transplantation between unaligned images. Results span human faces, animal faces, and churches, demonstrating applicability across several kinds of imagery while reusing an unconditional generator.
summary.tldr: A semantic mapper and cross-attention rearranging network give pretrained unconditional generators detailed mask-based spatial control.

title: Semantic Image Synthesis with Unconditional Generator

abstract: The recent advances in natural language processing (NLP), have led to a new trend of applying large language models (LLMs) to real-world scenarios. While the latest LLMs are astonishingly fluent when interacting with humans, they suffer from the misinformation problem by unintentionally generating factually false statements. This can lead to harmful consequences, especially when produced within sensitive contexts, such as healthcare. Yet few previous works have focused on evaluating misinformation in the long-form (LF) generation of LLMs, especially for knowledge-intensive topics. Moreover, although LLMs have been shown to perform well in different languages, misinformation evaluation has been mostly conducted in English. To this end, we present a benchmark, CARE-MI, for evaluating LLM misinformation in: 1) a sensitive topic, specifically the maternity and infant care domain; and 2) a language other than English, namely Chinese. Most importantly, we provide an innovative paradigm for building LF generation evaluation benchmarks that can be transferred to other knowledge-intensive domains and low-resourced languages. Our proposed benchmark fills the gap between the extensive usage of LLMs and the lack of datasets for assessing the misinformation generated by these models. It contains 1,612 expert-checked questions, accompanied with human-selected references. Using our benchmark, we conduct extensive experiments and found that current Chinese LLMs are far from perfect in the topic of maternity and infant care. In an effort to minimize the reliance on human resources for performance evaluation, we offer off-the-shelf judgment models for automatically assessing the LF output of LLMs given benchmark questions. Moreover, we compare potential solutions for LF generation evaluation and provide insights for building better automated metrics.

The paper targets two gaps in evaluating these errors: limited attention to long-form, knowledge-intensive answers and a strong emphasis on English. CARE-MI creates a Chinese-language benchmark focused specifically on this sensitive healthcare domain.

The authors also present a benchmark-construction approach intended to transfer to other domains requiring substantial factual knowledge and to languages with fewer evaluation resources.

To reduce the human effort involved in assessment, the authors supply ready-to-use judgment models for evaluating generated answers. They also compare evaluation approaches, making the contribution both a domain-specific test resource and an investigation into how automated assessment of long-form answers can improve.
summary.tldr: CARE-MI evaluates misinformation in Chinese maternity and infant-care answers using expert-checked questions and automated judgment models.

title: CARE-MI: Chinese Benchmark for Misinformation Evaluation in Maternity and Infant Care

abstract: Real-time video matting on edge devices faces significant computational resource constraints, limiting the widespread use of video matting in applications such as online conferences and short-form video production. Binarization is a powerful compression approach that greatly reduces computation and memory consumption by using 1-bit parameters and bitwise operations. However, binarization of the video matting model is not a straightforward process, and our empirical analysis has revealed two primary bottlenecks: severe representation degradation of the encoder and massive redundant computations of the decoder. To address these issues, we propose BiMatting, an accurate and efficient video matting model using binarization. Specifically, we construct shrinkable and dense topologies of the binarized encoder block to enhance the extracted representation. We sparsify the binarized units to reduce the low-information decoding computation. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that BiMatting outperforms other binarized video matting models, including state-of-the-art (SOTA) binarization methods, by a significant margin. Our approach even performs comparably to the full-precision counterpart in visual quality. Furthermore, BiMatting achieves remarkable savings of 12.4$\times$ and 21.6$\times$ in computation and storage, respectively, showcasing its potential and advantages in real-world resource-constrained scenarios. Our code and models are released at https://github.com/htqin/BiMatting .

paragraphs: BiMatting addresses the computational demands of video matting on devices with limited resources. Binarization reduces memory and computation through one-bit parameters and bitwise operations, but applying it directly to a matting model can damage quality. The authors identify two empirical problems: the encoder loses substantial representational ability, and the decoder performs many redundant computations.

The method changes both parts of the model to address these distinct bottlenecks. Its binarized encoder blocks use shrinkable and densely connected topologies to improve the representations they extract. In the decoder, sparsifying binarized units reduces computation that contributes little information. The design therefore combines representation improvements with selective reductions in decoding work.

Experiments show substantial gains over other binarized video matting models, including leading binarization methods. The authors also report visual quality comparable to the full-precision counterpart, alongside computation and storage savings of 12.4 times and 21.6 times, respectively. These results indicate that architecture changes can help preserve useful visual quality while realizing the resource benefits of binarization.
summary.tldr: BiMatting redesigns a binarized video matting encoder and decoder to retain visual quality while sharply reducing computation and storage.

title: BiMatting: Efficient Video Matting via Binarization

abstract: Adaptivity to the difficulties of a problem is a key property in sequential decision-making problems to broaden the applicability of algorithms. Follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL) has recently emerged as one of the most promising approaches for obtaining various types of adaptivity in bandit problems. Aiming to further generalize this adaptivity, we develop a generic adaptive learning rate, called stability-penalty-adaptive (SPA) learning rate for FTRL. This learning rate yields a regret bound jointly depending on stability and penalty of the algorithm, into which the regret of FTRL is typically decomposed. With this result, we establish several algorithms with three types of adaptivity: sparsity, game-dependency, and best-of-both-worlds (BOBW). Despite the fact that sparsity appears frequently in real problems, existing sparse multi-armed bandit algorithms with $k$-arms assume that the sparsity level $s \leq k$ is known in advance, which is often not the case in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, we first establish $s$-agnostic algorithms with regret bounds of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{sT})$ in the adversarial regime for $T$ rounds, which matches the existing lower bound up to a logarithmic factor. Meanwhile, BOBW algorithms aim to achieve a near-optimal regret in both the stochastic and adversarial regimes. Leveraging the SPA learning rate and the technique for $s$-agnostic algorithms combined with a new analysis to bound the variation in FTRL output in response to changes in a regularizer, we establish the first BOBW algorithm with a sparsity-dependent bound. Additionally, we explore partial monitoring and demonstrate that the proposed SPA learning rate framework allows us to achieve a game-dependent bound and the BOBW simultaneously.

title: Stability-penalty-adaptive follow-the-regularized-leader: Sparsity, game-dependency, and best-of-both-worlds

abstract: Hyperparameter optimization is an important subfield of machine learning that focuses on tuning the hyperparameters of a chosen algorithm to achieve peak performance. Recently, there has been a stream of methods that tackle the issue of hyperparameter optimization, however, most of the methods do not exploit the dominant power law nature of learning curves for Bayesian optimization. In this work, we propose Deep Power Laws (DPL), an ensemble of neural network models conditioned to yield predictions that follow a power-law scaling pattern. Our method dynamically decides which configurations to pause and train incrementally by making use of gray-box evaluations. We compare our method against 7 state-of-the-art competitors on 3 benchmarks related to tabular, image, and NLP datasets covering 59 diverse tasks. Our method achieves the best results across all benchmarks by obtaining the best any-time results compared to all competitors.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization must decide which training configurations deserve more computation. Learning curves offer information before training finishes, and this paper exploits their dominant power-law behavior to guide that decision. Deep Power Laws, or DPL, uses predicted learning trajectories to allocate effort among candidate configurations during the search.

DPL is an ensemble of neural networks constrained to produce predictions that follow a power-law scaling pattern. Using gray-box evaluations, which expose information from ongoing training, it dynamically chooses which configurations to pause and which to train further in increments. This connects a structured prediction of future performance with concrete decisions about how to spend the optimization budget.

The authors compare DPL with seven state-of-the-art competitors on three benchmarks covering tabular, image, and language data across 59 tasks. They report the best anytime results across all benchmarks relative to those competitors. This means the evaluation considers the quality of the solution available as optimization proceeds, supporting the usefulness of learning-curve structure for managing training effort throughout a search.
summary.tldr: Deep Power Laws predicts power-law learning curves to allocate hyperparameter search effort, achieving the best reported anytime results across three benchmarks.

title: Scaling Laws for Hyperparameter Optimization

abstract: Transferable graph learning involves knowledge transferability from a source graph to a relevant target graph. The major challenge of transferable graph learning is the distribution shift between source and target graphs induced by individual node attributes and complex graph structures. To solve this problem, in this paper, we propose a generic graph-structured Gaussian process framework (GraphGP) for adaptively transferring knowledge across graphs with either homophily or heterophily assumptions. Specifically, GraphGP is derived from a novel graph structure-aware neural network in the limit on the layer width. The generalization analysis of GraphGP explicitly investigates the connection between knowledge transferability and graph domain similarity. Extensive experiments on several transferable graph learning benchmarks demonstrate the efficacy of GraphGP over state-of-the-art Gaussian process baselines.

paragraphs: Transferring knowledge between graphs is difficult because both node attributes and graph structure can change. A model learned on a source graph therefore faces a distribution shift when applied to a related target graph. This paper introduces GraphGP, a graph-structured Gaussian process framework designed to adaptively transfer knowledge across such graph domains.

The framework accommodates either homophily or heterophily assumptions, allowing it to address graphs with different patterns of connection between nodes. GraphGP is derived from a new neural network that accounts for graph structure, by taking a limit in which its layers become infinitely wide. This construction connects the proposed graph neural architecture to a Gaussian process formulation for transfer learning.

The authors’ generalization analysis explicitly examines how transferability relates to similarity between graph domains. Their experiments on several transferable graph learning benchmarks show that GraphGP is effective relative to state-of-the-art Gaussian process baselines. Together, the analysis and experiments tie the transfer problem to both node information and structural relationships, providing a framework for studying when related graphs support useful knowledge transfer.
summary.tldr: GraphGP derives a graph-aware Gaussian process for knowledge transfer and analyzes how transferability relates to similarity between graph domains.

title: Graph-Structured Gaussian Processes for Transferable Graph Learning

abstract: Procedural Content Generation (PCG) is a technique to generate complex and diverse environments in an automated way. However, while generating content with PCG methods is often straightforward, generating meaningful content that reflects specific intentions and constraints remains challenging. Furthermore, many PCG algorithms lack the ability to generate content in an open-ended manner. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown to be incredibly effective in many diverse domains. These trained LLMs can be fine-tuned, re-using information and accelerating training for new tasks. Here, we introduce MarioGPT, a fine-tuned GPT2 model trained to generate tile-based game levels, in our case Super Mario Bros levels. MarioGPT can not only generate diverse levels, but can be text-prompted for controllable level generation, addressing one of the key challenges of current PCG techniques. As far as we know, MarioGPT is the first text-to-level model and combined with novelty search it enables the generation of diverse levels with varying play-style dynamics (i.e. player paths) and the open-ended discovery of an increasingly diverse range of content. Code available at https://github.com/shyamsn97/mario-gpt.

paragraphs: Procedural content generation can automatically produce game environments, but producing content that reflects a particular intention remains challenging. MarioGPT explores whether a language model can make generation more controllable through text. It uses a fine-tuned GPT2 model to create tile-based Super Mario Bros levels, applying an existing language model to a new kind of structured output.

Text prompts guide the kinds of levels the model generates. This addresses the gap between obtaining varied content and obtaining content shaped by a user’s request. The paper presents MarioGPT as, to the authors’ knowledge, the first text-to-level model, with diversity and prompt-based control as central capabilities.

The authors also combine MarioGPT with novelty search to support open-ended exploration. The resulting levels vary in their player paths, linking diversity to play-style dynamics as well as generated layouts. The contribution brings together language-based steering and a search process for discovering increasingly varied content, offering a way to keep exploration going while retaining a means of expressing generation intentions.
summary.tldr: MarioGPT generates Mario levels from text prompts and combines with novelty search to discover increasingly diverse layouts and player paths.

title: MarioGPT: Open-Ended Text2Level Generation through Large Language Models

abstract: We introduce a transformation framework that can be utilized to develop online algorithms with low $\epsilon$-approximate regret in the random-order model from offline approximation algorithms. We first give a general reduction theorem that transforms an offline approximation algorithm with low average sensitivity to an online algorithm with low $\epsilon$-approximate regret. We then demonstrate that offline approximation algorithms can be transformed into a low-sensitivity version using a coreset construction method. To showcase the versatility of our approach, we apply it to various problems, including online $(k,z)$-clustering, online matrix approximation, and online regression, and successfully achieve polylogarithmic $\epsilon$-approximate regret for each problem. Moreover, we show that in all three cases, our algorithm also enjoys low inconsistency, which may be desired in some online applications.

paragraphs: Offline algorithms work with a dataset as a whole, while online algorithms must make decisions as observations arrive. This paper develops a way to reuse offline approximation algorithms in online settings where the observations arrive in random order. The goal is low approximate regret: keeping cumulative performance close to an approximation-adjusted benchmark.

The central reduction requires the offline algorithm to have low average sensitivity, meaning that changes to its input do not substantially disrupt its output on average. The authors then show how a coreset construction can produce this stability. A coreset provides a compact representation of the data, connecting an offline approximation method to the requirements of the online reduction.

The framework yields polylogarithmic approximate regret for online clustering, matrix approximation, and regression. In each application, it also provides low inconsistency, limiting changes to the algorithm's decisions. These results establish a reusable route from offline approximation to stable online performance, with the random-order assumption forming an explicit part of the setting.
summary.tldr: A general reduction turns sufficiently stable offline approximation algorithms into online algorithms with low approximate regret under random arrival order.

title: A Batch-to-Online Transformation under Random-Order Model

abstract: Neural radiance field (NeRF) shows powerful performance in novel view synthesis and 3D geometry reconstruction, but it suffers from critical performance degradation when the number of known viewpoints is drastically reduced. Existing works attempt to overcome this problem by employing external priors, but their success is limited to certain types of scenes or datasets. Employing monocular depth estimation (MDE) networks, pretrained on large-scale RGB-D datasets, with powerful generalization capability may be a key to solving this problem: however, using MDE in conjunction with NeRF comes with a new set of challenges due to various ambiguity problems exhibited by monocular depths. In this light, we propose a novel framework, dubbed DäRF, that achieves robust NeRF reconstruction with a handful of real-world images by combining the strengths of NeRF and monocular depth estimation through online complementary training. Our framework imposes the MDE network's powerful geometry prior to NeRF representation at both seen and unseen viewpoints to enhance its robustness and coherence. In addition, we overcome the ambiguity problems of monocular depths through patch-wise scale-shift fitting and geometry distillation, which adapts the MDE network to produce depths aligned accurately with NeRF geometry. Experiments show our framework achieves state-of-the-art results both quantitatively and qualitatively, demonstrating consistent and reliable performance in both indoor and outdoor real-world datasets.

paragraphs: A neural radiance field can reconstruct a scene and generate new views, but its performance can deteriorate sharply when only a few camera views are available. DäRF addresses this shortage by combining a radiance field with a pretrained monocular depth estimation network, which supplies geometric information inferred from individual images.

Simply adding these depth predictions creates difficulties because monocular depth contains ambiguities. DäRF uses complementary training: the depth network guides the radiance field at both observed and unobserved viewpoints, while the radiance field helps adapt the depth network. Patch-wise scale and shift fitting and geometry distillation align the predicted depths with the geometry being reconstructed.

This exchange aims to make the two sources of geometric information more consistent instead of treating pretrained depth as a fixed answer. The authors report state-of-the-art quantitative and qualitative results on indoor and outdoor real-world datasets. Their findings support the usefulness of adapting the depth prior during reconstruction when only a handful of images is available.
summary.tldr: DäRF jointly adapts monocular depth estimation and radiance fields to improve scene reconstruction from a handful of images.

title: DäRF: Boosting Radiance Fields from Sparse Input Views with Monocular Depth Adaptation

abstract: This paper focuses on the high-dimensional sampling of log-concave distributions with composite structures: $p^*(\mathrm{d}x)\propto \exp(-g(x)-f(x))\mathrm{d}x$. We develop a double randomization technique, which leads to a fast underdamped Langevin algorithm with a dimension-independent convergence guarantee. We prove that the algorithm enjoys an overall $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{\left(\mathrm{tr}(H)\right)^{1/3}}{\epsilon^{2/3}}\right)$ iteration complexity to reach an $\epsilon$-tolerated sample whose distribution $p$ admits $W_2(p,p^*)\leq \epsilon$. Here, $H$ is an upper bound of the Hessian matrices for $f$ and does not explicitly depend on dimension $d$. For the posterior sampling over linear models with normalized data, we show a clear superiority of convergence rate which is dimension-free and outperforms the previous best-known results by a $d^{1/3}$ factor. The analysis to achieve a faster convergence rate brings new insights into high-dimensional sampling.

paragraphs: The paper studies sampling from high-dimensional log-concave distributions whose density has the composite form exp(−g(x)−f(x)), up to normalization. The aim is to produce samples whose distribution is close to the desired target. Its contribution is a double-randomization technique incorporated into an underdamped Langevin sampling algorithm.

The authors prove an iteration bound of approximately (tr(H))^(1/3)/ε^(2/3), suppressing logarithmic factors. Here H bounds the Hessian matrices of f, so the guarantee is expressed through a curvature quantity rather than an explicit dimension term. Accuracy is measured using the Wasserstein-2 distance: the output distribution must lie within ε of the target distribution.

For posterior sampling in linear models with normalized data, the authors establish a dimension-free convergence rate that improves on previous best-known results by a factor of d^(1/3). This application makes the benefit concrete under its stated data normalization condition. The broader result shows how double randomization can yield sharper sampling guarantees for the composite log-concave setting, with the bound retaining its explicit dependence on curvature and requested accuracy.
summary.tldr: Double randomization yields an underdamped Langevin sampler with curvature-based convergence guarantees and dimension-free rates for normalized linear-model posteriors.

title: Double Randomized Underdamped Langevin with Dimension-Independent Convergence Guarantee

abstract: Differentiable NAS (DARTS) is a simple and efficient neural architecture search method that has been extensively adopted in various machine learning tasks.% Nevertheless, DARTS still encounters several robustness issues, mainly the domination of skip connections.% The resulting architectures are full of parametric-free operations, leading to performance collapse.% Existing methods suggest that the skip connection has additional advantages in optimization compared to other parametric operations and propose to alleviate the domination of skip connections by eliminating these additional advantages.% In this paper, we analyze this issue from a simple and straightforward perspective and propose that the domination of skip connections results from parametric operations overfitting the training data while architecture parameters are trained on the validation data, leading to undesired behaviors.% Based on this observation, we propose the operation-level early stopping (OLES) method to overcome this issue and robustify DARTS without introducing any computation overhead.% Extensive experimental results can verify our hypothesis and the effectiveness of OLES.
