paragraphs: Differentiable architecture search, particularly DARTS, can produce networks dominated by skip connections. Because these operations have no learned parameters, excessive selection of them can lead to architectures with collapsed performance. The paper investigates why the search process develops this preference and proposes a way to make it more robust.

The authors attribute the problem to a mismatch between two parts of training. Parameterized operations can overfit the training data, while the parameters governing architecture selection are learned from validation data. Under this explanation, overfitting changes how the candidate operations appear to the architecture-selection process, encouraging undesirable dominance by skip connections.

Their response is operation-level early stopping, or OLES, which targets the proposed overfitting mechanism within the search. The method is presented as adding no computational overhead. Extensive experiments support both the authors’ hypothesis and the effectiveness of OLES. The contribution connects a specific failure mode in architecture selection to the training behavior of individual operations, providing a focused intervention within DARTS.
summary.tldr: OLES uses operation-level early stopping to address overfitting that the authors link to skip-connection dominance in DARTS.

title: Operation-Level Early Stopping for Robustifying Differentiable NAS

abstract: The Finite Element Method, an important technique in engineering, is aided by Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR), which dynamically refines mesh regions to allow for a favorable trade-off between computational speed and simulation accuracy. Classical methods for AMR depend on task-specific heuristics or expensive error estimators, hindering their use for complex simulations. Recent learned AMR methods tackle these problems, but so far scale only to simple toy examples. We formulate AMR as a novel Adaptive Swarm Markov Decision Process in which a mesh is modeled as a system of simple collaborating agents that may split into multiple new agents. This framework allows for a spatial reward formulation that simplifies the credit assignment problem, which we combine with Message Passing Networks to propagate information between neighboring mesh elements. We experimentally validate the effectiveness of our approach, Adaptive Swarm Mesh Refinement (ASMR), showing that it learns reliable, scalable, and efficient refinement strategies on a set of challenging problems. Our approach significantly speeds up computation, achieving up to 30-fold improvement compared to uniform refinements in complex simulations. Additionally, we outperform learned baselines and achieve a refinement quality that is on par with a traditional error-based AMR strategy without expensive oracle information about the error signal.

paragraphs: Finite-element simulations use meshes whose resolution affects both accuracy and computational cost. Adaptive mesh refinement concentrates detail where it is useful, but traditional approaches rely on task-specific rules or expensive error estimates. This paper develops a learned refinement method intended to handle challenging simulations beyond the simple examples supported by earlier learned approaches.

The method treats mesh elements as collaborating agents that can split into new agents as refinement proceeds. This adaptive swarm formulation supports spatial rewards, making it easier to identify which local decisions deserve credit. Message-passing networks let neighboring elements exchange information, connecting local refinement choices to the surrounding mesh.

Experiments show reliable, scalable, and efficient strategies across the tested problems. The method achieves up to a thirtyfold computational speedup compared with uniform refinement in complex simulations. It also outperforms learned baselines and matches the refinement quality of a traditional error-based strategy without expensive oracle error information. These results support learning where to spend simulation computation through coordinated local decisions.
summary.tldr: ASMR learns coordinated local mesh refinement, achieving up to thirtyfold speedups over uniform refinement in the evaluated complex simulations.

title: Swarm Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Mesh Refinement

abstract: We study offline model-based optimization to maximize a black-box objective function with a static dataset of designs and scores. These designs encompass a variety of domains, including materials, robots, DNA sequences, and proteins. A common approach trains a proxy on the static dataset and performs gradient ascent to obtain new designs. However, this often results in poor designs due to the proxy inaccuracies for out-of-distribution designs. Recent studies indicate that (a) gradient ascent with a mean ensemble of proxies generally outperforms simple gradient ascent, and (b) a trained proxy provides weak ranking supervision signals for design selection. Motivated by (a) and (b), we propose $\textit{parallel-mentoring}$ as an effective and novel method that facilitates mentoring among proxies, creating a more robust ensemble to mitigate the out-of-distribution issue. We focus on the three-proxy case in the main paper and our method consists of two modules. The first module, $\textit{voting-based pairwise supervision}$, operates on three parallel proxies and captures their ranking supervision signals as pairwise comparison labels. These labels are combined through majority voting to generate consensus labels, which incorporates ranking supervision signals from all proxies and enables mutual mentoring. Yet, label noise arises due to possible incorrect consensus. To alleviate this, we introduce an $\textit{adaptive soft-labeling}$ module with soft-labels initialized as consensus labels. Based on bi-level optimization, this module fine-tunes proxies in the inner level and learns more accurate labels in the outer level to adaptively mentor proxies, resulting in a more robust ensemble. Experiments validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available here.

A learned proxy can guide gradient ascent toward new candidates, but predictions may become inaccurate outside the training distribution. Optimizing those predictions can consequently produce poor designs.

Parallel mentoring strengthens an ensemble by letting its proxies supervise one another. In the main three-proxy setting, each proxy supplies pairwise rankings of designs. Majority voting combines these judgments into consensus comparison labels. This uses the ranking information from all three models to support mutual mentoring.

Consensus can still be wrong, so the method adds adaptive soft labeling. Starting from the consensus labels, a bi-level procedure fine-tunes the proxies in its inner optimization and improves the labels in its outer optimization. This aims to reduce the effect of noisy supervision and produce a more robust ensemble. Experiments support the method's effectiveness. Its main contribution is a mechanism for improving collective proxy guidance despite the distribution shift encountered when searching for new designs.
summary.tldr: Parallel mentoring combines proxy ranking votes with adaptive soft labels to improve offline design optimization.

title: Parallel-mentoring for Offline Model-based Optimization

abstract: We propose adaptive weight decay, which automatically tunes the hyper-parameter for weight decay during each training iteration. For classification problems, we propose changing the value of the weight decay hyper-parameter on the fly based on the strength of updates from the classification loss (i.e., gradient of cross-entropy), and the regularization loss (i.e., $\ell_2$-norm of the weights). We show that this simple modification can result in large improvements in adversarial robustness — an area which suffers from robust overfitting — without requiring extra data accros various datasets and architecture choices. For example, our reformulation results in 20\% relative robustness improvement for CIFAR-100, and 10\% relative robustness improvement on CIFAR-10 comparing to the best tuned hyper-parameters of traditional weight decay resulting in models that have comparable performance to SOTA robustness methods. In addition, this method has other desirable properties, such as less sensitivity to learning rate, and smaller weight norms, which the latter contributes to robustness to overfitting to label noise, and pruning.

paragraphs: The paper proposes adapting weight decay during training instead of keeping its strength fixed. Weight decay discourages large model weights. Its strength determines how much this pressure influences training alongside the objective of correctly classifying examples. The proposed method automatically adjusts that strength at every training iteration.

For classification, the adjustment depends on the strength of updates associated with two objectives: cross-entropy, which measures classification error, and regularization based on the weights’ ℓ2 norm. This makes the regularization strength responsive to the updates occurring during training, rather than relying on a single setting chosen beforehand.

The authors report that this change can substantially improve adversarial robustness, in a setting where robust overfitting is a concern. Across multiple datasets and architectures, the improvements require no extra data. Compared with traditional weight decay using its best-tuned hyperparameters, they report relative robustness gains of 20% on CIFAR-100 and 10% on CIFAR-10. These are relative improvements, not percentage-point increases. The resulting models have robustness comparable to state-of-the-art methods.

The abstract also reports lower sensitivity to the learning rate and smaller weight norms. The authors connect those smaller norms with resistance to overfitting noisy labels and with robustness to pruning. Together, these findings suggest that adjusting regularization during training can benefit several aspects of model robustness.
summary.tldr: Adaptive weight decay adjusts regularization at every training step and can improve adversarial robustness without extra data.

title: Improving Robustness with Adaptive Weight Decay

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that can bypass their safety guardrails. In many domains, adversarial training has proven to be one of the most promising methods to reliably improve robustness against such attacks. Yet, in the context of LLMs, current methods for adversarial training are hindered by the high computational costs required to perform discrete adversarial attacks at each training iteration. We address this problem by instead calculating adversarial attacks in the continuous embedding space of the LLM, which is orders of magnitudes more efficient. We propose a fast adversarial training algorithm (C-AdvUL) composed of two losses: the first makes the model robust on continuous embedding attacks computed on an adversarial behaviour dataset; the second ensures the usefulness of the final model by fine-tuning on utility data. Moreover, we introduce C-AdvIPO, an adversarial variant of IPO that does not require utility data for adversarially robust alignment. Our empirical evaluation on five models from different families (Gemma, Phi3, Mistral, Zephyr, Llama2) and at different scales (2B, 3.8B, 7B) shows that both algorithms substantially enhance LLM robustness against discrete attacks (GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR), while maintaining utility. Our results demonstrate that robustness to continuous perturbations can extrapolate to discrete threat models. Thereby, we present a path toward scalable adversarial training algorithms for robustly aligning LLMs.

This paper instead computes attacks in the model’s continuous embedding space. The authors report that generating these perturbations is orders of magnitude more efficient, making repeated adversarial training steps more practical.

The paper introduces two algorithms. C-AdvUL combines a loss for resisting continuous attacks on an adversarial behavior dataset with a separate fine-tuning loss on utility data. The second component preserves useful behavior alongside robustness. C-AdvIPO provides an adversarial variant of IPO that does not require utility data, offering another route to robust alignment.

Evaluations cover five models from several families and scales, testing robustness against the discrete attacks GCG, AutoDAN, and PAIR. Both algorithms substantially improve resistance while maintaining utility in those experiments. The central finding is empirical transfer: training against continuous perturbations can improve robustness to discrete attacks. It supports a more scalable training approach without establishing protection against every possible textual attack.
summary.tldr: Training against efficient continuous embedding attacks improves resistance to tested discrete language-model attacks while maintaining utility.

title: Efficient Adversarial Training in LLMs with Continuous Attacks

abstract: The goal of data attribution for text-to-image models is to identify the training images that most influence the generation of a new image. Influence is defined such that, for a given output, if a model is retrained from scratch without the most influential images, the model would fail to reproduce the same output. Unfortunately, directly searching for these influential images is computationally infeasible, since it would require repeatedly retraining models from scratch. In our work, we propose an efficient data attribution method by simulating unlearning the synthesized image. We achieve this by increasing the training loss on the output image, without catastrophic forgetting of other, unrelated concepts. We then identify training images with significant loss deviations after the unlearning process and label these as influential. We evaluate our method with a computationally intensive but "gold-standard" retraining from scratch and demonstrate our method's advantages over previous methods.

paragraphs: This paper asks which training images most influenced a particular image produced by a text-to-image model. It defines influence through a demanding test: removing influential images and retraining from scratch would prevent the model from reproducing that output. Searching directly with repeated retraining is computationally impractical, so the authors seek an efficient way to approximate this investigation.

Their method starts from the generated image and simulates unlearning it. They increase the model’s training loss on that image while avoiding catastrophic forgetting of unrelated concepts. They then examine how the losses of training images change after this intervention. Images whose losses shift substantially are identified as influential, using the model’s response to targeted forgetting as an attribution signal.

The authors evaluate this method against retraining from scratch, which they treat as the expensive reference standard for attribution. They report advantages over previous methods. The contribution is an efficiently obtainable influence signal evaluated against the removal-and-retraining definition, connecting a practical attribution procedure to the behavior it is intended to explain.
summary.tldr: Targeted unlearning of a generated image helps identify influential training images without repeatedly retraining the entire model.

title: Data Attribution for Text-to-Image Models by Unlearning Synthesized Images

abstract: We study the fundamental problem of sequential probability assignment, also known as online learning with logarithmic loss, with respect to an arbitrary, possibly nonparametric hypothesis class. Our goal is to obtain a complexity measure for the hypothesis class that characterizes the minimax regret and to determine a general, minimax optimal algorithm. Notably, the sequential $\ell_{\infty}$ entropy, extensively studied in the literature (Rakhlin and Sridharan, 2015, Bilodeau et al., 2020, Wu et al., 2023), was shown to not characterize minimax regret in general. Inspired by the seminal work of Shtarkov (1987) and Rakhlin, Sridharan, and Tewari (2010), we introduce a novel complexity measure, the \emph{contextual Shtarkov sum}, corresponding to the Shtarkov sum after projection onto a multiary context tree, and show that the worst case log contextual Shtarkov sum equals the minimax regret. Using the contextual Shtarkov sum, we derive the minimax optimal strategy, dubbed \emph{contextual Normalized Maximum Likelihood} (cNML). Our results hold for sequential experts, beyond binary labels, which are settings rarely considered in prior work. To illustrate the utility of this characterization, we provide a short proof of a new regret upper bound in terms of sequential $\ell_{\infty}$ entropy, unifying and sharpening state-of-the-art bounds by Bilodeau et al. (2020) and Wu et al. (2023).

paragraphs: Sequential probability assignment predicts outcomes over time and evaluates those predictions with logarithmic loss. The paper asks what determines the smallest achievable worst-case regret relative to a hypothesis class, including classes without a finite-dimensional parameterization. A previously studied complexity measure, sequential infinity-norm entropy, does not fully characterize this regret in general.

The authors introduce the contextual Shtarkov sum, formed by projecting a Shtarkov-style construction onto a branching context tree. They prove that its worst-case logarithm equals minimax regret. This supplies an exact characterization of prediction difficulty and leads to a minimax-optimal strategy called contextual Normalized Maximum Likelihood, or cNML.

The characterization also yields a short proof of a new upper bound expressed through sequential infinity-norm entropy, unifying and sharpening previous bounds. Thus, a measure that was insufficient for exact characterization still remains useful for bounding regret within the new framework.
summary.tldr: The contextual Shtarkov sum exactly characterizes minimax log-loss regret and yields a general optimal prediction strategy.

title: Sequential Probability Assignment with Contexts: Minimax Regret, Contextual Shtarkov Sums, and Contextual Normalized Maximum Likelihood

abstract: Large-scale foundation models have demonstrated exceptional performance in language and vision tasks. However, the numerous dense matrix-vector operations involved in these large networks pose significant computational challenges during inference. To address these challenges, we introduce the Block-Level Adaptive STructured (BLAST) matrix, designed to learn and leverage efficient structures prevalent in the weight matrices of linear layers within deep learning models. Compared to existing structured matrices, the BLAST matrix offers substantial flexibility, as it can represent various types of structures that are either learned from data or computed from pre-existing weight matrices. We demonstrate the efficiency of using the BLAST matrix for compressing both language and vision tasks, showing that (i) for medium-sized models such as ViT and GPT-2, training with BLAST weights boosts performance while reducing complexity by 70\% and 40\%, respectively; and (ii) for large foundation models such as Llama-7B and DiT-XL, the BLAST matrix achieves a 2x compression while exhibiting the lowest performance degradation among all tested structured matrices. Our code is available at https://github.com/changwoolee/BLAST.

paragraphs: BLAST addresses the computational burden of the dense matrix operations used throughout large neural networks. These operations are central to linear layers, so representing their weights more efficiently can reduce inference complexity. The paper introduces a structured matrix representation that adapts at the block level to capture useful patterns in those weights.

Its distinguishing feature is flexibility. BLAST can represent several kinds of structure, either learned during training or obtained from existing weight matrices. This lets the authors study both training models with structured weights and compressing larger pretrained models, using the same general representation across language and vision tasks.

For the medium-sized ViT and GPT-2 models, training with BLAST improves performance while reducing complexity by 70% and 40%, respectively. For Llama-7B and DiT-XL, it achieves twofold compression with the smallest performance loss among the structured matrices tested. These results support the value of adaptable structure: in the reported comparisons, efficiency gains need not require the same performance tradeoff as more restrictive structured representations.
summary.tldr: BLAST compresses neural-network weights with flexible block-level structure, reducing complexity while preserving or improving performance in the reported experiments.

title: BLAST: Block-Level Adaptive Structured Matrices for Efficient Deep Neural Network Inference

abstract: Designing causal bandit algorithms depends on two central categories of assumptions: (i) the extent of information about the underlying causal graphs and (ii) the extent of information about interventional statistical models. There have been extensive recent advances in dispensing with assumptions on either category. These include assuming known graphs but unknown interventional distributions, and the converse setting of assuming unknown graphs but access to restrictive hard/$\operatorname{do}$ interventions, which removes the stochasticity and ancestral dependencies. Nevertheless, the problem in its general form, i.e., _unknown_ graph and _unknown_ stochastic intervention models, remains open. This paper addresses this problem and establishes that in a graph with $N$ nodes, maximum in-degree $d$ and maximum causal path length $L$, after $T$ interaction rounds the regret upper bound scales as $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}((cd)^{L-\frac{1}{2}}\sqrt{T} + d + RN)$ where $c>1$ is a constant and $R$ is a measure of intervention power. A universal minimax lower bound is also established, which scales as $\Omega(d^{L-\frac{3}{2}}\sqrt{T})$. Importantly, the graph size $N$ has a diminishing effect on the regret as $T$ grows. These bounds have matching behavior in $T$, exponential dependence on $L$, and polynomial dependence on $d$ (with the gap $d\ $). On the algorithmic aspect, the paper presents a novel way of designing a computationally efficient CB algorithm, addressing a challenge that the existing CB algorithms using soft interventions face.

paragraphs: Causal bandit algorithms learn which interventions produce desirable outcomes. Many approaches assume either a known causal graph or restrictive interventions that remove randomness and dependencies on upstream variables. This paper tackles linear causal bandits when both the graph and the stochastic intervention models are unknown.

The authors provide a computationally efficient algorithm together with upper and minimax lower regret bounds. Regret captures the accumulated cost of learning which interventions to choose. Both bounds scale with the square root of the number of interaction rounds. They also expose exponential dependence on the longest causal path and polynomial dependence on maximum in-degree, with a remaining gap in the bounds.

The upper bound includes the number of graph nodes through an additive term involving intervention power. Consequently, graph size has a diminishing relative influence as interaction rounds accumulate. The results clarify how causal depth, connectivity, and intervention power shape learning difficulty while addressing the computational challenge associated with algorithms that use soft, stochastic interventions.
summary.tldr: An efficient linear causal-bandit algorithm handles unknown graphs and stochastic interventions, with regret bounds exposing the role of causal structure.

title: Linear Causal Bandits: Unknown Graph and Soft Interventions

abstract: Traditionally, 3d indoor datasets have generally prioritized scale over ground-truth accuracy in order to obtain improved generalization. However, using these datasets to evaluate dense geometry tasks, such as depth rendering, can be problematic as the meshes of the dataset are often incomplete and may produce wrong ground truth to evaluate the details. In this paper, we propose SCRREAM, a dataset annotation framework that allows annotation of fully dense meshes of objects in the scene and registers camera poses on the real image sequence, which can produce accurate ground truth for both sparse 3D as well as dense 3D tasks. We show the details of the dataset annotation pipeline and showcase four possible variants of datasets that can be obtained from our framework with example scenes, such as indoor reconstruction and SLAM, scene editing \& object removal, human reconstruction and 6d pose estimation. Recent pipelines for indoor reconstruction and SLAM serve as new benchmarks. In contrast to previous indoor dataset, our design allows to evaluate dense geometry tasks on eleven sample scenes against accurately rendered ground truth depth maps.

paragraphs: SCRREAM addresses a ground-truth problem in evaluating indoor 3D reconstruction. Large datasets often prioritize scale, but their meshes can be incomplete. When those meshes are used to produce reference depth images, missing geometry can make evaluation of fine details inaccurate. The paper therefore focuses on creating sufficiently dense and accurate annotations for geometry tasks.

The framework annotates fully dense object meshes and registers camera poses against real image sequences. This combination supports accurate reference data for both sparse and dense 3D tasks. The authors describe the annotation pipeline and illustrate four dataset variants covering indoor reconstruction and SLAM, scene editing and object removal, human reconstruction, and 6D pose estimation.

Recent indoor reconstruction and SLAM pipelines are evaluated as benchmarks. The dataset design enables dense geometry evaluation on eleven example scenes using accurately rendered reference depth maps. The central contribution is the connection between detailed scene annotation and reliable evaluation: improving the reference geometry makes it possible to assess details that incomplete indoor meshes could otherwise score incorrectly.
summary.tldr: SCRREAM combines dense mesh annotation with camera registration to provide more accurate ground truth for indoor 3D evaluation.

title: SCRREAM : SCan, Register, REnder And Map: A Framework for Annotating Accurate and Dense 3D Indoor Scenes with a Benchmark

abstract: We introduce a novel, training-free method for sampling *differentiable representations* (diffreps) using pretrained diffusion models. Rather than merely mode-seeking, our method achieves sampling by "pulling back" the dynamics of the reverse-time process—from the image space to the diffrep parameter space—and updating the parameters according to this pulled-back process. We identify an implicit constraint on the samples induced by the diffrep and demonstrate that addressing this constraint significantly improves the consistency and detail of the generated objects. Our method yields diffreps with substantially **improved quality and diversity** for images, panoramas, and 3D NeRFs compared to existing techniques. Our approach is a general-purpose method for sampling diffreps, expanding the scope of problems that diffusion models can tackle.

Rather than merely mode-seeking, our method achieves sampling by "pulling back" the dynamics of the reverse-time process—from the image space to the diffrep parameter space—and updating the parameters according to this pulled-back process. We identify an implicit constraint on the samples induced by the diffrep and demonstrate that addressing this constraint significantly improves the consistency and detail of the generated objects. Our method yields diffreps with substantially **improved quality and diversity** for images, panoramas, and 3D NeRFs compared to existing techniques. Our approach is a general-purpose method for sampling diffreps, expanding the scope of problems that diffusion models can tackle.

paragraphs: Pretrained diffusion models generate images, but the desired output may instead be a parameterized representation, such as a panorama or a 3D NeRF. This paper introduces a training-free method for sampling these differentiable representations. Its central objective is to obtain varied samples, going beyond procedures that mainly search for a particularly favored output.

The method transfers the reverse-time diffusion dynamics from image space into the representation’s parameter space. The authors describe this as pulling back the process: the representation’s parameters are updated according to the transferred dynamics. They also identify an implicit constraint that the representation places on possible samples and show that accounting for it improves consistency and detail.

Experiments cover images, panoramas, and 3D NeRFs, reporting substantial improvements in both quality and diversity over existing techniques. These findings matter because quality alone would not establish that a procedure samples a useful range of outputs. The work presents a general-purpose route for applying pretrained diffusion models to representations whose parameters, rather than image pixels alone, must be generated.
summary.tldr: A training-free method transfers diffusion dynamics into representation parameters, improving the quality and diversity of images, panoramas, and 3D NeRFs.

title: Diffusing Differentiable Representations

abstract: In this paper, we study differentially private (DP) algorithms for computing the geometric median (GM) of a dataset: Given $n$ points, $x_1,\dots,x_n$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the goal is to find a point $\theta$ that minimizes the sum of the Euclidean distances to these points, i.e., $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lVert|\theta - x_i\rVert_2$. Off-the-shelf methods, such as DP-GD, require strong a priori knowledge locating the data within a ball of radius $R$, and the excess risk of the algorithm depends linearly on $R$. In this paper, we ask: can we design an efficient and private algorithm with an excess error guarantee that scales with the (unknown) radius containing the majority of the datapoints? Our main contribution is a pair of polynomial-time DP algorithms for the task of private GM with an excess error guarantee that scales with the effective diameter of the datapoints. Additionally, we propose an inefficient algorithm based on the inverse smooth sensitivity mechanism, which satisfies the more restrictive notion of pure DP. We complement our results with a lower bound and demonstrate the optimality of our polynomial-time algorithms in terms of sample complexity.

In this paper, we ask: can we design an efficient and private algorithm with an excess error guarantee that scales with the (unknown) radius containing the majority of the datapoints? Our main contribution is a pair of polynomial-time DP algorithms for the task of private GM with an excess error guarantee that scales with the effective diameter of the datapoints. Additionally, we propose an inefficient algorithm based on the inverse smooth sensitivity mechanism, which satisfies the more restrictive notion of pure DP. We complement our results with a lower bound and demonstrate the optimality of our polynomial-time algorithms in terms of sample complexity.

paragraphs: The geometric median is the point minimizing the sum of Euclidean distances to a dataset's points. Computing it with differential privacy introduces an accuracy challenge. Standard approaches such as private gradient descent require advance knowledge of a ball containing the data, and their excess error grows linearly with that ball's radius.

This paper asks whether private estimation can instead adapt to the unknown radius containing most of the data. Its main contribution is two polynomial-time algorithms whose excess error guarantees scale with the data's effective diameter. This ties the guarantee to a more representative measure of data spread rather than relying only on the broader enclosing radius.

The authors also propose an inefficient algorithm based on inverse smooth sensitivity that satisfies the stricter requirement of pure differential privacy. A lower bound establishes sample-complexity optimality for the polynomial-time algorithms. Together, these results address accuracy, computational efficiency, and privacy strength, with distinct contributions for efficient estimation and the stronger pure-privacy requirement.
summary.tldr: New private geometric median algorithms achieve error guarantees tied to effective data diameter and optimal sample complexity.

title: Private Geometric Median

paragraphs: Scientific and probabilistic models often require functions of matrices that grow with the dataset or the number of model parameters. Evaluating those functions efficiently is only part of the problem: tuning the models also requires derivatives. This paper tackles efficient differentiation through Lanczos and Arnoldi iterations, established numerical methods for evaluating such quantities.

The authors derive adjoint systems for both iterative methods and implement them in JAX. These systems provide a way to compute the derivatives needed for optimization through the underlying matrix calculations. The contribution connects efficient large-matrix evaluation to gradient-based model tuning, extending the usefulness of numerical tools already central to these workloads.

The resulting code competes with Diffrax for differentiating partial differential equations and with GPyTorch for Gaussian-process model selection. It also outperforms standard factorization methods for calibrating Bayesian neural networks in the reported evaluations. These comparisons are achieved without problem-specific code optimization, suggesting that the derived differentiation machinery can be useful across several distinct scientific and probabilistic modeling tasks.
summary.tldr: New adjoint systems enable efficient differentiation through Lanczos and Arnoldi iterations, supporting gradient-based tuning across several large-matrix applications.

title: Gradients of Functions of Large Matrices

abstract: Domain Generalization (DG) aims to enable models to generalize to unseen target domains by learning from multiple source domains. Existing DG methods primarily rely on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which inherently learn texture biases due to their limited receptive fields, making them prone to overfitting source domains. While some works have introduced transformer-based methods (ViTs) for DG to leverage the global receptive field, these methods incur high computational costs due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Recently, advanced state space models (SSMs), represented by Mamba, have shown promising results in supervised learning tasks by achieving linear complexity in sequence length during training and fast RNN-like computation during inference. Inspired by this, we investigate the generalization ability of the Mamba model under domain shifts and find that input-dependent matrices within SSMs could accumulate and amplify domain-specific features, thus hindering model generalization. To address this issue, we propose a novel SSM-based architecture with saliency-based token-aware transformation (namely START), which achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performances and offers a competitive alternative to CNNs and ViTs. Our START can selectively perturb and suppress domain-specific features in salient tokens within the input-dependent matrices of SSMs, thus effectively reducing the discrepancy between different domains. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate that START outperforms existing SOTA DG methods with efficient linear complexity. Our code is available at https://github.com/lingeringlight/START.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks a model trained on several source domains to perform well on an unseen domain. This paper investigates state space models as an efficient alternative to convolutional networks and vision transformers. The motivation combines the need to avoid source-specific visual biases with the appeal of computation that scales linearly with sequence length.

The authors find that Mamba’s input-dependent matrices can accumulate and amplify features tied to particular domains, harming transfer. START addresses this within the state space architecture using a saliency-based, token-aware transformation. It selectively perturbs and suppresses domain-specific features in salient tokens within those matrices, aiming to reduce differences between domain representations.

Experiments on five benchmarks show START outperforming existing state-of-the-art domain generalization methods while retaining linear complexity. The finding links generalization problems to a specific part of the state space computation and demonstrates a targeted intervention there. It supports START as a competitive architecture for domain shifts, combining the reported predictive improvements with the computational scaling that motivated using state space models.
summary.tldr: START suppresses domain-specific features inside state space computations to improve unseen-domain performance while retaining linear complexity.

title: START: A Generalized State Space Model with Saliency-Driven Token-Aware Transformation

abstract: Exploring the intricate dynamics between muscular and skeletal structures is pivotal for understanding human motion. This domain presents substantial challenges, primarily attributed to the intensive resources required for acquiring ground truth muscle activation data, resulting in a scarcity of datasets.In this work, we address this issue by establishing Muscles in Time (MinT), a large-scale synthetic muscle activation dataset.For the creation of MinT, we enriched existing motion capture datasets by incorporating muscle activation simulations derived from biomechanical human body models using the OpenSim platform, a common framework used in biomechanics and human motion research.Starting from simple pose sequences, our pipeline enables us to extract detailed information about the timing of muscle activations within the human musculoskeletal system.Muscles in Time contains over nine hours of simulation data covering 227 subjects and 402 simulated muscle strands. We demonstrate the utility of this dataset by presenting results on neural network-based muscle activation estimation from human pose sequences with two different sequence-to-sequence architectures.

paragraphs: Muscles in Time, or MinT, addresses the scarcity of muscle activation data for studying human movement. Observing poses reveals how the body moves, while muscle activity provides another level of information about the muscular and skeletal processes involved. Collecting ground-truth activations is resource-intensive, so the authors create a large synthetic dataset through biomechanical simulation.

The pipeline starts with existing motion-capture sequences and enriches them using human body models in OpenSim. From pose sequences, it produces simulated information about when muscles activate during movement. MinT contains more than nine hours of simulation data across 227 subjects and 402 simulated muscle strands, linking motion observations with detailed activation sequences.

The authors demonstrate the dataset's utility by training two different sequence-to-sequence neural network architectures to estimate muscle activations from human poses. These results establish a use for MinT in learning the relationship between visible movement and simulated muscular activity. The synthetic nature of the activations is central to the contribution: biomechanical modeling supplies the additional information used to enrich existing motion data.
summary.tldr: MinT enriches motion-capture data with simulated muscle activations and supports learning to estimate those activations from pose sequences.

title: Muscles in Time: Learning to Understand Human Motion In-Depth by Simulating Muscle Activations

abstract: Many animals learn cognitive maps of their environment - a simultaneous representation of context, experience, and position. Place cells in the hippocampus, named for their explicit encoding of position, are believed to be a neural substrate of these maps, with place cell "remapping" explaining how this system can represent different contexts. Briefly, place cells alter their firing properties, or "remap", in response to changes in experiential or sensory cues. Substantial sensory changes, produced, e.g., by moving between environments, cause large subpopulations of place cells to change their tuning entirely. While many studies have looked at the physiological basis of remapping, we lack explicit calculations of how the contextual capacity of the place cell system changes as a function of place field firing properties. Here, we propose a geometric approach to understanding population level activity of place cells. Using known firing field statistics, we investigate how changes to place cell firing properties affect the distances between representations of different environments within firing rate space. Using this approach, we find that the number of contexts storable by the hippocampus grows exponentially with the number of place cells, and calculate this exponent for environments of different sizes. We identify a fundamental trade-off between high resolution encoding of position and the number of storable contexts. This trade-off is tuned by place cell width, which might explain the change in firing field scale along the dorsal-ventral axis of the hippocampus. We demonstrate that clustering of place cells near likely points of confusion, such as boundaries, increases the contextual capacity of the place system within our framework and conclude by discussing how our geometric approach could be extended to include other cell types and abstract spaces.

paragraphs: Hippocampal place cells encode position and change their firing patterns across contexts, a process called remapping. This paper asks how their firing properties affect the number of contexts that a population can represent. It develops a geometric account of population activity using known statistics of place-cell firing fields.

The approach measures distances between different environments’ representations in firing-rate space. Within this framework, the number of storable contexts grows exponentially with the number of place cells, and the authors calculate the growth exponent for different environment sizes. They also identify a trade-off: more precise encoding of location reduces the capacity to distinguish contexts.

Place-field width adjusts this trade-off, which the authors suggest might explain changes in firing-field scale along the hippocampus’s dorsal-ventral axis. Their framework also shows that concentrating place cells near likely confusion points, such as boundaries, increases contextual capacity. These results provide a quantitative link between spatial resolution and contextual storage, with the anatomical explanation presented as a possibility rather than an established cause.
summary.tldr: A geometric model of hippocampal place cells reveals a trade-off between precise location coding and the number of representable contexts.

title: Trading Place for Space: Increasing Location Resolution Reduces Contextual Capacity in Hippocampal Codes

abstract: Despite the availability of international prize-money competitions, scaled vehicles, and simulation environments, research on autonomous racing and the control of sports cars operating close to the limit of handling has been limited by the high costs of vehicle acquisition and management, as well as the limited physics accuracy of open-source simulators. In this paper, we propose a racing simulation platform based on the simulator Assetto Corsa to test, validate, and benchmark autonomous driving algorithms, including reinforcement learning (RL) and classical Model Predictive Control (MPC), in realistic and challenging scenarios. Our contributions include the development of this simulation platform, several state-of-the-art algorithms tailored to the racing environment, and a comprehensive dataset collected from human drivers. Additionally, we evaluate algorithms in the offline RL setting. All the necessary code (including environment and benchmarks), working examples, and datasets are publicly released and can be found at: https://github.com/dasGringuen/assetto_corsa_gym.

paragraphs: Autonomous racing asks driving algorithms to control cars close to their handling limits. Studying this with physical vehicles is expensive, while limited physics accuracy can make open-source simulators less useful for this purpose. This paper introduces a simulation platform built on Assetto Corsa to support testing, validation, and comparison of autonomous racing algorithms in realistic, challenging scenarios.

The contribution combines an environment with algorithms adapted to racing and a substantial dataset collected from human drivers. The platform accommodates reinforcement learning and classical Model Predictive Control, giving researchers a shared setting for examining different approaches to vehicle control. Human driving data adds another resource alongside the simulation itself.

The authors also evaluate algorithms in offline reinforcement learning, where learning uses previously collected experience. They publicly release the environment, benchmarks, working examples, and datasets. The paper's stated contribution is therefore research infrastructure spanning simulation, reference algorithms, and human data, making several parts of an autonomous racing study available together.
summary.tldr: A racing platform built on Assetto Corsa combines simulation, adapted control algorithms, and human driving data for autonomous racing research.

title: A Simulation Benchmark for Autonomous Racing with Large-Scale Human Data

abstract: We develop new conformal inference methods for obtaining validity guarantees on the output of large language models (LLMs). Prior work in conformal language modeling identifies a subset of the text that satisfies a high-probability guarantee of correctness. These methods work by filtering claims from the LLM's original response if a scoring function evaluated on the claim fails to exceed a threshold calibrated via split conformal prediction. Existing methods in this area suffer from two deficiencies. First, the guarantee stated is not conditionally valid. The trustworthiness of the filtering step may vary based on the topic of the response. Second, because the scoring function is imperfect, the filtering step can remove many valuable and accurate claims. We address both of these challenges via two new conformal methods. First, we generalize the conditional conformal procedure of Gibbs et al. (2023) in order to adaptively issue weaker guarantees when they are required to preserve the utility of the output. Second, we show how to systematically improve the quality of the scoring function via a novel algorithm for differentiating through the conditional conformal procedure. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on biography and medical question-answering datasets.

paragraphs: Conformal language-modeling methods can filter an answer’s claims to retain text with a high-probability correctness guarantee. Existing approaches score each claim and compare it with a calibrated threshold. This paper identifies two problems: the guarantee may vary in trustworthiness across response topics, and imperfect scores can remove valuable claims that are actually accurate.

The first proposed method extends conditional conformal inference so that it can adaptively issue weaker guarantees when needed to preserve useful output. This makes the strength of the guarantee part of the method’s response to the task. The second method improves the scoring function through an algorithm that differentiates through the conditional conformal procedure.

The authors evaluate their approach on biography and medical question-answering datasets and report evidence of its effectiveness. Together, the methods address both how a guarantee is assigned and how claims are scored before filtering. The contribution explicitly balances validity and retained usefulness; its adaptive weakening of guarantees is a central design feature that matters when interpreting the resulting outputs.
summary.tldr: Two conformal methods adapt correctness guarantees and improve claim scoring to retain more useful language-model output.

title: Large language model validity via enhanced conformal prediction methods

abstract: The cortico-spinal neural pathway is fundamental for motor control and movement execution, and in humans it is typically studied using concurrent electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG) recordings. However, current approaches for capturing high-level and contextual connectivity between these recordings have important limitations. Here, we present a novel application of statistical dependence estimators based on orthonormal decomposition of density ratios to model the relationship between cortical and muscle oscillations. Our method extends from traditional scalar-valued measures by learning eigenvalues, eigenfunctions, and projection spaces of density ratios from realizations of the signal, addressing the interpretability, scalability, and local temporal dependence of cortico-muscular connectivity. We experimentally demonstrate that eigenfunctions learned from cortico-muscular connectivity can accurately classify movements and subjects. Moreover, they reveal channel and temporal dependencies that confirm the activation of specific EEG channels during movement.

paragraphs: Understanding how brain and muscle activity relate is central to studying movement control. Researchers commonly record EEG and EMG together to examine that relationship. This paper develops a way to characterize their statistical dependence that provides more structure than a single numerical connectivity score, addressing contextual and time-local relationships between the recordings.

The method uses an orthonormal decomposition of density ratios to learn eigenvalues, eigenfunctions, and projection spaces from the observed signals. These learned components describe different aspects of the dependence between cortical and muscle oscillations. The approach is intended to address interpretability and scalability while capturing how connectivity varies over local time periods.

Experiments show that the learned eigenfunctions can accurately classify movements and subjects. They also expose dependencies across recording channels and time, confirming activation of specific EEG channels during movement. The findings give the learned representation two roles: it supports classification and provides interpretable information about the structure of brain-muscle connectivity observed in the recordings.
summary.tldr: A structured statistical-dependence model links EEG and EMG recordings, supporting movement classification and revealing channel and temporal relationships.

title: Learning Cortico-Muscular Dependence through Orthonormal Decomposition of Density Ratios

abstract: Cooperative bargaining games are widely used to model resource allocation and conflict resolution. Traditional solutions assume the mediator can access agents’ utility function values and gradients. However, there is an increasing number of settings, such as human-AI interactions, where utility values may be inaccessible or incomparable due to unknown, nonaffine transformations. To model such settings, we consider that the mediator has access only to agents' $\textit{most preferred directions}-$normalized utility gradients in the decision space. To this end, we propose a cooperative bargaining algorithm where a mediator has access to only the direction oracle of each agent. We prove that unlike popular approaches such as the Nash and Kalai-Smorodinsky bargaining solutions, our approach is invariant to monotonic nonaffine transformations, and that under strong convexity and smoothness assumptions, this approach enjoys global asymptotic convergence to Pareto stationary solutions. Moreover, we show that the bargaining solutions found by our algorithm also satisfy the axioms of symmetry and (under slightly stronger conditions) independence of irrelevant alternatives, which are popular in the literature. Finally, we conduct experiments in two domains, multi-agent formation assignment and mediated stock portfolio allocation, which validate these theoretical results.

paragraphs: Cooperative bargaining asks how a mediator can help agents agree on resource allocation or resolve conflicts. Standard approaches assume access to numerical utilities and their gradients. This paper considers situations where utility values are unavailable or cannot be compared reliably, including human-AI interactions where the numerical scale of preferences may be unknown.

The mediator instead receives each agent’s most preferred direction, represented by a normalized utility gradient. This preserves information about which changes an agent favors without requiring the magnitude of its utility or gradient. The proposed algorithm is invariant to monotonic nonaffine transformations, meaning that order-preserving changes to utility scales do not change its bargaining outcome.

Under strong convexity and smoothness assumptions, the authors prove global asymptotic convergence to Pareto stationary solutions. They also establish symmetry and, under somewhat stronger conditions, independence of irrelevant alternatives. Experiments in multi-agent formation assignment and mediated portfolio allocation support the theoretical results. The contribution is a bargaining procedure with explicit guarantees when the available preference information consists only of directions.
summary.tldr: A bargaining algorithm uses preferred directions instead of utility values and provides conditional convergence and fairness-related guarantees.

title: Cooperative Bargaining Games Without Utilities: Mediated Solutions from Direction Oracles

abstract: Document Visual Question Answering (DocVQA) faces dual challenges in processing lengthy multimodal documents (text, images, tables) and performing cross-modal reasoning. Current document retrieval-augmented generation (DocRAG) methods remain limited by their text-centric approaches, frequently missing critical visual information. The field also lacks robust benchmarks for assessing multimodal evidence selection and integration. We introduce MMDocRAG, a comprehensive benchmark featuring 4,055 expert-annotated QA pairs with multi-page, cross-modal evidence chains. Our framework introduces innovative metrics for evaluating multimodal quote selection and enables answers that interleave text with relevant visual elements. Through large-scale experiments with 60 VLM/LLM models and 14 retrieval systems, we identify persistent challenges in multimodal evidence retrieval, selection, and integration. Key findings reveal that advanced proprietary LVMs show superior performance than open-sourced alternatives. Also, they show moderate advantages using multimodal inputs over text-only inputs, while open-source alternatives show significant performance degradation. Notably, fine-tuned LLMs achieve substantial improvements when using detailed image descriptions. MMDocRAG establishes a rigorous testing ground and provides actionable insights for developing more robust multimodal DocVQA systems.

paragraphs: Answering questions about long documents requires finding evidence across text, images, and tables, then combining it into a coherent answer. Text-centered retrieval can overlook visual evidence even when that evidence is essential. This paper introduces MMDocRAG to evaluate how systems handle the full process of retrieving, selecting, and integrating information across document formats and pages.

The benchmark contains 4,055 expert-annotated question-answer pairs with evidence chains spanning multiple pages and modalities. Its evaluation framework includes metrics for selecting multimodal quotations and supports answers that combine written explanations with relevant visual elements. This makes evidence selection itself an explicit evaluation target, alongside the resulting answer.

Experiments cover 60 vision-language or language models and 14 retrieval systems. Proprietary models perform better overall and gain moderately from multimodal inputs, while open-source alternatives suffer substantial degradation with those inputs. Fine-tuned language models improve substantially when given detailed image descriptions. These findings show that access to images alone does not ensure effective document reasoning; how systems represent and integrate visual evidence matters.
summary.tldr: MMDocRAG benchmarks document question answering across text and visuals, revealing persistent weaknesses in retrieving and integrating multimodal evidence.

title: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Multimomal Generation for Document Question Answering

abstract: Recent work has revealed that state space models (SSMs), while efficient for long-sequence processing, are fundamentally limited in their ability to represent formal languages—particularly due to time-invariant and real-valued recurrence structures. In this work, we draw inspiration from adaptive and structured dynamics observed in biological neural systems and introduce the Adaptive Unitary State Space Model (AUSSM): a novel class of SSMs that leverages skew-symmetric, input-dependent recurrence to achieve unitary evolution and high expressive power. Using algebraic automata theory, we prove that AUSSM can perform modulo counting and simulate solvable group automata at finite precision, enabling SSMs to model a broad class of regular languages out of reach for other SSM architectures. To overcome the practical inefficiencies of adaptive recurrence, we develop a separable convolution formulation and a CUDA implementation that enables scalable parallel training. Empirically, we show that AUSSM and its hybrid variant—interleaved with Mamba—outperform prior SSMs on formal algorithmic tasks such as parity and modular arithmetic, and achieve competent performance on real-world long time-series classification benchmarks. Our results demonstrate that adaptive unitary recurrence provides a powerful and efficient inductive bias for both symbolic and continuous sequence modeling. The code is available at https://github.com/arjunkaruvally/AUSSM

paragraphs: State space models efficiently process long sequences, but their recurrence structure can restrict which symbolic patterns they represent. The paper identifies time-invariant, real-valued recurrence as an important source of these limitations. Its Adaptive Unitary State Space Model, or AUSSM, instead uses input-dependent, skew-symmetric recurrence to produce unitary state evolution and increase expressive power.

Using algebraic automata theory, the authors prove that AUSSM can count modulo a number and simulate solvable group automata at finite precision. These results establish access to a broad class of regular languages beyond the capabilities of other SSM architectures considered in the work. They give a formal explanation for why changing the recurrence can improve symbolic sequence processing.

Adaptive recurrence also creates practical efficiency challenges. The authors address them with a separable convolution formulation and CUDA implementation for parallel training. AUSSM and a hybrid interleaved with Mamba outperform prior SSMs on parity and modular arithmetic tasks, while achieving competent long time-series classification performance. The findings connect stronger formal capabilities with a scalable implementation.
summary.tldr: AUSSM combines adaptive unitary recurrence with parallel training to expand state space models’ symbolic capabilities and support long-sequence tasks.

title: Bridging Expressivity and Scalability with Adaptive Unitary SSMs

abstract: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods are foundational algorithms for Bayesian inference and probabilistic modeling. However, most MCMC algorithms are inherently sequential and their time complexity scales linearly with the sequence length. Previous work on adapting MCMC to modern hardware has therefore focused on running many independent chains in parallel. Here, we take an alternative approach: we propose algorithms to evaluate MCMC samplers in parallel across the chain length. To do this, we build on recent methods for parallel evaluation of nonlinear recursions that formulate the state sequence as a solution to a fixed-point problem and solve for the fixed-point using a parallel form of Newton's method. We show how this approach can be used to parallelize Gibbs, Metropolis-adjusted Langevin, and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling across the sequence length. In several examples, we demonstrate the simulation of up to hundreds of thousands of MCMC samples with only tens of parallel Newton iterations. Additionally, we develop two new parallel quasi-Newton methods to evaluate nonlinear recursions with lower memory costs and reduced runtime. We find that the proposed parallel algorithms accelerate MCMC sampling across multiple examples, in some cases by more than an order of magnitude compared to sequential evaluation.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo usually generates samples sequentially, so producing a longer chain requires more sequential work. Common hardware-oriented approaches run multiple independent chains at once. This paper instead studies parallel computation across the positions of a chain, aiming to accelerate the evaluation of the sequence itself despite dependencies between successive states.

The method represents the entire state sequence as the solution of a fixed-point problem. A parallel form of Newton’s method then solves that problem. The authors show how this approach applies to Gibbs sampling, Metropolis-adjusted Langevin sampling, and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. They also develop two parallel quasi-Newton methods to reduce the memory requirements and runtime of evaluating nonlinear recursions.

In several examples, the approach simulates up to hundreds of thousands of samples using only tens of parallel Newton iterations. Reported speedups exceed an order of magnitude in some cases compared with sequential evaluation. These results demonstrate that chain-length parallelism can be practically useful across multiple sampling examples, beyond parallelizing independent chains.
summary.tldr: Parallel fixed-point solvers accelerate computation across MCMC chain positions, producing more than tenfold speedups in some reported examples.

title: Parallelizing MCMC Across the Sequence Length

abstract: Autonomy is a hallmark of animal intelligence, enabling adaptive and intelligent behavior in complex environments without relying on external reward or task structure. Existing reinforcement learning approaches to exploration in reward-free environments, including a class of methods known as *model-based intrinsic motivation*, exhibit inconsistent exploration patterns and do not converge to an exploratory policy, thus failing to capture robust autonomous behaviors observed in animals. Moreover, systems neuroscience has largely overlooked the neural basis of autonomy, focusing instead on experimental paradigms where animals are motivated by external reward rather than engaging in ethological, naturalistic and task-independent behavior. To bridge these gaps, we introduce a novel model-based intrinsic drive explicitly designed after the principles of autonomous exploration in animals. Our method (3M-Progress) achieves animal-like exploration by tracking divergence between an online world model and a fixed prior learned from an ecological niche. To the best of our knowledge, we introduce the first autonomous embodied agent that predicts brain data entirely from self-supervised optimization of an intrinsic goal—without any behavioral or neural training data—demonstrating that 3M-Progress agents capture the explainable variance in behavioral patterns and whole-brain neural-glial dynamics recorded from autonomously behaving larval zebrafish, thereby providing the first goal-driven, population-level model of neural-glial computation. Our findings establish a computational framework connecting model-based intrinsic motivation to naturalistic behavior, providing a foundation for building artificial agents with animal-like autonomy.

abstract: Accurate 3D reconstruction of hands and instruments is critical for vision-based analysis of ophthalmic microsurgery, yet progress has been hampered by the lack of realistic, large-scale datasets and reliable annotation tools. In this work, we introduce OphNet-3D, the first extensive RGB-D dynamic 3D reconstruction dataset for ophthalmic surgery, comprising 41 sequences from 40 surgeons and totaling 7.1 million frames, with fine-grained annotations of 12 surgical phases, 10 instrument categories, dense MANO hand meshes, and full 6-DoF instrument poses. To scalably produce high-fidelity labels, we design a multi-stage automatic annotation pipeline that integrates multi-view data observation, data-driven motion prior with cross-view geometric consistency and biomechanical constraints, along with a combination of collision-aware interaction constraints for instrument interactions. Building upon OphNet-3D, we establish two challenging benchmarks—bimanual hand pose estimation and hand–instrument interaction reconstruction—and propose two dedicated architectures: H-Net for dual-hand mesh recovery and OH-Net for joint reconstruction of two-hand–two-instrument interactions. These models leverage a novel spatial reasoning module with weak-perspective camera modeling and collision-aware center-based representation. Both architectures outperform existing methods by substantial margins, achieving improvements of over 2mm in Mean Per Joint Position Error (MPJPE) and up to 23\% in ADD-S metrics for hand and instrument reconstruction, respectively.

title: Towards Dynamic 3D Reconstruction of Hand-Instrument Interaction in Ophthalmic Surgery

abstract: Fine-grained video action recognition can be formulated as a video–text matching problem. Previous approaches primarily rely on global video semantics to consolidate video embeddings, often leading to misaligned video–text pairs due to inaccurate atomic-level action understanding. This inaccuracy arises due to i) videos with distinct global semantics may share similar atomic actions or visual appearances, and ii) atomic actions can be momentary, gradual, or not directly aligned with overarching video semantics. Inspired by storyboarding, where a script is segmented into individual shots, we propose a multi-granularity framework, SFAR. SFAR generates fine-grained descriptions of common atomic actions for each global semantic using a large language model. Unlike existing works that refine global semantics with auxiliary video frames, SFAR introduces a filtering metric to ensure correspondence between the descriptions and the global semantics, eliminating the need for direct video involvement and thereby enabling more nuanced recognition of subtle actions. By leveraging both global semantics and fine-grained descriptions, our SFAR effectively identifies prominent frames within videos, thereby improving the accuracy of embedding aggregation. Extensive experiments on various video action recognition datasets demonstrate the competitive performance of our SFAR in supervised, few-shot, and zero-shot settings.

paragraphs: Recognizing a fine-grained video action requires relating the overall activity to its smaller component actions. Global descriptions alone can misalign videos and text because different activities share visual appearances or atomic actions. Some relevant actions are also brief or gradual, making them difficult to capture in a single overall video representation.

SFAR uses a storyboarding-inspired approach to describe actions at multiple levels. A language model generates descriptions of common atomic actions for each global semantic description. A filtering metric checks their correspondence with that global meaning without requiring video input for this description-refinement stage. The method then uses both levels of description to identify prominent frames and aggregate video embeddings more accurately.

Experiments across several action-recognition datasets report competitive performance in supervised, few-shot, and zero-shot settings. The stated contribution is a better connection between broad activity descriptions, their component actions, and the frames used to represent a video. This helps the matching process account for subtle actions that can be obscured by an exclusively global view.
summary.tldr: SFAR uses filtered atomic-action descriptions to select informative frames and improve fine-grained video–text alignment.

title: Storyboard-guided Alignment for Fine-grained Video Action Recognition

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has achieved major advances in natural images and video understanding, but challenges remain in domains like echocardiography (heart ultrasound) due to subtle anatomical structures, complex temporal dynamics, and the current lack of domain-specific pre-trained models. Existing SSL approaches such as contrastive, masked modeling, and clustering-based methods struggle with high intersample similarity, sensitivity to low PSNR inputs common in ultrasound, or aggressive augmentations that distort clinically relevant features. We present DISCOVR (Distilled Image Supervision for Cross Modal Video Representation), a self-supervised dual-branch framework for cardiac ultrasound video representation learning. DISCOVR combines a clustering-based video encoder that models temporal dynamics with an online image encoder that extracts fine-grained spatial semantics. These branches are connected through a semantic cluster distillation loss that transfers anatomical knowledge from the evolving image encoder to the video encoder, enabling temporally coherent representations enriched with fine-grained semantic understanding. Evaluated on six echocardiography datasets spanning fetal, pediatric, and adult populations, DISCOVR outperforms both specialized video anomaly detection methods and state-of-the-art video-SSL baselines in zero-shot and linear probing setups, achieving superior segmentation transfer and strong downstream performance on clinically relevant tasks such as LVEF prediction. **Code available at:** [https://github.com/mdivyanshu97/DISCOVR](https://github.com/mdivyanshu97/DISCOVR)

paragraphs: Learning from heart-ultrasound videos requires sensitivity to both subtle anatomy and changing motion. The video branch uses clustering to model temporal dynamics. An image encoder learns fine-grained spatial meaning and continues evolving during training. A semantic cluster distillation loss transfers anatomical knowledge from this image encoder into the video encoder. This connects detailed spatial understanding with representations that remain coherent over time.

The authors evaluate DISCOVR on six echocardiography datasets covering fetal, pediatric, and adult populations. It outperforms specialized video anomaly-detection methods and state-of-the-art video self-supervised baselines in zero-shot and linear-probing evaluations. The paper also reports stronger segmentation transfer and downstream performance on tasks including left ventricular ejection fraction prediction. summary.tldr: DISCOVR transfers anatomical information from an evolving image encoder into a video encoder to improve self-supervised heart-ultrasound representations.

title: Self-supervised Learning of Echocardiographic Video Representations via Online Cluster Distillation

abstract: In order to train, test, and evaluate nudity detection models, machine learning researchers typically rely on nude images scraped from the Internet. Our research finds that this content is collected and, in some cases, subsequently \emph{distributed} by researchers without consent, leading to potential misuse and exacerbating harm against the subjects depicted. \textbf{This position paper argues that the distribution of nonconsensually collected nude images by researchers perpetuates image-based sexual abuse and that the machine learning community should stop the nonconsensual use of nude images in research.} To characterize the scope and nature of this problem, we conducted a systematic review of papers published in computing venues that collect and use nude images. Our results paint a grim reality: norms around the usage of nude images are sparse, leading to a litany of problematic practices like distributing and publishing nude images with uncensored faces, and intentionally collecting and sharing abusive content. We conclude with a call-to-action for publishing venues and a vision for research in nudity detection that balances user agency with concrete research objectives.

This position paper examines what happens when researchers collect or redistribute those images without the depicted people’s consent. It argues that distributing nonconsensually collected nude images perpetuates image-based sexual abuse and that the research community should stop their nonconsensual use.

They find sparse norms governing these practices and identify concrete problems, including publishing or distributing images with uncensored faces and intentionally collecting and sharing abusive content. The concern therefore extends beyond initial collection to researchers’ subsequent handling and dissemination of images.

The paper calls on publishing venues to respond and proposes a vision for nudity-detection research that balances user agency with concrete research objectives. Its contribution combines evidence about current research practices with an explicit ethical position. The stated harms and potential misuse make consent and distribution central questions in how this research is conducted.
summary.tldr: A systematic review documents harmful nude-image research practices and supports a call to end nonconsensual use and distribution.

title: Stop the Nonconsensual Use of Nude Images in Research

abstract: Reasoning methods that adaptively allocate test-time compute have advanced LLM performance on easy to verify domains such as math and code. In this work, we study how to utilize this approach to train models that exhibit a degree of robustness to safety vulnerabilities, and show that doing so can provide benefits. We build a recipe called $\textit{\textbf{TARS}}$ (Training Adaptive Reasoners for Safety), a reinforcement learning (RL) approach that trains models to reason about safety using chain-of-thought traces and a reward signal that balances safety with task completion. To build TARS, we identify three critical design choices: (1) a ``lightweight'' warmstart SFT stage, (2) a mix of harmful, harmless, and ambiguous prompts to prevent shortcut behaviors such as too many refusals, and (3) a reward function to prevent degeneration of reasoning capabilities during training. Models trained with TARS exhibit adaptive behaviors by spending more compute on ambiguous queries, leading to better safety-refusal trade-offs. They also internally learn to better distinguish between safe and unsafe prompts and attain greater robustness to both white-box (e.g., GCG) and black-box attacks (e.g., PAIR). Overall, our work provides an effective, open recipe for training LLMs against jailbreaks and harmful requests by reasoning per prompt.

It introduces TARS, a reinforcement-learning recipe that trains models to reason about safety using chain-of-thought traces. Its reward balances avoiding harmful responses with completing legitimate tasks, making useful assistance part of the training objective.

The authors identify three key choices: a lightweight supervised warm start, a mixture of harmful, harmless, and ambiguous prompts, and a reward designed to preserve reasoning capabilities. The prompt mixture helps prevent shortcuts such as excessive refusal. Together, these choices aim to teach a model when careful consideration is useful and when a request can be answered.

TARS-trained models spend more computation on ambiguous queries and achieve better safety-refusal trade-offs. They also show improved internal differentiation between safe and unsafe prompts and greater robustness to white-box and black-box attacks. These are improvements in resistance to vulnerabilities rather than a claim of complete protection. The paper provides an open training recipe for developing this adaptive behavior.
summary.tldr: TARS trains language models to spend more reasoning effort on ambiguous requests, improving safety-refusal trade-offs and resistance to attacks.

title: Reasoning as an Adaptive Defense for Safety

abstract: Differential Transformer has recently gained significant attention for its impressive empirical performance, often attributed to its ability to perform noise canceled attention. However, precisely how differential attention achieves its empirical benefits remains poorly understood. Moreover, Differential Transformer architecture demands large-scale training from scratch, hindering utilization of open pretrained weights. In this work, we conduct an in-depth investigation of Differential Transformer, uncovering three key factors behind its success: (1) enhanced expressivity via negative attention, (2) reduced redundancy among attention heads, and (3) improved learning dynamics. Based on these findings, we propose DEX, a novel method to efficiently integrate the advantages of differential attention into pretrained language models. By reusing the softmax attention scores and adding a lightweight differential operation on the output value matrix, DEX effectively incorporates the key advantages of differential attention while remaining lightweight in both training and inference. Evaluations confirm that DEX substantially improves the pretrained LLMs across diverse benchmarks, achieving significant performance gains with minimal adaptation data (< 0.01%).
