paragraphs: Differential Transformers have shown strong empirical performance, but the explanation for their benefits has remained unclear. Their architecture also requires large-scale training from scratch, making existing pretrained weights difficult to reuse. This paper investigates the mechanism and uses its findings to design an adaptation method for pretrained language models.

The analysis identifies three contributing factors: greater expressivity through negative attention, less redundancy among attention heads, and improved learning dynamics. DEX incorporates these advantages by reusing existing softmax attention scores and adding a lightweight differential operation to the output value matrix. This places the new operation around computations that pretrained attention already provides.

Evaluations report substantial improvements across diverse language-model benchmarks with minimal adaptation data, stated as less than 0.01%. DEX is described as lightweight during both training and inference. The findings connect a mechanistic account of differential attention to a practical reuse strategy: pretrained models can gain its identified advantages through a small adaptation, making the analysis useful for architecture modification as well as understanding.
summary.tldr: DEX adds a lightweight differential operation to pretrained attention, bringing reported benchmark gains informed by an analysis of differential Transformers.

title: Understanding Differential Transformer Unchains Pretrained Self-Attentions

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) typically generate identical or similar responses for all users given the same prompt, posing serious safety risks in high-stakes applications where user vulnerabilities differ widely. Existing safety evaluations primarily rely on context-independent metrics—such as factuality, bias, or toxicity—overlooking the fact that the same response may carry divergent risks depending on the user's background or condition. We introduce ``personalized safety'' to fill this gap and present PENGUIN—a benchmark comprising 14,000 scenarios across seven sensitive domains with both context-rich and context-free variants. Evaluating six leading LLMs, we demonstrate that personalized user information significantly improves safety scores by 43.2%, confirming the effectiveness of personalization in safety alignment. However, not all context attributes contribute equally to safety enhancement. To address this, we develop RAISE—a training-free, two-stage agent framework that strategically acquires user-specific background. RAISE improves safety scores by up to 31.6% over six vanilla LLMs, while maintaining a low interaction cost of just 2.7 user queries on average. Our findings highlight the importance of selective information gathering in safety-critical domains and offer a practical solution for personalizing LLM responses without model retraining. This work establishes a foundation for safety research that adapts to individual user contexts rather than assuming a universal harm standard.

title: Personalized Safety in LLMs: A Benchmark and A Planning-Based Agent Approach

abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) derive their capabilities from extensive training on vast corpora of visual and textual data. Empowered by large-scale parameters, these models often exhibit strong memorization of their training data, rendering them susceptible to membership inference attacks (MIAs). Existing MIA methods for LVLMs typically operate under white- or gray-box assumptions, by extracting likelihood-based features for the suspected data samples based on the target LVLMs. However, mainstream LVLMs generally only expose generated outputs while concealing internal computational features during inference, limiting the applicability of these methods. In this work, we propose the first black-box MIA framework for LVLMs, based on a prior knowledge-calibrated memory probing mechanism. The core idea is to assess the model memorization of the private semantic information embedded within the suspected image data, which is unlikely to be inferred from general world knowledge alone. We conducted extensive experiments across four LVLMs and three datasets. Empirical results demonstrate that our method effectively identifies training data of LVLMs in a purely black-box setting and even achieves performance comparable to gray-box and white-box methods. Further analysis reveals the robustness of our method against potential adversarial manipulations, and the effectiveness of the methodology designs. Our code and data are available at \url{https://github.com/spmede/KCMP}.

paragraphs: Membership inference asks whether a particular example was part of a model's training data. For large vision-language models, existing approaches often depend on internal information, such as likelihood-based features. That makes them difficult to apply when a service exposes only generated responses and conceals its internal computations.

This paper proposes probing memory through those visible responses alone. The central distinction is between information a model could infer from general world knowledge and private semantic details associated with a suspected training image. The method calibrates its probing against prior knowledge, aiming to make recalled image-specific information more informative evidence of training membership.

Experiments cover four vision-language models and three datasets. The authors report effective identification of training examples in this black-box setting, with performance comparable to approaches using greater internal access. Additional analyses support robustness against the adversarial manipulations considered. These results show that withholding internal model features does not, by itself, eliminate the tested form of training-data exposure through generated outputs.
summary.tldr: The proposed attack identifies likely training images from visible model responses by probing private details beyond general world knowledge.

title: Black-Box Membership Inference Attack for LVLMs via Prior Knowledge-Calibrated Memory Probing

abstract: Efficient fine-tuning of pre-trained Text-to-Image (T2I) models involves adjusting the model to suit a particular task or dataset while minimizing computational resources and limiting the number of trainable parameters. However, it often faces challenges in striking a trade-off between aligning with the target distribution: learning a novel concept from a limited image for personalization and retaining the instruction ability needed for unifying multiple tasks, all while maintaining editability (aligning with a variety of prompts or in-context generation). In this work, we introduce DEFT, Decompositional Efficient Fine-Tuning, an efficient fine-tuning framework that adapts a pre-trained weight matrix by decomposing its update into two components with two trainable matrices: (1) a projection onto the complement of a low-rank subspace spanned by a low-rank matrix, and (2) a low-rank update. The single trainable low-rank matrix defines the subspace, while the other trainable low-rank matrix enables parameter adaptation within that subspace. We conducted extensive experiments on the Dreambooth and Dreambench Plus datasets for personalization, the InsDet dataset for object and scene adaptation, and the VisualCloze dataset for a universal image generation framework through visual in-context learning with both Stable Diffusion and a unified model. Our results demonstrated state-of-the-art performance, highlighting the emergent properties of efficient fine-tuning. Our code is available on \href{https://github.com/MAXNORM8650/DEFT}{DEFT}.

The single trainable low-rank matrix defines the subspace, while the other trainable low-rank matrix enables parameter adaptation within that subspace. We conducted extensive experiments on the Dreambooth and Dreambench Plus datasets for personalization, the InsDet dataset for object and scene adaptation, and the VisualCloze dataset for a universal image generation framework through visual in-context learning with both Stable Diffusion and a unified model. Our results demonstrated state-of-the-art performance, highlighting the emergent properties of efficient fine-tuning. Our code is available on \href{https://github.com/MAXNORM8650/DEFT}{DEFT}.

paragraphs: Adapting a text-to-image model requires balancing several goals. It should learn a new concept or image distribution while continuing to follow instructions and respond flexibly to different prompts. DEFT addresses this balance through a structured way to update pretrained weights while keeping the number of trainable parameters small.

The framework decomposes each weight update into two components involving two trainable low-rank matrices. One component uses a projection onto the complement of a learned low-rank subspace; the other supplies a low-rank update. One matrix defines the subspace, and the other supports adaptation within it. This makes the geometry of the update an explicit part of efficient fine-tuning.

The authors evaluate DEFT on personalization using Dreambooth and Dreambench Plus, object and scene adaptation using InsDet, and visual in-context generation using VisualCloze. The experiments include Stable Diffusion and a unified model, and the abstract reports state-of-the-art performance. These results support the proposed decomposition across several adaptation settings, linking parameter-efficient updates to the broader goal of learning task-specific behavior while retaining useful generation capabilities.
summary.tldr: DEFT structures text-to-image weight updates into complementary projection and low-rank components, achieving strong results across several adaptation tasks.

title: DEFT: Decompositional Efficient Fine-Tuning for Text-to-Image Models

abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) pretrained on large-scale multimodal data have shown promising capabilities in Video Anomaly Detection (VAD). However, their ability to reason about abnormal events based on scene semantics remains underexplored. In this paper, we investigate LVLMs’ behavior in VAD from a visual-textual co-occurrence perspective, focusing on whether their decisions are driven by statistical shortcuts between visual instances and textual phrases. By analyzing visual-textual co-occurrence in pretraining data and conducting experiments under different data settings, we reveal a hallucination phenomenon: LVLMs tend to rely on co-occurrence patterns between visual instances and textual phrases associated with either normality or abnormality, leading to incorrect predictions when these high-frequency objects appear in semantically mismatched contexts. To address this issue, we propose VAD-DPO, a direct preference optimization method supervised with counter-example pairs. By constructing visually similar but semantically contrasting video clips, VAD-DPO encourages the model to align its predictions with the semantics of scene rather than relying on co-occurrence patterns. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of VAD-DPO in enhancing both anomaly detection and reasoning performance, particularly in scene-dependent scenarios.

paragraphs: Detecting an abnormal event in a video requires interpreting what is happening in context. To address this, VAD-DPO uses direct preference optimization with counter-examples: video clips that look similar but have contrasting meanings.

These paired examples encourage predictions to follow the event's scene semantics, weakening reliance on superficial co-occurrence cues. Experiments on six benchmark datasets report improvements in both anomaly detection and reasoning, particularly when the judgment depends on the scene. The contribution connects an observed failure pattern to a targeted training intervention, showing that visually similar examples with different meanings can help models make more context-sensitive judgments.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies co-occurrence shortcuts in video anomaly judgments and improves contextual reasoning using preference training on contrasting video pairs.

title: Do LVLMs Truly Understand Video Anomalies? Revealing Hallucination via Co-Occurrence Patterns

abstract: The emergence of advanced multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has significantly enhanced AI assistants' ability to process complex information across modalities. Recently, egocentric videos, by directly capturing user focus, actions, and context in an unified coordinate, offer an exciting opportunity to enable proactive and personalized AI user experiences with MLLMs. However, existing benchmarks overlook the crucial role of gaze as an indicator of user intent. To address this gap, we introduce EgoGazeVQA, an egocentric gaze-guided video question answering benchmark that leverages gaze information to improve the understanding of longer daily-life videos. EgoGazeVQA consists of gaze-based QA pairs generated by MLLMs and refined by human annotators. Our experiments reveal that existing MLLMs struggle to accurately interpret user intentions using only global visual tokens. In contrast, our gaze-guided intent prompting methods significantly enhance performance by integrating spatial, temporal, and intent-related cues. We further conduct experiments on gaze-related fine-tuning and analyze how gaze estimation accuracy impacts prompting effectiveness. These results underscore the value of gaze for more personalized and effective AI assistants in egocentric settings.

paragraphs: First-person videos capture a person's actions and surroundings from a shared viewpoint, creating opportunities for assistants that respond to personal context. Understanding intent also requires attention to what the person is looking at. This paper introduces EgoGazeVQA to evaluate that connection, addressing the limited attention previous benchmarks give to gaze.

The benchmark contains gaze-based questions and answers about longer videos of everyday life. Multimodal language models generate the initial pairs, and human annotators refine them. The authors also develop gaze-guided intent prompts that combine spatial information, temporal information, and cues related to intent. This makes gaze an explicit part of how the model is directed to interpret a video.

Experiments show that existing models struggle to infer intentions when relying only on global visual tokens, while gaze-guided prompting significantly improves performance. The study additionally examines gaze-related fine-tuning and how gaze estimation accuracy affects prompting. These results support gaze as a useful source of context for more personalized assistants and establish a benchmark for studying how models connect visual attention with user intent.
summary.tldr: EgoGazeVQA shows that gaze-guided prompting improves multimodal models' understanding of user intent in first-person videos.

title: In the Eye of MLLM: Benchmarking Egocentric Video Intent Understanding with Gaze-Guided Prompting

abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) models have achieved remarkable success in generating visual content from text inputs. Although multiple safety alignment strategies have been proposed to prevent harmful outputs, they often lead to overly cautious behavior---rejecting even benign prompts---a phenomenon known as \textit{over-refusal} that reduces the practical utility of T2I models. Despite over-refusal having been observed in practice, there is no large-scale benchmark that systematically evaluates this phenomenon for T2I models. In this paper, we present an automatic workflow to construct synthetic evaluation data, resulting in OVERT (\textbf{OVE}r-\textbf{R}efusal evaluation on \textbf{T}ext-to-image models), the first large-scale benchmark for assessing over-refusal behaviors in T2I models. OVERT includes 4,600 seemingly harmful but benign prompts across nine safety-related categories, along with 1,785 genuinely harmful prompts (OVERT-unsafe) to evaluate the safety–utility trade-off. Using OVERT, we evaluate several leading T2I models and find that over-refusal is a widespread issue across various categories (Figure 1), underscoring the need for further research to enhance the safety alignment of T2I models without compromising their functionality. As a preliminary attempt to reduce over-refusal, we explore prompt rewriting; however, we find it often compromises faithfulness to the meaning of the original prompts.Finally, we demonstrate the flexibility of our generation framework in accommodating diverse safety requirements by generating customized evaluation data adapting to user-defined policies.

paragraphs: Text-to-image safety systems sometimes reject harmless requests because they appear risky. OVERT provides a large-scale benchmark for measuring this over-refusal, making the loss of legitimate functionality an explicit evaluation target. The authors construct the evaluation material through an automatic workflow for generating synthetic prompts.

The benchmark includes 4,600 benign prompts that seem harmful, spanning nine safety-related categories. A companion set, OVERT-unsafe, contains 1,785 genuinely harmful prompts. Evaluating both supports examination of the safety–utility tradeoff: a model should handle benign requests while still responding appropriately to genuinely harmful ones.

Tests of several leading text-to-image models reveal widespread over-refusal across categories. The authors also investigate prompt rewriting as an initial remedy, but find that it often changes the meaning of the original request. Finally, they demonstrate that the data-generation framework can produce evaluations tailored to user-defined safety policies. This makes the contribution both a concrete benchmark and a flexible method for constructing policy-specific evaluations.
summary.tldr: OVERT measures unnecessary refusals of benign image-generation prompts alongside safety on harmful prompts, revealing widespread over-refusal.

title: OVERT: A Benchmark for Over-Refusal Evaluation on Text-to-Image Models

abstract: In scientific domains---from biology to the social sciences---many questions boil down to \textit{What effect will we observe if we intervene on a particular variable?} If the causal relationships (e.g.~a causal graph) are known, its possible to estimate the intervention distributions. In the absence of this domain knowledge, the causal structure must be discovered from the available observational data. However, observational data are often compatible with multiple causal graphs, making methods that commit to a single structure prone to overconfidence. A principled way to manage this structural uncertainty is via Bayesian inference, which averages over a posterior distribution on possible causal structures and functional mechanisms. Unfortunately, the number of causal structures grows super-exponentially with the number of nodes in the graph, making computations intractable. We propose to circumvent these challenges by using meta-learning to create an end-to-end model: the Model-Averaged Causal Estimation Transformer Neural Process (MACE-TNP). The model is trained to predict the Bayesian model-averaged interventional posterior distribution, and its end-to-end nature bypasses the need for expensive calculations. Empirically, we demonstrate that MACE-TNP outperforms strong Bayesian baselines. Our work established meta-learning as a flexible and scalable paradigm for approximating complex Bayesian causal inference, that can be scaled to increasingly challenging settings in the future.

paragraphs: Estimating what happens after an intervention requires reasoning about causal relationships. Observational data can support several different causal graphs, so selecting just one can produce unjustified confidence. Bayesian inference addresses this by averaging over possible structures and mechanisms, but the rapidly growing number of graphs makes that calculation difficult.

MACE-TNP uses meta-learning to approximate this Bayesian calculation with an end-to-end model. Its training target is the model-averaged posterior distribution of intervention outcomes. The aim is therefore to predict an uncertainty-aware distribution that reflects multiple possible causal explanations, rather than first committing to one graph. Once learned, this mapping bypasses the expensive calculations otherwise needed for model averaging.

The authors report that MACE-TNP empirically outperforms strong Bayesian baselines. They present meta-learning as a flexible and scalable approach to approximating complex causal inference, with more challenging settings left as a direction for future scaling. The contribution matters because it treats uncertainty about causal structure as part of the prediction problem while pursuing a more computationally practical approximation.
summary.tldr: MACE-TNP learns to approximate Bayesian intervention predictions that average over uncertain causal structures and mechanisms.

title: Estimating Interventional Distributions with Uncertain Causal Graphs through Meta-Learning

abstract: Despite their superior performance on a wide range of domains, large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to misuse for generating harmful content, a risk that has been further amplified by various jailbreak attacks. Existing jailbreak attacks mainly follow sequential logic, where LLMs understand and answer each given task one by one. However, concurrency, a natural extension of the sequential scenario, has been largely overlooked. In this work, we first propose a word-level method to enable task concurrency in LLMs, where adjacent words encode divergent intents. Although LLMs maintain strong utility in answering concurrent tasks, which is demonstrated by our evaluations on mathematical and general question-answering benchmarks, we notably observe that combining a harmful task with a benign one significantly reduces the probability of it being filtered by the guardrail, showing the potential risks associated with concurrency in LLMs. Based on these findings, we introduce $\texttt{JAIL-CON}$, an iterative attack framework that $\underline{\text{JAIL}}$breaks LLMs via task $\underline{\text{CON}}$currency. Experiments on widely-used LLMs demonstrate the strong jailbreak capabilities of $\texttt{JAIL-CON}$ compared to existing attacks. Furthermore, when the guardrail is applied as a defense, compared to the sequential answers generated by previous attacks, the concurrent answers in our $\texttt{JAIL-CON}$ exhibit greater stealthiness and are less detectable by the guardrail, highlighting the unique feature of task concurrency in jailbreaking LLMs.

paragraphs: This paper investigates a safety problem that arises when language models handle multiple tasks concurrently. Most jailbreak approaches organize tasks sequentially, so the model encounters and answers them one after another. The authors instead introduce a word-level method in which neighboring words can belong to different intents, allowing tasks to be represented together.

Evaluations on mathematics and general question answering show that models retain strong usefulness under this concurrent arrangement. However, combining a harmful task with a benign one substantially lowers the probability that a guardrail filters it. The same ability to interpret intertwined tasks therefore creates a setting in which useful task performance and safety filtering can come apart.

The authors develop JAIL-CON, an iterative attack framework built around this finding. Experiments on widely used models report strong jailbreak performance relative to existing attacks. Its concurrent answers are also less detectable by the evaluated guardrail than previous attacks’ sequential answers. These findings identify task organization as a consequential factor in evaluating model safeguards.
summary.tldr: JAIL-CON shows that concurrent task processing can preserve language-model usefulness while making harmful requests and responses harder for guardrails to detect.

title: Adjacent Words, Divergent Intents: Jailbreaking Large Language Models via Task Concurrency

abstract: Graph anomaly detection (GAD) has become a critical research area, with successful applications in financial fraud and telecommunications. Traditional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) face significant challenges: at the topology level, they suffer from over-smoothing that averages out anomalous signals; at the feature level, discriminative models struggle when fraudulent nodes obfuscate their features to evade detection. In this paper, we propose a Conditional Graph Anomaly Diffusion Model (CGADM) that addresses these issues through the iterative refinement and denoising reconstruction properties of diffusion models. Our approach incorporates a prior-guided diffusion process that injects a pre-trained conditional anomaly estimator into both forward and reverse diffusion chains, enabling more accurate anomaly detection. For computational efficiency on large-scale graphs, we introduce a prior confidence-aware mechanism that adaptively determines the number of reverse denoising steps based on prior confidence. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that CGADM achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining significant computational advantages for large-scale graph applications.

paragraphs: Detecting unusual nodes in a graph becomes difficult when information sharing blurs the very signals that distinguish them. The paper identifies two obstacles: graph neural networks can smooth away anomalies across connected nodes, and fraudulent nodes can disguise their features. CGADM approaches detection through repeated denoising and reconstruction, using diffusion to refine evidence about anomalous behavior.

Its central design is a diffusion process guided by an existing anomaly estimator. This pretrained estimator influences both the forward process and the reverse reconstruction process, so anomaly-related guidance is incorporated throughout the model. The approach connects prior predictions with iterative refinement rather than relying solely on a discriminative decision from node features.

For large graphs, CGADM also adjusts the number of reverse denoising steps according to confidence in the prior estimator. This makes computation adaptive to the available guidance. Benchmark experiments report state-of-the-art detection performance alongside significant computational advantages, suggesting that guided reconstruction can address detection quality and the cost of applying diffusion at graph scale.
summary.tldr: CGADM uses anomaly-guided diffusion and confidence-dependent denoising to improve graph anomaly detection while reducing computational demands.

title: Conditional Diffusion Anomaly Modeling on Graphs

abstract: Existing multi-view clustering methods employ various strategies to address data-level sparsity and view-level dynamic fusion. However, we identify a critical yet overlooked issue: varying sparsity across views. Cross-view sparsity variations lead to encoding discrepancies, heightening sample-level semantic heterogeneity and making view-level dynamic weighting inappropriate. To tackle these challenges, we propose Adaptive Sparse Autoencoders for Multi-View Clustering (SparseMVC), a framework with three key modules. Initially, the sparse autoencoder probes the sparsity of each view and adaptively adjusts encoding formats via an entropy-matching loss term, mitigating cross-view inconsistencies. Subsequently, the correlation-informed sample reweighting module employs attention mechanisms to assign weights by capturing correlations between early-fused global and view-specific features, reducing encoding discrepancies and balancing contributions. Furthermore, the cross-view distribution alignment module aligns feature distributions during the late fusion stage, accommodating datasets with an arbitrary number of views. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SparseMVC achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance. Our framework advances the field by extending sparsity handling from the data-level to view-level and mitigating the adverse effects of encoding discrepancies through sample-level dynamic weighting. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/cleste-pome/SparseMVC.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups examples described through several representations or sources. This paper identifies differences in sparsity across views as a cause of inconsistent encodings. Those inconsistencies vary between samples, making a single dynamic weight for an entire view inappropriate for addressing the resulting semantic differences.

SparseMVC tackles this through three modules. An adaptive sparse autoencoder measures each view’s sparsity and adjusts its encoding using an entropy-matching objective. An attention-based module then weights samples by examining relationships between early-fused global features and individual-view features. Finally, a late-fusion module aligns feature distributions across views and supports datasets with an arbitrary number of views.

The design addresses representation mismatch before fusion, balances contributions at the sample level, and aligns distributions afterward. Extensive experiments report state-of-the-art clustering performance. The paper’s central contribution is to treat differing sparsity across views as a distinct modeling problem and connect that diagnosis to adaptive encoding and more finely targeted weighting.
summary.tldr: SparseMVC improves multi-view clustering by adapting to differences in sparsity and balancing view contributions separately for individual samples.

title: SparseMVC: Probing Cross-view Sparsity Variations for Multi-view Clustering

abstract: In this paper, we study an online strategic classification problem, where a principal aims to learn an accurate binary linear classifier from sequentially arriving agents. For each agent, the principal announces a classifier. The agent can strategically exercise costly manipulations on his features to be classified as the favorable positive class. The principal is unaware of the true feature-label distribution, but observes all reported features and only labels of positively classified agents. We assume that the true feature-label distribution is given by a halfspace model subject to arbitrary feature-dependent bounded noise (i.e., Massart Noise). This problem faces the combined challenges of agents' strategic feature manipulations, partial label observations, and label noises. We tackle these challenges by a novel learning algorithm. We show that the proposed algorithm yields classifiers that converge to the clairvoyant optimal one and attains a regret rate of $ O(\sqrt{T})$ up to poly-logarithmic and constant factors over $T$ cycles.

paragraphs: This paper studies a classifier that learns from people arriving sequentially, each of whom can pay a cost to alter reported features in pursuit of a favorable decision. The learner announces a binary linear classifier before each interaction. It sees everyone’s reported features but receives true labels only for people assigned the positive class.

Learning therefore combines three obstacles: strategic changes to inputs, selectively observed labels, and noisy outcomes. The analysis assumes the underlying feature-label distribution follows a halfspace model with Massart noise. This allows bounded label noise to depend arbitrarily on the features, making the stated noise assumption part of the scope of the result.

The authors propose an algorithm whose classifiers converge to the clairvoyant optimum under this setup. They also establish regret growing as O(√T), apart from polylogarithmic and constant factors, over T interactions. This gives a quantitative guarantee that accumulated performance loss grows sublinearly, despite manipulation and incomplete feedback. The result concerns learning under the combined modeled challenges rather than treating each in isolation.
summary.tldr: An online classifier achieves convergence and sublinear regret despite strategic feature manipulation, positive-only label feedback, and bounded feature-dependent noise.

title: Online Strategic Classification With Noise and Partial Feedback

abstract: After deployment, machine learning models often experience performance degradation due to shifts in data distribution. It is challenging to assess post-deployment performance accurately when labels are missing or delayed. Existing proxy methods, such as data drift detection, fail to measure the effects of these shifts adequately. To address this, we introduce a new method for evaluating binary classification models on unlabeled tabular data that accurately estimates model performance under covariate shift and call it Probabilistic Adaptive Performance Estimation (PAPE). It can be applied to any performance metric defined with elements of the confusion matrix. Crucially, PAPE operates independently of the original model, relying only on its predictions and probability estimates, and does not need any assumptions about the nature of covariate shift, learning directly from data instead. We tested PAPE using over 900 dataset-model combinations from US census data, assessing its performance against several benchmarks through various metrics. Our findings show that PAPE outperforms other methodologies, making it a superior choice for estimating the performance of binary classification models.

paragraphs: A deployed classifier may encounter inputs whose distribution differs from the data it previously saw. Detecting that shift alone does not reveal how much predictive performance has changed, especially when correct labels are unavailable or delayed. This paper introduces Probabilistic Adaptive Performance Estimation, or PAPE, to estimate performance for binary classifiers on unlabeled tabular data under covariate shift.

PAPE works independently of the classifier's internal architecture, using its predictions and probability estimates. The method supports any metric expressible through confusion-matrix entries, connecting its estimates to familiar ways of measuring classification performance. According to the authors, it learns from data without requiring assumptions about the particular form of the covariate shift.

The evaluation covers more than 900 combinations of datasets and models drawn from US census data, with comparisons across several metrics and benchmarks. PAPE outperforms the other evaluated approaches. These results support estimating the consequences of a distribution change directly, rather than using the presence of drift as a substitute for performance measurement. The stated setting remains binary classification on tabular data under covariate shift.
summary.tldr: PAPE estimates binary-classifier performance on unlabeled tabular data under covariate shift using predictions and probability estimates.

title: Estimating Model Performance Under Covariate Shift Without Labels

abstract: We present Rectified Point Flow, a unified parameterization that formulates pairwise point cloud registration and multi-part shape assembly as a single conditional generative problem. Given unposed point clouds, our method learns a continuous point-wise velocity field that transports noisy points toward their target positions, from which part poses are recovered. In contrast to prior work that regresses part-wise poses with ad-hoc symmetry handling, our method intrinsically learns assembly symmetries without symmetry labels. Together with an overlap-aware encoder focused on inter-part contacts, Rectified Point Flow achieves a new state-of-the-art performance on six benchmarks spanning pairwise registration and shape assembly. Notably, our unified formulation enables effective joint training on diverse datasets, facilitating the learning of shared geometric priors and consequently boosting accuracy. Our code and models are available at https://rectified-pointflow.github.io/.

In contrast to prior work that regresses part-wise poses with ad-hoc symmetry handling, our method intrinsically learns assembly symmetries without symmetry labels. Together with an overlap-aware encoder focused on inter-part contacts, Rectified Point Flow achieves a new state-of-the-art performance on six benchmarks spanning pairwise registration and shape assembly. paragraphs: Aligning two point clouds and assembling several shape parts both require recovering spatial arrangements from unposed geometry. Rectified Point Flow expresses these tasks through one conditional generative formulation. This creates a shared way to represent the problem across pairwise registration and multipart assembly.

The method learns a continuous velocity field for individual points, moving noisy points toward their target locations. Part poses are then recovered from those positions. This formulation learns assembly symmetries without symmetry labels. An overlap-aware encoder emphasizes contacts between parts, giving the model information about the geometric relationships that matter for placing components together.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on six benchmarks covering registration and assembly. The unified formulation also supports joint training across diverse datasets, which improves accuracy by helping the model learn shared geometric priors. The findings suggest that representing pose recovery through point motion can serve multiple geometric tasks and make training data from different sources useful within a common model.
summary.tldr: Rectified Point Flow unifies point-cloud registration and shape assembly by learning point motions from which poses are recovered.

title: Rectified Point Flow: Generic Point Cloud Pose Estimation

abstract: Multi-objective optimization problems (MOPs) are prevalent in numerous real-world applications. Recently, Pareto Set Learning (PSL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving MOPs. PSL can produce a neural network for modeling the set of all Pareto optimal solutions. However, applying PSL to black-box objectives, particularly those exhibiting non-separability, high dimensionality, and/or other complex properties, remains very challenging. To address this issue, we propose leveraging evolution strategies (ESs), a class of specialized black-box optimization algorithms, within the PSL paradigm. Traditional ESs capture the complex dimensional dependencies less efficiently, which can significantly hinder their performance in PSL. To tackle this issue, we suggest encapsulating the dependencies within a neural network, which is then trained using a novel gradient estimation method. The proposed method, termed Neural-ES, is evaluated using a bespoke benchmark suite for black-box PSL. Experimental comparisons with other methods demonstrate the efficiency of Neural-ES, underscoring its ability to learn the Pareto sets of challenging black-box MOPs.

paragraphs: Multi-objective optimization involves finding solutions that balance competing goals. Pareto Set Learning uses a neural network to model the set of Pareto-optimal solutions. Applying this idea to black-box objectives becomes difficult when problems are high-dimensional, involve strong dependencies between dimensions, or have other complex properties.

Neural-ES brings evolution strategies into Pareto Set Learning to address those difficulties. The authors identify inefficient handling of dependencies between dimensions as a weakness of traditional evolution strategies in this setting. Their method represents those dependencies within a neural network and trains it using a new gradient-estimation procedure.

Evaluation uses a benchmark suite designed specifically for black-box Pareto Set Learning. Comparisons with other methods demonstrate the efficiency of Neural-ES and its ability to learn Pareto sets for challenging problems. The approach matters because the learning target is a collection of trade-off solutions, making dependencies across the search space relevant to the whole set. Its contribution combines a neural representation of those dependencies with an optimization strategy suited to black-box objectives.
summary.tldr: Neural-ES models dependencies between dimensions to improve evolution-strategy learning of Pareto sets for difficult black-box objectives.

title: Neural Evolution Strategy for Black-box Pareto Set Learning

abstract: Estimating divergences between probability distributions in a consistent way is of great importance in many machine learning tasks. Although this is a fundamental problem in nonparametric statistics, to the best of our knowledge there has been no finite sample exponential inequality convergence bound derived for any divergence estimators. The main contribution of our work is to provide such a bound for an estimator of Renyi divergence for a smooth Holder class of densities on the d-dimensional unit cube. We also illustrate our theoretical results with a numerical experiment.
originalAbstract: Estimating divergences between probability distributions in a consistent way is of great importance in many machine learning tasks. Although this is a fundamental problem in nonparametric statistics, to the best of our knowledge there has been no finite sample exponential inequality convergence bound derived for any divergence estimators. The main contribution of our work is to provide such a bound for an estimator of Renyi divergence for a smooth Holder class of densities on the d-dimensional unit cube. We also illustrate our theoretical results with a numerical experiment.

paragraphs: Divergence estimation measures differences between probability distributions using observed data. A consistent estimator approaches the desired quantity as the sample grows, but consistency alone does not describe uncertainty at a finite sample size. This paper addresses that more specific question for an estimator of Renyi divergence.

Its main result is a finite-sample exponential concentration bound. Such a bound controls the probability that an estimate deviates from its target, providing a quantitative statement about estimation error before taking an infinite-data limit. The theorem applies to densities in a smooth Holder class defined on the d-dimensional unit cube. Smoothness and the specified domain are therefore part of the result's scope.

The authors identify the lack of such bounds for divergence estimators as a gap, qualified by their knowledge of prior work. They also provide a numerical experiment illustrating the theory. The contribution is principally a statistical guarantee for a particular estimator and density class, giving more precise control over finite-sample behavior than consistency by itself provides.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes a finite-sample exponential concentration bound for Renyi divergence estimation under specified smoothness and domain assumptions.

title: Generalized Exponential Concentration Inequality for Renyi Divergence Estimation

abstract: Lifelong reinforcement learning provides a promising framework for developing versatile agents that can accumulate knowledge over a lifetime of experience and rapidly learn new tasks by building upon prior knowledge. However, current lifelong learning methods exhibit non-vanishing regret as the amount of experience increases, and include limitations that can lead to suboptimal or unsafe control policies. To address these issues, we develop a lifelong policy gradient learner that operates in an adversarial setting to learn multiple tasks online while enforcing safety constraints on the learned policies. We demonstrate, for the first time, sublinear regret for lifelong policy search, and validate our algorithm on several benchmark dynamical systems and an application to quadrotor control.

However, current lifelong learning methods exhibit non-vanishing regret as the amount of experience increases, and include limitations that can lead to suboptimal or unsafe control policies. To address these issues, we develop a lifelong policy gradient learner that operates in an adversarial setting to learn multiple tasks online while enforcing safety constraints on the learned policies. We demonstrate, for the first time, sublinear regret for lifelong policy search, and validate our algorithm on several benchmark dynamical systems and an application to quadrotor control.

paragraphs: Lifelong reinforcement learning seeks agents that accumulate knowledge across tasks and use it to learn new tasks more quickly. The paper identifies two shortcomings in existing methods: regret that does not vanish with increasing experience, and limitations that can produce suboptimal or unsafe control policies. It develops a policy-gradient learner to address both concerns.

The algorithm learns multiple tasks online in an adversarial setting while enforcing safety constraints on the policies it learns. This places constraints within the learning process itself. The objective is to retain the benefits of accumulating experience across tasks while controlling which policies the learner can produce.

The authors establish sublinear regret for lifelong policy search. Sublinear growth means that cumulative regret increases more slowly than the learning horizon, so regret per step diminishes as experience grows. They also validate the method on benchmark dynamical systems and a quadrotor-control application. The contribution combines a long-run learning guarantee with explicit policy constraints and empirical control demonstrations, with safety expressed through the constraints enforced by the algorithm.
summary.tldr: A lifelong policy-gradient learner enforces safety constraints while achieving sublinear regret in an adversarial online setting.

title: Safe Policy Search for Lifelong Reinforcement Learning with Sublinear Regret

abstract: Have you ever wanted to multiply an n \times d matrix X, with n ≫d, on the left by an m \times n matrix \tilde G of i.i.d. Gaussian random variables, but could not afford to do it because it was too slow? In this work we propose a new randomized m \times n matrix T, for which one can compute T ⋅X in only O(nnz(X)) + \tilde O(m^1.5 ⋅d^3) time, for which the total variation distance between the distributions T ⋅X and \tilde G ⋅X is as small as desired, i.e., less than any positive constant. Here nnz(X) denotes the number of non-zero entries of X. Assuming nnz(X) ≫m^1.5 ⋅d^3, this is a significant savings over the naïve O(nnz(X) m) time to compute \tilde G ⋅X. Moreover, since the total variation distance is small, we can provably use T ⋅X in place of \tilde G ⋅X in any application and have the same guarantees as if we were using \tilde G ⋅X, up to a small positive constant in error probability. We apply this transform to nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) and support vector machines (SVM).

paragraphs: The paper tackles the cost of multiplying a tall data matrix by a Gaussian random matrix. It constructs a different randomized transform whose output distribution can be made arbitrarily close, in total variation distance, to the output of the Gaussian multiplication. The objective is to preserve the probabilistic usefulness of the original operation while reducing computation.

For an n-by-d input X and an m-by-n transform, the stated runtime is O(nnz(X)) plus a term of order m^1.5 times d^3 with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here nnz(X) counts nonzero entries. This improves substantially on the direct O(nnz(X) times m) computation when the input’s nonzero count is much larger than m^1.5 times d^3.

The distributional guarantee makes the replacement broadly useful: applications can retain the Gaussian transform’s guarantees up to a small additive change in error probability. Thus, the result concerns downstream probabilistic guarantees as well as speed. The authors apply the transform to nonnegative matrix factorization and support vector machines, illustrating two uses of the construction.
summary.tldr: A randomized transform approximates Gaussian matrix multiplication in distribution, offering substantial speedups under a stated size condition.

title: How to Fake Multiply by a Gaussian Matrix

abstract: Online sparse linear regression is an online problem where an algorithm repeatedly chooses a subset of coordinates to observe in an adversarially chosen feature vector, makes a real-valued prediction, receives the true label, and incurs the squared loss. The goal is to design an online learning algorithm with sublinear regret to the best sparse linear predictor in hindsight. Without any assumptions, this problem is known to be computationally intractable. In this paper, we make the assumption that data matrix satisfies restricted isometry property, and show that this assumption leads to computationally efficient algorithms with sublinear regret for two variants of the problem. In the first variant, the true label is generated according to a sparse linear model with additive Gaussian noise. In the second, the true label is chosen adversarially.

The goal is to design an online learning algorithm with sublinear regret to the best sparse linear predictor in hindsight. Without any assumptions, this problem is known to be computationally intractable. In this paper, we make the assumption that data matrix satisfies restricted isometry property, and show that this assumption leads to computationally efficient algorithms with sublinear regret for two variants of the problem. In the first variant, the true label is generated according to a sparse linear model with additive Gaussian noise. In the second, the true label is chosen adversarially.

paragraphs: This paper studies prediction when examples arrive sequentially and the learner observes only selected features of each example. On every round, it chooses coordinates, predicts a numerical outcome, and then receives the true label and a squared-error loss. The feature vectors may be chosen adversarially, making feature selection part of the learning challenge.

The target is sublinear regret against the best sparse linear predictor chosen after seeing all the data. This means the accumulated disadvantage relative to that predictor grows more slowly than the number of rounds. Without assumptions, obtaining an efficient solution is computationally intractable. The authors instead assume the data matrix satisfies the restricted isometry property, a structural condition concerning sparse directions.

Under that assumption, they obtain computationally efficient algorithms with sublinear regret for two versions of the problem. One generates labels from a sparse linear model with additive Gaussian noise; the other allows adversarial labels. The result shows how the stated structural assumption enables efficient learning even with selective feature observation and, in the second variant, adversarial outcomes.
summary.tldr: A restricted isometry assumption enables efficient online sparse regression with sublinear regret despite selective feature observation.

title: Adaptive Feature Selection: Computationally Efficient Online Sparse Linear Regression under RIP

abstract: Ensemble methods are arguably the most trustworthy techniques for boosting the performance of machine learning models. Popular independent ensembles (IE) relying on naive averaging/voting scheme have been of typical choice for most applications involving deep neural networks, but they do not consider advanced collaboration among ensemble models. In this paper, we propose new ensemble methods specialized for deep neural networks, called confident multiple choice learning (CMCL): it is a variant of multiple choice learning (MCL) via addressing its overconfidence issue.In particular, the proposed major components of CMCL beyond the original MCL scheme are (i) new loss, i.e., confident oracle loss, (ii) new architecture, i.e., feature sharing and (iii) new training method, i.e., stochastic labeling. We demonstrate the effect of CMCL via experiments on the image classification on CIFAR and SVHN, and the foreground-background segmentation on the iCoseg. In particular, CMCL using 5 residual networks provides 14.05\% and 6.60\% relative reductions in the top-1 error rates from the corresponding IE scheme for the classification task on CIFAR and SVHN, respectively.

paragraphs: Combining several neural networks can improve prediction, but independently training them and then averaging or voting leaves their collaboration largely unstructured. This paper introduces confident multiple choice learning, or CMCL, as an ensemble method designed specifically for deep networks. It builds on multiple choice learning while addressing an overconfidence issue in that approach.

CMCL changes three parts of the ensemble: its objective, architecture, and training procedure. These components are a confident oracle loss, feature sharing, and stochastic labeling. Together, they make collaboration part of how the models are trained, rather than relying solely on a final aggregation of independently learned predictions.

The authors evaluate CMCL on image classification using CIFAR and SVHN and on foreground-background segmentation using iCoseg. With five residual networks, CMCL reduces top-1 classification error relative to the corresponding independent ensemble by 14.05% on CIFAR and 6.60% on SVHN. These are relative error reductions, supporting the benefits of coordinated ensemble learning in the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: CMCL addresses overconfidence in multiple choice learning through a new loss, feature sharing, and stochastic labeling, improving reported ensemble results.

title: Confident Multiple Choice Learning

abstract: Tensor decomposition is an important problem with many applications across several disciplines, and a popular approach for this problem is the tensor power method. However, previous works with theoretical guarantee based on this approach can only find the top eigenvectors one after one, unlike the case for matrices. In this paper, we show how to find the eigenvectors simultaneously with the help of a new initialization procedure. This allows us to achieve a better running time in the batch setting, as well as a lower sample complexity in the streaming setting.

paragraphs: Tensor decomposition is used across several disciplines, and the tensor power method is a common approach to the problem. Earlier theoretically guaranteed versions recover leading eigenvectors one at a time. This paper addresses whether those eigenvectors can instead be found simultaneously, bringing a capability available for matrices into the tensor setting.

The central contribution is a new initialization procedure that enables simultaneous recovery through power iteration. Initialization is therefore a key part of the change in how the decomposition is computed. The method moves from a sequence of individual eigenvector searches to a procedure that finds multiple eigenvectors together, with theoretical support for that approach.

The authors report two resulting improvements: better running time when working with a batch of data and lower sample complexity when processing data in a streaming setting. These address distinct resources, computation in one case and required observations in the other. The work shows how changing initialization and recovery together can improve both aspects of tensor decomposition.
summary.tldr: A new initialization enables simultaneous tensor eigenvector recovery, improving batch running time and streaming sample complexity.

title: Tensor Decomposition via Simultaneous Power Iteration

abstract: A standard way to obtain convergence guarantees in stochastic convex optimization is to run an online learning algorithm and then output the average of its iterates: the actual iterates of the online learning algorithm do not come with individual guarantees. We close this gap by introducing a black-box modification to any online learning algorithm whose iterates converge to the optimum in stochastic scenarios. We then consider the case of smooth losses, and show that combining our approach with optimistic online learning algorithms immediately yields a fast convergence rate of $O(L/T^{3/2}+\sigma/\sqrt{T})$ on $L$-smooth problems with $\sigma^2$ variance in the gradients. Finally, we provide a reduction that converts any adaptive online algorithm into one that obtains the optimal accelerated rate of $\tilde O(L/T^2 + \sigma/\sqrt{T})$, while still maintaining $\tilde O(1/\sqrt{T})$ convergence in the non-smooth setting. Importantly, our algorithms adapt to $L$ and $\sigma$ automatically: they do not need to know either to obtain these rates.

We then consider the case of smooth losses, and show that combining our approach with optimistic online learning algorithms immediately yields a fast convergence rate of $O(L/T^{3/2}+\sigma/\sqrt{T})$ on $L$-smooth problems with $\sigma^2$ variance in the gradients. paragraphs: A standard route from online learning to stochastic convex optimization guarantees the quality of an average of successive iterates. The individual iterates do not automatically receive comparable guarantees. This paper introduces a black-box modification of online learning algorithms so that the resulting iterates themselves converge to the optimum in stochastic settings.

For smooth losses, the authors combine this modification with optimistic online learning. They obtain a convergence rate of O(L/T^(3/2) + σ/√T), where T counts iterations, L describes smoothness, and σ² is the gradient variance. The two terms distinguish the contribution associated with smoothness from the contribution associated with noisy gradients.

A further reduction converts adaptive online algorithms into methods with the optimal accelerated rate Õ(L/T² + σ/√T), while retaining Õ(1/√T) convergence for nonsmooth problems. The tilde notation suppresses logarithmic factors. These methods automatically adapt to L and σ without requiring either in advance, making the stated guarantees compatible with uncertainty about the problem's smoothness and noise.
summary.tldr: Black-box reductions give individual optimization iterates convergence guarantees and adaptive accelerated rates without prior knowledge of smoothness or gradient noise.

title: Anytime Online-to-Batch, Optimism and Acceleration

abstract: Extensive-form games (EFGs) are a common model of multi-agent interactions with imperfect information. State-of-the-art algorithms for solving these games typically perform full walks of the game tree that can prove prohibitively slow in large games. Alternatively, sampling-based methods such as Monte Carlo Counterfactual Regret Minimization walk one or more trajectories through the tree, touching only a fraction of the nodes on each iteration, at the expense of requiring more iterations to converge due to the variance of sampled values. In this paper, we extend recent work that uses baseline estimates to reduce this variance. We introduce a framework of baseline-corrected values in EFGs that generalizes the previous work. Within our framework, we propose new baseline functions that result in significantly reduced variance compared to existing techniques. We show that one particular choice of such a function — predictive baseline — is provably optimal under certain sampling schemes. This allows for efficient computation of zero-variance value estimates even along sampled trajectories.

paragraphs: Extensive-form games describe multi-agent interactions with imperfect information using a game tree. Solving large games by repeatedly traversing the full tree can be prohibitively slow. Sampling a few trajectories reduces the work per iteration, but introduces noisy value estimates that can increase the number of iterations needed for convergence.

The paper develops a general framework for correcting sampled values with baseline estimates. It extends earlier baseline-based variance reduction and introduces new baseline functions that substantially reduce variance compared with existing techniques. The goal is to make limited visits to the game tree more informative without requiring full traversals.

One proposed function, the predictive baseline, is proved optimal under certain sampling schemes. Under those conditions, the framework allows zero-variance value estimates to be computed efficiently even along sampled trajectories. The qualification about sampling matters: the result establishes a particularly strong outcome for supported schemes. It shows how an appropriate baseline can remove the sampling variability in these estimates while retaining trajectory-based computation.
summary.tldr: A generalized baseline framework reduces game-tree sampling variance and enables zero-variance value estimates under certain sampling schemes.

title: Low-Variance and Zero-Variance Baselines for Extensive-Form Games

abstract: Motivated by economic applications such as recommender systems, we study the behavior of stochastic bandits algorithms under \emph{strategic behavior} conducted by rational actors, i.e., the arms. Each arm is a \emph{self-interested} strategic player who can modify its own reward whenever pulled, subject to a cross-period budget constraint, in order to maximize its own expected number of times of being pulled. We analyze the robustness of three popular bandit algorithms: UCB, $\varepsilon$-Greedy, and Thompson Sampling. We prove that all three algorithms achieve a regret upper bound $\mathcal{O}(\max \{ B, K\ln T\})$ where $B$ is the total budget across arms, $K$ is the total number of arms and $T$ is the running time of the algorithms. This regret guarantee holds for \emph{arbitrary adaptive} manipulation strategy of arms. Our second set of main results shows that this regret bound is \emph{tight}— in fact, for UCB, it is tight even when we restrict the arms’ manipulation strategies to form a \emph{Nash equilibrium}. We do so by characterizing the Nash equilibrium of the game induced by arms’ strategic manipulations and show a regret lower bound of $\Omega(\max \{ B, K\ln T\})$ at the equilibrium.

paragraphs: In some bandit applications, the available options correspond to self-interested actors who want to be selected more often. This paper models each arm as a strategic player that can alter its reported reward when selected. Each player faces a budget across time and aims to maximize its expected number of selections.

The authors analyze UCB, epsilon-Greedy, and Thompson Sampling under this manipulation model. All three receive a regret upper bound of order max{B, K ln T}, where B is the total manipulation budget, K the number of arms, and T the time horizon. The guarantee covers arbitrary adaptive manipulation strategies, allowing arms to change their behavior as the process unfolds.

The authors also prove that the bound is tight. For UCB, they establish tightness even when the arms’ strategies form a Nash equilibrium, by characterizing that equilibrium and proving a matching-order lower bound. Thus, the budget-dependent regret is not merely an artifact of allowing arbitrary manipulation; it can also arise from equilibrium behavior among self-interested arms.
summary.tldr: Three standard bandit algorithms have tight budget-dependent regret guarantees against strategic reward manipulation, with UCB’s lower bound holding even at Nash equilibrium.

title: The Intrinsic Robustness of Stochastic Bandits to Strategic Manipulation

abstract: How can multiple distributed entities train a shared deep net on their private data while protecting data privacy? This paper introduces InstaHide, a simple encryption of training images. Encrypted images can be used in standard deep learning pipelines (PyTorch, Federated Learning etc.) with no additional setup or infrastructure. The encryption has a minor effect on test accuracy (unlike differential privacy). Encryption consists of mixing the image with a set of other images (in the sense of Mixup data augmentation technique (Zhang et al., 2018)) followed by applying a random pixel-wise mask on the mixed image. Other contributions of this paper are: (a) Use of large public dataset of images (e.g. ImageNet) for mixing during encryption; this improves security. (b) Experiments demonstrating effectiveness in protecting privacy against known attacks while preserving model accuracy. (c) Theoretical analysis showing that successfully attacking privacy requires attackers to solve a difficult computational problem. (d) Demonstration that Mixup alone is insecure as (contrary to recent proposals), by showing some efficient attacks. (e) Release of a challenge dataset to allow design of new attacks.

paragraphs: InstaHide addresses training a shared neural network across entities that wish to protect their private images. The proposed transformation mixes each image with other images and then applies a random mask at the pixel level. The resulting images can enter standard deep learning and federated learning pipelines without additional infrastructure.

The paper reports only a minor effect on test accuracy and studies mixing with images from a large public dataset as a way to improve security. Its experiments demonstrate protection against the known attacks evaluated while preserving model accuracy. A theoretical analysis also connects successful privacy attacks to solving a difficult computational problem.

The authors separately show that Mixup alone is insecure by constructing efficient attacks, distinguishing that component from the full InstaHide procedure. They also release a challenge dataset to support development of further attacks. The stated evidence combines practical attack evaluations and computational analysis; the empirical protection described concerns the tested attacks rather than establishing immunity to every possible attack.
summary.tldr: InstaHide combines image mixing and random pixel masks to protect training images, with reported accuracy preservation and resistance to evaluated attacks.

title: InstaHide: Instance-hiding Schemes for Private Distributed Learning

abstract: This paper studies few-shot relation extraction, which aims at predicting the relation for a pair of entities in a sentence by training with a few labeled examples in each relation. To more effectively generalize to new relations, in this paper we study the relationships between different relations and propose to leverage a global relation graph. We propose a novel Bayesian meta-learning approach to effectively learn the posterior distribution of the prototype vectors of relations, where the initial prior of the prototype vectors is parameterized with a graph neural network on the global relation graph. Moreover, to effectively optimize the posterior distribution of the prototype vectors, we propose to use the stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, which is related to the MAML algorithm but is able to handle the uncertainty of the prototype vectors. The whole framework can be effectively and efficiently optimized in an end-to-end fashion. Experiments on two benchmark datasets prove the effectiveness of our proposed approach against competitive baselines in both the few-shot and zero-shot settings.

paragraphs: Few-shot relation extraction identifies the relationship between two entities in a sentence using only a small number of labeled examples per relation. This paper seeks better generalization to new relations by using information about how different relations are connected. It represents that information in a global relation graph.

The method gives each relation a prototype vector and learns a posterior distribution over these prototypes. A graph neural network operating on the relation graph parameterizes their initial prior. This lets the graph inform what the model expects before adapting to the available examples, while the posterior represents uncertainty about the resulting relation prototypes.

To optimize these distributions, the authors use stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, which they relate to MAML while emphasizing its ability to handle prototype uncertainty. The complete framework supports efficient end-to-end optimization. The central contribution is bringing relation structure and uncertainty together when direct labeled evidence for a relation is scarce.
summary.tldr: A relation graph supplies Bayesian priors for uncertain relation prototypes, improving extraction when labeled examples are scarce or absent.

title: Few-shot Relation Extraction via Bayesian Meta-learning on Relation Graphs

abstract: Particle-based Variational Inference methods (ParVIs), like Stein Variational Gradient Descent, are nonparametric variational inference methods that optimize a set of particles to best approximate a target distribution. ParVIs have been proposed as efficient approximate inference algorithms and as potential alternatives to MCMC methods. However, to our knowledge, the quality of the posterior approximation of particles from ParVIs has not been examined before for large-scale Bayesian inference problems. We conduct this analysis and evaluate the sample quality of particles produced by ParVIs, and we find that existing ParVI approaches using stochastic gradients converge insufficiently fast under sample quality metrics. We propose a novel variance reduction and quasi-Newton preconditioning framework for ParVIs, by leveraging the Riemannian structure of the Wasserstein space and advanced Riemannian optimization algorithms. Experimental results demonstrate the accelerated convergence of variance reduction and quasi-Newton methods for ParVIs for accurate posterior inference in large-scale and ill-conditioned problems.

paragraphs: Particle-based variational inference approximates a target distribution by optimizing a collection of particles. Methods such as Stein Variational Gradient Descent have been proposed as efficient approximate inference procedures and possible alternatives to MCMC. This paper examines the quality of the posterior approximations they produce in large-scale Bayesian inference, making particle sample quality central to the evaluation.

The analysis finds that existing particle methods using stochastic gradients converge too slowly under sample-quality metrics. To address this, the authors propose a framework combining variance reduction with quasi-Newton preconditioning. They build the framework using the Riemannian structure of Wasserstein space and advanced Riemannian optimization methods, connecting the optimization changes to the geometry of distributions.

Experiments demonstrate accelerated convergence for accurate posterior inference in large-scale and ill-conditioned problems. The contribution concerns how quickly the particles form a useful approximation, rather than merely whether optimization can be performed. It also highlights the importance of evaluating the resulting posterior samples when judging the practical efficiency of particle-based inference methods.
summary.tldr: Variance reduction and quasi-Newton preconditioning accelerate particle-based posterior inference in large-scale and ill-conditioned problems.

title: Variance Reduction and Quasi-Newton for Particle-Based Variational Inference

abstract: The article introduces an elementary cost and storage reduction method for spectral clustering and principal component analysis. The method consists in randomly “puncturing” both the data matrix $X\in\mathbb{C}^{p\times n}$ (or $\mathbb{R}^{p\times n}$) and its corresponding kernel (Gram) matrix $K$ through Bernoulli masks: $S\in\{0,1\}^{p\times n}$ for $X$ and $B\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$ for $K$. The resulting “two-way punctured” kernel is thus given by $K=\frac1p[(X\odot S)^\H (X\odot S)]\odot B$. We demonstrate that, for $X$ composed of independent columns drawn from a Gaussian mixture model, as $n,p\to\infty$ with $p/n\to c_0\in(0,\infty)$, the spectral behavior of $K$ – its limiting eigenvalue distribution, as well as its isolated eigenvalues and eigenvectors – is fully tractable and exhibits a series of counter-intuitive phenomena. We notably prove, and empirically confirm on various image databases, that it is possible to drastically puncture the data, thereby providing possibly huge computational and storage gains, for a virtually constant (clustering or PCA) performance. This preliminary study opens as such the path towards rethinking, from a large dimensional standpoint, computational and storage costs in elementary machine learning models.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis and spectral clustering rely on matrix structure that can be costly to compute and store. This paper proposes randomly removing entries at two stages: first in the data matrix, then in its corresponding Gram matrix. Bernoulli masks determine which entries remain, producing what the authors call a two-way punctured kernel.

The theoretical analysis assumes independent data columns drawn from a Gaussian mixture. It studies the limit where both sample count and dimension grow while their ratio approaches a positive finite constant. In that setting, the authors characterize the kernel’s limiting eigenvalue distribution, isolated eigenvalues, and eigenvectors, making the consequences of puncturing mathematically tractable.

The analysis shows that substantial puncturing can be possible with nearly unchanged clustering or PCA performance, and image-database experiments support this finding. Such behavior offers potentially large computational and storage gains. The result identifies an opportunity to retain useful spectral information despite extensive removal of entries, within the analyzed regime and the demonstrated applications.
summary.tldr: Randomly puncturing both data and Gram matrices can preserve PCA or clustering performance while potentially greatly reducing computation and storage.

title: Two-way kernel matrix puncturing: towards resource-efficient PCA and spectral clustering

abstract: While maximizing deep neural networks’ (DNNs’) acceleration efficiency requires a joint search/design of three different yet highly coupled aspects, including the networks, bitwidths, and accelerators, the challenges associated with such a joint search have not yet been fully understood and addressed. The key challenges include (1) the dilemma of whether to explode the memory consumption due to the huge joint space or achieve sub-optimal designs, (2) the discrete nature of the accelerator design space that is coupled yet different from that of the networks and bitwidths, and (3) the chicken and egg problem associated with network-accelerator co-search, i.e., co-search requires operation-wise hardware cost, which is lacking during search as the optimal accelerator depending on the whole network is still unknown during search. To tackle these daunting challenges towards optimal and fast development of DNN accelerators, we propose a framework dubbed Auto-NBA to enable jointly searching for the Networks, Bitwidths, and Accelerators, by efficiently localizing the optimal design within the huge joint design space for each target dataset and acceleration specification. Our Auto-NBA integrates a heterogeneous sampling strategy to achieve unbiased search with constant memory consumption, and a novel joint-search pipeline equipped with a generic differentiable accelerator search engine. Extensive experiments and ablation studies validate that both Auto-NBA generated networks and accelerators consistently outperform state-of-the-art designs (including co-search/exploration techniques, hardware-aware NAS methods, and DNN accelerators), in terms of search time, task accuracy, and accelerator efficiency. Our codes are available at: https://github.com/RICE-EIC/Auto-NBA.

paragraphs: Efficient neural-network acceleration depends on three connected choices: the network architecture, numerical precision, and accelerator design. Auto-NBA searches these choices together. The challenge is that their combined design space is large, accelerator choices are discrete, and the hardware cost of a network operation depends on an accelerator that has not yet been selected.

The framework combines a heterogeneous sampling strategy with a joint-search pipeline and a differentiable accelerator search engine. The sampling strategy provides unbiased search with constant memory consumption. The pipeline handles the dependence between network and hardware decisions while searching for designs suited to a target dataset and acceleration specification.

Experiments and ablation studies report that the resulting networks and accelerators consistently outperform the evaluated state-of-the-art designs in search time, task accuracy, and accelerator efficiency. These findings support treating the three design choices as a connected optimization problem. The contribution is both a way to manage the search’s computational burden and a method for coordinating decisions whose costs and benefits depend on one another.
summary.tldr: Auto-NBA jointly searches network architectures, numerical precisions, and accelerators using a memory-efficient framework that improves evaluated design outcomes.

title: Auto-NBA: Efficient and Effective Search Over the Joint Space of Networks, Bitwidths, and Accelerators

abstract: Pre-trained representations are becoming crucial for many NLP and perception tasks. While representation learning in NLP has transitioned to training on raw text without human annotations, visual and vision-language representations still rely heavily on curated training datasets that are expensive or require expert knowledge. For vision applications, representations are mostly learned using datasets with explicit class labels such as ImageNet or OpenImages. For vision-language, popular datasets like Conceptual Captions, MSCOCO, or CLIP all involve a non-trivial data collection (and cleaning) process. This costly curation process limits the size of datasets and hence hinders the scaling of trained models. In this paper, we leverage a noisy dataset of over one billion image alt-text pairs, obtained without expensive filtering or post-processing steps in the Conceptual Captions dataset. A simple dual-encoder architecture learns to align visual and language representations of the image and text pairs using a contrastive loss. We show that the scale of our corpus can make up for its noise and leads to state-of-the-art representations even with such a simple learning scheme. Our visual representation achieves strong performance when transferred to classification tasks such as ImageNet and VTAB. The aligned visual and language representations enables zero-shot image classification and also set new state-of-the-art results on Flickr30K and MSCOCO image-text retrieval benchmarks, even when compared with more sophisticated cross-attention models. The representations also enable cross-modality search with complex text and text + image queries.

paragraphs: Learning visual and vision-language representations often depends on expensive dataset curation, which limits training scale. This paper explores whether a much larger, noisier collection can support strong representations with a simple learning method. It uses more than one billion image and alt-text pairs obtained without expensive filtering or post-processing.
