They support cross-modality search using complex text queries and combined text-and-image queries. These findings demonstrate the value of large-scale noisy supervision for both visual recognition and language-linked retrieval, without making scale a universal guarantee against arbitrary data noise.
summary.tldr: Training a simple dual encoder on over one billion noisy image–text pairs produces strong transferable visual and aligned vision-language representations.

title: Scaling Up Visual and Vision-Language Representation Learning With Noisy Text Supervision

abstract: This paper presents a novel approach for hierarchical time series forecasting that produces coherent, probabilistic forecasts without requiring any explicit post-processing reconciliation. Unlike the state-of-the-art, the proposed method simultaneously learns from all time series in the hierarchy and incorporates the reconciliation step into a single trainable model. This is achieved by applying the reparameterization trick and casting reconciliation as an optimization problem with a closed-form solution. These model features make end-to-end learning of hierarchical forecasts possible, while accomplishing the challenging task of generating forecasts that are both probabilistic and coherent. Importantly, our approach also accommodates general aggregation constraints including grouped and temporal hierarchies. An extensive empirical evaluation on real-world hierarchical datasets demonstrates the advantages of the proposed approach over the state-of-the-art.

Unlike the state-of-the-art, the proposed method simultaneously learns from all time series in the hierarchy and incorporates the reconciliation step into a single trainable model. This is achieved by applying the reparameterization trick and casting reconciliation as an optimization problem with a closed-form solution. These model features make end-to-end learning of hierarchical forecasts possible, while accomplishing the challenging task of generating forecasts that are both probabilistic and coherent. paragraphs: Hierarchical forecasting must describe uncertainty while respecting relationships between series at different aggregation levels. Forecasts are coherent when those relationships hold together. This paper presents a model that learns probabilistic forecasts and their reconciliation in one training process, removing the need for an explicit reconciliation stage after prediction.

The model learns simultaneously from all series in the hierarchy. It expresses reconciliation as an optimization problem with a closed-form solution and uses the reparameterization trick to support end-to-end learning. These components allow the consistency-enforcing operation to participate in training, connecting what the model learns with the aggregation relationships its forecasts must satisfy.

The approach also supports broader aggregation constraints, including grouped and temporal hierarchies. Its contribution therefore extends beyond a single form of hierarchical organization. An extensive evaluation on real-world hierarchical datasets demonstrates advantages over the state of the art. The stated findings support integrating reconciliation into a trainable probabilistic model as a way to produce forecasts that express uncertainty and agree across the required aggregations.
summary.tldr: A single trainable model incorporates reconciliation to produce probabilistic hierarchical forecasts that satisfy aggregation constraints.

title: End-to-End Learning of Coherent Probabilistic Forecasts for Hierarchical Time Series

abstract: We propose a residual randomization procedure designed for robust inference using Lasso estimates in the high-dimensional setting. Compared to earlier work that focuses on sub-Gaussian errors, the proposed procedure is designed to work robustly in settings that also include heavy-tailed covariates and errors. Moreover, our procedure can be valid under clustered errors, which is important in practice, but has been largely overlooked by earlier work. Through extensive simulations, we illustrate our method’s wider range of applicability as suggested by theory. In particular, we show that our method outperforms state-of-art methods in challenging, yet more realistic, settings where the distribution of covariates is heavy-tailed or the sample size is small, while it remains competitive in standard, “well behaved" settings previously studied in the literature.

Compared to earlier work that focuses on sub-Gaussian errors, the proposed procedure is designed to work robustly in settings that also include heavy-tailed covariates and errors. Moreover, our procedure can be valid under clustered errors, which is important in practice, but has been largely overlooked by earlier work. Through extensive simulations, we illustrate our method’s wider range of applicability as suggested by theory. In particular, we show that our method outperforms state-of-art methods in challenging, yet more realistic, settings where the distribution of covariates is heavy-tailed or the sample size is small, while it remains competitive in standard, “well behaved" settings previously studied in the literature.

paragraphs: This paper addresses statistical inference built on Lasso estimates in high-dimensional linear models. Its emphasis is robustness when the data depart from the well-behaved error assumptions common in earlier work. The authors propose a residual randomization procedure designed to accommodate settings that include heavy-tailed covariates and errors.

Heavy tails make unusually large observations more relevant to the analysis. The procedure also can remain valid when errors are clustered, so the inferential setting need not always treat errors as independent across observations. The authors highlight clustered errors as practically important and comparatively neglected in previous work. These features broaden the types of data conditions considered by the method.

Extensive simulations illustrate the wider applicability suggested by the theory. The method outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives in challenging evaluated settings involving heavy-tailed covariates or small samples, while remaining competitive in standard, well-behaved settings. The contribution is therefore a more robust route to inference using Lasso estimates, supported by theory and empirical comparisons across both difficult and conventional data regimes.
summary.tldr: Residual randomization supports robust inference from high-dimensional Lasso estimates in settings including heavy tails and potentially clustered errors.

title: Robust Inference for High-Dimensional Linear Models via Residual Randomization

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches rely on discrete-time state transition models whereas physical systems and the vast majority of control tasks operate in continuous-time. To avoid time-discretization approximation of the underlying process, we propose a continuous-time MBRL framework based on a novel actor-critic method. Our approach also infers the unknown state evolution differentials with Bayesian neural ordinary differential equations (ODE) to account for epistemic uncertainty. We implement and test our method on a new ODE-RL suite that explicitly solves continuous-time control systems. Our experiments illustrate that the model is robust against irregular and noisy data, and can solve classic control problems in a sample-efficient manner.
originalAbstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches rely on discrete-time state transition models whereas physical systems and the vast majority of control tasks operate in continuous-time. To avoid time-discretization approximation of the underlying process, we propose a continuous-time MBRL framework based on a novel actor-critic method. Our approach also infers the unknown state evolution differentials with Bayesian neural ordinary differential equations (ODE) to account for epistemic uncertainty. We implement and test our method on a new ODE-RL suite that explicitly solves continuous-time control systems. Our experiments illustrate that the model is robust against irregular and noisy data, and can solve classic control problems in a sample-efficient manner.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning uses a learned description of how a system evolves to support decision-making. The paper points out a mismatch: these models usually describe transitions at discrete time steps, while physical systems and many control tasks evolve continuously. It proposes modeling the dynamics directly in continuous time to avoid approximating the underlying process through time discretization.

The framework combines a new actor-critic method with Bayesian neural ordinary differential equations. These equations learn the unknown rates of state evolution. Their Bayesian formulation accounts for epistemic uncertainty, meaning uncertainty about dynamics that the model has not yet established from data. The dynamics model therefore represents both an evolution rule and uncertainty about that rule.

The authors implement the approach in a new ODE-RL suite that explicitly solves continuous-time control systems. Experiments illustrate robustness to irregular and noisy data, together with sample-efficient solutions to classic control problems. The findings support continuous-time modeling as a useful foundation for learning control from imperfect observations.
summary.tldr: A continuous-time actor-critic framework learns uncertain dynamics with Bayesian neural ODEs and demonstrates sample-efficient control from irregular, noisy data.

title: Continuous-time Model-based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: To rapidly learn a new task, it is often essential for agents to explore efficiently - especially when performance matters from the first timestep. One way to learn such behaviour is via meta-learning. Many existing methods however rely on dense rewards for meta-training, and can fail catastrophically if the rewards are sparse. Without a suitable reward signal, the need for exploration during meta-training is exacerbated. To address this, we propose HyperX, which uses novel reward bonuses for meta-training to explore in approximate hyper-state space (where hyper-states represent the environment state and the agent’s task belief). We show empirically that HyperX meta-learns better task-exploration and adapts more successfully to new tasks than existing methods.

Without a suitable reward signal, the need for exploration during meta-training is exacerbated. paragraphs: An agent facing a new task often needs to explore before it knows how to obtain rewards. Meta-learning aims to teach this adaptation behavior across tasks, but the training process itself also needs useful exploration. Existing approaches can rely on frequent rewards during meta-training and fail severely when rewards are sparse, leaving little feedback about which behavior is productive.

HyperX addresses this problem by adding reward bonuses during meta-training. These bonuses encourage exploration in an approximate hyper-state space, where a hyper-state combines the current environment state with the agent's belief about its task. Including task belief makes the exploration target reflect both where the agent is and what it currently understands about the problem.

Experiments show that HyperX learns better task-exploration behavior and adapts more successfully to new tasks than existing methods. The contribution is an exploration mechanism for the process of learning to adapt: improving the experiences available during meta-training helps the agent acquire behavior useful when it later encounters an unfamiliar task.
summary.tldr: HyperX rewards exploration of environment states and task beliefs during meta-training, improving adaptation to new tasks empirically.

title: Exploration in Approximate Hyper-State Space for Meta Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Algorithmic recourse seeks to provide actionable recommendations for individuals to overcome unfavorable classification outcomes from automated decision-making systems. Recourse recommendations should ideally be robust to reasonably small uncertainty in the features of the individual seeking recourse. In this work, we formulate the adversarially robust recourse problem and show that recourse methods that offer minimally costly recourse fail to be robust. We then present methods for generating adversarially robust recourse for linear and for differentiable classifiers. Finally, we show that regularizing the decision-making classifier to behave locally linearly and to rely more strongly on actionable features facilitates the existence of adversarially robust recourse.

Recourse recommendations should ideally be robust to reasonably small uncertainty in the features of the individual seeking recourse. In this work, we formulate the adversarially robust recourse problem and show that recourse methods that offer minimally costly recourse fail to be robust. We then present methods for generating adversarially robust recourse for linear and for differentiable classifiers. Finally, we show that regularizing the decision-making classifier to behave locally linearly and to rely more strongly on actionable features facilitates the existence of adversarially robust recourse.

paragraphs: Algorithmic recourse recommends actions someone can take to obtain a favorable decision from a classifier. A recommendation is less useful if small uncertainty in that person’s recorded features causes it to fail. This paper formalizes recourse that must withstand such uncertainty, treating robustness as part of the recommendation problem.

The authors show that methods offering minimally costly recourse fail to be robust. This reveals a tension between finding the cheapest change and finding one whose success survives small feature perturbations. They then develop methods for producing adversarially robust recourse for linear classifiers and for differentiable classifiers, addressing robustness directly rather than considering only action cost.

The paper also examines how the classifier itself can make reliable recourse easier to obtain. Regularizing it to behave locally like a linear model and to rely more heavily on actionable features facilitates the existence of robust recommendations. This finding connects decision-model design with recourse quality: robustness depends partly on how the classifier uses information, as well as on the recommendation procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper develops recourse methods robust to feature uncertainty and shows how classifier design can help such recommendations exist.

title: On the Adversarial Robustness of Causal Algorithmic Recourse

abstract: This work develops mixup for graph data. Mixup has shown superiority in improving the generalization and robustness of neural networks by interpolating features and labels between two random samples. Traditionally, Mixup can work on regular, grid-like, and Euclidean data such as image or tabular data. However, it is challenging to directly adopt Mixup to augment graph data because different graphs typically: 1) have different numbers of nodes; 2) are not readily aligned; and 3) have unique typologies in non-Euclidean space. To this end, we propose G-Mixup to augment graphs for graph classification by interpolating the generator (i.e., graphon) of different classes of graphs. Specifically, we first use graphs within the same class to estimate a graphon. Then, instead of directly manipulating graphs, we interpolate graphons of different classes in the Euclidean space to get mixed graphons, where the synthetic graphs are generated through sampling based on the mixed graphons. Extensive experiments show that G-Mixup substantially improves the generalization and robustness of GNNs.

paragraphs: Mixup creates training examples by interpolating between existing samples and their labels. Applying that idea directly to graphs is difficult because graphs can have different numbers of nodes, lack a natural alignment, and have different connectivity structures. This paper moves the interpolation to a representation of how graphs are generated.

G-Mixup first estimates a graphon for each class using graphs belonging to that class. A graphon acts as a graph generator. The method interpolates between these class generators in Euclidean space and then samples synthetic graphs from the resulting mixed generator. It therefore constructs new graphs without requiring a direct correspondence between the nodes of two individual input graphs.

The approach matters because it gives graph augmentation a shared space in which mixing is feasible despite differences in graph size and structure. Extensive experiments report substantial improvements in the generalization and robustness of graph neural networks. These results support generator-level interpolation as a useful way to bring mixup's benefits to graph classification, where ordinary sample-level interpolation is difficult to define.
summary.tldr: G-Mixup augments graph datasets by mixing class-level graph generators and sampling new graphs from the mixtures.

title: G-Mixup: Graph Data Augmentation for Graph Classification

abstract: Multi-head attention is a driving force behind state-of-the-art transformers, which achieve remarkable performance across a variety of natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision tasks. It has been observed that for many applications, those attention heads learn redundant embedding, and most of them can be removed without degrading the performance of the model. Inspired by this observation, we propose Transformer with a Mixture of Gaussian Keys (Transformer-MGK), a novel transformer architecture that replaces redundant heads in transformers with a mixture of keys at each head. These mixtures of keys follow a Gaussian mixture model and allow each attention head to focus on different parts of the input sequence efficiently. Compared to its conventional transformer counterpart, Transformer-MGK accelerates training and inference, has fewer parameters, and requires fewer FLOPs to compute while achieving comparable or better accuracy across tasks. Transformer-MGK can also be easily extended to use with linear attention. We empirically demonstrate the advantage of Transformer-MGK in a range of practical applications, including language modeling and tasks that involve very long sequences. On the Wikitext-103 and Long Range Arena benchmark, Transformer-MGKs with 4 heads attain comparable or better performance to the baseline transformers with 8 heads.

paragraphs: Multi-head attention gives transformers multiple ways to attend to their inputs, but attention heads can learn redundant representations. This paper takes that observation as motivation to change what each head contains. Transformer-MGK replaces redundant heads with mixtures of attention keys, allowing individual heads to focus efficiently on different parts of a sequence.

The keys follow a Gaussian mixture model. This provides multiple key components within a head and changes the allocation of attention capacity. Compared with conventional transformer counterparts, the proposed architecture uses fewer parameters and floating-point operations, speeds training and inference, and achieves comparable or better accuracy across the evaluated tasks. It can also be extended to linear attention.

The empirical study includes language modeling and applications with very long sequences. On Wikitext-103 and Long Range Arena, four-head Transformer-MGK models perform comparably to or better than eight-head baseline transformers. These results support probabilistic key mixtures as a way to use attention capacity more efficiently in the tested settings, with computational savings accompanying the prediction results.
summary.tldr: Gaussian mixtures of attention keys let transformers use fewer heads and less computation while maintaining or improving performance in reported benchmarks.

title: Improving Transformers with Probabilistic Attention Keys

abstract: Machine learning methods on graphs have proven useful in many applications due to their ability to handle generally structured data. The framework of Gaussian Markov Random Fields (GMRFs) provides a principled way to define Gaussian models on graphs by utilizing their sparsity structure. We propose a flexible GMRF model for general graphs built on the multi-layer structure of Deep GMRFs, originally proposed for lattice graphs only. By designing a new type of layer we enable the model to scale to large graphs. The layer is constructed to allow for efficient training using variational inference and existing software frameworks for Graph Neural Networks. For a Gaussian likelihood, close to exact Bayesian inference is available for the latent field. This allows for making predictions with accompanying uncertainty estimates. The usefulness of the proposed model is verified by experiments on a number of synthetic and real world datasets, where it compares favorably to other both Bayesian and deep learning methods.

paragraphs: Gaussian Markov random fields define probabilistic models using the sparse relationships in a graph. Deep versions add a multilayer structure, but the earlier framework was designed for lattice graphs. This paper extends that approach to general graphs, broadening the range of structured data it can represent.

The key contribution is a new layer designed for scalability. It supports efficient training through variational inference and can use existing graph neural-network software frameworks. This combines the probabilistic structure of a Gaussian field with a layered model that can operate on large graphs.

When the observation likelihood is Gaussian, the method permits nearly exact Bayesian inference for the latent field. Predictions can therefore come with uncertainty estimates, an explicit benefit of the probabilistic formulation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets compare favorably with both Bayesian and deep-learning alternatives. The result is a more broadly applicable Deep GMRF framework whose scalability and uncertainty capabilities are considered together.
summary.tldr: A new Deep GMRF layer extends scalable probabilistic modeling to general graphs, with nearly exact latent inference under Gaussian likelihoods.

title: Scalable Deep Gaussian Markov Random Fields for General Graphs

abstract: Despite the broad use of fixed-point iterations throughout applied mathematics, the optimal convergence rate of general fixed-point problems with nonexpansive nonlinear operators has not been established. This work presents an acceleration mechanism for fixed-point iterations with nonexpansive operators, contractive operators, and nonexpansive operators satisfying a Hölder-type growth condition. We then provide matching complexity lower bounds to establish the exact optimality of the acceleration mechanisms in the nonexpansive and contractive setups. Finally, we provide experiments with CT imaging, optimal transport, and decentralized optimization to demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the acceleration mechanism.
originalAbstract: Despite the broad use of fixed-point iterations throughout applied mathematics, the optimal convergence rate of general fixed-point problems with nonexpansive nonlinear operators has not been established. This work presents an acceleration mechanism for fixed-point iterations with nonexpansive operators, contractive operators, and nonexpansive operators satisfying a Hölder-type growth condition. We then provide matching complexity lower bounds to establish the exact optimality of the acceleration mechanisms in the nonexpansive and contractive setups. Finally, we provide experiments with CT imaging, optimal transport, and decentralized optimization to demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the acceleration mechanism.

paragraphs: A fixed-point problem seeks an input that remains unchanged when an operator is applied to it. Repeatedly applying the operator is a widely used solution strategy, but the best possible convergence rate for general nonlinear nonexpansive operators had remained unresolved. Nonexpansive operators do not increase distances, while contractive operators satisfy a stronger distance-shrinking property.

The paper develops acceleration mechanisms for nonexpansive operators, contractive operators, and nonexpansive operators with an additional Hölder-type growth condition. Acceleration here concerns reaching a fixed-point solution more efficiently through an improved iteration procedure. Treating these operator classes separately allows the analysis to reflect the mathematical structure available in each setting.

For the nonexpansive and contractive settings, matching lower bounds establish the exact optimality of the proposed acceleration mechanisms. The lower bounds are crucial because they show that the achieved complexity meets the corresponding theoretical limit. Experiments in CT imaging, optimal transport, and decentralized optimization additionally demonstrate practical effectiveness. The abstract's exact-optimality claim covers the first two settings, while the growth-conditioned setting also receives an acceleration method.
summary.tldr: Accelerated fixed-point methods achieve provably exact optimal complexity for nonexpansive and contractive operator settings.

title: Exact Optimal Accelerated Complexity for Fixed-Point Iterations

abstract: Foundational work on the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis has suggested an exciting corollary: winning tickets found in the context of one task can be transferred to similar tasks, possibly even across different architectures. This has generated broad interest, but methods to study this universality are lacking. We make use of renormalization group theory, a powerful tool from theoretical physics, to address this need. We find that iterative magnitude pruning, the principal algorithm used for discovering winning tickets, is a renormalization group scheme, and can be viewed as inducing a flow in parameter space. We demonstrate that ResNet-50 models with transferable winning tickets have flows with common properties, as would be expected from the theory. Similar observations are made for BERT models, with evidence that their flows are near fixed points. Additionally, we leverage our framework to study winning tickets transferred across ResNet architectures, observing that smaller models have flows with more uniform properties than larger models, complicating transfer between them.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket perspective suggests that useful sparse subnetworks found for one task may transfer to similar tasks, potentially even across architectures. This paper develops a way to study that possibility using renormalization group theory from physics. Its focus is understanding shared structure in the pruning process associated with transferable winning tickets.

The authors identify iterative magnitude pruning as a renormalization group scheme that induces a flow through parameter space. ResNet-50 models with transferable winning tickets exhibit common flow properties, consistent with the theory. BERT models show related observations, along with evidence that their flows are near fixed points. These observations connect transfer behavior with properties of the pruning trajectory.

The framework is also applied to transfer across ResNet architectures. Smaller models have more uniform flow properties than larger ones, a difference that complicates transfer between them. The findings offer a language and analytical approach for investigating universality, while retaining the conditional nature of transfer: shared patterns provide evidence about particular models, rather than a guarantee that winning tickets transfer across arbitrary tasks or architectures.
summary.tldr: A renormalization group view of iterative pruning reveals shared parameter-flow properties associated with transferable winning tickets in studied ResNet and BERT models.

title: Universality of Winning Tickets: A Renormalization Group Perspective

abstract: Recent studies indicate that kernel machines can often perform similarly or better than deep neural networks (DNNs) on small datasets. The interest in kernel machines has been additionally bolstered by the discovery of their equivalence to wide neural networks in certain regimes. However, a key feature of DNNs is their ability to scale the model size and training data size independently, whereas in traditional kernel machines model size is tied to data size. Because of this coupling, scaling kernel machines to large data has been computationally challenging. In this paper, we provide a way forward for constructing large-scale general kernel models, which are a generalization of kernel machines that decouples the model and data, allowing training on large datasets. Specifically, we introduce EigenPro 3.0, an algorithm based on projected dual preconditioned SGD and show scaling to model and data sizes which have not been possible with existing kernel methods. We provide a PyTorch based implementation which can take advantage of multiple GPUs.

paragraphs: Kernel machines can be competitive with deep neural networks on small datasets, but scaling them creates a structural difficulty. In traditional kernel methods, model size is tied to the amount of training data. This coupling makes larger datasets computationally challenging, whereas neural networks can vary model size and training-set size independently.

The paper develops general kernel models that separate those two choices. Its central algorithm, EigenPro 3.0, uses projected dual preconditioned stochastic gradient descent to train these models. The aim is to make large-data kernel learning feasible without requiring model size to track dataset size in the traditional way. Decoupling the model and data is the organizing contribution.

The authors demonstrate scaling to model and dataset sizes that existing kernel methods had not supported. They also provide a PyTorch implementation capable of using multiple GPUs. These findings concern the computational reach of kernel learning, expanding the sizes at which such models can be trained. The abstract's small-data accuracy motivation does not establish that the new large-scale models universally outperform deep neural networks.
summary.tldr: EigenPro 3.0 scales general kernel models by decoupling model size from training-data size.

title: Toward Large Kernel Models

abstract: The Arcade Learning Environment (ALE) has become an essential benchmark for assessing the performance of reinforcement learning algorithms. However, the computational cost of generating results on the entire 57-game dataset limits ALE’s use and makes the reproducibility of many results infeasible. We propose a novel solution to this problem in the form of a principled methodology for selecting small but representative subsets of environments within a benchmark suite. We applied our method to identify a subset of five ALE games, we call Atari-5 , which produces 57-game median score estimates within 10% of their true values. Extending the subset to 10-games recovers 80% of the variance for log-scores for all games within the 57-game set. We show this level of compression is possible due to a high degree of correlation between many of the games in ALE.

paragraphs: The Arcade Learning Environment evaluates reinforcement learning algorithms across 57 games, but running the full suite is computationally expensive. That cost limits how often researchers can use the benchmark and reproduce results. This paper develops a principled way to select a much smaller collection of environments that still represents performance across the larger suite.

Applying the method produces Atari-5, a subset of five games. The authors report that this subset estimates the full suite's median score within 10% of its actual value. A larger subset of ten games recovers 80% of the variance in log-scores across all 57 games. These are two distinct measures of how much information a reduced benchmark preserves.

The explanation is that performance on many ALE games is highly correlated, so the full suite contains substantial overlapping information. Carefully chosen games can therefore stand in for part of that repeated evidence. The findings support cheaper estimates of broad benchmark performance; the stated results concern median scores and log-score variance, rather than exact reconstruction of every game's result.
summary.tldr: A carefully selected five-game Atari subset estimates the full 57-game median score within 10%.

title: Atari-5: Distilling the Arcade Learning Environment down to Five Games

abstract: Inspired by applications in pricing and contract design, we study the maximization of one-sided Lipschitz functions, which only provide the (weaker) guarantee that they do not grow too quickly in one direction. We show that it is possible to learn a maximizer for such a function while incurring $O(\log \log T)$ total regret (with a universal constant independent of the number of discontinuities / complexity of the function). This regret bound is asymptotically optimal in $T$ due to a lower bound of Kleinberg and Leighton. By applying this algorithm, we show that one can sell digital goods to multiple buyers and learn the optimal linear contract in the principal-agent setting while incurring at most $O(\log \log T)$ regret.

paragraphs: Learning to maximize a function becomes challenging when the function can have discontinuities. This paper studies one-sided Lipschitz functions, which satisfy the weaker requirement that growth is controlled in one direction. Pricing and contract design motivate the question of how much reward must be sacrificed while learning a maximizer.

The authors give an algorithm whose total regret grows as O(log log T), where T is the interaction horizon. Regret measures the accumulated shortfall associated with learning instead of already using an optimal choice. The bound has a universal constant independent of the function’s number of discontinuities or complexity, making that independence a central feature of the result.

A known lower bound establishes that the dependence on T is asymptotically optimal. Applying the algorithm, the authors obtain the same regret order for selling digital goods to multiple buyers and learning an optimal linear contract in a principal-agent setting. These results show that the specified one-sided regularity can support very low learning cost despite allowing more irregular functions than ordinary two-sided smoothness assumptions.
summary.tldr: One-sided Lipschitz functions can be maximized with asymptotically optimal O(log log T) regret, with applications to pricing and contracts.

title: Optimal No-Regret Learning for One-Sided Lipschitz Functions

abstract: Chaotic dynamical systems (DS) are ubiquitous in nature and society. Often we are interested in reconstructing such systems from observed time series for prediction or mechanistic insight, where by reconstruction we mean learning geometrical and invariant temporal properties of the system in question (like attractors). However, training reconstruction algorithms like recurrent neural networks (RNNs) on such systems by gradient-descent based techniques faces severe challenges. This is mainly due to exploding gradients caused by the exponential divergence of trajectories in chaotic systems. Moreover, for (scientific) interpretability we wish to have as low dimensional reconstructions as possible, preferably in a model which is mathematically tractable. Here we report that a surprisingly simple modification of teacher forcing leads to provably strictly all-time bounded gradients in training on chaotic systems, and, when paired with a simple architectural rearrangement of a tractable RNN design, piecewise-linear RNNs (PLRNNs), allows for faithful reconstruction in spaces of at most the dimensionality of the observed system. We show on several DS that with these amendments we can reconstruct DS better than current SOTA algorithms, in much lower dimensions. Performance differences were particularly compelling on real world data with which most other methods severely struggled. This work thus led to a simple yet powerful DS reconstruction algorithm which is highly interpretable at the same time.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a chaotic system from time series means learning its geometry and persistent temporal properties, including structures such as attractors. Training recurrent networks for this purpose is difficult because chaotic trajectories diverge exponentially, producing exploding gradients. The paper also seeks compact reconstructions, since lower-dimensional, mathematically tractable models are desirable for scientific interpretation.

The authors introduce a simple modification of teacher forcing and prove that it keeps training gradients bounded at all times. They pair this training change with an architectural rearrangement of piecewise-linear recurrent neural networks. Together, these modifications allow faithful reconstruction in spaces whose dimensionality is no greater than that of the observed system.

Across several dynamical systems, the proposed approach reconstructs dynamics better than the state-of-the-art algorithms considered while using substantially fewer dimensions. The reported differences are especially compelling on real-world data, where most competing methods struggle. The contribution connects stable training with compact modeling: controlling gradients helps make a tractable recurrent architecture useful for reconstructing chaotic behavior without relying on a much larger state representation.
summary.tldr: Modified teacher forcing guarantees bounded training gradients and, with a revised recurrent architecture, enables compact reconstructions of chaotic dynamics.

title: Generalized Teacher Forcing for Learning Chaotic Dynamics

abstract: Recent innovations on hardware (e.g. Nvidia A100) have motivated learning N:M structured sparsity masks from scratch for fast model inference. However, state-of-the-art learning recipes in this regime (e.g. SR-STE) are proposed for non-adaptive optimizers like momentum SGD, while incurring non-trivial accuracy drop for Adam-trained models like attention-based LLMs. In this paper, we first demonstrate such gap origins from poorly estimated second moment (i.e. variance) in Adam states given by the masked weights. We conjecture that learning N:M masks with Adam should take the critical regime of variance estimation into account. In light of this, we propose STEP, an Adam-aware recipe that learns N:M masks with two phases: first, STEP calculates a reliable variance estimate ( precondition phase ) and subsequently, the variance remains fixed and is used as a precondition to learn N:M masks ( mask-learning phase ). STEP automatically identifies the switching point of two phases by dynamically sampling variance changes over the training trajectory and testing the sample concentration. Empirically, we evaluate STEP and other baselines such as ASP and SR-STE on multiple tasks including CIFAR classification, machine translation and LLM fine-tuning (BERT-Base, GPT-2). We show STEP mitigates the accuracy drop of baseline recipes and is robust to aggressive structured sparsity ratios.

paragraphs: Hardware support for N:M structured sparsity motivates learning masks that remove weights in a regular pattern for faster inference. However, recipes developed for non-adaptive optimizers can reduce accuracy when applied to Adam-trained models. This paper traces that gap to poor second-moment estimates in Adam's optimizer states associated with masked weights.

STEP responds with two training phases. First, it obtains a reliable variance estimate. It then fixes that estimate and uses it as a preconditioner while learning the sparsity mask. The transition is selected automatically by sampling changes in the variance estimates during training and testing how concentrated those samples are.

The authors evaluate STEP against approaches including ASP and SR-STE on CIFAR classification, machine translation, and fine-tuning of BERT-Base and GPT-2. They report that STEP reduces the accuracy drop seen with baseline recipes and remains robust under aggressive structured sparsity ratios. The method makes the optimizer's state estimation part of the sparsity-learning procedure, following the authors' conjecture that successful mask learning with Adam should account for the critical variance-estimation regime.
summary.tldr: STEP stabilizes Adam's variance estimates before learning structured sparsity masks, reducing reported accuracy losses.

title: STEP: Learning N:M Structured Sparsity Masks from Scratch with Precondition

abstract: We investigate the problem of stochastic, combinatorial multi-armed bandits where the learner only has access to bandit feedback and the reward function can be non-linear. We provide a general framework for adapting discrete offline approximation algorithms into sublinear $\alpha$-regret methods that only require bandit feedback, achieving $\mathcal{O}\left(T^\frac{2}{3}\log(T)^\frac{1}{3}\right)$ expected cumulative $\alpha$-regret dependence on the horizon $T$. The framework only requires the offline algorithms to be robust to small errors in function evaluation. The adaptation procedure does not even require explicit knowledge of the offline approximation algorithm — the offline algorithm can be used as black box subroutine. To demonstrate the utility of the proposed framework, the proposed framework is applied to multiple problems in submodular maximization, adapting approximation algorithms for cardinality and for knapsack constraints. The new CMAB algorithms for knapsack constraints outperform a full-bandit method developed for the adversarial setting in experiments with real-world data.

paragraphs: The paper studies decisions made by selecting combinations of items when the learner observes only the reward for the whole selection. This limited feedback makes learning difficult because it does not reveal each item's contribution. The setting is stochastic, and the reward of a combination can depend on its items in a nonlinear way.

The authors provide a framework that turns existing offline approximation algorithms into online learning methods. The key requirement is that the offline algorithm tolerate small errors in evaluating rewards. Its internal workings need not be known: the framework can call it as a black box. This makes established optimization procedures reusable under bandit feedback.

The resulting methods have expected cumulative α-regret growing on the order of T^(2/3) log(T)^(1/3), where T is the decision horizon and α reflects the approximation benchmark. Sublinear growth means average regret against that benchmark decreases over time. Applications cover submodular maximization with cardinality and knapsack constraints. On real-world data, the knapsack methods outperform a full-bandit comparison method designed for an adversarial setting.
summary.tldr: A black-box framework converts error-tolerant offline approximation algorithms into combinatorial bandit methods with sublinear expected α-regret.

title: A Framework for Adapting Offline Algorithms to Solve Combinatorial Multi-Armed Bandit Problems with Bandit Feedback

abstract: Models that can predict the occurrence of events ahead of time with low false-alarm rates are critical to the acceptance of decision support systems in the medical community. This challenging task is typically treated as a simple binary classification, ignoring temporal dependencies between samples, whereas we propose to exploit this structure. We first introduce a common theoretical framework unifying dynamic survival analysis and early event prediction. Following an analysis of objectives from both fields, we propose Temporal Label Smoothing (TLS), a simpler, yet best-performing method that preserves prediction monotonicity over time. By focusing the objective on areas with a stronger predictive signal, TLS improves performance over all baselines on two large-scale benchmark tasks. Gains are particularly notable along clinically relevant measures, such as event recall at low false-alarm rates. TLS reduces the number of missed events by up to a factor of two over previously used approaches in early event prediction.

This challenging task is typically treated as a simple binary classification, ignoring temporal dependencies between samples, whereas we propose to exploit this structure. We first introduce a common theoretical framework unifying dynamic survival analysis and early event prediction. paragraphs: Early event prediction aims to warn about an event before it occurs while keeping false alarms low. Treating each observation as an isolated binary classification example ignores relationships across time. This paper uses that temporal structure to improve prediction, motivated by the requirements of medical decision-support systems.

The authors first introduce a theoretical framework connecting dynamic survival analysis with early event prediction. Comparing objectives from these areas leads to Temporal Label Smoothing, or TLS. The method preserves prediction monotonicity over time and concentrates the training objective on regions with a stronger predictive signal. Its design makes the temporal organization of the task part of how the model learns.

On two large benchmark tasks, TLS outperforms all evaluated baselines. Gains are especially notable for clinically relevant measures such as event recall when false-alarm rates are low. The reported reduction in missed events reaches a factor of two relative to previously used approaches. This connects the training change to the practical goal of catching more events without excessive alarms.
summary.tldr: Temporal Label Smoothing uses time structure to improve early event detection, with fewer missed events at low false-alarm rates.

title: Temporal Label Smoothing for Early Event Prediction

abstract: Modern computer vision pipelines handle large images in one of two sub-optimal ways: down-sampling or cropping. These two methods incur significant losses in the amount of information and context present in an image. There are many downstream applications in which global context matters as much as high frequency details, such as in real-world satellite imagery; in such cases researchers have to make the uncomfortable choice of which information to discard. We introduce xT, a simple framework for vision transformers which effectively aggregates global context with local details and can model large images end-to-end on contemporary GPUs. We select a set of benchmark datasets across classic vision tasks which accurately reflect a vision model’s ability to understand truly large images and incorporate fine details over large scales and assess our method’s improvement on them. xT is a streaming, two-stage architecture that adapts existing vision backbones and long sequence language models to effectively model large images without quadratic memory growth. We are able to increase accuracy by up to 8.6% on challenging classification tasks and F1 score by 11.6 on context-dependent segmentation on images as large as 29,000 x 29,000 pixels.

The paper introduces xT to combine these two scales of information.

They report classification accuracy improvements of up to 8.6% and an F1-score increase of 11.6 for context-dependent segmentation, using images as large as 29,000 by 29,000 pixels. These results support the value of preserving both local information and broader context in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: xT combines local detail and global context in very large images through a streaming architecture without quadratic memory growth.

title: xT: Nested Tokenization for Larger Context in Large Images

abstract: Transformers are the dominant architecture for sequence modeling, but there is growing interest in models that use a fixed-size latent state that does not depend on the sequence length, which we refer to as ”generalized state space models” (GSSMs). In this paper we show that while GSSMs are promising in terms of inference-time efficiency, they are limited compared to transformer models on tasks that require copying from the input context. We start with a theoretical analysis of the simple task of string copying and prove that a two layer transformer can copy strings of exponential length while GSSMs are fundamentally limited by their fixed-size latent state. Empirically, we find that transformers outperform GSSMs in terms of efficiency and generalization on synthetic tasks that require copying the context. Finally, we evaluate pretrained large language models and find that transformer models dramatically outperform state space models at copying and retrieving information from context. Taken together, these results suggest a fundamental gap between transformers and GSSMs on tasks of practical interest.

paragraphs: Sequence models with a fixed-size latent state offer promising inference efficiency, but their state size does not grow with the input. This paper groups such architectures as generalized state space models and studies what that design means for copying information from context. Copying provides a concrete task for comparing their capabilities with those of transformers.

The theoretical analysis shows that a two-layer transformer can copy strings of exponential length, while fixed-state models face a fundamental restriction from their bounded latent state. The result identifies a capacity difference relevant to retaining input information for later reproduction. Its focus is the copying task rather than a claim that transformers dominate every kind of sequence processing.

Synthetic experiments find transformer advantages in both efficiency and generalization on tasks requiring context copying. Evaluations of pretrained language models also show large transformer advantages in copying and retrieving contextual information. The theoretical and empirical evidence therefore point in the same direction: fixed-size state can be a consequential constraint when a task requires reproducing or recovering information from the input.
summary.tldr: Theory and experiments identify copying and context-retrieval advantages for transformers over sequence models constrained to a fixed-size latent state.

title: Repeat After Me: Transformers are Better than State Space Models at Copying

abstract: Coverage path planning (CPP) is the problem of finding a path that covers the entire free space of a confined area, with applications ranging from robotic lawn mowing to search-and-rescue. When the environment is unknown, the path needs to be planned online while mapping the environment, which cannot be addressed by offline planning methods that do not allow for a flexible path space. We investigate how suitable reinforcement learning is for this challenging problem, and analyze the involved components required to efficiently learn coverage paths, such as action space, input feature representation, neural network architecture, and reward function. We propose a computationally feasible egocentric map representation based on frontiers, and a novel reward term based on total variation to promote complete coverage. Through extensive experiments, we show that our approach surpasses the performance of both previous RL-based approaches and highly specialized methods across multiple CPP variations.

paragraphs: Coverage path planning asks an agent to traverse all accessible space within an area. When the environment is unknown, the agent must decide where to move while simultaneously discovering the map. This makes the problem different from computing a fixed route over a fully known layout, with applications including robotic mowing and search-and-rescue.

The paper studies how reinforcement learning can handle this setting by examining several connected design choices: the available actions, the information shown to the model, its neural architecture, and its reward. It proposes a computationally feasible map representation organized around the agent and based on frontiers, which mark boundaries relevant to further exploration.

The authors also introduce a reward term based on total variation to encourage complete coverage. The representation and reward address complementary needs: making the evolving environment manageable for the learner and guiding it toward the coverage objective. Extensive experiments across multiple coverage-planning variations show performance exceeding earlier reinforcement-learning approaches and highly specialized methods, supporting the effectiveness of the combined design.
summary.tldr: An agent-centered frontier map and a coverage-promoting reward improve learned routes through unknown environments.

title: Learning Coverage Paths in Unknown Environments with Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In many interactive decision-making problems, there is contextual side information that remains fixed within the course of an interaction. This problem has been studied quite extensively under the assumption the context is fully observed, as well as in the opposing limit when the context is unobserved, a special type of POMDP also referred to as a Latent MDP (LMDP). In this work, we consider a class of decision problems that interpolates between the settings, namely, between the case the context is fully observed, and the case the context is unobserved. We refer to this class of decision problems as LMDPs with prospective side information. In such an environment an agent receives additional, weakly revealing, information on the latent context at the beginning of each episode. We show that, surprisingly, this problem is not captured by contemporary POMDP settings and is not solved by RL algorithms designed for partially observed environments. We then establish that any sample efficient algorithm must suffer at least $\Omega(K^{2/3})$-regret, as opposed to standard $\Omega(\sqrt{K})$ lower bounds. We design an algorithm with a matching upper bound that depends only polynomially on the problem parameters. This establishes exponential improvement in the sample complexity relative to the existing LMDP lower bound, when prospective information is not given in prior work.

paragraphs: Some decision problems have a hidden context that stays fixed throughout an interaction. This paper studies an intermediate setting between fully observing that context and receiving no direct information about it. At the beginning of each episode, the agent receives a weak clue about the context, termed prospective side information.

The authors show that contemporary partially observed decision-process settings and their reinforcement learning algorithms do not capture or solve this problem as formulated. They establish that any sample-efficient algorithm must incur regret of at least order K^(2/3), where K counts episodes. This is a stronger lower bound than the familiar square-root dependence on K.

They then construct an algorithm with a matching regret upper bound and only polynomial dependence on the problem parameters. Compared with the existing latent-MDP sample-complexity lower bound without prospective information, this yields an exponential improvement. The result shows that even weak initial information can change learning difficulty substantially, while the matching regret bounds identify a distinct challenge within the new setting.
summary.tldr: Weak clues about hidden episode context enable an exponential sample-complexity improvement, with matching K^(2/3) regret bounds for sample-efficient learning.

title: Prospective Side Information for Latent MDPs

abstract: Topological deep learning (TDL) is a rapidly evolving field that uses topological features to understand and design deep learning models. This paper posits that TDL is the new frontier for relational learning. TDL may complement graph representation learning and geometric deep learning by incorporating topological concepts, and can thus provide a natural choice for various machine learning settings. To this end, this paper discusses open problems in TDL, ranging from practical benefits to theoretical foundations. For each problem, it outlines potential solutions and future research opportunities. At the same time, this paper serves as an invitation to the scientific community to actively participate in TDL research to unlock the potential of this emerging field.

The field brings topological features and concepts into the understanding and design of neural models. The authors argue that this perspective may complement graph representation learning and geometric deep learning, broadening the available approaches to relational problems.

The paper organizes its case around open questions, covering both practical benefits and theoretical foundations. For each problem, it discusses possible solutions and opportunities for further research. This connects the question of when topological methods are useful with the question of how their behavior and design should be understood.

The contribution is a research agenda and an invitation to develop the field. The authors suggest that topological ideas can make these models a natural choice in various machine learning settings, while treating that potential as something the community should investigate. The paper's significance lies in identifying directions for progress and connecting practical ambitions with foundational questions about relational learning.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes topological deep learning as a promising complement to graph and geometric learning and maps open practical and theoretical questions.

title: Position: Topological Deep Learning is the New Frontier for Relational Learning

abstract: Recent vision-language models have achieved tremendous advances. However, their computational costs are also escalating dramatically, making model acceleration exceedingly critical. To pursue more efficient vision-language Transformers, this paper introduces Cross-Guided Ensemble of Tokens (CrossGET), a general acceleration framework for vision-language Transformers. This framework adaptively combines tokens in real-time during inference, significantly reducing computational costs while maintaining high performance. CrossGET features two primary innovations: 1) Cross-Guided Matching and Ensemble. CrossGET leverages cross-modal guided token matching and ensemble to effectively utilize cross-modal information, achieving wider applicability across both modality-independent models, e.g., CLIP, and modality-dependent ones, e.g., BLIP2. 2) Complete-Graph Soft Matching. CrossGET introduces an algorithm for the token-matching mechanism, ensuring reliable matching results while facilitating parallelizability and high efficiency. Extensive experiments have been conducted on various vision-language tasks, such as image-text retrieval, visual reasoning, image captioning, and visual question answering. The performance on both classic multimodal architectures and emerging multimodal LLMs demonstrates the framework’s effectiveness and versatility. The code is available at https://github.com/sdc17/CrossGET.

paragraphs: Vision-language Transformers process information from images and text, but their growing computational requirements make efficient inference increasingly important. CrossGET addresses this by adaptively combining tokens while a model is running. Reducing the number of separate tokens lowers computational work while aiming to retain the information needed for strong task performance.

Its first contribution uses information across modalities to guide which tokens should be matched and combined. This allows the framework to apply to architectures with different relationships between image and language processing, including CLIP and BLIP2. Its second contribution, complete-graph soft matching, supplies a matching procedure designed for reliable results and efficient parallel computation.

The authors evaluate CrossGET on image-text retrieval, visual reasoning, image captioning, and visual question answering. Results across established multimodal architectures and multimodal large language models support its effectiveness and broad applicability. The reported outcome is a substantial reduction in computation while maintaining high performance, making token combination a practical point of intervention for accelerating several kinds of vision-language systems.
summary.tldr: CrossGET combines tokens using cross-modal guidance to reduce vision-language Transformer computation while maintaining high performance.

title: CrossGET: Cross-Guided Ensemble of Tokens for Accelerating Vision-Language Transformers

abstract: Reversing a diffusion process by learning its score forms the heart of diffusion-based generative modeling and for estimating properties of scientific systems. The diffusion processes that are tractable center on linear processes with a Gaussian stationary distribution, limiting the kinds of models that can be built to those that target a Gaussian prior or more generally limits the kinds of problems that can be generically solved to those that have conditionally linear score functions. In this work, we introduce a family of tractable denoising score matching objectives, called local-DSM, built using local increments of the diffusion process. We show how local-DSM melded with Taylor expansions enables automated training and score estimation with nonlinear diffusion processes. To demonstrate these ideas, we use automated-DSM to train generative models using non-Gaussian priors on challenging low dimensional distributions and the CIFAR10 image dataset. Additionally, we use the automated-DSM to learn the scores for nonlinear processes studied in statistical physics.

paragraphs: Learning the score of a diffusion process is central to reversing that process for generative modeling and studying scientific systems. Common tractable approaches focus on linear processes with Gaussian stationary distributions. This restricts the priors and process structures that can be handled using those approaches.

The paper introduces local-DSM, a family of denoising score-matching objectives constructed from local increments of a diffusion process. Combining these objectives with Taylor expansions enables automated training and score estimation for nonlinear diffusions. The approach expands the kinds of diffusion processes available for modeling beyond the familiar linear setting.

The authors demonstrate automated-DSM by training generative models with non-Gaussian priors on challenging low-dimensional distributions and the CIFAR10 image dataset. They also learn scores for nonlinear processes from statistical physics. These demonstrations cover both data generation and scientific process modeling. The contribution is a tractable route to score estimation for nonlinear diffusions, supported by examples in these different settings rather than a stated claim of universal superiority in generation quality.
summary.tldr: Local denoising score-matching objectives combined with Taylor expansions enable automated score learning for nonlinear diffusions and generative models with non-Gaussian priors.

title: What’s the score? Automated Denoising Score Matching for Nonlinear Diffusions

abstract: RNA properties, such as function and stability, are intricately tied to their two-dimensional conformations. This has spurred the development of computational models for predicting the RNA secondary structures, leveraging dynamic programming or machine learning (ML) techniques. These structures are governed by specific rules; for example, only Watson-Crick and Wobble pairs are allowed, and sequences must not form sharp bends. Recent efforts introduced a systematic approach to post-process the predictions made by ML algorithms, aiming to modify them to respect the constraints. However, we still observe instances violating the requirements, significantly reducing biological relevance. To address this challenge, we present a novel post-processing framework for ML-based predictions on RNA secondary structures, inspired by the assignment problem in integer linear programming. Our algorithm offers a theoretical guarantee, ensuring that the resulting predictions adhere to the fundamental constraints of RNAs. Empirical evidence supports the efficacy of our approach, demonstrating improved predictive performance with no constraint violation, while requiring less running time.

paragraphs: RNA function and stability depend closely on its secondary structure, the pattern of pairings that gives it a two-dimensional conformation. Predicted structures must obey biological rules, including allowed pairing types and restrictions against sharp bends. Machine learning predictions can violate these rules, and existing post-processing approaches can still leave invalid structures.

The paper introduces a post-processing framework inspired by the assignment problem in integer linear programming. It acts on machine learning predictions to make them satisfy the relevant structural constraints. The central contribution is a theoretical guarantee that the resulting predictions obey fundamental RNA constraints, giving the correction procedure a formal basis beyond empirical success alone.

The authors report improved predictive performance, no constraint violations, and lower running time in their empirical evaluation. These outcomes matter together: a correction method should produce valid structures without sacrificing its usefulness as a predictor or adding excessive computational cost. The work connects a constrained optimization formulation to biological structure prediction, providing a way to enforce structural requirements after an ML model has produced its initial output.
summary.tldr: An assignment-inspired post-processing method guarantees fundamental RNA constraints while improving prediction performance and runtime in the reported evaluation.

title: Enforcing Constraints in RNA Secondary Structure Predictions: A Post-Processing Framework Based on the Assignment Problem

abstract: Recent research in molecular discovery has primarily been devoted to small, drug-like molecules, leaving many similarly important applications in material design without adequate technology. These applications often rely on more complex molecular structures with fewer examples that are carefully designed using known substructures. We propose a data-efficient and interpretable model for representing and reasoning over such molecules in terms of graph grammars that explicitly describe the hierarchical design space featuring motifs to be the design basis. We present a novel representation in the form of random walks over the design space, which facilitates both molecule generation and property prediction. We demonstrate clear advantages over existing methods in terms of performance, efficiency, and synthesizability of predicted molecules, and we provide detailed insights into the method’s chemical interpretability.

It proposes a representation designed to make the available structural knowledge useful for both molecular generation and property prediction.

The method uses graph grammars to describe a hierarchical design space whose building blocks are molecular motifs. Molecules are represented through random walks over this space. This connects the representation to explicit construction rules, giving the model an interpretable account of molecular organization while supporting reasoning over complex structures.

The authors demonstrate advantages over existing methods in performance, efficiency, and the synthesizability of predicted molecules. They also provide detailed analysis of the method’s chemical interpretability. The contribution is a shared representation for proposing molecules and predicting their properties, grounded in the substructures used to design them. Its reported data efficiency is especially relevant to the motivating setting, where carefully designed molecules are complex and examples are scarce.
summary.tldr: Random walks over interpretable molecular graph grammars support data-efficient molecule generation and property prediction.

title: Representing Molecules as Random Walks Over Interpretable Grammars

abstract: The secondary structure of ribonucleic acid (RNA) is more stable and accessible in the cell than its tertiary structure, making it essential for functional prediction. Although deep learning has shown promising results in this field, current methods suffer from poor generalization and high complexity. In this work, we reformulate the RNA secondary structure prediction as a K-Rook problem, thereby simplifying the prediction process into probabilistic matching within a finite solution space. Building on this innovative perspective, we introduce RFold, a simple yet effective method that learns to predict the most matching K-Rook solution from the given sequence. RFold employs a bi-dimensional optimization strategy that decomposes the probabilistic matching problem into row-wise and column-wise components to reduce the matching complexity, simplifying the solving process while guaranteeing the validity of the output. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RFold achieves competitive performance and about eight times faster inference efficiency than the state-of-the-art approaches. The code is available at https://github.com/A4Bio/RFold.

paragraphs: RNA secondary structure is important for predicting biological function and is more stable and accessible in cells than tertiary structure. The paper addresses the complexity and poor generalization associated with existing deep learning approaches. Its central move is to express secondary structure prediction as a K-Rook problem, turning prediction into probabilistic matching within a finite collection of candidate solutions.

The resulting method, RFold, learns to select the matching solution best suited to an input sequence. To make this manageable, it separates the matching optimization into row-wise and column-wise components. This two-dimensional decomposition reduces the complexity of solving the matching problem while guaranteeing that the produced output satisfies the formulation's validity requirements.

Extensive experiments show competitive predictive performance and inference approximately eight times faster than the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The result connects a simpler mathematical formulation with a practical speed advantage. Output validity and predictive accuracy are separate claims here: the construction guarantees validity, while the experiments provide the evidence that its predictions remain competitive.
summary.tldr: RFold reformulates RNA secondary structure prediction as probabilistic K-Rook matching, delivering valid outputs and competitive accuracy with roughly eightfold faster inference.

title: Deciphering RNA Secondary Structure Prediction: A Probabilistic K-Rook Matching Perspective

abstract: Neuron-level interpretations aim to explain network behaviors and properties by investigating neurons responsive to specific perceptual or structural input patterns. Although there is emerging work in the vision and language domains, none is explored for acoustic models. To bridge the gap, we introduce AND, the first Audio Network Dissection framework that automatically establishes natural language explanations of acoustic neurons based on highly responsive audio. AND features the use of LLMs to summarize mutual acoustic features and identities among audio. Extensive experiments are conducted to verify AND’s precise and informative descriptions. In addition, we highlight two acoustic model behaviors with analysis by AND. First, models discriminate audio with a combination of basic acoustic features rather than high-level abstract concepts. Second, training strategies affect neuron behaviors. Supervised training guides neurons to gradually narrow their attention, while self-supervised learning encourages neurons to be polysemantic for exploring high-level features. Finally, we demonstrate a potential use of AND in audio model unlearning by conducting concept-specific pruning based on the descriptions.

paragraphs: AND explains acoustic networks at the level of individual neurons. It examines audio that strongly activates a neuron and automatically produces a natural-language description of what those recordings share. Large language models summarize common acoustic features and identities, turning activation patterns into descriptions that people can inspect.

Experiments support the precision and informativeness of these descriptions. The resulting analysis suggests that the studied models distinguish audio through combinations of basic acoustic features rather than primarily through abstract concepts. It also reveals differences associated with training strategy: supervised training progressively narrows neurons’ attention, while self-supervised training encourages neurons to respond to multiple meanings or patterns as they explore higher-level features.

These findings make the framework useful for studying how acoustic representations develop, beyond simply naming what a neuron responds to. The paper also demonstrates a potential application to model unlearning: descriptions guide the pruning of neurons associated with particular concepts. That demonstration presents concept-specific pruning as a possible use of the interpretation framework, rather than establishing a general solution to unlearning.
summary.tldr: AND describes acoustic neurons in natural language and uses those descriptions to analyze training effects and explore concept-specific pruning.

title: AND: Audio Network Dissection for Interpreting Deep Acoustic Models

abstract: We introduce Reprompting, an iterative sampling algorithm that automatically learns the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) recipes for a given task without human intervention. Through Gibbs sampling, Reprompting infers the CoT recipes that work consistently well for a set of training samples by iteratively sampling new recipes using previously sampled recipes as parent prompts to solve other training problems. We conduct extensive experiments on 20 challenging reasoning tasks. Results show that Reprompting outperforms human-written CoT prompts substantially by +9.4 points on average. It also achieves consistently better performance than the state-of-the-art prompt optimization and decoding algorithms.

Through Gibbs sampling, Reprompting infers the CoT recipes that work consistently well for a set of training samples by iteratively sampling new recipes using previously sampled recipes as parent prompts to solve other training problems. We conduct extensive experiments on 20 challenging reasoning tasks. Results show that Reprompting outperforms human-written CoT prompts substantially by +9.4 points on average. paragraphs: A chain-of-thought prompt provides a recipe for approaching a reasoning task, but designing that recipe by hand can leave useful alternatives unexplored. Reprompting automates this task-specific search. It learns recipes from training examples without requiring a person to write or revise the reasoning prompts during the procedure.

The algorithm uses Gibbs sampling in an iterative process. Previously sampled recipes become parent prompts for solving other training problems, which produces new candidate recipes. The aim is to find approaches that work consistently across a set of examples. This makes earlier prompt candidates part of the mechanism for exploring subsequent candidates, connecting prompt discovery across the training set.

The authors evaluate Reprompting on 20 challenging reasoning tasks and report an average improvement of 9.4 points over human-written chain-of-thought prompts. It also consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art prompt-optimization and decoding algorithms. These results indicate that automatically searching for task-specific reasoning recipes can substantially improve performance in the evaluated settings, and that the particular iterative sampling procedure is effective relative to the alternatives tested.
summary.tldr: Reprompting automatically discovers reasoning prompts through Gibbs sampling, outperforming human-written prompts by 9.4 points on average across 20 tasks.

title: Reprompting: Automated Chain-of-Thought Prompt Inference Through Gibbs Sampling

abstract: Machine learning (ML) has been actively adopted in Linear Programming (LP) and Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP), whose potential is hindered by instance scarcity. Current synthetic instance generation methods often fall short in closely mirroring the distribution of original datasets or ensuring the feasibility and boundedness of the generated data — a critical requirement for obtaining reliable supervised labels in model training. In this paper, we present a diffusion-based LP/MILP instance generative framework called MILP-FBGen. It strikes a balance between structural similarity and novelty while maintaining feasibility/boundedness via a meticulously designed structure-preserving generation module and a feasibility/boundedness-constrained sampling module. Our method shows superiority on two fronts: 1) preservation of key properties (hardness, feasibility, and boundedness) of LP/MILP instances, and 2) enhanced performance on downstream tasks. Extensive studies show two-fold superiority that our method ensures higher distributional similarity and 100% feasibility in both easy and hard datasets, surpassing current state-of-the-art techniques.
