paragraphs: Machine learning for linear and mixed-integer linear programming needs suitable training problems, but real instances can be scarce. Synthetic instances must resemble the original data while preserving properties needed for reliable labels. In particular, feasibility concerns whether a valid solution exists, and boundedness prevents the objective from improving without a finite limit.

MILP-FBGen is a diffusion-based framework for generating these optimization instances. It combines a structure-preserving generation module with sampling constrained by feasibility and boundedness. The design aims to balance resemblance to existing instances with novelty, while retaining properties that matter for solving and learning from the generated problems.

The reported studies show stronger distributional similarity and 100% feasibility on both easy and hard datasets compared with existing techniques. They also demonstrate preservation of key properties, including hardness, and improved downstream task performance. These findings matter because realistic structure and usable optimization labels must work together for synthetic instances to serve as effective training data.
summary.tldr: MILP-FBGen generates realistic optimization instances using diffusion and constrained sampling to preserve feasibility, boundedness, and useful problem structure.

title: MILP-FBGen: LP/MILP Instance Generation with Feasibility/Boundedness

abstract: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models rely on 2D inputs, lacking integration with the broader realm of the 3D physical world. Furthermore, they perform action prediction by learning a direct mapping from perception to action, neglecting the vast dynamics of the world and the relations between actions and dynamics. In contrast, human beings are endowed with world models that depict imagination about future scenarios to plan action accordingly. To this end, we propose 3D-VLA by introducing a new family of embodied foundation models that seamlessly link 3D perception, reasoning, and action through a generative world model. Specifically, 3D-VLA is built on top of a 3D-based large language model (LLM) and a set of action tokens is introduced to engage with the embodied environment. Furthermore, to inject generation abilities into the model, we train the embodied diffusion models and align them into the LLM for predicting the goal image and point cloud. To train our 3D-VLA, we curate a large-scale 3D embodied instruction dataset by extracting vast 3D-related information from existing robotics datasets. Our experiments on held-in datasets demonstrate that 3D-VLA significantly improves the reasoning, multimodality generation and planning capabilities in embodied environments, showcasing its potential in real-world applications.

The paper addresses two gaps in earlier vision-language-action systems: their reliance on two-dimensional inputs and their direct mapping from observations to actions. summary.tldr: 3D-VLA combines 3D perception, language, action tokens, and diffusion-based goal generation to improve embodied reasoning and planning on held-in datasets.

title: 3D-VLA: A 3D Vision-Language-Action Generative World Model

abstract: Predictive posterior densities (PPDs) are essential in approximate inference for quantifying predictive uncertainty and comparing inference methods. Typically, PPDs are estimated by simple Monte Carlo (MC) averages. In this paper, we expose a critical under-recognized issue: the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the simple MC estimator can sometimes be extremely low, leading to unreliable estimates. Our main contribution is a theoretical analysis demonstrating that even with exact inference, SNR can decay rapidly with an increase in (a) the mismatch between training and test data, (b) the dimensionality of the latent space, or (c) the size of test data relative to training data. Through several examples, we empirically verify these claims and show that these factors indeed lead to poor SNR and unreliable PPD estimates (sometimes, estimates are off by hundreds of nats even with a million samples). While not the primary focus, we also explore an adaptive importance sampling approach as an illustrative way to mitigate the problem, where we learn the proposal distribution by maximizing a variational proxy to the SNR. Taken together, our findings highlight an important challenge and provide essential insights for reliable estimation.

paragraphs: Posterior predictive densities support uncertainty quantification and comparisons between inference methods. They are often estimated by averaging Monte Carlo samples. This paper shows that such averages can have extremely low signal-to-noise ratios, making the estimates unreliable even when the underlying posterior inference is exact.

The theoretical analysis identifies three factors that can rapidly worsen the estimator's signal-to-noise ratio: mismatch between training and test data, a larger latent space, and more test data relative to training data. Examples empirically confirm these effects. In some cases, estimates remain wrong by hundreds of nats despite using a million samples, illustrating how a large sample count can coexist with poor estimation.

The authors also explore adaptive importance sampling as a possible mitigation. They learn its proposal distribution by maximizing a variational proxy for signal-to-noise ratio. This is an illustrative response rather than the paper's primary contribution. The main finding separates the quality of posterior inference from the reliability of a predictive-density estimate, showing why accurate inference alone does not remove this particular source of estimation error.
summary.tldr: Simple Monte Carlo posterior predictive estimates can be highly unreliable even with exact inference and very large sample counts.

title: Understanding the difficulties of posterior predictive estimation

abstract: In many classification applications, the prediction of a deep neural network (DNN) based classifier needs to be accompanied by some confidence indication. Two popular approaches for that aim are: 1) Calibration: modifies the classifier’s softmax values such that the maximal value better estimates the correctness probability; and 2) Conformal Prediction (CP): produces a prediction set of candidate labels that contains the true label with a user-specified probability, guaranteeing marginal coverage but not, e.g., per class coverage. In practice, both types of indications are desirable, yet, so far the interplay between them has not been investigated. Focusing on the ubiquitous Temperature Scaling (TS) calibration, we start this paper with an extensive empirical study of its effect on prominent CP methods. We show that while TS calibration improves the class-conditional coverage of adaptive CP methods, surprisingly, it negatively affects their prediction set sizes. Motivated by this behavior, we explore the effect of TS on CP beyond its calibration application and reveal an intriguing trend under which it allows to trade prediction set size and conditional coverage of adaptive CP methods. Then, we establish a mathematical theory that explains the entire non-monotonic trend. Finally, based on our experiments and theory, we offer guidelines for practitioners to effectively combine adaptive CP with calibration, aligned with user-defined goals.

paragraphs: A classifier can express confidence through calibrated probabilities or through a set of plausible labels. Conformal prediction constructs such sets with a specified marginal coverage guarantee, but that guarantee does not ensure the same coverage for every class. This paper studies how temperature scaling, a common calibration method, interacts with conformal prediction.

An extensive empirical study finds that temperature scaling improves class-conditional coverage for adaptive conformal methods while making prediction set sizes worse. The result exposes a tension between two desirable properties: more even coverage across classes and smaller, more informative candidate sets. Better probability calibration therefore does not automatically improve every aspect of the resulting prediction sets.

The authors then investigate temperature scaling beyond its usual calibration purpose. They identify a non-monotonic relationship that allows trading set size against conditional coverage, and develop mathematical theory explaining the full trend. Based on the theory and experiments, they offer practical guidance for combining calibration with adaptive conformal prediction according to the user’s priorities.
summary.tldr: Temperature scaling creates a theoretically explained trade-off between prediction set size and class-conditional coverage in adaptive conformal prediction.

title: On Temperature Scaling and Conformal Prediction of Deep Classifiers

abstract: We consider a distributed learning problem, where agents minimize a global objective function by exchanging information over a network. Our approach has two distinct features: (i) It substantially reduces communication by triggering communication only when necessary, and (ii) it is agnostic to the data-distribution among the different agents. We can therefore guarantee convergence even if the local data-distributions of the agents are arbitrarily distinct. We analyze the convergence rate of the algorithm both in convex and nonconvex settings and derive accelerated convergence rates in a convex setting. We also characterize the effect of communication failures and demonstrate that our algorithm is robust to communication failures. The article concludes by presenting numerical results from distributed learning tasks on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. The experiments underline communication savings of 35% or more due to the event-based communication strategy, show resilience towards heterogeneous data-distributions, and highlight that our approach outperforms common baselines such as FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD and FedADMM.

paragraphs: Distributed learning asks multiple agents to improve a shared objective by exchanging information over a network. Communication can be costly, and different agents may hold very different data. This paper develops an ADMM-based approach that triggers communication only when needed and does not require similar data distributions across participating agents.

The authors analyze convergence in both convex and nonconvex settings, with accelerated convergence rates established in a convex setting. Their guarantees accommodate arbitrarily distinct local data distributions. They also characterize how communication failures affect the algorithm and demonstrate robustness to such failures, addressing another practical obstacle to coordinating learning across a network.

Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 report communication savings of at least 35% from the event-based strategy. They also show resilience to heterogeneous data and better performance than FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, and FedADMM in the evaluated tasks. Together, the analysis and experiments support selective communication as a way to reduce network traffic while continuing to learn effectively from agents with different local datasets.
summary.tldr: Event-triggered distributed learning reduces communication while supporting convergence across agents with arbitrarily different local data distributions.

title: Distributed Event-Based Learning via ADMM

abstract: Boosting provides a practical and provably effective framework for constructing accurate learning algorithms from inaccurate rules of thumb. It extends the promise of sample-efficient learning to settings where direct Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) may not be implementable efficiently. In the realizable setting, boosting is known to offer this computational reprieve without compromising on sample efficiency. However, in the agnostic case, existing boosting algorithms fall short of achieving the optimal sample complexity. We highlight a previously unexplored avenue of improvement: unlabeled samples. We design a computationally efficient agnostic boosting algorithm that matches the sample complexity of ERM, given polynomially many additional unlabeled samples. In fact, we show that the total number of samples needed, unlabeled and labeled inclusive, is never more than that for the best known agnostic boosting algorithm – so this result is never worse – while only a vanishing fraction of these need to be labeled for the algorithm to succeed. This is particularly fortuitous for learning-theoretic applications of agnostic boosting, which often take place in the distribution-specific setting, where unlabeled samples can be availed for free. We also prove that the resultant guarantee is resilient against mismatch between the distributions governing the labeled and unlabeled samples. Finally, we detail an application of this result in reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Boosting combines imperfect learning rules into a more accurate predictor. In the agnostic setting, where the learning problem need not admit a perfectly correct predictor, existing boosting methods have required more samples than the optimal benchmark. This paper investigates whether additional unlabeled examples can close that gap while preserving computational efficiency.

The proposed algorithm matches the labeled sample complexity of empirical risk minimization when given polynomially many extra unlabeled samples. Its total sample requirement, counting both labeled and unlabeled examples, is no greater than that of the best known agnostic boosting algorithm. Only a vanishing fraction of those examples need labels, making the distinction between the two sample types central to the result.

This tradeoff is particularly useful in distribution-specific learning settings where unlabeled examples can be available for free. The authors also prove resilience to mismatch between the distributions supplying labeled and unlabeled data and describe a reinforcement learning application. The contribution is a theoretical route to sample-optimal labeled learning through a broader use of unlabeled information.
summary.tldr: Additional unlabeled data lets an efficient agnostic boosting algorithm match optimal labeled sample complexity without increasing the best known total sample requirement.

title: Sample-Optimal Agnostic Boosting with Unlabeled Data

abstract: Foundation models are strong data compressors, but when accounting for their parameter size, their compression ratios are inferior to standard compression algorithms. Naively reducing the parameter count does not necessarily help as it deteriorates predictions and, accordingly, compression. We conduct a large-scale empirical study to find a sweet spot where pre-trained vanilla transformers can achieve competitive compression ratios. To this end, we train models on 165GB of raw byte sequences of either text, image, or audio data (and all possible combinations of the three) and then compress 1GB of out-of-distribution (OOD) data from each modality. We find that relatively small models (millions of parameters) can outperform standard general-purpose compression algorithms (gzip, LZMA2) and even domain-specific compressors (PNG, JPEG-XL, FLAC) — even when accounting for parameter size. We achieve, e.g., the lowest compression ratio of 0.49 on OOD audio data (vs. 0.54 for FLAC). We conduct extensive ablations and hyperparameter sweeps to study the impact of model- and dataset scale, and we investigate the effect of unimodal versus multimodal training. We find that even small models can be trained to perform well on multiple modalities, but unlike large-scale foundation models, transfer to unseen modalities is generally weak.

This paper empirically searches for a useful balance between model size and compression quality using ordinary pretrained transformers.

summary.tldr: Small byte-level transformers can outperform conventional compressors even when their parameter storage is counted, though unseen-modality transfer remains weak.

title: Compression via Pre-trained Transformers: A Study on Byte-Level Multimodal Data

abstract: Motivated by applications in trajectory inference and particle tracking, we introduce Smooth Schrödinger Bridges. Our proposal generalizes prior work by allowing the reference process in the multi-marginal Schrödinger Bridge problem to be a smooth Gaussian process, leading to more regular and interpretable trajectories in applications. Though naïvely smoothing the reference process leads to a computationally intractable problem, we identify a class of processes (including the Matérn processes) for which the resulting Smooth Schrödinger Bridge problem can be lifted to a simpler problem on phase space, which can be solved in polynomial time. We develop a practical approximation of this algorithm that outperforms existing methods on numerous simulated and real single-cell RNAseq datasets.

paragraphs: Trajectory inference seeks a coherent account of movement or change from observations across time. This paper introduces Smooth Schrödinger Bridges for that setting, including particle tracking. The proposal lets the reference process in a multi-marginal Schrödinger Bridge be a smooth Gaussian process, so the inferred trajectories can be more regular and easier to interpret.

Smoothness creates a computational obstacle: simply replacing the reference process with a smoother one can make the problem intractable. The authors identify a class of processes, including Matérn processes, for which a transformation into phase space yields a simpler problem. For this class, the transformed problem can be solved in polynomial time.

They also develop a practical approximation of the algorithm and report improvements over existing methods on numerous simulated and real single-cell RNA sequencing datasets. The contribution combines a richer trajectory model with a route to computation. Its tractability result applies to the identified process class, providing a specific way to obtain smoother inferred trajectories without relying on an arbitrary smoothing choice.
summary.tldr: Smooth Schrödinger Bridges enable more regular trajectory inference through a tractable phase-space formulation for a specified class of Gaussian processes.

title: Trajectory Inference with Smooth Schrödinger Bridges

abstract: Intermediate Representations (IRs) play a critical role in compiler design and program analysis, yet their comprehension by Large Language Models (LLMs) remains underexplored. In this paper, we present an explorative empirical study evaluating the capabilities of six state-of-the-art LLMs—GPT-4, GPT-3, DeepSeek, Gemma 2, Llama 3, and Code Llama—in understanding IRs. Specifically, we assess model performance across four core tasks: control flow graph reconstruction, decompilation, code summarization, and execution reasoning. While LLMs exhibit competence in parsing IR syntax and identifying high-level structures, they consistently struggle with instruction-level reasoning, especially in control flow reasoning, loop handling, and dynamic execution. Common failure modes include misinterpreting branching instructions, omitting critical operations, and relying on heuristic reasoning rather than on precise instruction-level logic. Our findings highlight the need for IR-specific enhancements in LLM design. We recommend fine-tuning on structured IR datasets and integrating control-flow-sensitive architectures to improve the models’ effectiveness on IR-related tasks. All the experimental data and source code are publicly available at https://github.com/hjiang13/LLM4IR.

paragraphs: Compiler intermediate representations describe programs in a form used for compilation and analysis. This paper investigates how well language models understand them through an empirical study of six models: GPT-4, GPT-3, DeepSeek, Gemma 2, Llama 3, and Code Llama. The study examines several kinds of understanding instead of treating familiarity with the notation as sufficient.

The evaluation covers reconstructing control flow graphs, decompiling code, summarizing code, and reasoning about execution. The models can parse the syntax and recognize broad program structures, but consistently struggle to reason precisely through individual instructions. Branches, loops, and dynamic execution are particularly difficult, exposing a gap between recognizing a program’s shape and tracking what its operations actually do.

Observed errors include misreading branches, leaving out essential operations, and substituting heuristic reasoning for instruction-level logic. These findings motivate the authors’ recommendations to fine-tune on structured intermediate-representation datasets and incorporate architectures sensitive to control flow. Those recommendations are proposed improvements; the reported evidence establishes the models’ strengths and failure patterns across the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Six evaluated language models recognize compiler IR syntax and broad structures but struggle with precise instruction-level execution reasoning.

title: Can Large Language Models Understand Intermediate Representations in Compilers?

abstract: A fundamental question in data-driven decision making is how to quantify the uncertainty of predictions to inform risk-sensitive downstream actions, as often required in domains such as medicine. We develop a decision-theoretic foundation linking prediction sets to risk-averse decision-making, addressing three questions: (1) What is the correct notion of uncertainty quantification for risk-averse decision makers? We prove that prediction sets are optimal for decision makers who wish to optimize their value at risk. (2) What is the optimal policy that a risk averse decision maker should use to map prediction sets to actions? We show that a simple max-min decision policy is optimal for risk-averse decision makers. Finally, (3) How can we derive prediction sets that are optimal for such decision makers? We provide an exact characterization in the population regime and a distribution free finite-sample construction. These insights leads to Risk-Averse Calibration (RAC), a principled algorithm that is both practical—exploiting black-box predictions to enhance downstream utility—and safe—adhering to user-defined risk thresholds. We experimentally demonstrate RAC’s advantages in medical diagnosis and recommendation systems, showing that it substantially improves the trade-off between safety and utility, delivering higher utility than existing methods while avoiding critical errors.

paragraphs: Uncertainty estimates become useful when they help someone choose an action. This paper develops a decision-theoretic connection between prediction sets and decisions that prioritize protection against unfavorable outcomes. Its results focus specifically on decision makers optimizing value at risk, giving the uncertainty representation a precise downstream objective.

For that objective, the authors prove that prediction sets are optimal and that a max-min policy is the optimal way to turn those sets into actions. Such a policy evaluates an action through its least favorable outcome within the set. The paper also characterizes optimal prediction sets in the population setting and provides a distribution-free construction for finite samples.

These results lead to Risk-Averse Calibration, or RAC, which uses black-box predictions to improve decision utility while respecting user-chosen risk thresholds. Experiments in medical diagnosis and recommendation report a better safety–utility trade-off than existing methods, with higher utility while avoiding critical errors. The contribution connects how uncertainty is represented, how actions are selected, and how the representation is calibrated around the same risk-sensitive objective.
summary.tldr: RAC connects prediction sets and max-min decisions to value-at-risk optimization, improving the reported safety–utility trade-off under user-defined risk thresholds.

title: Decision Theoretic Foundations for Conformal Prediction: Optimal Uncertainty Quantification for Risk-Averse Agents

abstract: Foundation models (FMs) have emerged as a promising approach for time series forecasting. While effective, FMs typically remain fixed during deployment due to the high computational costs of learning them online. Consequently, deployed FMs fail to adapt their forecasts to current data characteristics, despite the availability of online feedback from newly arriving data. This raises the question of whether FM performance can be enhanced by the efficient usage of this feedback. We propose ELF to answer this question. ELF is a lightweight mechanism for the online adaption of FM forecasts in response to online feedback. ELF consists of two parts: a) the ELF-Forecaster which is used to learn the current data distribution; and b) the ELF-Weighter which is used to combine the forecasts of the FM and the ELF-Forecaster. We evaluate the performance of ELF in conjunction with several recent FMs across a suite of standard time series datasets. In all of our experiments we find that using ELF improves performance. This work demonstrates how efficient usage of online feedback can be used to improve FM forecasts.

paragraphs: A deployed forecasting model receives a useful stream of feedback as new observations reveal what actually happened. Time series foundation models often remain fixed because updating these large models online is computationally expensive. Consequently, their forecasts may not adjust to the current characteristics of the data, even when recent feedback is available.

ELF introduces a lightweight way to use that feedback. It contains an ELF-Forecaster that learns the current data distribution and an ELF-Weighter that combines this forecaster’s predictions with those of the foundation model. Adaptation therefore happens through a smaller forecasting and weighting mechanism around the existing model, making new observations useful without requiring online learning of the foundation model itself.

The authors evaluate ELF alongside several recent foundation models on standard time series datasets and report improvements in every experiment they conduct. That consistency applies to the tested combinations of models and datasets. The findings show that an additional adaptive mechanism can make practical use of incoming feedback and improve forecasts from otherwise fixed foundation models.
summary.tldr: ELF improves fixed foundation-model forecasts by combining them with a lightweight forecaster that learns from incoming data.

title: Lightweight Online Adaption for Time Series Foundation Model Forecasts

abstract: Online advertising is a vital revenue source for major internet platforms. Recently, joint advertising, which assigns a bundle of two advertisers in an ad slot instead of allocating a single advertiser, has emerged as an effective method for enhancing allocation efficiency and revenue. However, existing mechanisms for joint advertising fail to realize the optimality, as they tend to focus on individual advertisers and overlook bundle structures. This paper identifies an optimal mechanism for joint advertising in a single-slot setting. For multi-slot joint advertising, we propose BundleNet, a novel bundle-based neural network approach specifically designed for joint advertising. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that the mechanisms generated by BundleNet approximate the theoretical analysis results in the single-slot setting and achieve state-of-the-art performance in the multi-slot setting. This significantly increases platform revenue while ensuring approximate dominant strategy incentive compatibility and individual rationality.

paragraphs: Joint advertising allocates a bundle of two advertisers to an advertising slot. Designing auctions for this setting requires accounting for the bundle structure, which existing mechanisms can overlook when focusing on individual advertisers. This paper studies mechanisms that use that structure to improve allocation and platform revenue.

For a single advertising slot, the authors identify an optimal mechanism. For the more complex multi-slot setting, they introduce BundleNet, a neural network approach built around advertiser bundles. Experiments in the single-slot case show that mechanisms produced by BundleNet approximate the theoretical results. This provides a connection between the learned approach and the setting where the paper supplies an optimal solution.

In multi-slot experiments, BundleNet achieves leading performance and significantly increases platform revenue. The generated mechanisms also maintain approximate dominant strategy incentive compatibility and individual rationality, properties concerning truthful participation and participants’ willingness to take part. These approximate properties should be distinguished from exact guarantees, just as the multi-slot empirical results differ from the single-slot optimality result.
summary.tldr: The paper derives an optimal single-slot joint advertising mechanism and introduces BundleNet for strong multi-slot revenue with approximate incentive properties.

title: Optimal Auction Design in the Joint Advertising

abstract: Recent embodied agents are primarily built based on reinforcement learning (RL) or large language models (LLMs). Among them, RL agents are efficient for deployment but only perform very few tasks. By contrast, giant LLM agents (often more than 1000B parameters) present strong generalization while demanding enormous computing resources. In this work, we combine their advantages while avoiding the drawbacks by conducting the proposed referee RL on our developed large auto-regressive model (LARM). Specifically, LARM is built upon a lightweight LLM (fewer than 5B parameters) and directly outputs the next action to execute rather than text. We mathematically reveal that classic RL feedbacks vanish in long-horizon embodied exploration and introduce a giant LLM based referee to handle this reward vanishment during training LARM. In this way, LARM learns to complete diverse open-world tasks without human intervention. Especially, LARM successfully harvests enchanted diamond equipment in Minecraft, which demands significantly longer decision-making chains than the highest achievements of prior best methods.

paragraphs: Embodied agents need to choose actions over long sequences, often before useful feedback becomes available. LARM aims to combine the deployment efficiency associated with reinforcement-learning agents and the generalization associated with large language models. It builds an action-producing agent from a language model with fewer than five billion parameters.

LARM directly predicts the next action to execute. During training, a much larger language model serves as a referee. The authors mathematically analyze how conventional reinforcement-learning feedback vanishes during long-horizon embodied exploration, and introduce referee reinforcement learning to address this problem. This places the large model's evaluative capability within the training process for the smaller acting model.

The resulting agent learns diverse open-world tasks without human intervention. A highlighted achievement is obtaining enchanted diamond equipment in Minecraft, which the authors describe as requiring substantially longer decision chains than prior leading achievements. This result supports the approach's ability to sustain progress across extended action sequences, where useful training feedback is particularly difficult to obtain.
summary.tldr: LARM uses a large-language-model referee during reinforcement learning to train a smaller action model for long-horizon embodied tasks.

title: LARM: Large Auto-Regressive Model for Long-Horizon Embodied Intelligence

abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are ubiquitous in numerous real-world applications, and watermarking facilitates protecting intellectual property and preventing potential harm from AI-generated content. Existing watermarking methods mainly focus on static plain text or image data, while they can hardly be applied to dynamic graphs due to spatial and temporal variations of structured data. This motivates us to propose KGMark, the first graph watermarking framework that aims to generate robust, detectable, and transparent diffusion fingerprints for dynamic KG data. Specifically, we propose a novel clustering-based alignment method to adapt the watermark to spatial variations. Meanwhile, we present a redundant embedding strategy to harden the diffusion watermark against various attacks, facilitating the robustness of the watermark to the temporal variations. Additionally, we introduce a novel learnable mask matrix to improve the transparency of diffusion fingerprints. By doing so, our KGMark properly tackles the variation challenges of structured data. Experiments on various public benchmarks show the effectiveness of our proposed KGMark.

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs contain structured information that can change across space and time, making watermarking more complicated than for static text or images. KGMark is a framework for placing diffusion fingerprints in dynamic knowledge graphs. It aims to make these fingerprints detectable and robust while preserving transparency in the marked data.

The framework addresses graph variation through several coordinated mechanisms. A clustering-based alignment method adapts the watermark to spatial changes. Redundant embedding strengthens the watermark against attacks and helps it withstand temporal variation. A learnable mask matrix improves fingerprint transparency, addressing another requirement alongside detectability and robustness.

Experiments on multiple public benchmarks support KGMark’s effectiveness. The contribution is a watermarking design that explicitly accounts for the changing structure of graph data, with different components addressing alignment, persistence, and transparency. This matters for the paper’s motivating uses of watermarking, including intellectual property protection and reducing potential harm associated with AI-generated content, where a fingerprint needs to remain useful as the underlying structured data varies.
summary.tldr: KGMark combines alignment, redundant embedding, and learnable masking to watermark knowledge graphs that change over space and time.

title: KGMark: A Diffusion Watermark for Knowledge Graphs

abstract: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) aims to integrate the complementary strengths of offline and online RL by pre-training an agent offline and subsequently fine-tuning it through online interactions. However, recent studies reveal that offline pre-trained agents often underperform during online fine-tuning due to inaccurate value estimation caused by distribution shift, with random initialization proving more effective in certain cases. In this work, we propose a novel method, Online Pre-Training for Offline-to-Online RL (OPT), explicitly designed to address the issue of inaccurate value estimation in offline pre-trained agents. OPT introduces a new learning phase, Online Pre-Training, which allows the training of a new value function tailored specifically for effective online fine-tuning. Implementation of OPT on TD3 and SPOT demonstrates an average 30% improvement in performance across a wide range of D4RL environments, including MuJoCo, Antmaze, and Adroit.

paragraphs: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning starts with recorded experience and then improves an agent through new interactions. That transition can expose inaccurate value estimates because the experience encountered online differs from the offline data. Prior studies cited in the abstract find that this problem can sometimes make offline pretraining less useful than starting from random initialization.

OPT introduces an additional phase called Online Pre-Training. Its purpose is to train a new value function specifically suited to the later online fine-tuning stage. The method therefore targets the quality of the agent's estimates during the transition, treating preparation of those estimates as an explicit learning step.

The authors implement OPT with TD3 and SPOT and evaluate it across D4RL environments spanning MuJoCo, Antmaze, and Adroit. They report an average performance improvement of 30%. These results support preparing a new value function as a useful intervention for offline-to-online learning in the tested settings. The average summarizes performance across the evaluations rather than specifying an identical gain in every environment.
summary.tldr: OPT adds a phase that trains a new value function for online fine-tuning, reporting a 30% average performance improvement in its evaluations.

title: Online Pre-Training for Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The Robust Regularized Markov Decision Process (RRMDP) is proposed to learn policies robust to dynamics shifts by adding regularization to the transition dynamics in the value function. Existing methods mostly use unstructured regularization, potentially leading to conservative policies under unrealistic transitions. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework, the $d$-rectangular linear RRMDP ($d$-RRMDP), which introduces latent structures into both transition kernels and regularization. We focus on offline reinforcement learning, where an agent learns policies from a precollected dataset in the nominal environment. We develop the Robust Regularized Pessimistic Value Iteration (R2PVI) algorithm that employs linear function approximation for robust policy learning in $d$-RRMDPs with $f$-divergence based regularization terms on transition kernels. We provide instance-dependent upper bounds on the suboptimality gap of R2PVI policies, demonstrating that these bounds are influenced by how well the dataset covers state-action spaces visited by the optimal robust policy under robustly admissible transitions. We establish information-theoretic lower bounds to verify that our algorithm is near-optimal. Finally, numerical experiments validate that R2PVI learns robust policies and exhibits superior computational efficiency compared to baseline methods.

paragraphs: Robust offline reinforcement learning seeks policies that tolerate changes in environment dynamics while learning from previously collected data. Regularizing transition dynamics can support robustness, but unstructured regularization may lead to overly conservative policies by considering unrealistic transitions. This paper introduces a framework that places latent structure in both the transition model and its regularization.

The framework is a d-rectangular linear Robust Regularized Markov Decision Process. Its proposed algorithm, Robust Regularized Pessimistic Value Iteration, uses linear function approximation and f-divergence regularization of transition kernels. Learning uses a dataset collected in the nominal environment, while the policy objective accounts for admissible changes to that environment's dynamics.

The authors derive instance-dependent upper bounds on policy suboptimality. Those bounds depend on how well the dataset covers state-action pairs visited by the optimal robust policy under robustly admissible transitions. Information-theoretic lower bounds establish near-optimality of the algorithm. Numerical experiments also report robust policies and better computational efficiency than baselines, connecting the structured formulation to both theoretical performance and practical computation.
summary.tldr: R2PVI learns robust offline policies using structured transition regularization, with near-optimal guarantees that depend on dataset coverage.

title: Robust Offline Reinforcement Learning with Linearly Structured $f$-Divergence Regularization

abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) has become a popular and effective method to apply strong foundation models to specific downstream tasks. In this work, we explore the learning dynamics throughout the CPT process for large language models (LLMs). We specifically focus on how general and downstream domain performance evolves at each training step, with domain performance measured via validation losses. We have observed that the CPT loss curve fundamentally characterizes the transition from one curve to another hidden curve, and could be described by decoupling the effects of distribution shift and learning rate (LR) annealing. We derive a CPT scaling law that combines the two factors, enabling the prediction of loss at any (continual) training steps and across learning rate schedules (LRS) in CPT. Our formulation presents a comprehensive understanding of several critical factors in CPT, including the learning rate, the training steps, and the distribution distance between PT and CPT datasets. Moreover, our approach can be adapted to customize training hyper-parameters to different CPT goals such as balancing general and domain-specific performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our scaling law holds across various CPT datasets and training hyper-parameters.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a language model’s performance changes during continual pretraining, when a pretrained model receives further training on a particular domain. It tracks both general and domain-specific performance through validation loss. The goal is to understand the learning trajectory well enough to predict it and choose training settings for different objectives.

The authors observe that the loss trajectory can be understood as a transition between an initial curve and another hidden curve. Their formulation separates the effect of changing the training-data distribution from the effect of gradually reducing the learning rate. Combining these factors yields a scaling law for predicting loss across continual-training steps and learning-rate schedules.

The formulation accounts for training duration, learning rate, and the distance between the original and continual-pretraining data distributions. It can also guide hyperparameter choices when balancing general performance against domain specialization. Experiments across multiple continual-pretraining datasets and settings support the scaling law, providing empirical evidence that this decomposition captures useful regularities in adaptation.
summary.tldr: A continual-pretraining scaling law separates distribution shift from learning-rate effects to predict loss trajectories and guide training choices.

title: Learning Dynamics in Continual Pre-Training for Large Language Models

abstract: The ability of agents to collaborate with previously unknown teammates on the fly, known as ad hoc teamwork (AHT), is crucial in many real-world applications. Existing approaches to AHT require online interactions with the environment and some carefully designed teammates. However, these prerequisites can be infeasible in practice. In this work, we extend the AHT problem to the offline setting, where the policy of the ego agent is directly learned from a multi-agent interaction dataset. We propose a hierarchical sequence modeling framework called TAGET that addresses critical challenges in the offline setting, including limited data, partial observability and online adaptation. The core idea of TAGET is to dynamically predict teammate-aware rewards-to-go and sub-goals, so that the ego agent can adapt to the changes of teammates’ behaviors in real time. Extensive experimental results show that TAGET significantly outperforms existing solutions to AHT in the offline setting.

paragraphs: Ad hoc teamwork asks an agent to cooperate with teammates it has not encountered before. Training for this situation commonly depends on interacting with an environment and having carefully designed teammates available. This paper studies an offline alternative: learning the focal agent’s policy directly from recorded interactions among multiple agents.

The proposed framework, TAGET, uses hierarchical sequence modeling to address limited training data, incomplete observations, and adaptation during use. Its central mechanism predicts both teammate-aware rewards-to-go and sub-goals dynamically. These predictions describe anticipated future reward and intermediate objectives while accounting for teammates, giving the agent a way to adjust as their behavior changes.

The experiments report substantial improvements over existing ad hoc teamwork approaches in the offline setting. The contribution is therefore a way to connect training from fixed records with responsive collaboration at deployment. Offline learning describes how the policy is acquired; TAGET’s changing predictions provide the mechanism for adapting its behavior when working with unfamiliar teammates.
summary.tldr: TAGET learns teamwork from recorded interactions and dynamically predicts teammate-aware goals and future rewards to adapt to unfamiliar collaborators.

title: Ad Hoc Teamwork via Offline Goal-Based Decision Transformers

abstract: As large language models (LLMs) see wide adoption in software engineering, the reliable assessment of the correctness and security of LLM-generated code is crucial. Notably, prior work showed that LLMs are prone to generating code with security vulnerabilities, highlighting that security is often overlooked. These insights were enabled by specialized benchmarks crafted by security experts through significant manual effort. However, benchmarks (i) inevitably end up contaminating training data, (ii) must extend to new tasks to provide a more complete picture, and (iii) must increase in difficulty to challenge more capable LLMs. In this work, we address these challenges and present AutoBaxBuilder, an automated pipeline that generates code security benchmarking tasks from scratch. It leverages the code-understanding capabilities of LLMs combined with robust reliability checks to construct functional tests and end-to-end security-probing exploits. The quality of the pipeline is quantitatively confirmed by aligning its predictions with an expert-written baseline and qualitatively validated through manual soundness verification. We use AutoBaxBuilder to construct a new benchmark and release it to the public as AutoBaxBench, together with a thorough evaluation on contemporary LLMs. AutoBaxBuilder generates new tasks in under 2 hours, for less than USD 4. Including a manual verification, this reduces the required human effort for benchmark construction by a factor of 12.

paragraphs: Evaluating generated code requires checking both whether it works and whether it contains exploitable weaknesses. Security benchmarks have typically required substantial expert effort, yet they need continual renewal as existing tasks enter training data and models become more capable. AutoBaxBuilder addresses this maintenance problem by automatically creating new code security evaluation tasks.

The pipeline combines language models’ code understanding with reliability checks. It constructs functional tests alongside end-to-end exploits that probe security, making intended behavior and vulnerability detection part of the same task-building process. The authors assess its quality by comparing its predictions with an expert-written baseline and manually checking task soundness.

The resulting public benchmark, AutoBaxBench, accompanies an evaluation of contemporary language models. The authors report task generation in under two hours for less than four US dollars. Even when manual verification is included, benchmark construction requires twelve times less human effort. The contribution is therefore a practical way to refresh security evaluations while retaining explicit checks on the reliability of generated tasks.
summary.tldr: AutoBaxBuilder automates security benchmark construction with functional tests and exploits, reducing human effort twelvefold including manual verification.

title: AutoBaxBuilder: Bootstrapping Code Security Benchmarking

abstract: Safe reinforcement learning (Safe RL) aims to maximize expected return while satisfying safety constraints, typically modeled as Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs). While primal-dual methods scale well to deep RL, they often suffer from delayed constraint correction, leading to oscillatory behavior and prolonged safety violations. In this paper, we propose Constraint-Sensitive Policy Optimization (CSPO), a first-order primal-dual method that incorporates local constraint sensitivity into policy updates. CSPO augments the primal objective with a constraint-sensitive correction derived from the shortest signed distance to the safety boundary, enabling smarter recovery steps back to safety, compensating for delayed Lagrange multiplier updates, reducing oscillations near the boundary, and preserving the KKT solutions of the original constrained problem. Experiments on navigation and locomotion benchmarks demonstrate that CSPO achieves faster safety recovery and high reward preservation, resulting in higher constrained returns compared to state-of-the-art primal-dual and penalty-based methods.

In this paper, we propose Constraint-Sensitive Policy Optimization (CSPO), a first-order primal-dual method that incorporates local constraint sensitivity into policy updates. CSPO augments the primal objective with a constraint-sensitive correction derived from the shortest signed distance to the safety boundary, enabling smarter recovery steps back to safety, compensating for delayed Lagrange multiplier updates, reducing oscillations near the boundary, and preserving the KKT solutions of the original constrained problem. Experiments on navigation and locomotion benchmarks demonstrate that CSPO achieves faster safety recovery and high reward preservation, resulting in higher constrained returns compared to state-of-the-art primal-dual and penalty-based methods.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning seeks high reward while satisfying safety constraints. Primal-dual methods adjust both the policy and the multipliers that govern constraint pressure. Their corrections can arrive too late, allowing violations to persist and causing the policy to oscillate near the boundary between safe and unsafe behavior.

Constraint-Sensitive Policy Optimization, or CSPO, adds local information about constraint sensitivity directly to policy updates. Its correction comes from the shortest signed distance to the safety boundary. This supplies a more immediate recovery signal, compensating for delayed multiplier updates and reducing oscillation. The method uses first-order optimization and preserves the original problem's KKT solutions, the constrained optimality conditions considered in the paper.

On navigation and locomotion benchmarks, CSPO returns to safety faster while retaining high reward. It achieves higher constrained returns than the evaluated state-of-the-art primal-dual and penalty methods. These findings concern improved recovery and reward preservation during constrained learning; the mechanism specifically addresses how policy updates respond when safety correction is needed.
summary.tldr: CSPO uses local constraint sensitivity to accelerate safety recovery and reduce oscillations while preserving reward in tested reinforcement-learning tasks.

title: CSPO: Constraint-Sensitive Policy Optimization for Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Symmetry is fundamental to understanding physical systems and can improve performance and sample efficiency in machine learning. Both pursuits require knowledge of the underlying symmetries in data, yet discovering these symmetries automatically is challenging. We propose LieFlow, a novel framework that reframes symmetry discovery as a distribution learning problem on Lie groups. Instead of searching for the symmetry generators, our approach operates directly in group space, modeling a symmetry distribution over a large hypothesis group $G$. The support of the learned distribution reveals the underlying symmetry group $H \subseteq G$. Unlike previous works, LieFlow can discover both continuous and discrete symmetries within a unified framework, without assuming a fixed Lie algebra basis or a specific distribution over the group elements. Experiments on synthetic 2D and 3D point clouds, ModelNet10, and a real-world MI-Motion dataset show that LieFlow accurately discovers continuous and discrete subgroups, significantly outperforming a state-of-the-art baseline, LieGAN, in identifying discrete symmetries.

paragraphs: LieFlow addresses automatic discovery of the symmetries present in data. Knowing these symmetries can help explain physical systems and improve machine-learning performance and sample efficiency. The challenge is to infer the relevant transformations without already specifying the precise symmetry structure that the data obey.

The framework treats discovery as learning a distribution over a larger candidate Lie group. Instead of searching directly for symmetry generators, it works with group elements themselves. The support of the learned distribution reveals the subgroup representing the underlying symmetries. This formulation accommodates both continuous and discrete symmetries without requiring a fixed Lie algebra basis or a prescribed distribution over group elements.

The authors evaluate LieFlow on synthetic two- and three-dimensional point clouds, ModelNet10, and MI-Motion data. They report accurate recovery of continuous and discrete subgroups, with especially strong improvements over LieGAN for discrete symmetries. The findings support distribution learning in group space as a unified route to identifying different kinds of symmetry.
summary.tldr: LieFlow learns distributions over transformation groups to discover both continuous and discrete symmetries in data.

title: Discovering Symmetry Groups with Flow Matching

abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) has emerged as a promising paradigm for vision–language models (VLMs) to bridge the distribution gap between pre-training and test data. Recent works have focused on backpropagation-free TTA methods that rely on cache-based designs, but these introduce two key limitations. First, inference latency increases as the cache grows with the number of classes, leading to inefficiencies in large-scale settings. Second, suboptimal performance occurs when the cache contains insufficient or incorrect samples. Particularly, knowledge prototypes are adaptively weighted based on the zero-shot class confidence of each test sample, incorporating the sample’s visual features into the corresponding class-specific prototype. It is worth highlighting that the knowledge from past test samples is integrated and utilized solely in the prototypes, eliminating the overhead of cache population and retrieval that hinders the efficiency of existing TTA methods. For example, PTA improves CLIP’s accuracy from 65.64% to 69.38% on 10 cross-domain benchmarks, while retaining 92% of CLIP’s inference speed on large-scale ImageNet-1K. title: Prototype-Based Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) extend the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by combining heterogeneous model architectures to handle diverse modalities like images and audio. However, this inherent heterogeneity in MLLM model structure and data types makes makeshift extensions to existing LLM training frameworks unsuitable for efficient MLLM training, especially in distributed training. In this paper, we present Cornstarch, an efficient distributed MLLM training framework that contemplates MLLM’s unique characteristics in both model and data parallelization. Cornstarch introduces frozen-aware pipeline parallelism and workload-balanced context parallelism to improve MLLM training throughput. Our extensive evaluation shows that Cornstarch outperforms state-of-the-art solutions by $2.26\times$ on average in terms of MLLM training throughput. Cornstarch is an open-source project and available on Github.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models combine components and data types for inputs such as text, images, and audio. That mixture creates distributed-training demands that differ from those of language-only models. This paper introduces Cornstarch, a framework designed around those differences, arguing that makeshift extensions to existing language-model training systems leave substantial efficiency unrealized.

Cornstarch changes both model and data parallelization. Its frozen-aware pipeline parallelism accounts for components whose parameters are held fixed during training. Its workload-balanced context parallelism addresses how work is distributed when processing context. Together, these mechanisms treat the model’s heterogeneous structure and the workload’s heterogeneous data as central scheduling concerns.

In the authors’ extensive evaluation, Cornstarch achieves an average training-throughput improvement of 2.26 times over the state-of-the-art solutions compared. The reported gain concerns how much training work the system processes, rather than a claim about improved model prediction quality. The contribution is an open-source training framework showing that explicit support for multimodal structure can substantially improve distributed execution in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Cornstarch adapts distributed parallelism to multimodal workloads and reports 2.26-times higher average training throughput than compared systems.

title: Efficient Distributed MLLM Training with Cornstarch

abstract: Generative sequence modeling faces a fundamental tension between the expressivity of Transformers and the efficiency of linear sequence models. Existing efficient architectures are theoretically bounded by shallow, single-step linear updates, while powerful iterative methods like Test-Time Training (TTT) break hardware parallelism due to two dimensions of serial dependency: token-level state reliance and step-level iteration loops. We propose PRISM (Parallel Residual Iterative Sequence Model) to resolve this tension. PRISM explicitly reconstructs the expressive gate $\times$ residual $\times$ direction iteration pattern of TTT in a parallelizable form. We employ a Write-Forget Decoupling strategy that isolates non-linearity within the injection operator. To bypass the serial dependency of explicit solvers, PRISM utilizes a two-stage proxy architecture: a short-convolution anchors the initial residual using local history energy, while a learned predictor estimates the refinement updates directly from the input. This design distills structural patterns associated with iterative correction into a parallelizable feedforward operator. Theoretically, we prove that this formulation achieves Rank-$L$ accumulation, structurally expanding the update scheme beyond the single-step Rank-$1$ bottleneck. Empirically, it achieves comparable performance to explicit optimization methods while achieving 174x higher throughput. Codes are available in https://github.com/gpr-prism/prism/.

summary.tldr: PRISM approximates iterative sequence-model corrections with a parallel feedforward architecture, reporting comparable performance and 174-fold higher throughput.

title: PRISM: Parallel Residual Iterative Sequence Model

abstract: Many materials properties depend on higher-order derivatives of the potential energy surface, yet machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) trained with a standard loss on energy, force, and stress errors can exhibit error in curvature, degrading the prediction of vibrational properties. We introduce phonon fine-tuning (PFT), which directly supervises second-order force constants of materials by matching MLIP energy Hessians to DFT-computed force constants from finite displacement phonon calculations. To scale to large supercells, PFT stochastically samples Hessian columns and computes the loss with a single Hessian-vector product. We also use a simple co-training scheme to incorporate upstream data to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. On the MDR Phonon benchmark, PFT improves Nequix MP by 55% on average across phonon thermodynamic properties and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among models trained on Materials Project trajectories. PFT also generalizes to improve properties beyond second-derivatives, improving thermal conductivity predictions that rely on third-order derivatives of the potential energy.

Phonon fine-tuning directly targets this mismatch instead of relying on standard training losses to constrain it indirectly.

To make this practical for large supercells, it randomly samples Hessian columns and evaluates the loss using a single Hessian-vector product. Co-training with upstream data helps mitigate forgetting while the model learns this additional physical information.

On the MDR Phonon benchmark, PFT improves Nequix MP by an average of 55% across phonon thermodynamic properties. It achieves leading accuracy among models trained on Materials Project trajectories. The benefits also extend to thermal conductivity predictions, which depend on third-order energy derivatives. This shows that explicitly supervising second-order behavior can improve both the directly targeted vibrational properties and a reported property involving higher-order derivatives.
summary.tldr: Phonon fine-tuning directly supervises energy curvature, improving vibrational-property predictions and extending benefits to thermal conductivity.

title: PFT: Phonon Fine-tuning for Machine Learned Interatomic Potentials

abstract: While sparse autoencoders provide features more interpretable than individual neurons, reliably characterizing them remains challenging. We propose Query Lens, which extends Logit Lens to enable more comprehensive and faithful interpretations of sparse features. By jointly considering encoder-side key features and decoder-side value features, we identify both the inputs that activate a feature and the outputs it promotes. We also account for indirect, module-mediated effects that arise when the feature is processed by downstream modules, going beyond the direct effect captured by Logit Lens. In experiments, we find that Query Lens yields coherent token signatures for features that remain uninterpretable under Logit Lens. Finally, we propose the Subspace Channel Hypothesis, suggesting that downstream modules read features through layer-specific subspaces.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders can expose features that are easier to interpret than individual neurons, but explaining what those features do remains difficult. Query Lens expands the interpretation task to include both what activates a feature and what that feature promotes in the model’s output. This provides a more complete account of its role.

The method jointly examines encoder-side key features and decoder-side value features. It also follows indirect effects produced when downstream modules process a feature, extending beyond the direct output effect captured by Logit Lens. This matters because a feature’s eventual influence can depend on how later computation transforms or reads it.

Experiments find coherent token signatures for features that remain uninterpretable under Logit Lens. The authors also propose the Subspace Channel Hypothesis: downstream modules may read features through layer-specific subspaces. This is presented as a hypothesis about the organization of feature use, alongside empirical evidence that including activation conditions and indirect effects improves interpretability.
summary.tldr: Query Lens interprets sparse features through their activating inputs, promoted outputs, and indirect effects in downstream modules.

title: Query Lens: Interpreting Sparse Key-Value Features with Indirect Effects

abstract: This work studies online episodic tabular Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known transitions and develops best-of-both-worlds algorithms that achieve refined data-dependent regret bounds in the adversarial regime and variance-dependent regret bounds in the stochastic regime. We quantify MDP complexity using a first-order quantity and several new data-dependent measures for the adversarial regime, including a second-order quantity and a path-length measure, as well as variance-based measures for the stochastic regime. To adapt to these measures, we develop algorithms based on global optimization and policy optimization, both built on optimistic follow-the-regularized-leader with log-barrier regularization. For global optimization, our algorithms achieve first-order, second-order, and path-length regret bounds in the adversarial regime, and in the stochastic regime, they achieve a variance-aware gap-independent bound and a variance-aware gap-dependent bound that is polylogarithmic in the number of episodes. For policy optimization, our algorithms achieve the same data- and variance-dependent adaptivity, up to a factor of the episode horizon, by exploiting a new optimistic $Q$-function estimator. Finally, we establish regret lower bounds in terms of data-dependent complexity measures for the adversarial regime and a variance measure for the stochastic regime, implying that the regret upper bounds achieved by the global-optimization approach are nearly optimal.

paragraphs: This paper studies episodic decision-making in finite-state, finite-action environments whose transition rules are known. It develops algorithms with regret guarantees that adapt to the observed problem's difficulty. Regret measures the accumulated disadvantage relative to a comparison policy, so a more adaptive bound can distinguish easier learning sequences from worst-case ones.

The analysis covers both adversarial and stochastic regimes. For adversarial settings, it introduces several data-dependent complexity measures, including second-order and path-length quantities. For stochastic settings, the guarantees depend on variance. Both global-optimization and policy-optimization algorithms use optimistic follow-the-regularized-leader with log-barrier regularization. A new optimistic Q-function estimator enables the policy-optimization approach to obtain similar adaptivity, with an additional episode-horizon factor.

For global optimization, the stochastic results include a variance-aware bound independent of gaps and a gap-dependent bound growing only polylogarithmically with episode count. Matching lower-bound analysis shows that its guarantees are nearly optimal in terms of the studied complexity measures. These are theoretical results under known transitions, explaining how achievable regret can depend on data structure and variability.
summary.tldr: For tabular MDPs with known transitions, new algorithms achieve regret bounds that adapt to data complexity and stochastic variance.

title: Data- and Variance-dependent Regret Bounds for Online Tabular MDPs

abstract: Classical optimization theory establishes that zeroth-order (ZO) algorithms suffer from a dimension-dependent slowdown, with convergence rates typically scaling with the model dimension compared to first-order methods. However, in contrast to these theoretical expectations, a growing body of recent work demonstrates the successful application of ZO methods to fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) with billions of parameters. To explain this paradox, we derive the one-step learning dynamics of ZO SGD, where the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (eNTK) naturally emerges as the key term governing the learning behavior. Inspection of the eNTK produced by ZO-SGD reveals that each element corresponds to the inner product of neural tangent vectors projected onto a random low-dimensional subspace. Thus, by invoking the Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma, our analysis shows that the fidelity of the ZO eNTK is governed primarily by the number of perturbations. Crucially, the approximation error depends on the model output size rather than the massive parameter dimension. This dimension-free property provides a theoretical justification for the scalability of ZO methods to LLMs finetuning tasks. We believe that this kernel-based framework offers a novel perspective for understanding ZO methods within the context of learning dynamics.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization learns through perturbations without directly using full gradients. Classical theory predicts a slowdown tied to the number of model parameters, making successful applications to enormous language models seem surprising. This paper investigates that tension by studying how one zeroth-order stochastic-gradient step changes the model’s learning behavior.

The analysis identifies the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel as the central quantity governing those changes. For zeroth-order updates, its entries correspond to inner products of neural tangent vectors after projection into a random low-dimensional space. Applying the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma connects the quality of this projected representation to the number of perturbations used.

The resulting approximation error depends on the size of the model output rather than its potentially massive parameter count. This gives a theoretical explanation for how zeroth-order methods can remain useful in language-model fine-tuning despite pessimistic dimension-dependent expectations. The result concerns the kernel approximation and one-step learning dynamics; it provides a different analytical perspective on scalability without asserting that all optimization costs become independent of model size.
summary.tldr: A kernel analysis explains zeroth-order fine-tuning scalability through approximation error governed by output size and perturbations rather than parameter count.

title: Learning Dynamics of Zeroth-Order Optimization: A Kernel Perspective

abstract: Imitation learning with diffusion models has advanced robotic control by capturing the multi-modal action distributions. However, existing methods typically treat observations only as high-level conditions to the denoising network, rather than integrating them into the stochastic dynamics of the diffusion process itself. As a result, the sampling is forced to begin from random noise, weakening the coupling between perception and control and often yielding suboptimal performance. We propose BridgePolicy, a generative visuomotor policy that directly integrates observations into the stochastic dynamics via a diffusion-bridge formulation. By constructing an observation-informed trajectory, BridgePolicy enables sampling to start from a rich and informative prior rather than random noise, substantially improving precision and reliability in control. A key difficulty is that diffusion bridge normally connects distributions of matched dimensionality, while robotic observations are heterogeneous and not naturally aligned with actions. To overcome this, we introduce a semantic aligner to unify the visual and state inputs and align the observations with action representations, making diffusion bridge applicable to heterogeneous robot data. Extensive experiments across 52 simulation tasks on three benchmarks and 5 real-world tasks demonstrate that BridgePolicy consistently outperforms state-of-the-art generative policies. Our code is available at https://github.com/jianghcsr/BridgePolicy.

paragraphs: BridgePolicy changes how diffusion-based robot policies use observations when generating actions. Existing approaches commonly give observations to the denoising network as conditions while starting the sampling process from random noise. The paper argues that this leaves perception and control less tightly connected than they could be.

The proposed policy embeds observations directly into the stochastic dynamics through a diffusion bridge. Sampling therefore begins from an informative prior shaped by what the robot observes. A technical obstacle is that diffusion bridges normally connect distributions with matching dimensionality, whereas images, robot states, and actions have different forms. This alignment makes the bridge formulation applicable to heterogeneous robot data. Across 52 simulation tasks from three benchmarks and five real-world tasks, BridgePolicy consistently outperforms state-of-the-art generative policies. The reported results support the value of observation-informed sampling for control precision and reliability. The key methodological shift is where observations enter: they shape the sampling trajectory itself, as well as informing the generated behavior.
summary.tldr: BridgePolicy starts action generation from an observation-informed prior and reports stronger robot-control performance across simulated and real tasks.

title: Sample from What You See: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Diffusion Bridge with Observation-Embedded Stochastic Differential Equation

abstract: Action values are foundational to many control algorithms such as Q-learning. Therefore, efficient action-value learning is central to reinforcement learning (RL). However, learning them can be slow, requiring many updates to move values from their initialization, typically near zero, to their true values, which may be far from zero. Moreover, action-value learning algorithms typically update each state-action pair independently, without learning a value that is common to all actions within a state. In this paper, we address these inefficiencies by introducing the mean-expansion layer, which accelerates action-value learning by sharing values across actions within a state and by changing the problem from directly learning potentially large action-values to learning a lower-norm representation of them. In deep RL, this layer can be applied as a parameter-free addition to Q-network architectures without altering the underlying algorithm. Applied to deep Q-networks and implicit quantile networks, it improves aggregate performance across 57 Atari 2600 games while increasing action gaps and dramatically reducing value overestimation.

paragraphs: Q-learning depends on estimates of how valuable each action is in a given state. Learning these estimates can take many updates when they start near zero but their eventual values are much larger. Another inefficiency is that action values are typically updated separately, even though actions available in the same state may share a substantial common value.

The paper introduces a mean-expansion layer that shares value information across actions within a state. It also changes the representation being learned so that the model learns quantities with a smaller norm instead of directly learning potentially large action values. For deep reinforcement learning, this is a parameter-free addition to the network architecture and leaves the underlying learning algorithm unchanged.

Applied to deep Q-networks and implicit quantile networks, the layer improves aggregate performance over 57 Atari games. The authors also report larger gaps between action values and much less value overestimation. These findings indicate that changing how values are represented and shared can improve learning without requiring a different control algorithm.
summary.tldr: A parameter-free network layer accelerates action-value learning by sharing values across actions and learning a smaller-norm representation.

title: Accelerating Q-learning through Efficient Value-Sharing across Actions

abstract: Realizing the full potential of quantum computation requires Quantum Error Correction (QEC). QEC reduces error rates by encoding logical information across redundant physical qubits, enabling errors to be detected and corrected. A common decoder used for this task is Minimum Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM) a graph-based algorithm that relies on edge weights to identify the most likely error chains. In this work, we propose a data-driven decoder named Neural Minimum Weight Perfect Matching (NMWPM). Our decoder utilizes a hybrid architecture that integrates Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to extract local syndrome features and Transformers to capture long-range global dependencies, which are then used to predict dynamic edge weights for the MWPM decoder. To facilitate training through the non-differentiable MWPM algorithm, we formulate a novel proxy loss function that enables end-to-end optimization. Our findings on the toric code under depolarizing noise demonstrate thresholds of 17.9% and 10.95%, nearing the 18.9% and 11.0% maximum likelihood bounds, highlighting the advantage of hybrid decoders that combine the predictive capabilities of neural networks with the algorithmic structure of classical matching.

In this work, we propose a data-driven decoder named Neural Minimum Weight Perfect Matching (NMWPM). Our decoder utilizes a hybrid architecture that integrates Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to extract local syndrome features and Transformers to capture long-range global dependencies, which are then used to predict dynamic edge weights for the MWPM decoder.
