paragraphs: Quantum error correction protects logical information by distributing it across redundant physical qubits. A decoder interprets detected error signals and chooses a correction. Minimum Weight Perfect Matching is a common graph-based decoder whose edge weights determine which error chains it considers most likely.

Neural Minimum Weight Perfect Matching learns dynamic edge weights while retaining the classical matching algorithm. A graph neural network extracts local features from the error syndrome, and a Transformer captures longer-range dependencies. Their predictions adapt the weights used by matching. Because the matching operation is not differentiable, the authors introduce a proxy loss that enables end-to-end training.

For the toric code under depolarizing noise, the paper reports thresholds of 17.9% and 10.95%, approaching the cited maximum-likelihood bounds of 18.9% and 11.0%. These findings support the hybrid design: neural components interpret local and global evidence, while a structured matching algorithm uses that information to decode errors. The reported results are specific to the code and noise setting studied.
summary.tldr: NMWPM learns context-dependent graph weights for classical quantum-error matching, reaching reported thresholds near maximum-likelihood bounds.

title: Neural Minimum Weight Perfect Matching for Quantum Error Codes

abstract: Hallucinations—plausible but factually incorrect responses—pose a major challenge to the reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs), especially in multi-step or agentic settings. Existing work largely frames hallucinations as a consequence of missing knowledge; we show instead that, even when the relevant factual knowledge is present, models still produce hallucinated answers, pointing to retrieval instability rather than knowledge gaps. Building on this observation, we introduce APORIA (Aggregate Prompt-wise Observation Retrieving Instability via Asymmetry—the Socratic state of "puzzlement-in-contradiction" that hallucinations embody), a geometric framework that studies repeated responses to the same prompt in sentence-embedding space. Our central hypothesis is that genuine responses cluster more tightly than hallucinated ones; we empirically validate this and show that, after Fisher projection, the two response classes become consistently separable. We leverage this asymmetry in geometry via APORIA-LP, an efficient label-propagation method that classifies large collections of responses from as few as 30–50 annotations, achieving F1 scores above 90% across ten small-sized LLMs. To support further research, we release SOCRATES-300K, a fully labelled dataset of 300,000 responses, together with the code for both dataset generation and result reproduction. Our key finding—framing hallucinations from a geometric perspective in the embedding space—complements traditional knowledge-centric and single-response evaluation paradigms, paving the way for further research.

abstract: Speech restoration aims to recover clean speech from degraded recordings affected by noise, reverberation, bandwidth reduction, or other distortions, where input and output sampling rates may differ. Existing approaches typically assume matched input–output rates and apply redundant resampling, limiting native multi-rate processing. We formulate this gap as the extended sampling-frequency-independent (xSFI) setting, where a model must operate under decoupled input–output rates, and propose TF-Restormer, a query-based xSFI modeling framework. The model encodes only the observed input band and synthesizes the unobserved high-frequency band through extension queries with band-partitioned cross-attention, yielding an asymmetric encoder–decoder that allocates capacity to analysis while keeping synthesis lightweight. Trained with a perceptual loss, a scaled log-spectral loss, and adversarial supervision via an SFI-STFT discriminator, TF-Restormer attains balanced fidelity–perceptual quality as a single unified model, without redundant resampling across denoising, dereverberation, bandwidth extension, and combined-distortion benchmarks under multiple sampling rates.

paragraphs: TF-Restormer restores speech when the recording's input sampling rate and the desired output rate can differ. The paper formalizes this as an extended sampling-frequency-independent setting. This matters because restoration can involve both removing distortions from observed audio and synthesizing frequency content absent from a bandwidth-limited recording, without repeatedly resampling signals to fit matched-rate assumptions.

The model encodes only the frequency band actually present in the input. Extension queries generate the missing higher-frequency band through band-partitioned cross-attention. Its asymmetric encoder–decoder places more capacity on analyzing the recording while keeping synthesis lightweight, making the different roles of observed and unobserved frequency content explicit in the architecture.

The result supports handling rate changes and restoration together within the model, without redundant resampling.
summary.tldr: TF-Restormer restores speech at independently chosen input and output rates by separating observed-band analysis from missing-band synthesis.

title: Query-Based Asymmetric Modeling with Decoupled Input–Output Rates for Speech Restoration

abstract: Recovering 3D human poses for multiple individuals from different camera views is a fundamental bottleneck for analyzing interacting behaviors. Existing self-supervised approaches leverage synthetic catalogues of 3D poses; however, this leads to poor generalization in real-world scenarios due to distribution shifts. We therefore introduce DisPOSE, a self-supervised framework that approximates the inherently discrete multi-view person-assignment problem as a generative diffusion process over the space of polystochastic tensors. By employing differentiable Sinkhorn projections during denoising, our model learns to guide solutions toward valid and feasible assignments based on 2D image priors. The complete 3D skeletons of localized individuals are then regressed using a Hypergraph-Convolutional Decoder that explicitly models relational structures and articulated joints across multiple views. The proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art self-supervised methods on standard datasets and demonstrates strong performance on a newly proposed benchmark featuring highly occluded scenes from surgical operating rooms. Our diffusion-based localization demonstrates high label efficiency, retaining 99% of its performance with only 10% of the pseudo-labels. Notably, disentangling the assignment and root regression components while maintaining differentiability makes DisPOSE nearly agnostic to different camera arrangements.

paragraphs: Estimating several people’s 3D poses from multiple cameras requires deciding which observations across views belong to the same person. Existing self-supervised methods can generalize poorly when they rely on synthetic pose catalogues that differ from real scenes. DisPOSE tackles the assignment problem directly through a diffusion process guided by information from 2D images.

Its diffusion localization retains 99% of its performance with 10% of the pseudo-labels. These results support the approach’s label efficiency and its usefulness for difficult scenes containing interacting or obscured people.
summary.tldr: DisPOSE uses constrained diffusion to match people across camera views before reconstructing 3D skeletons, achieving strong self-supervised results with few pseudo-labels.

title: DisPOSE: Projected Polystochastic Diffusion for Self-Supervised Multi-View 3D Human Pose Estimation

abstract: We build AICrypto, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate the cryptography capabilities of large language models (LLMs). The benchmark comprises 135 multiple-choice questions, 150 capture-the-flag challenges, and 30 proof problems, covering a broad range of skills from knowledge memorization to vulnerability exploitation and formal reasoning. All tasks are carefully reviewed or constructed by cryptography experts to improve correctness and rigor. For each proof problem, we provide detailed scoring rubrics and reference solutions that enable automated grading, achieving high correlation with human expert evaluations. We introduce strong human expert performance baselines for comparison across all task types. Our evaluation of 17 leading LLMs reveals that state-of-the-art models match or even surpass human experts in memorizing cryptographic concepts, exploiting common vulnerabilities, and routine proofs. However, our analysis reveals that they still lack a deep understanding of abstract mathematical concepts and struggle with tasks that require multi-step reasoning and dynamic analysis. We hope this work could provide insights for future research on LLMs in cryptographic applications. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/wangyu-ovo/aicrypto-agent.

These findings make the benchmark useful for separating strong performance on familiar cryptographic tasks from deeper reasoning abilities that remain challenging.
summary.tldr: AICrypto finds strong LLM performance on familiar cryptographic tasks but persistent difficulties with abstract mathematics and complex reasoning.

title: AICrypto: Evaluating Cryptography Capabilities of Large Language Models

abstract: Deep learning (DL) models, despite their remarkable success, remain vulnerable to small input perturbations that can cause erroneous outputs, motivating the recent proposal of probabilistic robustness (PR) as a complementary alternative to adversarial robustness (AR). However, existing PR formulations assume a fixed and known perturbation distribution, an unrealistic expectation in practice. To address this limitation, we propose non-parametric probabilistic robustness (NPPR), a more practical PR metric that does not rely on any predefined perturbation distribution. Following the non-parametric paradigm in statistical modeling, NPPR learns an optimized perturbation distribution directly from data, enabling conservative PR evaluation under distributional uncertainty. We further develop an NPPR estimator based on a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), covering various input-dependent and input-independent perturbation scenarios. Theoretical analyses establish the relationships among AR, PR, and NPPR. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet across ResNet18/50, WideResNet50 and VGG16 validate NPPR as a more practical robustness metric, showing conservative (lower) PR estimates compared to assuming those common perturbation distributions used in state-of-the-arts.

paragraphs: Probabilistic robustness evaluates a model under input perturbations drawn from a distribution. Its usefulness depends on how well that distribution represents the disturbances being considered. The paper targets a weakness in existing formulations: assuming the perturbation distribution is fixed and known, even when that knowledge is unavailable in practice.

Non-parametric probabilistic robustness learns an optimized perturbation distribution from data rather than requiring one to be specified beforehand. The aim is a conservative assessment under distributional uncertainty. The authors develop an estimator using a Gaussian mixture model, accommodating both input-dependent and input-independent perturbations, and provide theoretical relationships between adversarial robustness, ordinary probabilistic robustness, and their proposed metric.

The resulting robustness estimates are lower than estimates based on commonly assumed perturbation distributions. This is the intended conservative behavior: evaluation becomes less optimistic when the disturbance model is learned for that purpose, making the choice of perturbation distribution an explicit part of robustness assessment.
summary.tldr: NPPR learns perturbation distributions from data to produce more conservative probabilistic robustness estimates under distributional uncertainty.

title: Non-Parametric Probabilistic Robustness: A Conservative Risk Estimator under Unknown Perturbation Distributions

abstract: Despite the advanced capabilities of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), they frequently suffer from object hallucination. One reason is that visual features and pretrained textual representations often become intertwined in the deeper network layers. To address this, we propose REVIS, a training-free framework designed to explicitly re-activate this suppressed visual information. Rooted in latent space geometry, REVIS extracts the pure visual information vector via orthogonal projection and employs a calibrated strategy to perform sparse intervention only at the precise depth where suppression occurs. This surgical approach effectively restores visual information with minimal computational cost. Empirical evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate that REVIS reduces object hallucination rates by approximately 19% compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while preserving general reasoning capabilities.

paragraphs: Vision-language models sometimes describe objects that are absent from an image. This paper focuses on one proposed contributor: visual features become entangled with pretrained textual representations in deeper layers, suppressing useful image information. REVIS aims to restore that information directly within the model’s internal representations without additional training.

This makes the correction targeted both in what information it adds and where it acts, with the abstract reporting minimal computational cost.

The result supports targeted internal steering as a way to improve visual grounding without retraining the model. Its explanatory scope remains tied to the stated mechanism: interference between visual and textual representations is presented as one reason for hallucination, and reactivating suppressed visual information addresses that contributor.
summary.tldr: REVIS reduces object hallucination by selectively restoring suppressed visual information inside vision-language models without retraining.

title: REVIS: Sparse Latent Steering to Mitigate Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have garnered attention for their biological plausibility, energy efficiency, and temporal modeling capability. Due to the non-differentiability of spike generation, a widely used training method for SNNs is backpropagation through time with surrogate gradients, achieving competitive performance with few timesteps. Intuitively, scaling timesteps should improve performance by enriching temporal dynamics. However, we observe timestep scaling paradox (TSP), a counter-intuitive accuracy degradation when scaling timesteps. We investigate TSP and link it to long-term temporal gradient vanishing and weakened cross-timestep dependencies. To address this, we propose the Timestep-Scalable (TS) neuron model. It introduces long-term memory reconsolidation to enhance cross-timestep information flow and enable effective learning with more timesteps. In parallel, a temporal forgetting mechanism periodically truncates the accumulation path, suppressing excessive temporal buildup and improving training stability. Supported by theoretical analysis and extensive experiments, TS consistently improves performance when scaling timesteps. In addition, it attains state-of-the-art results on time-series and event-based tasks, while remaining strong on static image classification and object detection.

summary.tldr: The TS neuron combines long-term information flow with controlled forgetting to make additional timesteps beneficial in the reported spiking-network evaluations.

title: Resolving the Timestep Scaling Paradox in Spiking Neural Networks with a Timestep-Scalable Neuron Model

abstract: Precise alignment is a prerequisite for hyperspectral and multispectral image fusion, yet existing methods struggle with complex non-rigid deformations. Existing techniques either suffer from inter-task error accumulation by treating registration and fusion as disjoint processes or neglect the geometric nature of distortions by relying on isotropic Euclidean metrics. We propose Structure-Aware Riemannian Flow Matching (SA-RFM), a geometry-informed framework for joint registration and fusion of hyperspectral and multispectral images. SA-RFM reformulates registration as dynamic optimal transport on a structure-induced Riemannian manifold, where anisotropic costs are derived from MSI structural cues. To circumvent the complexity of explicit OT solvers, we incorporate this geometry into a conditional flow matching framework via a local cost approximation. This formulation is realized through two synergistic mechanisms: a Riemannian Flow Matching objective that enforces structure-aware error measurement, and an optimal transport direction regularization that aligns the velocity field with the induced metric, thereby resolving the fundamental mismatch between anisotropic costs and conventional Euclidean supervision. Extensive experiments on four datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method. Code is available at: https://github.com/ZhangQuan-hub.

paragraphs: Combining hyperspectral and multispectral images requires accurate alignment, particularly when their differences involve complex non-rigid deformation. Treating alignment and fusion as separate tasks can propagate errors between them. The paper also argues that measuring deformation equally in every direction overlooks image structure that should influence how alignment is evaluated.

SA-RFM jointly handles registration and fusion using geometry derived from structural cues in the multispectral image. It expresses registration as dynamic optimal transport on a Riemannian manifold, allowing movement costs to depend on direction and structure. A local cost approximation incorporates this geometry into conditional flow matching without requiring explicit optimal transport solvers.

Two mechanisms implement the approach. A Riemannian flow matching objective measures error according to the structural geometry, while direction regularization aligns the learned velocity field with that same metric. This keeps the learning signals consistent with the anisotropic costs used to describe deformation. Experiments on four datasets report superior performance. The contribution is a joint framework whose deformation model and supervision both account for image structure.
summary.tldr: SA-RFM jointly aligns and fuses hyperspectral and multispectral images using flow matching guided by structure-dependent geometry.

title: Structure-Aware Riemannian Flow Matching for Registration and Fusion of Hyperspectral and Multispectral Images

abstract: Visuo-tactile sensors have been widely adopted in robotic manipulation. However, inherent heterogeneity in sensor designs hinders the learning of unified tactile representations in cross-sensor scenarios. Existing methods that focus on reconstruction or task-specific supervision often fail to capture the common information between different tactile sensors, particularly in the presence of substantial sensor variations, resulting in limited generalization to unseen sensors. To address this, we propose Cross-Tactile Sensor Representation Learning (CTSRL), a unified framework for sensor-agnostic tactile representation learning. CTSRL introduces a Cross-Sensor Modulator (CSM) to eliminate sensor-specific biases and adopts a two-stage learning paradigm: (1) leveraging aligned synthetic data for cross-sensor self-supervised learning to extract shared latent representations across sensor domains; and (2) integrating real-world multimodal tactile data to bridge the sim-to-real semantic gap through cross-modal alignment, thereby enriching representations with fine-grained semantic attributes. Experimental results show that our method demonstrates strong multi-sensor generalization, significantly improving sensor-agnostic representation learning.

paragraphs: Visuo-tactile sensors support robotic manipulation, but differences in their designs make it difficult to learn representations that work across sensors. Training based on reconstruction or individual tasks can miss the information sensors share, especially when their outputs differ substantially. CTSRL addresses this problem with a unified tactile representation framework.

A Cross-Sensor Modulator targets sensor-specific biases, and training proceeds in two stages. First, aligned synthetic data provides self-supervised learning across sensor domains, encouraging a shared internal representation. Second, real-world multimodal tactile data connects these learned features to richer semantic information through cross-modal alignment. This stage is designed to bridge the semantic gap between simulated and real observations.

The experiments report strong generalization across multiple sensors and substantial improvement in sensor-agnostic representation learning. The approach matters because it explicitly addresses both sources of variation: differences among sensor designs and differences between synthetic and real data. Its reported results support learning common tactile information while retaining fine-grained semantic attributes useful for interpreting touch.
summary.tldr: CTSRL combines aligned synthetic training and real multimodal alignment to learn tactile representations that generalize across sensor designs.

title: Cross-Tactile Sensor Representation Learning

abstract: Regression with functional covariates poses fundamental challenges due to the infinite-dimensional nature of functional data, and its theoretical properties have been studied under specialized frameworks in classical nonparametric statistics. While deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated remarkable empirical success in high-dimensional regression, their theoretical behavior in settings involving infinite-dimensional covariates remains largely unexplored. In this work, we study the theoretical performance of DNN-based estimators for regression problems with functional covariates. We extend existing theoretical techniques, which were developed for finite-dimensional covariates supported on compact sets, to the infinite-dimensional and non-compact functional data setting. Under mild conditions, we show that DNN estimators attain minimax-optimal polynomial rates of convergence for both functional linear models and functional generalized linear models. For fully nonparametric regression with functional covariates, we establish a lower bound on the prediction error and further discuss the fundamental obstacles inherent to this problem and their connections to existing state-of-the-art methods in the literature.

paragraphs: Regression usually represents an input as a finite list of measurements. Functional regression instead takes an entire function as an input, creating an inherently infinite-dimensional problem. This paper studies when deep neural network estimators can make accurate predictions in that setting and how their accuracy improves as more data become available.

The authors extend theoretical tools previously developed for finite-dimensional inputs restricted to compact sets. Their analysis accommodates functional inputs without that compactness restriction. Under conditions described as mild, they prove polynomial convergence rates for functional linear and generalized linear models. These rates are minimax-optimal, meaning they match the best worst-case statistical rates for the model classes considered.

The fully nonparametric setting receives a different result: a lower bound on prediction error and an analysis of fundamental obstacles. This distinction matters because the optimal-rate guarantees for the structured models do not establish the same result for unrestricted functional regression. The paper clarifies where neural-network regression has strong theoretical support and where the complexity of functional inputs creates deeper statistical difficulties.
summary.tldr: The paper proves optimal neural-network regression rates for structured functional models under mild conditions and studies barriers in the fully nonparametric case.

title: Deep Neural Network Regression with Functional Covariates

abstract: Concept-based models (CMs), deep neural networks that ground their predictions on representations aligned with human-understandable concepts (e.g., "round", "stripes", etc.), have been shown to learn representations that leak concept-irrelevant information. As the traditional narrative goes, this leakage is undesirable and should be eradicated as it leads to uninterpretable models. In this paper, we posit that this conventional view of leakage in CMs is not only ill-posed, as the evidence of how leakage makes a model less interpretable is often inconclusive, but also bound to lead to impractical CMs under common real-world constraints. Specifically, we argue that in real-world settings where concept incompleteness is the norm, some leakage is often necessary for constructing accurate and intervenable CMs. To this end, we propose that there is such a thing as benign leakage and show that, by optimizing a reframing of the typical CM training objective, CMs can encourage and exploit this form of leakage without sacrificing accuracy or intervenability.
originalAbstract: Concept-based models (CMs), deep neural networks that ground their predictions on representations aligned with human-understandable concepts (e.g., "round", "stripes", etc.), have been shown to learn representations that leak concept-irrelevant information. As the traditional narrative goes, this leakage is undesirable and should be eradicated as it leads to uninterpretable models. In this paper, we posit that this conventional view of leakage in CMs is not only ill-posed, as the evidence of how leakage makes a model less interpretable is often inconclusive, but also bound to lead to impractical CMs under common real-world constraints. Specifically, we argue that in real-world settings where concept incompleteness is the norm, some leakage is often necessary for constructing accurate and intervenable CMs. To this end, we propose that there is such a thing as benign leakage and show that, by optimizing a reframing of the typical CM training objective, CMs can encourage and exploit this form of leakage without sacrificing accuracy or intervenability.

paragraphs: Concept-based models make predictions through representations associated with understandable properties, such as shape or texture. Those representations can also retain information unrelated to their assigned concepts, a phenomenon called leakage. This position paper challenges the assumption that all such information must be removed to keep a model interpretable.

The authors argue that evidence connecting leakage to reduced interpretability is often inconclusive. They also emphasize concept incompleteness: in many real-world settings, the supplied concepts do not capture everything needed for prediction. Under those conditions, they contend that some leakage is often necessary to obtain models that are accurate and still allow interventions on their concepts.

The paper proposes a category of benign leakage and reframes the usual training objective to encourage and use it. The authors show that this form can be exploited without sacrificing accuracy or intervenability. Their claim is conditional on the kind of leakage and the setting; it does not endorse every hidden information channel. The contribution is a more selective account of what concept representations should preserve.
summary.tldr: When concepts are incomplete, some leakage can support accurate, intervenable models, motivating a training objective that encourages benign leakage.

title: Position: In Defense of Information Leakage in Concept-based Models

abstract: Finding exact solutions to the quantum many-body problem is computationally intractable (QMA-hard). Traditional approximations for electrons in an atom or molecule—density functional theory and wavefunction methods—have been indispensable, but their development shows signs of saturation: DFT functionals have proliferated without converging toward the exact functional, and strong correlation remains largely unsolved after decades of effort. This position paper argues that machine learning represents the most promising path forward—not as a proof of logical necessity, but as a decision-theoretic argument: ML succeeds whether the underlying problems are truly hard or merely lack simple analytical solutions. We reframe recent traditional method development as “hand-crafted machine learning” that has exhausted the hypothesis space accessible to human intuition. Significant challenges remain, but these have clear research paths forward, unlike the fundamental barriers facing traditional approaches. ML-based approaches merit strategic priority in quantum chemistry’s next phase.

paragraphs: This paper argues for giving machine learning strategic priority in quantum chemistry. Exact solutions to the quantum many-body problem are computationally intractable, so traditional methods rely on approximations. The authors contend that development of density functional theory and wavefunction methods shows signs of saturation, including continuing difficulties with strong correlation and a proliferation of functionals without convergence toward the exact one.

Their argument is about how to allocate research effort under uncertainty. They maintain that ML offers a promising direction whether the underlying challenge reflects genuine computational hardness or the absence of simple analytical solutions. They also reinterpret recent traditional method development as a form of manually designed learning whose search possibilities have been limited by human intuition.

Despite the title’s strong wording, the paper explicitly avoids claiming that an ML transition follows as a logical necessity. It acknowledges substantial remaining challenges while arguing that these have clearer research paths than the barriers facing traditional approaches. The contribution is a case for research prioritization, grounded in the authors’ comparison of the prospects for these different methodological directions.
summary.tldr: The authors make a decision-theoretic case for prioritizing ML in quantum chemistry while explicitly avoiding a claim of logical inevitability.

title: Position: The Inevitable Transition to Machine Learning in Quantum Chemistry

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as digital agents that perform multi-step digital work on a computer, but the environments in which they operate remain fragmented and task-specific. Our position is that digital agents need Agent-Native Computer: interfaces that expose system capabilities through compositional observation and action spaces aligned with LLM strengths. To ground this position, we showcase AgentVM, an environment running on top of a modern operating system, which integrates Graphical User Interface (GUI)-based and text-based interactions over a shared system state, and factors interaction into modular environment views. Through quantitative and qualitative analysis, we show that a unified agent-native computer is essential for building general-purpose digital agents.

paragraphs: This position paper focuses on the computer environment used by language-model agents performing multistep digital work. The authors argue that existing environments are fragmented and tailored to particular tasks. They propose computers designed around agents, with observations and actions that can be combined and that fit the capabilities of language models.

To make the proposal concrete, they showcase AgentVM, an environment built on a modern operating system. It combines graphical and text-based interaction over a shared system state. Both forms of interaction therefore concern the same underlying computer, while modular environment views organize what the agent can observe and do. This makes the interface itself a central part of agent design.

The paper uses quantitative and qualitative analysis to support its position that a unified environment is essential for general-purpose digital agents. The broader implication is that agent capability depends on how system functionality is exposed, alongside the language model’s abilities. AgentVM illustrates how a common environment can bring different interaction modes into one coherent setting.
summary.tldr: The authors present AgentVM to argue that general-purpose digital agents need unified computer environments combining graphical and text interaction.

title: Position: Digital Agents Require Unified Agent-Native Computers

abstract: This position paper argues that Large Language Models (LLMs) should incorporate explicit mechanisms for human empathy. As LLMs become increasingly deployed in high-stakes human-centered settings, their success depends not only on correctness or fluency but on faithful preservation of human perspectives. Yet, current LLMs systematically fail at this requirement: even when well-aligned and policy-compliant, they often attenuate affect, misrepresent contextual salience, and rigidify relational stance in ways that distort meaning. We formalize empathy as an observable behavioral property: the capacity to model and respond to human perspectives while preserving intention, affect, and context. Under this framing, we identify four recurring mechanisms of empathic failure in contemporary LLMs–sentiment attenuation, empathic granularity mismatch, conflict avoidance, and linguistic distancing–arising as structural consequences of prevailing training and alignment practices. We further organize these failures along three dimensions: cognitive, cultural, and relational empathy, to explain their manifestation across tasks. Empirical analyses show that strong benchmark performance can mask systematic empathic distortions, motivating empathy-aware objectives, benchmarks, and training signals as first-class components of LLM development. Our code is available at: https://github.com/youxiaoxing/LLM_Empathy.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that language models need explicit mechanisms for preserving human perspectives. It defines empathy behaviorally: a model should understand and respond to a person while retaining their intention, emotion, and context. Under this definition, fluent, correct, or policy-compliant language can still distort what a person means.

The authors identify four recurring failures: weakening emotional content, responding at an inappropriate level of emotional detail, avoiding conflict, and creating linguistic distance. They connect these failures to prevailing training and alignment practices and organize them across cognitive, cultural, and relational dimensions. This framework makes empathy a collection of observable response properties that can be examined across tasks.

Their empirical analyses indicate that strong benchmark results can conceal systematic distortions of human perspectives. That finding matters for settings where the meaning of a response depends on whose viewpoint is represented and how it is expressed. The paper calls for empathy-aware objectives, benchmarks, and training signals to become explicit components of model development.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that LLM training and evaluation should explicitly measure and preserve human intention, emotion, and context.

abstract: We present a new subgoal-based method for automatically creating useful skills in reinforcement learning. Our method identifies subgoals by partitioning local state transition graphs—those that are constructed using only the most recent experiences of the agent. The local scope of our subgoal discovery method allows it to successfully identify the type of subgoals we seek—states that lie between two densely-connected regions of the state space—while producing an algorithm with low computational cost.
originalAbstract: We present a new subgoal-based method for automatically creating useful skills in reinforcement learning. Our method identifies subgoals by partitioning local state transition graphs—those that are constructed using only the most recent experiences of the agent. The local scope of our subgoal discovery method allows it to successfully identify the type of subgoals we seek—states that lie between two densely-connected regions of the state space—while producing an algorithm with low computational cost.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way for a reinforcement learning agent to create useful skills automatically by discovering subgoals. It seeks states that sit between two densely connected regions of the state space. Such states identify connections between regions and provide concrete intermediate destinations around which a skill can be organized.

To find these states, the method partitions state-transition graphs built from only the agent's most recent experiences. In these graphs, the relevant structure comes from transitions the agent has recently encountered. The discovery procedure therefore works with a local view of the state space instead of requiring a graph covering the entire environment.

The authors state that this local scope successfully identifies the desired kind of subgoal while keeping computational cost low. The contribution links the structure used to discover skills with the amount of experience processed during discovery. Its target is specifically states between densely connected regions, giving the method a clear structural definition of what makes a subgoal useful.
summary.tldr: Partitioning graphs of recent transitions discovers subgoals between densely connected regions at low computational cost.

title: Identifying useful subgoals in reinforcement learning by local graph partitioning

abstract: We propose a new stopping condition for a Support Vector Machine (SVM) solver which precisely reflects the objective of the Leave-One-Out error computation. The stopping condition guarantees that the output on an intermediate SVM solution is identical to the output of the optimal SVM solution with one data point excluded from the training set. A simple augmentation of a general SVM training algorithm allows one to use a stopping criterion equivalent to the proposed sufficient condition. A comprehensive experimental evaluation of our method shows consistent speedup of the exact LOO computation by our method, up to the factor of 13 for the linear kernel. The new algorithm can be seen as an example of constructive guidance of an optimization algorithm towards achieving the best attainable expected risk at optimal computational cost.
originalAbstract: We propose a new stopping condition for a Support Vector Machine (SVM) solver which precisely reflects the objective of the Leave-One-Out error computation. The stopping condition guarantees that the output on an intermediate SVM solution is identical to the output of the optimal SVM solution with one data point excluded from the training set. A simple augmentation of a general SVM training algorithm allows one to use a stopping criterion equivalent to the proposed sufficient condition. A comprehensive experimental evaluation of our method shows consistent speedup of the exact LOO computation by our method, up to the factor of 13 for the linear kernel. The new algorithm can be seen as an example of constructive guidance of an optimization algorithm towards achieving the best attainable expected risk at optimal computational cost.

paragraphs: Computing leave-one-out error requires evaluating predictions when individual training examples are excluded. For support vector machines, the paper develops a stopping condition tailored to this evaluation objective. The condition identifies when an intermediate solver result already gives the output needed for the leave-one-out calculation.

The proposed sufficient condition guarantees that this output matches the output of the optimal SVM trained without the excluded point. A simple addition to a general SVM training algorithm enables an equivalent stopping criterion. This allows optimization to stop once the relevant prediction is certified, while preserving exactness of the leave-one-out error computation.

A comprehensive empirical evaluation reports consistent speedups, reaching a factor of 13 for the linear kernel. The contribution is to align computational stopping with the purpose of the calculation: obtaining the correct held-out output. The condition is sufficient, so its guarantee applies when it is satisfied without claiming that it identifies every possible opportunity to stop. The reported speedups show that this guarantee can save substantial computation in practice.
summary.tldr: A sufficient stopping condition speeds exact SVM leave-one-out evaluation by certifying the needed prediction before optimization finishes.

title: Stopping conditions for exact computation of leave-one-out error in support vector machines

abstract: In this paper we develop a spectral framework for estimating mixture distributions, specifically Gaussian mixture models. In physics, spectroscopy is often used for the identification of substances through their spectrum. Treating a kernel function K(x,y) as "light" and the sampled data as "substance", the spectrum of their interaction (eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the kernel matrix K ) unveils certain aspects of the underlying parametric distribution p , such as the parameters of a Gaussian mixture. Our approach extends the intuitions and analyses underlying the existing spectral techniques, such as spectral clustering and Kernel Principal Components Analysis (KPCA). We construct algorithms to estimate parameters of Gaussian mixture models, including the number of mixture components, their means and covariance matrices, which are important in many practical applications. We provide a theoretical framework and show encouraging experimental results.

paragraphs: The paper develops a spectral approach to estimating mixture distributions, focusing on Gaussian mixtures. Its guiding analogy is spectroscopy: the interaction between a probe and a substance reveals something about the substance. Here, a kernel function acts as the probe, and the observed data supply the material being examined.

Computationally, the relevant spectrum consists of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a kernel matrix constructed from the samples. The authors show how this information can reveal aspects of the underlying distribution. Their framework extends ideas and analyses associated with spectral clustering and kernel principal component analysis toward estimating the parameters of a probabilistic mixture.

The resulting algorithms estimate the number of Gaussian components as well as their means and covariance matrices. This makes the spectral information useful for describing both the mixture’s structure and its individual components. The paper supplies a theoretical framework and encouraging experimental results, supporting spectral analysis as a route to distribution estimation in the studied setting.
summary.tldr: Data spectroscopy uses kernel-matrix eigenstructure to estimate Gaussian mixture components, including their number, means, and covariances.

title: Data spectroscopy: learning mixture models using eigenspaces of convolution operators

abstract: This paper examines two-stage techniques for learning kernels based on a notion of alignment. It presents a number of novel theoretical, algorithmic, and empirical results for alignment-based techniques. Our results build on previous work by Cristianini et al. (2001), but we adopt a different definition of kernel alignment and significantly extend that work in several directions: we give a novel and simple concentration bound for alignment between kernel matrices; show the existence of good predictors for kernels with high alignment, both for classification and for regression; give algorithms for learning a maximum alignment kernel by showing that the problem can be reduced to a simple QP; and report the results of extensive experiments with this alignment-based method in classification and regression tasks, which show an improvement both over the uniform combination of kernels and over other state-of-the-art learning kernel methods.
originalAbstract: This paper examines two-stage techniques for learning kernels based on a notion of alignment. It presents a number of novel theoretical, algorithmic, and empirical results for alignment-based techniques. Our results build on previous work by Cristianini et al. (2001), but we adopt a different definition of kernel alignment and significantly extend that work in several directions: we give a novel and simple concentration bound for alignment between kernel matrices; show the existence of good predictors for kernels with high alignment, both for classification and for regression; give algorithms for learning a maximum alignment kernel by showing that the problem can be reduced to a simple QP; and report the results of extensive experiments with this alignment-based method in classification and regression tasks, which show an improvement both over the uniform combination of kernels and over other state-of-the-art learning kernel methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies two-stage kernel learning methods based on alignment, a criterion used to guide the choice of a kernel. The authors adopt a different definition of alignment from earlier work and develop theoretical results, learning algorithms, and experiments around it. The central question is how alignment connects kernel selection to useful prediction.

The analysis provides a concentration bound for alignment between kernel matrices and proves that highly aligned kernels admit good predictors for both classification and regression. The authors also show that learning a maximum-alignment kernel can be reduced to a simple quadratic program. This gives an actionable optimization procedure alongside the theoretical motivation for the criterion.

Extensive classification and regression experiments show improvements over uniformly combining kernels and over other leading kernel-learning methods. The paper therefore supports alignment from several directions: its statistical behavior, its relationship to predictor quality, its computational optimization, and its observed performance. The existence result motivates the criterion without asserting that every predictor using a highly aligned kernel must perform well.
summary.tldr: Alignment-based kernel learning gains theoretical support, a quadratic-program formulation, and improved classification and regression results.

title: Two-Stage Learning Kernel Algorithms

abstract: This work explores the effects of relevant and irrelevant boolean variables on the accuracy of classifiers. The analysis uses the assumption that the variables are conditionally independent given the class, and focuses on a natural family of learning algorithms for such sources when the relevant variables have a small advantage over random guessing. The main result is that algorithms relying predominately on irrelevant variables have error probabilities that quickly go to 0 in situations where algorithms that limit the use of irrelevant variables have errors bounded below by a positive constant. We also show that accurate learning is possible even when there are so few examples that one cannot determine with high confidence whether or not any individual variable is relevant.

paragraphs: This paper examines a counterintuitive possibility: a classifier can benefit from using a collection of variables dominated by irrelevant ones. The analysis concerns Boolean variables and assumes they are conditionally independent given the class. It focuses on a natural family of learning algorithms in settings where relevant variables are only slightly more informative than random guessing.

The main result identifies situations where algorithms relying predominantly on irrelevant variables have error probabilities that rapidly approach zero. In those same situations, algorithms that restrict the use of irrelevant variables retain an error bounded away from zero. This comparison challenges the expectation that aggressively limiting irrelevant variables must improve learning.

The authors also show that accurate classification can be possible with too few examples to determine confidently whether any individual variable is relevant. Taken together, the results separate successful prediction from reliable identification of useful individual features. Their force comes from the specified assumptions and learning setting; they do not establish a universal advantage for adding irrelevant variables.
summary.tldr: Under the paper's assumptions, using mostly irrelevant variables can enable accurate classification even when individual relevance cannot be identified confidently.
